From the News Desk

Nov 26, 2026Open weights · BharatGenBharatGen launches Patram 1.5: a 7.8B document model built for messy Indian paperwork, on one 24 GB GPUBharatGen launched Patram 1.5 on Nov 26, 2026: a vision-language model that reads, parses, answers questions on and extracts from scanned, handwritten, stamped and mixed-language Indian documents — and is designed to say when it cannot answer rather than guess. The weights are Apache 2.0, verified from the repository by this desk, and BharatGen's own sizing guidance puts the model on a 24 GB GPU. The picture is BharatGen's own announcement art: Patram 1.5 pulling a clean billing-history table out of a Maharashtra electricity bill. BharatGen is India's sovereign AI programme, backed by the Department of Science and Technology and the IndiaAI Mission and anchored at IIT Bombay. This story was held this morning until the maker's own imagery could be verified and self-hosted; it is published now that it has been.
Act on this story:Patram 1.5 — the model page →Compare GPU prices →
Nov 26, 2026Open data · NVIDIANVIDIA opens Nemotron 3.5 Parse's training data and recipe — and clocks 20.44 pages a second on one H200NVIDIA published the training data, fine-tuning recipe and speed work behind its compact document-parsing model Nemotron 3.5 Parse on Nov 26, 2026: three synthetic datasets totalling about 18.9 million image-and-annotation pairs, a public supervised-fine-tuning to GRPO recipe, and a speculative decoder, DFlash2, that NVIDIA measures at 20.44 pages per second on a single H200 at high concurrency. The model itself is not new — it is a 0.63B parser published earlier in 2026 under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence — what opened today is everything around it. The picture is NVIDIA's own first figure from the post: a page on the left, the model's structured extraction of it on the right.

Price WatchLatest catch · Nov 26, 2026 — Spheron's stated snapshot regenerates again the same day — stated H100 $2.39 to $3.38, stated B300 $12.42 to $13.37
SpheronStated prices — For the second day running, Spheron's generated snapshot kept its date stamp but rewrote its own table between our morning and afternoon reads — stated figures only, never verified board prices; the verified board itself did not move this afternoon
$2.39→$3.38
H100 — Stated Nov 26, 2026 (morning read)Stated Nov 26, 2026 (afternoon read)

Spheron's generated pricing snapshot (its llms.txt file) still stamps itself ‘as of 26 Nov 2026’, but the file regenerated between this desk's morning and afternoon reads today (afternoon read about 20:24 UTC), and its stated on-demand figures moved: stated B300 $12.42 → $13.37 (up 7.6%), stated H100 $2.39 → $3.38 (up 41.4%), stated B200 $11.12 → $11.06, stated RTX PRO 6000 $2.39 → $2.35 and stated RTX 4090 $1.23 → $1.18; stated H200 ($5.22), A100 ($1.43), L40S ($1.06), RTX 5090 ($0.78) and RTX 6000 Ada ($0.80) held. Its pricing page's own data moved the other way on the same card over the same interval — H100 $3.38 → $2.39, with its FAQ now agreeing at $2.39 — so the two surfaces have effectively swapped their H100 figures intraday, and they now agree on 10 of 12 cards, disagreeing only on H100 and RTX 4090 (this morning: 9 of 12, disagreeing on B300, H100 and RTX PRO 6000). The standing cautions apply in full: these are figures Spheron states in its own files, reported as stated and never as verified board prices (Spheron has no verified prices on our board), and both sides of every move are dated by our reads (morning and afternoon, Nov 26, 2026). On the verified board this afternoon was flat: Verda held this morning's first-cut levels on all nine tracked cards (GB300 $14.41, B300 $12.53, B200 $9.603, H200 $6.768, H100 SXM $5.293, A100 80GB $2.410, A100 40GB $1.733, RTX PRO 6000 $2.864, L40S $2.079, both Verda pages agreeing) and Hyperstack was unchanged by the raw-page method (all 13 on-demand rows identical, as every day since Oct 31). No new Verda entry: a Verda story already ran this morning on the first cut, and no proportion-rule threshold is newly met. This is the newest of the 58 changes reported on Price Watch. Source: Spheron's own llms.txt pricing snapshot and pricing page (spheron.network), read Nov 26, 2026 morning and afternoon; Verda's own pricing pages (verda.com/pricing and verda.com/gpu-instances) and Hyperstack's own pricing page (hyperstack.cloud/pricing, raw-page read), read Nov 26, 2026 afternoon.

Nov 26, 2026Open weights · Ant GroupAnt Group open-sources Ming-Image-0.2-Design: a design image model under MIT, validated on one 80 GB GPUAnt Group's inclusionAI team listed the weights of Ming-Image-0.2-Design on Nov 25, 2026 and announced it on Nov 26: a design-focused text-to-image and image-editing model aimed at e-commerce hero images, UI drafts and spatial renderings, under the MIT licence. Ant's own validated setup is a single CUDA GPU with 80 GiB of memory — H100, H200 or A100 80GB territory. The picture is Ant Group's own example art from the model repository. Nov 25, 2026Models · AminiAmini's Soma-1X Lite: a 2B open-weight model that turns paper records into structured data on one GPUAmini released Soma-1X Lite on Nov 25, 2026: a 2.2-billion-parameter vision-language model, Apache 2.0, built to convert paper records — typed forms, handwriting, tables, faded scans — into structured, machine-readable data that preserves layout and reading order. The weights are a single 4.43 GB file, verified from the repository by this desk, and the licence is Apache 2.0 in both the model card and the README — commercial use allowed. The picture is Amini's own hero image from the model repository: its wordmark over a mosaic of the historical documents the model is built to read. Amini's pitch is sovereign digitisation: the model is small enough to run inside an institution's own infrastructure, so the records never leave it.

Nov 26, 2026Open weights · BharatGenBharatGen launches Patram 1.5: a 7.8B document model built for messy Indian paperwork, on one 24 GB GPUBharatGen launched Patram 1.5 on Nov 26, 2026: a vision-language model that reads, parses, answers questions on and extracts from scanned, handwritten, stamped and mixed-language Indian documents — and is designed to say when it cannot answer rather than guess. The weights are Apache 2.0, verified from the repository by this desk, and BharatGen's own sizing guidance puts the model on a 24 GB GPU. The picture is BharatGen's own announcement art: Patram 1.5 pulling a clean billing-history table out of a Maharashtra electricity bill. BharatGen is India's sovereign AI programme, backed by the Department of Science and Technology and the IndiaAI Mission and anchored at IIT Bombay. This story was held this morning until the maker's own imagery could be verified and self-hosted; it is published now that it has been.
Act on this story:Patram 1.5 — the model page →Compare GPU prices →
Nov 26, 2026Open data · NVIDIANVIDIA opens Nemotron 3.5 Parse's training data and recipe — and clocks 20.44 pages a second on one H200NVIDIA published the training data, fine-tuning recipe and speed work behind its compact document-parsing model Nemotron 3.5 Parse on Nov 26, 2026: three synthetic datasets totalling about 18.9 million image-and-annotation pairs, a public supervised-fine-tuning to GRPO recipe, and a speculative decoder, DFlash2, that NVIDIA measures at 20.44 pages per second on a single H200 at high concurrency. The model itself is not new — it is a 0.63B parser published earlier in 2026 under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence — what opened today is everything around it. The picture is NVIDIA's own first figure from the post: a page on the left, the model's structured extraction of it on the right.
Act on this story:Nemotron 3.5 Parse — the model page →Compare GPU prices →
Nov 26, 2026Prices · VerdaVerda cuts prices for the first time: seven cards fall in one day, five by about 6%Verda cut seven of its nine tracked on-demand GPU rates on Nov 26, 2026 — its first cut after rises on Nov 23 and Nov 24 and a flat Nov 25. GB300 fell $15.31 to $14.41 and B300 $13.31 to $12.53 (both −5.9%); H200, H100 SXM and RTX PRO 6000 each fell about 5.8%; B200 and A100 80GB fell by smaller steps. A100 40GB and L40S held. The chart is this desk's own record of Verda's published rates, read on Verda's own pages on both days — the subject of this story is our own price data, so our chart is the evidence.

/price-watch.html:
Price Watch

That’s our business — catch and report every change. Every rise, every cut and every inconsistency a provider publishes, caught against their own pages and reported with both observation dates and the source named. No entry appears without dated evidence on both sides.

58 changes caught and reported · 9 providers · newest first · latest catch Nov 26, 2026

SpheronStated pricesRate change

Spheron's generated pricing snapshot (its llms.txt file) still stamps itself ‘as of 26 Nov 2026’, but the file regenerated between this desk's morning and afternoon reads today (afternoon read about 20:24 UTC), and its stated on-demand figures moved: stated B300 $12.42 → $13.37 (up 7.6%), stated H100 $2.39 → $3.38 (up 41.4%), stated B200 $11.12 → $11.06, stated RTX PRO 6000 $2.39 → $2.35 and stated RTX 4090 $1.23 → $1.18; stated H200 ($5.22), A100 ($1.43), L40S ($1.06), RTX 5090 ($0.78) and RTX 6000 Ada ($0.80) held. Its pricing page's own data moved the other way on the same card over the same interval — H100 $3.38 → $2.39, with its FAQ now agreeing at $2.39 — so the two surfaces have effectively swapped their H100 figures intraday, and they now agree on 10 of 12 cards, disagreeing only on H100 and RTX 4090 (this morning: 9 of 12, disagreeing on B300, H100 and RTX PRO 6000). The standing cautions apply in full: these are figures Spheron states in its own files, reported as stated and never as verified board prices (Spheron has no verified prices on our board), and both sides of every move are dated by our reads (morning and afternoon, Nov 26, 2026). On the verified board this afternoon was flat: Verda held this morning's first-cut levels on all nine tracked cards (GB300 $14.41, B300 $12.53, B200 $9.603, H200 $6.768, H100 SXM $5.293, A100 80GB $2.410, A100 40GB $1.733, RTX PRO 6000 $2.864, L40S $2.079, both Verda pages agreeing) and Hyperstack was unchanged by the raw-page method (all 13 on-demand rows identical, as every day since Oct 31). No new Verda entry: a Verda story already ran this morning on the first cut, and no proportion-rule threshold is newly met.

Source: Spheron's own llms.txt pricing snapshot and pricing page (spheron.network), read Nov 26, 2026 morning and afternoon; Verda's own pricing pages (verda.com/pricing and verda.com/gpu-instances) and Hyperstack's own pricing page (hyperstack.cloud/pricing, raw-page read), read Nov 26, 2026 afternoon

Verda7 cards cutRate change

Verda's own two pricing pages (verda.com/pricing and verda.com/gpu-instances, read first-hand Nov 25 and Nov 26, 2026, agreeing exactly on both days) show the first broad cut of the recent pattern: GB300 $15.31 → $14.41 (−5.9%), B300 $13.31 → $12.53 (−5.9%), H200 $7.184 → $6.768 (−5.8%), H100 SXM $5.619 → $5.293 (−5.8%), RTX PRO 6000 $3.041 → $2.864 (−5.8%), A100 80GB $2.482 → $2.410 (−2.9%) and B200 $9.844 → $9.603 (−2.4%). A100 40GB ($1.733) and L40S ($2.079) held flat, and Verda's spot rates on the same page are exactly half the new on-demand rates, so the cut runs across the page. This is a direction change, not a return to lows: even after the cut, GB300 at $14.41 sits well above its levels from earlier in November, because the Nov 23–24 rises were larger than today's fall on most cards. How Price Watch reports

Figures are read from the provider’s own published pages or live offers — never from another aggregator. A figure stated on a provider’s pages is reported as stated, attributed to that provider; it becomes a verified board price only through our full pricing check — see How we price.

All three kinds of change are reported the same way: price rises, price cuts, and disagreements — where a provider’s own pages state different prices for the same card, the disagreement itself is the change, and it is reported as caught rather than smoothed over.

/for-providers.html:
For providers

The listing standard

  • Prices publicly checkable — your rates live on your own public pages, where anyone can read them.
  • Independently verified by us — we read your published pages ourselves; you never send us numbers to print.
  • Freshness maintained — fixed rates are re-verified daily; marketplace rates are stamped to the hour.
  • Listing never buys rank — Best offer goes to the lowest price, and no payment changes any order on this site.

What we check, and how often

Every price on the board is read from the provider's own published pricing pages or live offers — never from another aggregator. Fixed-rate providers are re-checked daily; marketplaces that move by the hour are labelled as live and stamped to the hour. When a provider publishes no price at all, we show no price rather than an estimate.

How to apply

Send us the public page where your prices live and the name you list under. /how-we-price.html:
How we price

Our sources

Providers' own published pricing pages and live offers only. No other aggregator is ever a source — if we cannot read it on the provider's own site, it does not appear here.

The cadence

Marketplaces refresh hourly and are stamped to the hour. Fixed-rate providers are re-verified daily. Every price on this site carries its checked date; no timestamp, no price.

What “verified” means

A price is verified when we have checked it against the provider's own published source. Verified and merely listed are never blurred: a GPU a provider lists without a published price appears as listed, quote-only, with no price shown. Anything we cannot verify is left out, never guessed.

The Best offer rule

Exactly one per GPU variant: the single lowest verified on-demand price, whoever offers it. Spot prices compete only for a separate Best spot price tag. The tag is arithmetic — it moves when prices move, and no one can pay to hold it.

The independence rule

GPUJournal sells nothing and rents nothing. No paid placement, no sponsored rows, no promoted listings. If referral terms are ever used, they will be disclosed — and they will never affect order.

Every change, reported

Catching and reporting every change is our business. When a check finds a price has moved, the board carries the new figure with its new date, and the change itself is reported on Price Watch — the old figure, the new figure, both observation dates and the source named. A change we cannot evidence on both sides is not reported as one.

Corrections

When we get something wrong, the correction is published here, not silently edited.

Oct 19, 2026

Every price on the board was re-checked against the provider's own pages, and the guides were re-costed on those rates. Any figure that could not be confirmed was removed rather than estimated. Two labelling quirks turned up along the way: Hyperstack publishes one H100 under two labels (both are listed, exactly as published), and TensorDock's A100 marketplace pages disagree with each other (the board uses its Managed Containers rate, labelled as such).

Guides that cover it

GPU Pricing · 2026-10-29 · 8 min

Six rises in seven days: what Verda's October says about GPU demand

One provider raised its GPU prices on Oct 23, Oct 24, Oct 26, Oct 27, Oct 28 and again on Oct 29 — six rises in seven days, across almost its whole range, each one small and each one in the same direction. We know the dates and the figures because we check and bank these prices every day. Here is the full record, what else moved in October, and the half of the market that still has not.

Model Deployment · 2026-10-29 · 10 min

Thinking of deploying Mistral Large 4? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

Mistral’s Large 4 — “Le Chonk” — landed on Hugging Face on Oct 29, 2026: about a trillion parameters, free to download, and far too big for any single graphics card. This page does the deployment maths in the open: how much memory each version needs, the smallest rental setups that honestly hold it, what those setups cost per hour, per day and per month — and the point where renting GPUs beats paying per token, and where it doesn’t.

GPU Pricing · 2026-10-30 · 7 min

Batch is the new spot: what RunPod’s 20% batch discount does to the maths for work that can wait

On Oct 28, 2026, RunPod made Serverless Batch Inference generally available: send requests in bulk, let them run when RunPod’s batch workers get to them, and pay 20% less than the on-demand rate on H100, H200, B200 and B300. This page does the maths on that trade — what the discount is worth in dollars, and what you give up for it.

Model Deployment · 2026-10-30 · 12 min

Thinking of deploying Kimi K3.1 Pro? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

The weights are out. Moonshot published Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face on Nov 4, 2026 — 96 safetensors shards summing to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes (about 1.56TB) in native MXFP4 — under its own Kimi K3.1-Pro License, with vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed named on the model card as the serving engines. This guide, first published Oct 30, 2026 as pre-release maths, was refreshed on Nov 6, 2026 with the real file sizes, the real licence and the official recipes: the smallest honest setup is one 8-GPU B300 node, the cheapest node-shaped setup on the current board is 16× H200 at $57.44/hr — and Moonshot’s own API, at $2.00 in / $10.00 out per 1M tokens, still beats self-hosting on price at ordinary volumes.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-05 · 11 min

MI355X vs B300: inference cost per token, priced from the board

Spheron's comparison of these two 288GB cards, published Nov 3, 2026, prices its verdicts from modelled rates — including MI355X rates no provider actually sells at. This page re-runs the same question from prices read on the providers' own pages and checked on Nov 5, 2026: TensorWave's published $2.95/GPU/hr MI355X rate and Oracle's $8.60 list price, against a B300 board that starts at $7.40/GPU/hr. The silicon is tied — same 288GB of HBM3e, same 8 TB/s of bandwidth on both makers' spec sheets. The rental market is not tied at all, and in this comparison the entry tickets matter more than the chips.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-08 · 12 min

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

Provider Comparisons · 2026-11-12 · 13 min

H100 or B200 sold out? What to rent instead — priced

A stock alert tells you the card you wanted is gone. It does not tell you what to rent instead, or what the substitute costs. This page does: every substitute below is a real offer on our verified price board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — the card, the provider, the rate, and the terms that change the bill. One honesty note before the table: we are not reporting any provider as sold out today — our checks found prices, not stock levels. This guide is for the moment you go to book an H100 SXM or a B200 and find it gone.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-12 · 15 min

Deploy Inkling 2 Small — what it actually costs

Thinking Machines put the Inkling 2 Small weights on Hugging Face on Nov 12, 2026, under Apache 2.0 — and the first question every builder asks is the rental question. The honest answer starts with size: a 594-billion-parameter model whose own card asks for a GPU cluster with at least 500GB of memory. There is no single-card route. What there is: a cheapest verified way in at $14.36 an hour, a more comfortable one for 44 cents an hour more, and a clear set of people who should not rent at all and should use the APIs the maker lists instead. The model facts come from the maker's own card and repos, read on release day; the prices from our verified board, checked Nov 12, 2026.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-13 · 15 min

Deploy MiniMax H3-Image on one GPU

MiniMax released the H3-Image weights on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image model that generates and edits at up to 16 megapixels natively, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU — the cheapest documented one-card route on our board is $1.69 an hour. The hard part is the licence, and it is not a footnote: the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License Agreement excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom, South Korea and the United States entirely, and requires MiniMax's prior written authorisation before anyone with over $1M in annualised revenue — or anyone offering the model as a hosted service — may use it at all. For most readers, the licence decides whether there is a deployment to price. This guide takes the decisions in the order they bind: licence first, memory second, rental third. The model facts come from MiniMax's own card, repo and LICENSE file, read Nov 13, 2026; the prices from our verified board, checked Nov 26, 2026.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-14 · 13 min

How much does it cost to rent a GPU in the cloud?

On the board we checked on Nov 14, 2026, the cheapest verified on-demand offers in the table below start at $0.34 an hour for an RTX 4090 and top out at $14.27 an hour for a GB300. That range is real, but it is not the whole answer. The lowest H100 SXM rate, TensorDock's $2.25 per GPU per hour, comes with an eight-GPU minimum — an $18.00 hourly commitment, not a $2.25 rental. This guide separates the sticker price from the amount you actually commit to, then adds the costs the hourly rate leaves out.

Provider Comparisons · 2026-11-19 · 16 min

Serverless GPU inference compared — AWS Lambda GPU functions vs RunPod Serverless vs keeping an instance

“Serverless GPU” now means two very different bills. RunPod Serverless charges for the seconds a worker actually runs. AWS’s new Lambda GPU functions, launched Nov 18, 2026, charge for EC2 instance time your capacity sits provisioned — plus a 9.75% management fee and $0.20 per million requests — with no per-request duration charge at all. And the third option is the oldest one: rent the GPU by the hour and pay for its idle time yourself. This guide prices all three shapes from the providers’ own published rates, checked Nov 19, 2026, works the cost of a million requests at two request lengths, and finds the utilisation line where the always-on instance starts winning.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-22 · 16 min

Deploy Hy4 on an 8-GPU node — the FP8 route, costed

Hy4 is Tencent's 770-billion-parameter flagship, and its FP8 checkpoint measures 786.31GB on disk — which is why every serving recipe is built around a single node, eight GPUs or four of the largest cards. This guide works the deployment the way a renter has to: the measured weights, the memory arithmetic that rules the H100 out outright, the two documented serving routes with their exact launch commands, what a node costs at prices checked Nov 22, 2026, and the licence clause that has to be read before the node is rented, not after.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-24 · 19 min

Deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview — what its FP8+FP4 weights need, priced

Baidu has open-sourced the first post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash: a 280B mixture-of-experts model with 14B active per token, a 1M-token context window and an Apache 2.0 licence, shipped in three builds — a default build whose routed experts are 4-bit (165.91GB measured), an FP8 build for hardware without FP4 kernels (301.87GB) and a BF16 build (599.59GB). Unusually for preview weights, the serving support is real on day one: SGLang publishes a cookbook with a verified hardware matrix, and vLLM serves it through Baidu’s own plugin. Just as unusually, Baidu says in plain words on the model card that this is “an intermediate checkpoint from post-training” and that training is not finished. This guide prices the documented routes against our board, works the memory maths build by build — including the shapes that fail by single-digit gigabytes — and keeps the preview caveat where it belongs: in the decision, not in a footnote.

Deploy MiniMax H3-Image on one GPU

MiniMax released the H3-Image weights on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image model that generates and edits at up to 16 megapixels natively, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU — the cheapest documented one-card route on our board is $1.69 an hour. The hard part is the licence, and it is not a footnote: the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License Agreement excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom, South Korea and the United States entirely, and requires MiniMax's prior written authorisation before anyone with over $1M in annualised revenue — or anyone offering the model as a hosted service — may use it at all. GB200 NVL72 pricing, minimums and lead times — the real total cost

A GB200 NVL72 is not a GPU you rent by the card. It is a 72-GPU rack — 36 GB200 Superchips in one NVLink domain — and almost every price quoted for it is a division of a whole-system price, not a rate you can buy one GPU at. On the board we checked on Nov 15, 2026, exactly two providers publish a verified on-demand price for it: Oracle OCI at $16.00 per GPU per hour and Google Cloud at $18.6875. But their smallest cheques differ by a factor of twenty-one: Oracle will sell you one 4-GPU node for $64.00 an hour, while Google’s own page sets an 18-VM minimum for this shape — 72 GPUs, the entire rack — so the smallest Google commitment is $1,345.50 an hour. This guide prices the rack, not the sticker.

Deploy Hy4 on an 8-GPU node — the FP8 route, costed

Hy4 is Tencent's 770-billion-parameter flagship, and its FP8 checkpoint measures 786.31GB on disk — which is why every serving recipe is built around a single node, eight GPUs or four of the largest cards. This guide works the deployment the way a renter has to: the measured weights, the memory arithmetic that rules the H100 out outright, the two documented serving routes with their exact launch commands, what a node costs at prices checked Nov 22, 2026, and the licence clause that has to be read before the node is rented, not after.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-24 · 19 min

Deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview — what its FP8+FP4 weights need, priced

Baidu has open-sourced the first post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash: a 280B mixture-of-experts model with 14B active per token, a 1M-token context window and an Apache 2.0 licence, shipped in three builds — a default build whose routed experts are 4-bit (165.91GB measured), an FP8 build for hardware without FP4 kernels (301.87GB) and a BF16 build (599.59GB). Unusually for preview weights, the serving support is real on day one: SGLang publishes a cookbook with a verified hardware matrix, and vLLM serves it through Baidu’s own plugin. Just as unusually, Baidu says in plain words on the model card that this is “an intermediate checkpoint from post-training” and that training is not finished. This guide prices the documented routes against our board, works the memory maths build by build — including the shapes that fail by single-digit gigabytes — and keeps the preview caveat where it belongs: in the decision, not in a footnote.

Deploy MiniMax H3-Image on one GPU

MiniMax released the H3-Image weights on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image model that generates and edits at up to 16 megapixels natively, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU — the cheapest documented one-card route on our board is $1.69 an hour. The hard part is the licence, and it is not a footnote: the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License Agreement excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom, South Korea and the United States entirely, and requires MiniMax's prior written authorisation before anyone with over $1M in annualised revenue — or anyone offering the model as a hosted service — may use it at all. For most readers, the licence decides whether there is a deployment to price. This guide takes the decisions in the order they bind: licence first, memory second, rental third. Inkling 2 Mini is the rare new model that is a one-card job. This guide works the two honest routes: run the checkpoint exactly as shipped on one 32GB card, or run it dequantized at full precision on an 80GB card — what each route needs, which serving commands are documented today, and what each costs at prices checked Nov 26, 2026. Model Deployment · 2026-11-22 · 16 min

Deploy Hy4 on an 8-GPU node — the FP8 route, costed

Hy4 is Tencent's 770-billion-parameter flagship, and its FP8 checkpoint measures 786.31GB on disk — which is why every serving recipe is built around a single node, eight GPUs or four of the largest cards. This guide works the deployment the way a renter has to: the measured weights, the memory arithmetic that rules the H100 out outright, the two documented serving routes with their exact launch commands, what a node costs at prices checked Nov 22, 2026, and the licence clause that has to be read before the node is rented, not after.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-24 · 19 min

Deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview — what its FP8+FP4 weights need, priced

Baidu has open-sourced the first post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash: a 280B mixture-of-experts model with 14B active per token, a 1M-token context window and an Apache 2.0 licence, shipped in three builds — a default build whose routed experts are 4-bit (165.91GB measured), an FP8 build for hardware without FP4 kernels (301.87GB) and a BF16 build (599.59GB). Unusually for preview weights, the serving support is real on day one: SGLang publishes a cookbook with a verified hardware matrix, and vLLM serves it through Baidu’s own plugin. Just as unusually, Baidu says in plain words on the model card that this is “an intermediate checkpoint from post-training” and that training is not finished. This guide prices the documented routes against our board, works the memory maths build by build — including the shapes that fail by single-digit gigabytes — and keeps the preview caveat where it belongs: in the decision, not in a footnote.

Guides that cover it

Provider Comparisons · 2026-11-12 · 13 min

H100 or B200 sold out? What to rent instead — priced

A stock alert tells you the card you wanted is gone. It does not tell you what to rent instead, or what the substitute costs. This page does: every substitute below is a real offer on our verified price board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — the card, the provider, the rate, and the terms that change the bill. One honesty note before the table: we are not reporting any provider as sold out today — our checks found prices, not stock levels. This guide is for the moment you go to book an H100 SXM or a B200 and find it gone.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-12 · 12 min

Deploy Praxis-1 on one H100

Runway's Praxis-1 is a 27B robot policy that genuinely runs on one rented GPU — but “deploy” is three different jobs: serve a ready-made policy, adapt one to your task with LoRA, or fine-tune the base checkpoint for your own rig. Each prices differently, and one of them is not a one-card job at all. This guide prices all three from our verified board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — starting from the fact most coverage skips: the base checkpoint cannot drive a robot until you fine-tune it.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-13 · 15 min

Deploy MiniMax H3-Image on one GPU

MiniMax released the H3-Image weights on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image model that generates and edits at up to 16 megapixels natively, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU — the cheapest documented one-card route on our board is $1.69 an hour. The hard part is the licence, and it is not a footnote: the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License Agreement excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom, South Korea and the United States entirely, and requires MiniMax's prior written authorisation before anyone with over $1M in annualised revenue — or anyone offering the model as a hosted service — may use it at all. For most readers, the licence decides whether there is a deployment to price. This guide takes the decisions in the order they bind: licence first, memory second, rental third. The model facts come from MiniMax's own card, repo and LICENSE file, read Nov 13, 2026; the prices from our verified board, checked Nov 26, 2026.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-21 · 13 min

Deploy Inkling 2 Mini — how to run it and what it actually costs

Inkling 2 Mini is the rare new model that is a one-card job. Thinking Machines Lab released the weights on Nov 20, 2026 as a single checkpoint of about 20GB — a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts whose middle layers loop three times per token — and the cheapest verified card that a serving framework has actually verified for it rents for $0.69 an hour. This guide works the two honest routes: run the checkpoint exactly as shipped on one 32GB card, or run it dequantized at full precision on an 80GB card — what each route needs, which serving commands are documented today, and what each costs at prices checked Nov 26, 2026. It also names the cheap cards that look like they fit and, as of today, are not verified to run it.

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: self-host it or pay for the API?

NVIDIA’s open transcription model — 40 languages, speaker labels, translation, released Oct 28, 2026 — can be rented two ways: by the minute from a hosted API, or by the hour on a GPU you run yourself. The hosted price is public and tiny. The self-host price depends on one number nobody has independently measured yet — how fast the downloadable stack really runs — so this guide costs both routes honestly: the API at its published rate, self-hosting at a clearly printed planning assumption, and NVIDIA’s own published best case shown for what it is.

GPU Selection · 2026-11-04 · 13 min

Best GPU for video generation in 2026

A video model doesn’t bill you by the token. It bills you by the second of card time — so the right question is never “which GPU is fastest?” but “which is the smallest card that runs this model well, and what does one finished clip cost on it?” This guide answers that for the six open-weight video models people actually rent cards for in 2026 — Wan 2.2 in both sizes, HunyuanVideo-1.5, LTX-2, CogVideoX-1.5 and Mochi 1 — with verified prices checked Nov 4, 2026, and a cost per 5-second clip wherever the maker publishes a generation time. Where a maker publishes none, we price the model by the hour and say so, rather than invent a number.

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-21 · 13 min

Deploy Inkling 2 Mini — how to run it and what it actually costs

Inkling 2 Mini is the rare new model that is a one-card job. Thinking Machines Lab released the weights on Nov 20, 2026 as a single checkpoint of about 20GB — a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts whose middle layers loop three times per token — and the cheapest verified card that a serving framework has actually verified for it rents for $0.69 an hour. This guide works the two honest routes: run the checkpoint exactly as shipped on one 32GB card, or run it dequantized at full precision on an 80GB card — what each route needs, which serving commands are documented today, and what each costs at prices checked Nov 26, 2026. It also names the cheap cards that look like they fit and, as of today, are not verified to run it.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 19 min

Deploy Ternary Bonsai 2.5 on one small card — what 6 GB of weights actually costs to run

PrismML’s Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B is a 27B agent model whose weights are ternary — every weight is −1, 0 or +1 — so the fastest checkpoint measures 5.99 GB on disk (the maker headlines 5.93 GB) against 53.8 GB for the same model at FP16. That makes the rental question almost absurdly simple: every single card on our board can hold it, so the decision is not which card fits but which card is worth paying for, which of the three file packings your runtime will actually load, and whether the maker’s own speed tables — the only speed figures that exist for this model — justify skipping the ordinary 4-bit build of the base model instead. This guide works the arithmetic, prices the honest single-card routes, and prints the traps: the fastest file needs PrismML’s own llama.cpp fork, and the file that runs on stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage on an old build.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-02 · 14 min

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: self-host it or pay for the API?

NVIDIA’s open transcription model — 40 languages, speaker labels, translation, released Oct 28, 2026 — can be rented two ways: by the minute from a hosted API, or by the hour on a GPU you run yourself. The hosted price is public and tiny. The self-host price depends on one number nobody has independently measured yet — how fast the downloadable stack really runs — so this guide costs both routes honestly: the API at its published rate, self-hosting at a clearly printed planning assumption, and NVIDIA’s own published best case shown for what it is.

GPU Selection · 2026-11-04 · 13 min

Best GPU for video generation in 2026

A video model doesn’t bill you by the token. It bills you by the second of card time — so the right question is never “which GPU is fastest?” but “which is the smallest card that runs this model well, and what does one finished clip cost on it?” This guide answers that for the six open-weight video models people actually rent cards for in 2026 — Wan 2.2 in both sizes, HunyuanVideo-1.5, LTX-2, CogVideoX-1.5 and Mochi 1 — with verified prices checked Nov 4, 2026, and a cost per 5-second clip wherever the maker publishes a generation time. Where a maker publishes none, we price the model by the hour and say so, rather than invent a number.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-12 · 12 min

Deploy Praxis-1 on one H100

Runway's Praxis-1 is a 27B robot policy that genuinely runs on one rented GPU — but “deploy” is three different jobs: serve a ready-made policy, adapt one to your task with LoRA, or fine-tune the base checkpoint for your own rig. Each prices differently, and one of them is not a one-card job at all. This guide prices all three from our verified board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — starting from the fact most coverage skips: the base checkpoint cannot drive a robot until you fine-tune it.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-14 · 13 min

On the board we checked on Nov 14, 2026, the cheapest verified on-demand offers in the table below start at $0.34 an hour for an RTX 4090 and top out at $14.27 an hour for a GB300. That range is real, but it is not the whole answer. The lowest H100 SXM rate, TensorDock's $2.25 per GPU per hour, comes with an eight-GPU minimum — an $18.00 hourly commitment, not a $2.25 rental. This guide separates the sticker price from the amount you actually commit to, then adds the costs the hourly rate leaves out.

Provider Comparisons · 2026-11-19 · 16 min

Serverless GPU inference compared — AWS Lambda GPU functions vs RunPod Serverless vs keeping an instance

“Serverless GPU” now means two very different bills. RunPod Serverless charges for the seconds a worker actually runs. AWS’s new Lambda GPU functions, launched Nov 18, 2026, charge for EC2 instance time your capacity sits provisioned — plus a 9.75% management fee and $0.20 per million requests — with no per-request duration charge at all. And the third option is the oldest one: rent the GPU by the hour and pay for its idle time yourself. This guide prices all three shapes from the providers’ own published rates, checked Nov 19, 2026, works the cost of a million requests at two request lengths, and finds the utilisation line where the always-on instance starts winning.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-21 · 13 min

Deploy Inkling 2 Mini — how to run it and what it actually costs

Inkling 2 Mini is the rare new model that is a one-card job. Thinking Machines Lab released the weights on Nov 20, 2026 as a single checkpoint of about 20GB — a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts whose middle layers loop three times per token — and the cheapest verified card that a serving framework has actually verified for it rents for $0.69 an hour. This guide works the two honest routes: run the checkpoint exactly as shipped on one 32GB card, or run it dequantized at full precision on an 80GB card — what each route needs, which serving commands are documented today, and what each costs at prices checked Nov 26, 2026. It also names the cheap cards that look like they fit and, as of today, are not verified to run it.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 19 min

Deploy Ternary Bonsai 2.5 on one small card — what 6 GB of weights actually costs to run

PrismML’s Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B is a 27B agent model whose weights are ternary — every weight is −1, 0 or +1 — so the fastest checkpoint measures 5.99 GB on disk (the maker headlines 5.93 GB) against 53.8 GB for the same model at FP16. That makes the rental question almost absurdly simple: every single card on our board can hold it, so the decision is not which card fits but which card is worth paying for, which of the three file packings your runtime will actually load, and whether the maker’s own speed tables — the only speed figures that exist for this model — justify skipping the ordinary 4-bit build of the base model instead. This guide works the arithmetic, prices the honest single-card routes, and prints the traps: the fastest file needs PrismML’s own llama.cpp fork, and the file that runs on stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage on an old build.

Deploy Soma-1X Lite — paper records to structured data on one small card, priced

Amini’s Soma-1X Lite does one job: it takes a page — a typed form, a handwritten letter, a table, a faded scan — and returns the page as structured data, one labelled block per element with its position on the page, tables as HTML and maths as LaTeX. It is a 2.21-billion-parameter vision-language model whose whole weights file measures 4.43 GB, so the rental question is not whether it fits — every card on our board holds it several times over — but which serving route actually runs it today, what a page costs on the one throughput figure the maker publishes, and where the traps are: the model only answers properly with its own trained prompts and thinking switched off, the card prints no context length, and the 4-bit quantisations people usually reach for do not exist because the maker’s own tests found they degraded the layout detection. This guide works the arithmetic and prices the honest single-card routes.

Guides that cover it

GPU Selection · 2026-10-30 · 14 min

Best GPU for AI inference in 2026 — priced from a checked board

Most “best GPU for inference” pages price their verdicts from a rate card the seller itself publishes — prices stated on the seller’s own pages, with no check date a reader can test. This page works the other way round. Every price below was read on the provider’s own published page and checked on Oct 30, 2026, and every cost per token is built from a throughput assumption printed next to it, so the maths can be rerun with your own numbers. The result is not the ranking the spec sheets suggest: on a mid-size model, the cheapest tokens in our checks come off a $0.34-an-hour gaming card, and the fastest card on the board finishes mid-table.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-14 · 13 min

How much does it cost to rent a GPU in the cloud?

On the board we checked on Nov 14, 2026, the cheapest verified on-demand offers in the table below start at $0.34 an hour for an RTX 4090 and top out at $14.27 an hour for a GB300. That range is real, but it is not the whole answer. The lowest H100 SXM rate, TensorDock's $2.25 per GPU per hour, comes with an eight-GPU minimum — an $18.00 hourly commitment, not a $2.25 rental. This guide separates the sticker price from the amount you actually commit to, then adds the costs the hourly rate leaves out.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-21 · 13 min

Deploy Inkling 2 Mini — how to run it and what it actually costs

Inkling 2 Mini is the rare new model that is a one-card job. Thinking Machines Lab released the weights on Nov 20, 2026 as a single checkpoint of about 20GB — a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts whose middle layers loop three times per token — and the cheapest verified card that a serving framework has actually verified for it rents for $0.69 an hour. This guide works the two honest routes: run the checkpoint exactly as shipped on one 32GB card, or run it dequantized at full precision on an 80GB card — what each route needs, which serving commands are documented today, and what each costs at prices checked Nov 26, 2026. It also names the cheap cards that look like they fit and, as of today, are not verified to run it.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 19 min

Deploy Ternary Bonsai 2.5 on one small card — what 6 GB of weights actually costs to run

PrismML’s Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B is a 27B agent model whose weights are ternary — every weight is −1, 0 or +1 — so the fastest checkpoint measures 5.99 GB on disk (the maker headlines 5.93 GB) against 53.8 GB for the same model at FP16. That makes the rental question almost absurdly simple: every single card on our board can hold it, so the decision is not which card fits but which card is worth paying for, which of the three file packings your runtime will actually load, and whether the maker’s own speed tables — the only speed figures that exist for this model — justify skipping the ordinary 4-bit build of the base model instead. This guide works the arithmetic, prices the honest single-card routes, and prints the traps: the fastest file needs PrismML’s own llama.cpp fork, and the file that runs on stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage on an old build.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 17 min

Deploy Soma-1X Lite — paper records to structured data on one small card, priced

Amini’s Soma-1X Lite does one job: it takes a page — a typed form, a handwritten letter, a table, a faded scan — and returns the page as structured data, one labelled block per element with its position on the page, tables as HTML and maths as LaTeX. It is a 2.21-billion-parameter vision-language model whose whole weights file measures 4.43 GB, so the rental question is not whether it fits — every card on our board holds it several times over — but which serving route actually runs it today, what a page costs on the one throughput figure the maker publishes, and where the traps are: the model only answers properly with its own trained prompts and thinking switched off, the card prints no context length, and the 4-bit quantisations people usually reach for do not exist because the maker’s own tests found they degraded the layout detection. This guide works the arithmetic and prices the honest single-card routes.

One provider raised its GPU prices on Oct 23, Oct 24, Oct 26, Oct 27, Oct 28 and again on Oct 29 — six rises in seven days, across almost its whole range, each one small and each one in the same direction. Model Deployment · 2026-10-30 · 12 min

Thinking of deploying Kimi K3.1 Pro? Here’s how — and what it actually costs

The weights are out. Moonshot published Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face on Nov 4, 2026 — 96 safetensors shards summing to 1,561,293,160,568 bytes (about 1.56TB) in native MXFP4 — under its own Kimi K3.1-Pro License, with vLLM, SGLang and TokenSpeed named on the model card as the serving engines. This guide, first published Oct 30, 2026 as pre-release maths, was refreshed on Nov 6, 2026 with the real file sizes, the real licence and the official recipes: the smallest honest setup is one 8-GPU B300 node, the cheapest node-shaped setup on the current board is 16× H200 at $57.44/hr — and Moonshot’s own API, at $2.00 in / $10.00 out per 1M tokens, still beats self-hosting on price at ordinary volumes.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-08 · 12 min

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

Hy4 is Tencent's 770-billion-parameter flagship, and its FP8 checkpoint measures 786.31GB on disk — which is why every serving recipe is built around a single node, eight GPUs or four of the largest cards. Guides that cover it

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-15 · 13 min

GB200 NVL72 pricing, minimums and lead times — the real total cost

A GB200 NVL72 is not a GPU you rent by the card. It is a 72-GPU rack — 36 GB200 Superchips in one NVLink domain — and almost every price quoted for it is a division of a whole-system price, not a rate you can buy one GPU at. On the board we checked on Nov 15, 2026, exactly two providers publish a verified on-demand price for it: Oracle OCI at $16.00 per GPU per hour and Google Cloud at $18.6875. But their smallest cheques differ by a factor of twenty-one: Oracle will sell you one 4-GPU node for $64.00 an hour, while Google’s own page sets an 18-VM minimum for this shape — 72 GPUs, the entire rack — so the smallest Google commitment is $1,345.50 an hour. This guide prices the rack, not the sticker.

Full precision (FP16)
6 GB

8-bit

4-bit

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

Licence: MIT — free for any use, including commercial. Just keep the licence notice.

Worth knowing

Z.ai's lightweight MoE sibling to GLM-4.7, released Jan 19, 2026 — the model Z.ai bills as its 30B-A3B. The checkpoint itself counts 31.2B total parameters by its own safetensors total (47 layers, 64 routed experts with top-4 routing plus one shared expert, per its config), about 3B active per token, a 200K context (config maximum 202,752) and an MIT licence. Public and ungated on Hugging Face, in BF16.

What it needs

Full precision (FP16)
62 GB
the weights, uncompressed
8-bit
31 GB
the weights, compressed to 8-bit
4-bit
16 GB
the weights, compressed to 4-bit

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

What it needs

Full precision (FP16)
8 GB
the weights, uncompressed
8-bit
4 GB
the weights, compressed to 8-bit
4-bit
2 GB
the weights, compressed to 4-bit

How we work this out: memory = the model's total parameters × bytes per weight — 2 bytes at full precision (FP16), 1 byte at 8-bit, half a byte at 4-bit. Weights only — add room for the conversation memory (KV cache) and the serving software. A GPU counts as running a build when its memory covers the weights plus about 20% headroom. Real figures move with context length and software.

GPU Pricing · 2026-10-26 · 7 min

GPU rental prices are rising in 2026 — the dated evidence

If you rent GPUs at a provider's own list rates, you are probably paying more than you did a few weeks ago. This page shows the rises we have verified on providers' own pages — each one dated — and the half of the market that has not moved yet.

GPU Pricing · 2026-10-30 · 7 min

Batch is the new spot: what RunPod’s 20% batch discount does to the maths for work that can wait

On Oct 28, 2026, RunPod made Serverless Batch Inference generally available: send requests in bulk, let them run when RunPod’s batch workers get to them, and pay 20% less than the on-demand rate on H100, H200, B200 and B300. This page does the maths on that trade — what the discount is worth in dollars, and what you give up for it.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-08 · 12 min

Power is the new GPU shortage: why powered land decides your rental price

GPU rental prices have been rising for six weeks, and the usual explanation — not enough chips — no longer fits. The chips exist. What is scarce is somewhere powered to plug them in: an energised building, on a grid connection, under a signed power contract. This page walks through the verified rises, shows why they point at power rather than silicon, and tells you what to ask before you rent capacity that has not been switched on yet.

Provider Comparisons · 2026-11-19 · 16 min

Serverless GPU inference compared — AWS Lambda GPU functions vs RunPod Serverless vs keeping an instance

“Serverless GPU” now means two very different bills. RunPod Serverless charges for the seconds a worker actually runs. AWS’s new Lambda GPU functions, launched Nov 18, 2026, charge for EC2 instance time your capacity sits provisioned — plus a 9.75% management fee and $0.20 per million requests — with no per-request duration charge at all. And the third option is the oldest one: rent the GPU by the hour and pay for its idle time yourself. This guide prices all three shapes from the providers’ own published rates, checked Nov 19, 2026, works the cost of a million requests at two request lengths, and finds the utilisation line where the always-on instance starts winning.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-21 · 13 min

Deploy Inkling 2 Mini — how to run it and what it actually costs

Inkling 2 Mini is the rare new model that is a one-card job. Thinking Machines Lab released the weights on Nov 20, 2026 as a single checkpoint of about 20GB — a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts whose middle layers loop three times per token — and the cheapest verified card that a serving framework has actually verified for it rents for $0.69 an hour. This guide works the two honest routes: run the checkpoint exactly as shipped on one 32GB card, or run it dequantized at full precision on an 80GB card — what each route needs, which serving commands are documented today, and what each costs at prices checked Nov 26, 2026. It also names the cheap cards that look like they fit and, as of today, are not verified to run it.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-22 · 16 min

Deploy Hy4 on an 8-GPU node — the FP8 route, costed

Hy4 is Tencent's 770-billion-parameter flagship, and its FP8 checkpoint measures 786.31GB on disk — which is why every serving recipe is built around a single node, eight GPUs or four of the largest cards. This guide works the deployment the way a renter has to: the measured weights, the memory arithmetic that rules the H100 out outright, the two documented serving routes with their exact launch commands, what a node costs at prices checked Nov 22, 2026, and the licence clause that has to be read before the node is rented, not after.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 19 min

Deploy Ternary Bonsai 2.5 on one small card — what 6 GB of weights actually costs to run

PrismML’s Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B is a 27B agent model whose weights are ternary — every weight is −1, 0 or +1 — so the fastest checkpoint measures 5.99 GB on disk (the maker headlines 5.93 GB) against 53.8 GB for the same model at FP16. That makes the rental question almost absurdly simple: every single card on our board can hold it, so the decision is not which card fits but which card is worth paying for, which of the three file packings your runtime will actually load, and whether the maker’s own speed tables — the only speed figures that exist for this model — justify skipping the ordinary 4-bit build of the base model instead. This guide works the arithmetic, prices the honest single-card routes, and prints the traps: the fastest file needs PrismML’s own llama.cpp fork, and the file that runs on stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage on an old build.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 17 min

Deploy Hy4 Flash — the FP8 setup on two H200s, costed

Tencent's Hy4 Flash is a 220B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only about 12B parameters per token — but memory is always the full 220.3B, because every parameter has to sit in GPU memory whether a given token uses it or not. At FP8 the weights occupy about 220GB, which fits two H200s with room to spare; at BF16 they occupy about 440GB and need four. On the cheapest verified H200 rate on our board, checked Nov 25, 2026, the FP8 pair costs $7.18 an hour. This guide shows the memory maths, the serving routes Tencent actually documents — both written for tensor-parallel 8, so the two-GPU run is a memory fit, not a published recipe — what each setup costs across every H200 offer on the board, and the licence clause, §10.2 of the Tencent Hy License, that a commercial hoster needs to read before the download finishes.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 24 min

Deploy Sarvam-105B-1711 on one RTX PRO 6000 — and the $0.15/Mtok break-even

Sarvam's 105B checkpoint is the rare open-weight release whose pitch is a single workstation card: the NVFP4 build measures 70.15GB on disk and is documented by its maker to run on one 96GB RTX PRO 6000, at $1.69 an hour on the cheapest verified row of our board (checked Nov 25, 2026). In the same announcement, Sarvam cut its hosted price to a blended $0.15 per million tokens — and this guide works the honest break-even from Sarvam's own published throughput table. The answer is stark: at the throughput Sarvam itself measures on this card, the break-even volume is about 57 times what the card can produce in a month. You rent this card for control, not for savings — and the guide shows the arithmetic that proves it, both ways.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-25 · 17 min

Deploy Soma-1X Lite — paper records to structured data on one small card, priced

Amini’s Soma-1X Lite does one job: it takes a page — a typed form, a handwritten letter, a table, a faded scan — and returns the page as structured data, one labelled block per element with its position on the page, tables as HTML and maths as LaTeX. It is a 2.21-billion-parameter vision-language model whose whole weights file measures 4.43 GB, so the rental question is not whether it fits — every card on our board holds it several times over — but which serving route actually runs it today, what a page costs on the one throughput figure the maker publishes, and where the traps are: the model only answers properly with its own trained prompts and thinking switched off, the card prints no context length, and the 4-bit quantisations people usually reach for do not exist because the maker’s own tests found they degraded the layout detection. This guide works the arithmetic and prices the honest single-card routes.

GPU Pricing · 2026-11-15 · 13 min

GB200 NVL72 pricing, minimums and lead times — the real total cost

A GB200 NVL72 is not a GPU you rent by the card. It is a 72-GPU rack — 36 GB200 Superchips in one NVLink domain — and almost every price quoted for it is a division of a whole-system price, not a rate you can buy one GPU at. On the board we checked on Nov 15, 2026, exactly two providers publish a verified on-demand price for it: Oracle OCI at $16.00 per GPU per hour and Google Cloud at $18.6875. But their smallest cheques differ by a factor of twenty-one: Oracle will sell you one 4-GPU node for $64.00 an hour, while Google’s own page sets an 18-VM minimum for this shape — 72 GPUs, the entire rack — so the smallest Google commitment is $1,345.50 an hour. This guide prices the rack, not the sticker.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-24 · 19 min

Deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview — what its FP8+FP4 weights need, priced

Baidu has open-sourced the first post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash: a 280B mixture-of-experts model with 14B active per token, a 1M-token context window and an Apache 2.0 licence, shipped in three builds — a default build whose routed experts are 4-bit (165.91GB measured), an FP8 build for hardware without FP4 kernels (301.87GB) and a BF16 build (599.59GB). Unusually for preview weights, the serving support is real on day one: SGLang publishes a cookbook with a verified hardware matrix, and vLLM serves it through Baidu’s own plugin. Just as unusually, Baidu says in plain words on the model card that this is “an intermediate checkpoint from post-training” and that training is not finished. This guide prices the documented routes against our board, works the memory maths build by build — including the shapes that fail by single-digit gigabytes — and keeps the preview caveat where it belongs: in the decision, not in a footnote.

Model Deployment · 2026-11-24 · 19 min

Deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview — what its FP8+FP4 weights need, priced

Baidu has open-sourced the first post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash: a 280B mixture-of-experts model with 14B active per token, a 1M-token context window and an Apache 2.0 licence, shipped in three builds — a default build whose routed experts are 4-bit (165.91GB measured), an FP8 build for hardware without FP4 kernels (301.87GB) and a BF16 build (599.59GB). Unusually for preview weights, the serving support is real on day one: SGLang publishes a cookbook with a verified hardware matrix, and vLLM serves it through Baidu’s own plugin. Just as unusually, Baidu says in plain words on the model card that this is “an intermediate checkpoint from post-training” and that training is not finished. This guide prices the documented routes against our board, works the memory maths build by build — including the shapes that fail by single-digit gigabytes — and keeps the preview caveat where it belongs: in the decision, not in a footnote.

Best Single GPU for AI Inference in 2026: One Card, Decided Properly

Most inference guides assume an 8-GPU node. Most readers have one card and one job. Here is the single-card decision — by VRAM headroom and cost per finished request, using prices checked Oct 18, 2026.

The verdict

  • L40S — 7B–32B models, image generation, best all-rounder under $1/hr · $0.79/hr at RunPod Community
  • RTX PRO 6000 — 70B quantized on ONE card — the sleeper pick · $1.69/hr at RunPod Community
  • H100 — High-throughput serving, FP8, when requests per second pay the rent · $4.50/hr at Nebius
  • RTX 4090 — Tight budgets, 7B–14B models, dev and prototyping · $0.34/hr at RunPod Community

The deciding metric: cost per finished request, not $/hr

A GPU's hourly price tells you what the meter charges. It does not tell you what a request costs. Divide the hourly rate by the requests the card actually completes per hour at your batch size and context length, and the ranking flips: a $2.64/hr H100 pushing 3× the throughput of a $0.96/hr L40S is the cheaper card per request — until your traffic drops and the H100 sits idle at full price. Rule of thumb: if the card will be busy more than ~60% of the hour, buy throughput (H100 class). If it will idle between bursts, buy the cheapest card that fits the model with KV-cache headroom (L40S / RTX PRO 6000 class). Fit first, throughput second, headline price last.

Worked math: serving a 32B model for one day (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

Job: serve Qwen-class 32B, ~40 requests/min average, 24 hours. On an L40S (48GB, FP16 weights ≈ 65GB — too big; run AWQ INT4 ≈ 20GB, comfortable with KV cache): 24h × $0.96 = $23.04/day. On an H100 (FP16 fits with room to batch harder): 24h × $2.64 = $63.36/day. The H100 finishes each request faster, but at a steady 40 req/min the L40S is not saturated — you would pay $40.32/day extra for latency you may not need. Flip it: at 200 req/min the L40S queues, p95 latency blows up, and the H100's $63.36 buys the headroom that keeps the service usable. Same models, same day — the right card is decided by your request rate, not the spec sheet. Rerun this division with the current Price Board before you budget.

Steps

1. Size the weights first

Parameters × bytes per parameter: FP16 = 2 bytes, INT8 = 1, INT4 ≈ 0.5. A 32B model is ~65GB at FP16, ~20GB at INT4. If weights alone exceed the card, no flag will save you.

2. Reserve KV cache honestly

Budget at least 25–40% of VRAM on top of weights for KV cache at your real context length. A card that 'fits' the weights and OOMs at request #50 does not fit.

3. Match the card to your duty cycle

Busy >60% of the hour → throughput card (H100). Bursty or dev traffic → cheapest card that fits (L40S, RTX PRO 6000, 4090).

4. Cost the finished job

Hours the job actually runs × the dated $/hr from the Price Board. Include spin-up and idle-while-you-debug time — everyone forgets those, and they are real hours on the meter.

5. Rent for one hour and measure

Run your real prompts, record tokens/sec and p95 latency, then commit. One measured hour beats ten benchmark blog posts — including this one.

Alternatives

Two smaller cards instead of one big one

Two L40S (96GB total) can beat one H100 on price for embarrassingly parallel work — batch image generation, offline evals. For single-request latency, one fast card still wins.

An API instead of a rental

Below ~2 busy hours a day, a per-token API is usually cheaper than any rental once idle time is counted. The crossover is arithmetic, not ideology — do the division for your traffic.

Deploy Qwen 32B on a Single GPU with vLLM: The One-Card Runbook

A 32B model, one 48GB card, no cluster. VRAM math first, then the exact vLLM launch — flags explained, KV cache sized, cost per hour from the Oct 18, 2026 Price Board.

The verdict

  • Card — Smallest card that runs 32B AWQ comfortably with KV headroom
  • Weights — FP16 (≈65GB) does not fit a 48GB card — quantization is the decision
  • Context — KV cache budget ~18GB at 32k with the flags below
  • Job cost — A full working day of serving / evals

The deciding metric: VRAM after KV cache, not VRAM on the box

The spec sheet says 48GB. The model takes ~20GB in AWQ INT4. What remains — about 26GB after CUDA context and activations — is your KV cache, and KV cache is what decides how many conversations the card holds at once and how long each can run. At 32k context, one sequence's KV for a 32B-class model runs to several GB; plan for a handful of concurrent long sequences, not hundreds. If your workload is many short chats, you are fine. If it is a few very long documents, context — not the model — is your wall. Size for the workload you have, in that order: weights, KV at your context, concurrency.

RTX 4090 24GB24GB1,008 GB/sNot on the boardAWQ weights fit (~20GB) but KV headroom is ~2GB. Demo-grade only.
L40S 48GB48GB864 GB/sNot on the boardThe target card for this runbook. Balanced fit + headroom.
RTX PRO 6000 96GB96GB1,792 GB/sNot on the boardRun FP16 instead, or double concurrency. The headroom is the point.
H100 80GB80GB3,350 GB/sNot on the boardOverkill for one 32B — unless throughput per request pays.

Worked math: what a day of 32B actually costs (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

L40S on-demand at $0.96/hr: a focused 8-hour build-and-eval day = $7.68. A 24-hour always-on deployment = $23.04/day, $691.20 per 30-day month. Stepping up in VRAM from here means a bigger card class. Neither number includes storage or egress; on most providers those are small next to GPU hours, but check before a month-long commitment. Prices move — the Price Board carries the current checked date; rerun this math there.

Steps

1. Provision the card

Rent an L40S (48GB) with at least 100GB disk — model weights, cache and logs add up faster than you expect. Pick the region nearest your users; latency is geography.

2. Install vLLM

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate, then pip install vllm. Pin the version in your notes; 'latest' is a moving target when you return in a month.

3. Download the AWQ weights

Fetch the AWQ INT4 build of the 32B model from its official repo. Verify the size on disk (~20GB class) before launching — a partial download presents as a CUDA error later.

4. Launch with the flags that matter

vllm serve <model> --quantization awq --max-model-len 32768 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --enable-prefix-caching. gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 leaves breathing room; max-model-len is your KV budget made explicit — set it to the context you sized for, not the model's maximum.

5. Validate like a skeptic

Send one short prompt, one 20k-token prompt, and ten concurrent prompts. Watch VRAM and logs. The long + concurrent test is where undersized deployments confess.

6. Cost-guard the box

Set a calendar reminder or an auto-stop. The most expensive GPU is the one you forgot was running over a weekend: 60 idle hours on an L40S = $57.60 for nothing.

Alternatives

SGLang instead of vLLM

Comparable throughput, strong prefix-cache story. If your workload is many shared-prefix prompts (agents, few-shot templates), benchmark both for one hour each and keep the winner.

Step up to 70B on the RTX PRO 6000

Same runbook shape, INT4 weights ≈ 40GB, 96GB card. If 32B quality is your ceiling, the card — not the procedure — is the upgrade.

GPU PRICING →  ·  2026-10-18 · 10 min read

The True Cost of Renting a GPU: What the $/hr Isn't Telling You

$/hr is the beginning of the bill, not the bill. Spin-up, idle time, storage, egress and the spot-interruption tax — totalled honestly, with dated prices from Oct 18, 2026.

The verdict

  • Headline lie — $/hr ignores spin-up, idle, storage and egress — typically +15–40% on real jobs
  • H200 spot — Spot saves $1.48/hr vs on-demand — if interruptions don't eat the saving
  • Forgotten weekend — 60 idle hours nobody meant to buy
  • Rule — Budget the finished job, then add 25% the first time you run it

The deciding metric: cost per finished job

Nobody's goal is 'rent a GPU'. The goal is a trained adapter, a served model, a finished eval. So cost that. Finished-job cost = (spin-up + working + idle + teardown hours) × $/hr + storage + egress + the expected cost of interruptions. The $/hr ranking and the finished-job ranking regularly disagree: the cheapest hourly card that runs 30% longer and gets interrupted twice can cost more than the 'expensive' card that finished last night. Every worked example below uses one dated rate set — Oct 18, 2026 — so the arithmetic stays checkable. When rates move, the method doesn't.

GPUVRAMBandwidthLowest verified priceVerdict
Spin-up & setup——Not on the boardImage pulls, weight downloads, env fixes. Billed at full $/hr on most providers.
Idle time——Not on the boardThe silent budget-killer. Debugging locally while the box runs is paying rent to watch you think.
Storage——Not on the boardCheckpoints multiply. A 70B full checkpoint habit can outgrow the GPU bill on long runs.
Egress——Not on the boardDownloading a 140GB model repeatedly is a line item, not a rounding error.
Spot interruptions——Not on the boardPrice the restart: lost progress since last checkpoint + spin-up again, times how often it happens.

Worked math: spot vs on-demand on an H200 (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

On-demand H200: $4.80/hr. Spot H200: $3.32/hr — a $1.48/hr saving, 31% off. Take a 20-hour fine-tune with checkpoints every 2 hours. On-demand total: 20 × $4.80 = $96.00, done. Spot, uninterrupted: 20 × $3.32 = $66.40. Spot with two interruptions, each losing on average 1 hour of progress and 15 minutes of restart: effective hours ≈ 22.5 × $3.32 = $74.70 — still ahead by $21.30. Spot with six interruptions: ≈ 27.5 × $3.32 = $91.30, and your deadline is now fiction. Break-even sits around 7 interruptions for this job shape. Spot is a bet with knowable odds: checkpoint often, count your interruptions, and the math — not the discount — decides.

Steps

1. Write the job, not the rental

Define done: artifact produced, metric reached, service live. Estimate working hours from a one-hour pilot run, not from hope.

2. Add the invisible hours

Spin-up (measure it once), teardown, and an idle allowance: +10% if you're disciplined, +30% if you're honest.

3. Price interruptions for spot

Expected restarts × (average progress lost + spin-up) × spot rate. Compare against the on-demand total, not the on-demand hourly.

4. Cap storage before it caps you

Decide checkpoint retention before the run: keep last 2 + best 1 is a sane default. Delete on a schedule, not on a panic.

5. Set the kill switch first

Auto-stop, budget alert, calendar reminder — pick one before you start the meter. Every experienced renter has exactly one forgotten-weekend story.

Alternatives

Reserved / committed capacity

For steady, month-scale serving, committed rates can undercut on-demand by a wide margin — at the cost of flexibility. Worth it only when the workload is proven, not predicted.

Buy the card

Above roughly 55–65% sustained utilisation over the card's useful life, ownership starts to win on pure math — before power, cooling, and your time enter the ledger. Run your own numbers; the crossover is lower than most renters assume and higher than most buyers admit.

The deciding metric: what is actually scarce in your workload

Every workload is starved for exactly one thing. Throughput-bound serving is starved for memory bandwidth — the H100's 3,350 GB/s is 3.9× the L40S, and tokens/sec follows bandwidth at decode time. Capacity-bound work — a 70B model that must fit — is starved for VRAM, and there the RTX PRO 6000's 96GB beats the H100's 80GB outright — capacity and bandwidth are different currencies. Budget-bound mixed work is starved for dollars, and the L40S's sub-$1 rate with datacenter drivers wins by simply being rentable all month. Name your scarcity first. The 'best GPU' question dissolves the moment you do.

Worked math: a 30-day always-on deployment (prices as of Oct 18, 2026)

720 hours a month. L40S: 720 × $0.96 = $691.20. H100: 720 × $2.64 = $1,900.80. Read those as capabilities, not just costs: the $1,209.60 gap between them buys 3.9× decode bandwidth. The RTX PRO 6000 carries no monthly figure here — its rental rates are not on the board yet. If your service never saturates the L40S, the H100's extra $1,209.60 buys nothing measurable. If your model doesn't fit the L40S, its cheapness is irrelevant. Cost per month is the last step of the decision, never the first.

Steps

1. Name the scarcity

Bandwidth (tokens/sec), capacity (model must fit), or budget (hours per month). Write it down; it picks the winner in step 4.

2. Check the hard fit gate

Weights + KV at your context must fit with ≥20% headroom. Any card failing this is out, regardless of price.

3. Check the precision gate

Need FP8 for your serving plan? H100 and PRO 6000 (Blackwell/Ada-class paths differ) — verify your stack's support on the exact card before renting a month of it.

4. Let the scarcity decide

Bandwidth → H100. Capacity → PRO 6000. Budget with a fitting model → L40S. Ties are broken by the Price Board's current dated rates.
