/story/telekom-munich-b300-expansion-nov.html:
NEWS →  ·  Infrastructure · Deutsche Telekom

Deutsche Telekom expands its sold-out Munich AI factory with Blackwell Ultra B300s

Nov 9, 2026

Deutsche Telekom announced on Nov 9, 2026 that it will expand its Industrial AI Cloud — the “AI factory” at Munich’s Tucherpark — with additional NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra (B300) systems, after the first expansion phase sold out in seven months. The B300s join the site’s existing Blackwell B200 systems and double the number of chips in that class, taking the factory’s capacity to 20 megawatts. Telekom puts the new investment at nearly another quarter of a billion euros.

Image: Deutsche Telekom via telekom.com

What Telekom announced, in its own release (Deutsche Telekom media information, Nov 9, 2026): the Munich factory only went live in February 2026, and its initial expansion — which Telekom says alone increased Germany’s available AI computing capacity by 50 percent — was fully booked just seven months later; planning for further stages began as early as May. The site will keep using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs alongside the new B300s. A federal minister quoted in the release, Katherina Reiche, put the result as “doubling its capacity to 20,000 graphics processing units”. Trade coverage of the same Munich press conference (TelecomTV and Light Reading, Nov 9) put the expansion cost at about €250 million and current capacity at 12 MW, rising to the 20 MW Telekom states. Telekom says the factory runs at a PUE of 1.2 and its waste heat will supply the Tucherpark district.

Who is using it, per the same release: industrial companies and institutes including Siemens, Daimler Truck, Currenta, Synopsys, Agile Robots, Wandelbots, PhysicsX, Noxtua and EDAG, for simulations, digital twins, robotics and language models — including Soofi, a German language model trained on the infrastructure. Telekom is also exploring a further, larger expansion of its Bavarian commitment with partners, but states plainly that no final investment decision has been made on that stage — it is an exploration, not a commitment, and we report it as such.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and builders this is the European version of the same story this autumn keeps telling: sovereign, in-region Blackwell capacity sells out. A factory that opened in February was fully booked by September, and its owner is now spending roughly another quarter-billion euros to double its Blackwell-class fleet with B300s — the third demand data point today alone, after Edgevana’s $700 million-plus in take-or-pay Blackwell agreements and Verda’s eleventh list-price rise holding through our evening check. The honest limits: this is enterprise Industrial AI Cloud capacity sold to industry, research and the public sector under European data rules, not self-serve hourly rental — Telekom publishes no per-GPU price, and nothing in this announcement can be booked from our price board today. What it tells a renter planning European capacity for 2027 is that the queue for B300s in Europe is lengthening, not shortening.

Anthropic launched its IPO roadshow on Nov 10, 2026 and filed Amendment No. 2 to its Form S-1 with the SEC the same day: 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78, listing on Nasdaq as ANT, raising up to about $64.4 billion and valuing the company at about $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding. Alongside the offering, seven technology companies — the GPU supply chain itself — have agreed to buy $26 billion of Anthropic stock in a private placement at the IPO price.

Image: Anthropic via anthropic.com

The terms, from Amendment No. 2 to Anthropic's Form S-1 filed with the SEC on Nov 10, 2026, as reported the same day by Reuters, CNBC and Axios from the filing: Anthropic itself sells 801,351,354 of the 825 million shares and existing stockholders sell 23,648,646; underwriters hold a 30-day option on a further 123,750,000 shares, which at $78 would take the total raise to about $74 billion. A draft circulated to banks late on Nov 9 showed about 867 million shares at $70 to $80; Anthropic told the banks those details were inaccurate, and the Nov 10 amended filing — $70 to $78 — is the version of record. CNBC reports pricing on Nov 18 and trading from Nov 19; the filing itself gives no dates, so we report that timing as reported, not filed.

The placement is the part this desk cares about: Google and NVIDIA have each agreed to buy about $10 billion of non-voting Class N shares at the IPO price, AMD $2.5 billion, and Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC $1 billion, $1 billion, $1 billion and $500 million respectively — $26 billion in all, per the filing summaries. The filing's use-of-proceeds language covers general corporate purposes including compute and infrastructure. One widely flashed sub-claim — up to $120.5 billion of NVIDIA GPU compute agreements with SpaceX — appears in none of the detailed filing summaries we read, so we do not print it as fact.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and buyers, this is the largest single demand signal of the autumn. The companies buying the placement are the companies that make and sell the chips, the memory and the foundry capacity — and the buyer is one of the largest GPU consumers in the world, now capitalised at a trillion-dollar scale with compute named in its use of proceeds. A newly funded Anthropic is a multi-year buyer of exactly the capacity renters are competing for, which is the same direction as everything else in this week's record: Verda's twelfth rise today, Lambda's announced rises landing Nov 16, and CoreWeave reporting tonight with a backlog its last quarterly filing put at $103.7 billion. None of that makes any single rental cheaper.

NEWS →  ·  Prices · Verda

Verda raises prices for the twelfth time — the same four GPUs up about 1% again

Nov 10, 2026

Read on Verda's own GPU instances page today, Nov 10, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 9: the same four GPUs that rose yesterday rose again by about 1% — GB300, B300, H100 SXM and L40S. It is Verda's twelfth rise since Oct 23. The other five tracked GPUs held for a second straight day.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on verda.com/gpu-instances

What changed, read on verda.com/gpu-instances on Nov 10, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.58 → $13.72 [$13.720], B300 $11.81 → $11.93 [$11.930], H100 SXM $4.99 → $5.04 [$5.037] and L40S $1.96 → $1.98 [$1.978] — each about +1.0%, exactly the pattern of Nov 9. Held: B200 $9.14 [$9.138], H200 $6.44 [$6.440], A100 80GB $2.32 [$2.316], A100 40GB $1.66 [$1.657] and RTX PRO 6000 $2.73 [$2.725]. Verda's confidential-computing B300 rose the same ~1% ($12.05 → $12.17), which we do not list on the board. Across two days the four movers are up about 2.1% in all; Verda's GB300, this board's Best offer for that card, has gone from $11.82 an hour at our Oct 19 check to $13.72 today, up 16.1% in three weeks.

Everywhere else we checked today held: RunPod Secure (all 11 tracked offers), Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, SaladCloud and TensorDock were re-read on their own pages, and Hyperstack was checked by a first-hand read of its raw pricing page — all 13 of its on-demand rows unchanged. Lambda's page still prints only the rates it has announced for Nov 16 (about +15% on B200 and H100); its current rates sit behind a login, and nafnaf.ai again showed no GPUs available. Rising list prices are consistent with growing demand (our reading, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can produce the same shape).

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters the practical point is again narrow: Verda's GB300 is this board's Best offer for that card, so the cheapest verified GB300 in our index just rose to $13.72 an hour. The other three rises sit above their cards' Best offers and change no recommendation. Two identical selective rises in two days look less like a one-off adjustment and more like a daily step on those four cards — the next checks will show whether the step continues, and whether the held five ever join it.

PROVIDER COMPARISONS →  ·  2026-11-10 · 14 min read

Monetize idle GPUs, honestly: marketplace, colocation — or sell the card

Every guide to renting out your GPU starts at the signup button. This one starts at the arithmetic. What an idle card earns is decided by three numbers nobody can promise you — how many hours it rents, what the platform keeps, and what your power costs — so this page works all three openly, at rates verified on Nov 10, 2026, and then gives the option the funnel guides leave out: sometimes the best way to monetize an idle GPU is to sell it.

The verdict

  • One consumer card at home — List it on a host marketplace — and run the sell comparison below first. About $84–$146 a month after power at 40–70% utilisation, worked in full below. Selling the same card today brings roughly $2,400–$2,800 once — renting takes well over a year to match it.
  • A few gaming cards — Marketplace, all of them — colocation maths does not work at this size. The same per-card maths, times the cards: roughly $84–$146 per 4090-class card per month after power. Your real cost is babysitting uptime across several machines.
  • 8+ datacenter cards — Colocation, or a host programme — the facility contract comes first, the listing second. An 8× H100 node grosses $13,140 a month at the best verified node rate if rented every hour — and about $5,060 after power alone at 40%, before the fixed facility bill. The bill is owed whether the node rents or not.
  • An enterprise fleet — Contract / colocation at negotiated rates — you are running a small cloud, price it like one. No honest per-card net exists here: it is your negotiated facility cost against your booked utilisation. For scale, Spheron’s own cost model puts colocation plus networking at roughly $73 per GPU per month on a 1,024-GPU cluster (their figure, stated Oct 2026) — a small fleet pays more.
Compare prices→For providers→

The three routes, without the funnel

Every “net” figure here is worked step by step below — gross at three utilisation levels, minus power — where a platform takes a host-side cut, that depends on the model and is handled in the fee section. Nothing here is an earnings promise; utilisation is the renter’s decision, not yours. Route 1 — list on a marketplace that takes hosts. You install the platform’s software, pass its verification, set or accept a price, and renters find you. The platform handles the customer, the billing and the metering, and takes its side of the money — how much, and taken from whom, differs by platform and gets its own section below. Your costs are power, wear, and keeping the machine online. This is the only route that makes sense below a rack of hardware. Route 2 — colocation. You rent rack space, power, cooling and bandwidth in a data centre, put your machines in it, and list them yourself (or through a marketplace on top). The facility bill is fixed and monthly: it arrives at 100% whether your machines rent at 100% or at zero. Colocation buys the density and uptime a home connection cannot offer — an 8-GPU node wants kilowatts, not a wall socket — and only pays once the fleet is big enough that the fixed bill is a small slice of the gross. Route 3 — sell the hardware. No funnel will suggest this, because nobody earns a commission when you sell your own card. It belongs in the comparison anyway: a used RTX 4090 sells today for roughly what 16–34 months of realistic renting nets (worked below), and the card at the end of two years of renting is worth less than the card today. Renting wins when you want the card kept, or genuinely believe utilisation will run high for years. Selling wins more often than the hosting guides admit.

The marketplace maths: one RTX 4090

Worked at the cheapest verified renter price for a 4090 hour on our board — $0.34/hr (RunPod Community, checked Nov 10, 2026). That is what a renter actually pays for this card today, so it is the honest rate for a host listing to compete at. A month is 730 hours. Power is the card alone at its rated 450W TDP, at an assumed $0.12/kWh — home rates vary widely, and the rest of the PC draws more, so treat the power line as a floor.

One RTX 4090, listed at $0.34/hrRented every hour (100%)70% of hours40% of hours
Rented hours in a 730-hour month730511292
Gross$248.20$173.74$99.28
Power while rented (450W × hours × $0.12/kWh)−$39.42−$27.59−$15.77
Net before any host-side platform cut$208.78$146.15$83.51

Two honest footnotes. First, the platform’s cut: on nafnaf’s model the 5% fee is added on the renter’s side, so a host asking $0.34 receives $0.34 and the renter pays $0.357 — the table stands as written there. On a platform that deducts from the host’s side, take that percentage off the gross line before power; the section below says which models we could verify. Second, a PC left on around the clock draws idle power too — at an assumed 50–100W (labelled assumption), roughly $4–$9 a month, owed whether or not a job ever lands.

The same maths at node scale: 8× H100

Datacenter cards rent as nodes. The best verified 8-GPU H100 rate on our board is TensorDock’s $2.25 per GPU per hour at an 8-GPU minimum — $18.00 per node-hour (checked Nov 10, 2026). Power is the eight cards alone at the H100 SXM’s rated 700W TDP each — 5.6 kW, before CPUs, networking and cooling, so again a floor.

One 8× H100 node at $18.00/hr100%70%40%
Gross$13,140$9,198$5,256
Power while rented (5.6 kW × hours × $0.12/kWh)−$491−$343−$196
Net before facility bill and any platform cut$12,649$8,855$5,060

The node’s gross is just over fifty times the single 4090’s — and unlike the home card, the node has a landlord. The line missing from this table is the facility bill, and it is missing on purpose: there is no honest universal figure for it. It gets its own section, as a formula, below.

Compare prices→For providers→

What the platforms take — verified, and what is not published

PlatformWhat it takes — and what it does not publish
nafnaf5%, charged to the renter, not deducted from you. nafnaf’s own provider pages (read Nov 10, 2026) state a 5% consumer fee on your rate: “Ask $1.00, receive $1.00; the renter pays $1.05.” You set the rate for compute, storage and transfer; operating costs and taxes remain yours.
Vast.aiNo host-side hosting fee since June 2024; the renter-side surcharge is not published. Vast’s own 2024 round-up says it “eliminated hosting fees entirely” in June 2024 and moved to “a more flexible internal surcharge model” — the price a host sets is the price the host earns, and Vast’s margin sits inside the price the renter sees. What that surcharge is, Vast does not publish; third-party write-ups quote everything from the mid-teens to 25%, which tells you they are guessing. Treat any exact Vast percentage on a blog as unverified — including, if we ever printed one, ours.
SaladCloudYou are paid in Salad Balance, not cash. Salad’s own documentation (read Nov 10, 2026) says owners earn rewards in Salad Balance, redeemed through its storefront for PayPal, gift cards, games and subscriptions; the rate on a job is set by the priority the customer chose, and Salad’s own FAQ states many providers earn $100–$200 a month — Salad’s figure, not ours, and its terms guarantee no earnings. Balance is worth less than the same number in cash: you can only spend it where Salad lets you.
Everyone elseCheck the current split before you list. Host programmes revise their terms, and a percentage from last year’s blog post is how hosts get surprised. The split, the payout currency, the minimum payout and the payout schedule are four separate lines in every host agreement; read all four.

One structural point matters more than any percentage: whether the fee comes off your side or is added to the renter’s. A fee added on top (nafnaf’s model, and Vast’s since 2024) leaves your rate intact but makes your listing look pricier to a comparing renter. What decides your month is never the fee alone — it is the fee model multiplied by the utilisation that platform actually delivers to a card like yours.

Colocation: the fixed bill, as a formula

Colocation is priced per kilowatt or per rack per month, negotiated per facility, per region, per power contract — Spheron’s own colocation guide concedes the same point, in its words that a colocation quote “is closer to a real estate lease than a cloud price list.” So this guide will not quote you a colo price. It gives you the only number that matters, computable the moment a facility quotes you:

The break-even formula
Break-even utilisation = your fixed monthly facility bill ÷ (your hourly rate × 730)

That is the share of the month your machines must rent just to cover the facility, before power and before any platform cut. Worked example with a clearly illustrative bill: at a facility bill of $1,500 a month (illustrative — get quotes; your market will differ) and the node’s $18.00/hr, break-even is $1,500 ÷ $13,140 ≈ 11% of hours to cover the facility alone, and roughly 12% once the node’s power margin is counted. Double the bill to $3,000 and break-even doubles with it, to about 23%. The formula is the deliverable: a quote you cannot run through it is a quote you do not understand yet. Two anchors, both labelled. Spheron’s own cost model for a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster (their post, figures stated as of early Oct 2026) itemises colocation and networking at roughly $75,000 a month — about $73 per GPU per month — with power billed separately. That is a thousand-GPU buyer’s number; a single-rack tenant has none of that leverage and should expect a far higher per-GPU cost, which is why route 2 starts at “8+ datacenter cards” above and not at two. And density is the gate before price: Spheron states GPU colocation runs 10–15 kW per rack as the 2026 baseline against 3–5 kW for standard server colocation — so a standard enterprise colo contract may not be able to power your rack at any price.

The 70% question, tested

Hosting content routinely models 70% utilisation or better, because the numbers look good there. Nothing about a marketplace promises it: utilisation is set by how many renters want your exact card, in your location, at your price, against every other identical listing — for a consumer card, thousands of them. Look at the same 4090 across the range, from the table above: $208.78 a month rented every hour, $146.15 at 70%, $83.51 at 40%. The card did not change; the assumption did, and it moved the answer two and a half times. Any earnings figure quoted without its utilisation assumption printed next to it is marketing, not maths.

Renting one RTX 4090What it takes — or what it pays
Match $2,400 in one yearNet about $200 a month — the card would need to rent about 96% of all hours for a year straight, against a ceiling of $208.78 a month if it rents literally every hour.
Match $2,800 in one yearAbout $233 a month — no utilisation level gets there at all at the worked rates.
24 months at 70% utilisationAbout $3,500 net before any host-side cut, against $2,400–$2,800 today — while the rented card ends those two years older, more worn, and worth less.

Now the comparison the funnel leaves out — renting against selling. A used RTX 4090 sold for roughly $2,400–$2,800 in recent completed eBay sales (sold-listing trackers read Nov 10, 2026; condition and model move the figure, and trackers disagree with each other — the method works with whatever your card would actually fetch). At the worked rates above, matching even the low end within a year means netting about $200 a month, against a ceiling of $208.78 if the card rents literally every hour: the card would need to rent about 96% of all hours for a year straight. Against the top of the range ($2,800, or $233 a month), no utilisation level gets there at all. Over two years the picture flips, but only just, and only at sustained high utilisation: 24 months at 70% nets about $3,500 before any host-side cut, against $2,400–$2,800 today — while the rented card ends those two years older, more worn, and worth less, and the $0.34 rate has to survive a market that has repriced everything else. The honest summary: renting a single 4090 is a reasonable way to keep a card you want anyway and offset its cost. As a pure investment against selling, it needs years and luck.

The demand is real — and it still is not a promise

The renter side of this market is genuinely tight, and our own record shows it. Providers do not raise prices twelve times into weak demand:

ProviderWhat our Price Watch record shows
VerdaA mid-size provider on our board — has raised its prices twelve times since Oct 23, 2026; its GB300 rate is up ▲ 16.1% since Oct 19 ($11.82 → $13.72/hr, both read on Verda’s own pricing pages on those dates).
RunPod ServerlessIts B200 rate rose about 25% between our Oct 26 and Nov 2 reads.
LambdaHas announced rises of about 15% taking effect Nov 16, 2026.

Hold the counterweight in the same hand. A rising list price at a datacenter provider is evidence renters pay more for capacity in facilities — it is not evidence that your specific card, in your specific postcode, beside thousands of identical marketplace listings, rents one hour more. Datacenter demand concentrates on datacenter cards in datacenter buildings; the consumer-card end clears at $0.34 an hour precisely because supply there is deep. Both facts are in our record. Quote either one alone and you are selling something.

When not to bother

SituationWhy it does not pay
One old or low-memory cardThe maths scales with the hourly rate; a card renting for a few cents an hour cannot outrun its own power bill, let alone your time.
Expensive home electricityEvery figure here moves with your power price. At double the assumed $0.12/kWh, the 4090’s 40% month nets about $68 instead of $84 — run your own rate through the table before listing, not after.
You cannot keep the machine onlineMarketplaces verify hosts, rank on reliability, and delist or bury listings that drop offline or fail jobs. A gaming PC that sleeps, updates and reboots on its own schedule is not inventory; it is a future delisting.
You need the money soon, or certainlyRental income is variable and starts at zero; a sale is one amount, once, now. If the point is a known sum by a known date, route 3 is the only honest answer.
The payout is not moneyBalance, credits and tokens are worth what the platform lets you redeem them for, when it lets you. Price that in before counting the earnings.
Compare prices→For providers→

How we know

Rental rates are from GPUJournal’s verified price board, checked Nov 10, 2026 on providers’ own published pages and banked daily since Oct 19, 2026: RTX 4090 best verified offer RunPod Community $0.34/GPU/hr (RunPod Secure lists the same card at $0.89); 8× H100 node rate TensorDock $2.25/GPU/hr at an 8-GPU minimum, $18.00/node/hr. Platform terms were read on the platforms’ own pages on Nov 10, 2026: nafnaf’s provider pages state a 5% consumer fee added to the host’s rate (“Ask $1.00, receive $1.00; the renter pays $1.05”); Vast.ai’s 2024 round-up on vast.ai states hosting fees were eliminated in June 2024 in favour of an internal surcharge model whose percentage Vast does not publish — third-party percentages for Vast (mid-teens to 25% across the write-ups we found) conflict and are treated as unverified; Salad’s documentation states hosts earn Salad Balance redeemable via its storefront (PayPal, gift cards, games), that job rates depend on customer-set priority, and that many providers earn $100–$200/month (Salad’s own figure; its terms guarantee no earnings). Power figures are labelled planning assumptions: card draws are the manufacturers’ rated TDP (RTX 4090 450W, H100 SXM 700W), GPU only — whole-system draw is higher; electricity is an assumed $0.12/kWh; a month is 730 hours; idle draw of 50–100W is an assumption, not a measurement. The colocation worked example uses an explicitly illustrative facility bill of $1,500/month — no colocation price is quoted in this guide because none is published in a form we could verify; the $73/GPU/month colocation-and-networking figure and the 10–15 kW/rack density baseline are Spheron’s stated figures from its colocation post (stated as of early Oct 2026, read Nov 10, 2026), as are its supplier programme terms. Resale: two completed-eBay-sale trackers read Nov 10, 2026 (GetPCParts average ≈$2,387, sales through Nov 7, 2026; pcprice.watch median $2,780) — this guide uses the rounded range $2,400–$2,800, and the rent-vs-sell method works with any figure you substitute. Demand evidence is our own Price Watch record: Verda’s twelve rises, Oct 23 – Nov 10, 2026 (GB300 $11.82 read Oct 19 → $13.72 read Nov 10); RunPod Serverless B200 ($8.64 read Oct 26 → $10.79 read Nov 2); Lambda’s announced rises of Nov 6, 2026, effective Nov 16 — announced, not yet in effect, and not applied to our board.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Everything in this box is GPUJournal’s judgement on the verified record above it; the record itself is in the tables and the method note. We sell nothing, list nothing and take no commission from any route on this page — which is more than the author of the guide this one answers can say. Spheron’s posts on this question (read Nov 10, 2026) walk a rack owner through GPU colocation and land where you would expect: colocate the facility, then let a demand marketplace — theirs — fill it. For a datacenter fleet that framing is mostly fair, and their supplier programme’s stated terms (you set prices, you sign your own contracts, they handle billing and settle monthly) are reasonable ones to compare against. But the funnel starts at rack owners because that is who it can sell to. It does not run a home card’s net after power, does not test the utilisation its route implies for a card like yours, its programme covers H100-class datacenter SKUs only, and “sell” does not appear as a route. Start from your situation instead: one card — marketplace, with the sell comparison run first; a rack or more — get colo quotes, run the break-even formula on each, and only then argue about which marketplace’s demand is worth its cut.

MiniMax open-sources H3-Image: a 16-megapixel image model that serves on one GPU

Nov 10, 2026

MiniMax published the weights of H3-Image on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image generation and editing model that produces roughly 16-megapixel images — up to 4096×4096 — directly, with no upscaler, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU through vLLM-Omni or SGLang. It is released under MiniMax's own community licence, not a permissive one, and the full download is bigger than the headline checkpoint suggests.

Image: MiniMax via huggingface.co

What shipped, from MiniMax's blog (Nov 10, 2026) and the official Hugging Face card (MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image), both read first-hand: one checkpoint unifies text-to-image and image editing, accepts up to 16 reference images, and is distilled to six sampling steps with no classifier-free guidance. MiniMax claims 4K images in under 10 seconds — the maker's own figure, not measured by us — and says 4K-and-above API requests are 50% off for launch week. An optional prompt-expander model, MiniMax-H3-Image-PE (17.9 GB, NVFP4), shipped quietly alongside it.

The hardware maths, from the same card: the image checkpoint itself is 68.65 GB (66.28 GB transformer + 2.34 GB VAE), but its text encoder is NOT in the repository — it loads from the separate MiniMax-H3 release and adds 66.7 GB, so budget about 135 GB of downloads and memory for the full BF16 stack. The card lists NVIDIA H200, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and AMD Instinct MI350X as supported, gives a one-GPU start command for both vLLM-Omni and SGLang, and the serving recipes carry per-hardware configurations — on a 96 GB card the full BF16 stack plainly does not fit at once, so check the recipe for your card before renting. The licence is the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License Agreement, with a separate written-authorisation route described in the licence itself: read it before planning a commercial service.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For image workloads this changes the rental question. A flagship-class open image model that generates 16 megapixels natively and serves on one GPU means the default rental is a single high-memory card, not a node — and AMD's MI350X is a named day-one target alongside NVIDIA, which is still rare for a launch this size. The honest watch-outs are the two in the facts above: the real footprint is about twice the headline checkpoint once the text encoder is counted, and the community licence is MiniMax's own terms, not MIT or Apache. Teams that clear both can price this against per-image API bills from a single card's hourly rate on our board.

NEWS →  ·  Results · CoreWeave

CoreWeave Q3: revenue up 168% to $3.66 billion, a $132.5 billion backlog — and guidance raised again

Nov 10, 2026

CoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 results after the close on Nov 10, 2026: revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168% on a year earlier and more than $1 billion added in a single quarter, a revenue backlog of about $132.5 billion, and full-year guidance raised on every line. The cost of building that fast is in the same release: a $709 million net loss, with $846 million of net interest expense in the quarter alone.

Image: CoreWeave via coreweave.com

The reported numbers, from CoreWeave's own results release (Nov 10, 2026, quarter ended Sep 30, 2026), read first-hand: revenue $3,661 million against $1,365 million a year earlier; operating income $207 million (6% margin); adjusted operating income $379 million (10% margin), which the company says reached double digits a quarter ahead of plan; net loss $709 million, or $1.27 a share, against $110 million a year earlier, with net interest expense of $846 million against $310 million. Backlog — committed contracts not yet recognised as revenue, subject to delivery and availability requirements, in the release's own definition — was about $132.5 billion at Sep 30, up from about $104 billion at Jun 30 per the company's second-quarter reporting.

The build-out and the outlook, from the same release: CoreWeave added more than 200 MW of active power in the quarter to pass 1.7 GW, double its live footprint since the start of the year, and grew contracted power by more than 900 MW to over 4.6 GW. It says multi-rack NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 deployments are online, with first production workloads for Cognition at 4.8 times the token throughput of GB200 NVL72 (CoreWeave's own figure). Full-year 2026 guidance is raised: revenue to $13.0–$13.3 billion, adjusted operating income to $1.275–$1.375 billion, capital expenditure to $37–$39 billion, exit run-rate revenue to $20–$21 billion, with more than 1.85 GW of active power expected at year-end and fourth-quarter interest expense guided at $1.05–$1.15 billion. The chief executive says about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits is expected in the next three months alone.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For anyone renting GPUs, this is the demand side of the price board reporting itself. The largest listed neocloud grew revenue 168%, carries $132.5 billion of contracted backlog and is still raising guidance and capex — while paying $846 million a quarter in interest to do it. That combination is exactly the backdrop to the pattern our Price Watch has tracked all autumn: providers raising list prices in small, repeated steps because contracted demand keeps absorbing capacity. It does not make any single provider's hourly rate fair or unfair — our board still judges that card by card — but it explains why the rises keep coming, and why CoreWeave's own capacity is sold against contracts first and a public price list second. Next demand tests: Nebius reports Nov 12, Lambda's announced rises take effect Nov 16, and NVIDIA reports Nov 17.

AMD's 256-core EPYC ‘Venice’ is shipping — the host CPU built to feed GPU racks

Nov 11, 2026

AMD announced general availability of its 6th Gen EPYC server processors (‘Venice’, Zen 6, SP7) on Nov 10, 2026: systems are shipping from the leading server makers now, Meta is the named lead customer, and cloud instances follow at Microsoft Azure (HDv2 in preview) and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (Compute E7). The flagship EPYC 9996 carries 256 cores and 512 threads at a $14,904 list price.

Image: AMD via newsroom.amd.com

The launch, from AMD's own newsroom release dated Nov 10, 2026: 6th Gen EPYC SP7 platforms are shipping from leading OEMs and ODMs; the portfolio is workload-split across general-purpose, high-frequency host-node and high-density parts. The high-frequency host-node chips boost to 5.3 GHz, and AMD claims (vendor figures, from its release footnotes) up to 1.8× the LLM output throughput of the previous EPYC generation for host-node parts and up to 3.7× the SPECrate2017 performance of an NVIDIA Vera CPU-based system for the 9996. The same release folds in AMD's Helion agentic-AI rack blueprint (up to 73,728 threads per rack) and names Azure's forthcoming ND MI455X v7 — built on AMD's Helios rackscale design — for production AI inference.

Why a CPU launch belongs on a GPU desk: every GPU node a renter pays for is paired with host CPUs that feed the accelerators, run the agent sandboxes and orchestration around the models, and increasingly carry whole agent workloads themselves. Venice is the x86 host platform the next wave of GPU racks — AMD Instinct and multi-vendor alike — will ship with into 2027, and Azure HDv2 and OCI E7 are the first cloud doors renters will meet it through. It is also AMD's direct counter to NVIDIA's Vera CPU, whose first full independent reviews landed the same week.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters the practical read is about the whole node, not the card alone: when Venice-based instances reach Azure and OCI, the CPU side of those GPU-adjacent instances gets faster host feeding and far denser agent capacity per rack — worth checking in the spec sheet before comparing two otherwise identical GPU offers. No rental price changes follow from this launch today; it is the platform the 2027 capacity will stand on.

Runway open-sources Praxis-1: a 27B robot model that runs on one H100, under Apache 2.0

Nov 11, 2026

Runway released the weights of Praxis-1 on Nov 11, 2026: a 27-billion-parameter world action model that predicts video and robot actions together, tops NVIDIA's RoboLab-120 leaderboard on Runway's own figures, and is released — weights, inference code and fine-tuning code — under Apache 2.0, including for commercial use. It runs out of the box on a single H100.

Image: Runway via runway.com

What shipped, from Runway's own announcement (Nov 11, 2026), read first-hand: Praxis-1 is a 27B-parameter mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer, first introduced in September as Runway's first world action model, now open to every developer. Runway reports 46.2% success across 1,200 episodes on NVIDIA's RoboLab-120 benchmark, ahead of FLUX 3 Action at 42.9%, Cosmos3 Nano at 36.8% and π0.5 at 28.0% — Runway's figures, data as of November 2026, not measured by us. The release is on GitHub, on Hugging Face with native LeRobot support, and in vLLM-Omni, with hosted inference on Reactor; launch partners Noble Machines, Standard Bots and Ultra have been running it on their own hardware, and fine-tuned on Google's RT-1 robot — which never appeared in its training data — it reaches 80.0% on SimplerEnv against the original RT-1 policy's 52.4% (Runway's figure).

The hardware maths, from Runway's research page: 27.2 billion parameters in total, 54.4 GB in BF16 — so the full model fits one 80 GB GPU — and packing the routed experts in NVFP4 shrinks the policy weights to 17.5 GB. Runway lists H100 and B200 data-centre GPUs, RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 workstation cards, and Jetson Thor on the robot itself as running it out of the box. Three checkpoints are in the Hugging Face collection: the base model and DROID and bimanual YAM fine-tunes.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Most open-weight drops on this desk are language or image models; Praxis-1 is a frontier-class robot brain that a single rented H100 can run and fine-tune, under the most permissive licence there is — the exact opposite of this week's territorial community licences. For GPU renters it is a new, concrete workload to price: one 80 GB card for the BF16 model, a workstation card for the NVFP4 build, and LoRA fine-tuning without retraining the full model. Physical-AI teams no longer need a cluster, or a closed API, to work with the current RoboLab-120 leader.

Jensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA CEO — CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim chief

Nov 12, 2026

NVIDIA announced on Nov 12, 2026 that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer and Board member, effective immediately, ending 33 years leading the company he co-founded. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's Chief Financial Officer since 2013, serves as Interim CEO while keeping the CFO role; Harvey C. Jones becomes the company's first-ever Chair of the Board. NVIDIA's release gives no reason for the resignation.

Image: NVIDIA via nvidianews.nvidia.com

The announcement is NVIDIA's own, published via GlobeNewswire at 13:48 UTC on Nov 12, 2026, following press reports on Nov 11 that the Board was weighing Huang's future — reports this desk held as unverified until NVIDIA itself spoke. From the release: the Board is searching for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates; Kress joined NVIDIA in September 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft; Jones, Chair of the Board, is a former Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys. Jones, in the release: the Board expects “the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” Kress: “I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.” NVIDIA's third-quarter fiscal 2027 results stay on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, with the earnings call at 2 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled. Reuters reported NVIDIA shares fell more than 10% in premarket trading.

Why this belongs on a GPU desk: NVIDIA supplies effectively every card on this board, and its roadmap — Blackwell today, Vera Rubin next — sets the capacity and pricing weather for every provider a renter buys from. A leadership change at the top of that supplier, five days before earnings, is the single largest company event in the GPU market this year.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and buyers, the dated facts today are narrow and worth stating plainly: no product, pricing or roadmap change has been announced, and continuity of operations, customer commitments and the roadmap is NVIDIA's stated position in its own release. The first real test is the Nov 17 earnings call, now led by Interim CEO Kress. Anything beyond the release — including reporting about the circumstances around the resignation — is not something NVIDIA has confirmed, and this desk is not presenting it as fact.

Nebius reported third-quarter results before the open on Nov 12, 2026: revenue of $980.8m, up 571% year on year and ahead of the roughly $907.5m consensus, with adjusted EBITDA of $465.8m. The tracked neocloud also raised 2026 capex to about $27bn and gave its first 2027 outlook — revenue of $12–13bn on capex of $40–45bn.

Image: Nebius via nebius.com

From Nebius's own release (BusinessWire, Nov 12, 2026): AI Cloud revenue was $973.8m, up 643%; adjusted net income was +$90.9m against a GAAP net loss from continuing operations of $37.5m. Annualised recurring revenue reached $6.4bn at the end of September, and the $7bn ARR milestone now lands in February rather than December. Full-year 2026 revenue is guided to the low end of the $3.0–3.4bn range, 2026 capex rises to about $27bn (from $20–25bn), cash stood at $7.4bn, and the company signed more than $12bn of new contract value since the quarter began. Shares fell roughly 10–15% in premarket trading on the guidance and capex mix, despite the revenue beat.

Nebius is a priced provider on this board, and its numbers are the demand story in financial form: a neocloud spending $40–45bn on capacity in 2027 is building for contracted demand, not speculation — the same pattern as CoreWeave's $132.5bn backlog reported on Nov 10. The other side of the coin for renters: revenue recognition slipping a quarter (December into February) says new capacity is landing slightly later than planned, which is one more reason near-term GPU supply stays tight.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters the read is capacity, not the share price: Nebius is quadrupling down on build-out, which points to more Nebius inventory through 2027, while the slipped ARR milestone is a small, dated signal that supply arrives a little slower than promised. No Nebius board prices changed today — its rates were re-read unchanged in today's check.

H100 or B200 sold out? What to rent instead — priced

A stock alert tells you the card you wanted is gone. It does not tell you what to rent instead, or what the substitute costs. This page does: every substitute below is a real offer on our verified price board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — the card, the provider, the rate, and the terms that change the bill. One honesty note before the table: we are not reporting any provider as sold out today — our checks found prices, not stock levels. This guide is for the moment you go to book an H100 SXM or a B200 and find it gone.

The verdict

  • H100 SXM — one card — H200 at RunPod Community — same Hopper generation, 141GB of memory instead of 80GB, rented by the single card. On-demand, no minimum.
  • H100 SXM — an 8-GPU training job — The H100 SXM itself, at TensorDock — “gone” is usually one provider's shelf, not the market's; this is the cheapest verified H100 SXM rate on our board. On-demand, 8-GPU minimum — $18.00/hr for the node.
  • H100 SXM — single card, budget first — H100 PCIe at RunPod Community — same chip family, same 80GB; no NVLink and lower power, so a single-card substitute, not a training-node one. On-demand, no minimum.
  • B200 — B300 at Hyperstack — Blackwell Ultra, a step up not down: 288GB instead of 192GB. On-demand (RunPod Secure lists the same card at $8.99). · $5.98/hr at RunPod Community
  • B200 — budget first — H200 at RunPod Community — a generation down, 141GB instead of 192GB, and 40% below the cheapest B200 on the board. On-demand, no minimum.
  • Either card — and your work fits in 80GB without FP8 — A100 80GB at Thunder Compute — the previous generation, the honest workhorse; no FP8, so the newest serving speed-ups do not apply. On-demand, no minimum.
  • B200 — you actually need more card, not less — GB300 at Verda — rack-scale Blackwell Ultra, listed per GPU-hour on Verda's own page. On-demand.

First move: check the same card somewhere else

Every rate in the verdict above is the lowest verified on-demand price for that card on our board on Nov 12, 2026 — one best offer per card, the same rule the board itself uses. Terms that change the bill (minimums, whole-node rental, VAT) are printed with the price wherever they apply. “Sold out” is almost always a sentence about one provider's shelf. The H100 SXM is listed by eight providers on our board, and the spread between them is wider than the gap between most substitutes: on Nov 12, 2026 the same card, on-demand, runs from $2.25 to $5.14 a GPU-hour before you reach the hyperscalers — TensorDock $2.25 (8-GPU minimum), RunPod Community $2.69, Thunder Compute and Hyperstack $3.20 each, RunPod Secure and Lambda $3.99 each, Verda $5.14. Microsoft Azure lists it at $12.29 per GPU — but that is an 8-GPU VM at $98.32 an hour, a whole machine, not a card you can rent one of (see “What not to do”). Before you substitute anything, price the card itself across the board — the substitute decision only starts when the card is gone everywhere you would actually rent it. The B200 tells the same story. Nine verified offers, Nov 12, 2026: RunPod Community $5.98, Hyperstack $6.00, Lambda $6.69, RunPod Secure $7.99, Nebius $8.50 (excluding VAT), CoreWeave $8.60 (an 8-GPU node — $68.80 an hour for the node), Verda $9.32, then the whole-node hyperscalers, Oracle OCI $14.00 and Google Cloud $18.53, both per-GPU figures divided out of 8-GPU machines. One warning with a date on it: Lambda has announced its B200 rises to $7.69 on Nov 16, 2026 (Lambda's own announcement of Nov 6) — if your fallback plan is “Lambda when RunPod is full,” it gets 15% more expensive on Monday.

Why these two cards go first

The H100 SXM and the B200 sit where the demand is: the H100 is the default training and serving card of the last three years, and the B200 is what the biggest jobs moved to. Our own record — every move read on providers' own pages and banked daily — shows what that demand does to prices:

Rising prices are consistent with growing demand — that is our reading of the pattern, labelled as interpretation; capacity and cost moves can push the same way. Either way, the practical fact is the same: the two most-wanted cards are the two whose shelves empty first — and whose prices move against you while you wait. A substitute plan made in advance, at checked prices, beats a scramble.

The substitutes, ranked by closeness

Same class, one step up — H200 for H100, B300 for B200. The H200 is the H100's own generation with 141GB of faster memory: anything an H100 SXM runs, an H200 runs, with headroom. Its best verified rate is RunPod Community's $3.59/GPU/hr (Nov 12, 2026) — $0.90 an hour above the cheapest single-card H100 SXM, and cheaper than four of the eight H100 SXM offers on the board. For the B200, the B300 is the same Blackwell family one step up, with 288GB: Hyperstack $7.40, RunPod Secure $8.99, Nebius $9.50 excluding VAT (all Nov 12, 2026). Stepping up costs more per hour and can cost less per job — a bigger card finishes sooner — but we publish prices, not benchmarks, so we make that claim no further than this sentence.

The same chip in a different shape — H100 PCIe and H100 NVL. The H100 PCIe is the same silicon at a lower power limit, without NVLink: for one card doing serving or fine-tuning, the difference barely shows; for cards that must work together, it is the whole ballgame. RunPod Community $1.99, Hyperstack $2.50, RunPod Secure $2.89 (Nov 12, 2026). The H100 NVL carries 94GB — the card for a model that nearly fits on 80GB — at RunPod Community $2.59 and RunPod Secure $3.19, but it is sold as linked pairs, not as a lone card, so budget for two. One step down — A100 80GB. The honest workhorse: same 80GB as the H100, an older generation, no FP8. If your stack predates FP8 or your work is 32B–70B models in INT8/INT4, it does the job at about 40% of the H100's cheapest single-card rate: Thunder Compute $1.09, RunPod Community $1.19 (PCIe) and $1.39 (SXM), TensorDock $1.50 (Nov 12, 2026). Below it, the A100 40GB (Verda $1.69, Lambda $1.99) covers smaller models and learning workloads — but 40GB fills up fast, and a substitute that runs out of memory is not a substitute. One step sideways — two smaller cards, or a different 96GB. For work that splits — batch jobs, parallel experiments, one model replica per card — two cards can beat one big one on price: two A100 80GB at Thunder Compute cost $2.18 an hour together, less than one single-card H100 SXM at RunPod Community ($2.69), and put 160GB of memory on the table across two cards. What two cards cannot do is pool that memory into one fast whole without NVLink; a single model that needs 100GB in one place still needs one big card. For exactly that job there is a sideways option this board keeps flagging: the RTX PRO 6000, 96GB on a single card at RunPod Community $1.69/GPU/hr (Nov 12, 2026) — our board's most VRAM per dollar, and enough for a 70B model on one card, quantized or in FP8. And one specialist: CoreWeave's GH200 ($6.50, 1-GPU instance, 96GB) pairs its GPU with an ARM processor on one fabric — powerful for work built for it, and a software-change risk for work that was not.

What not to do

The trapWhy it costs you
Do not compare a per-GPU rate with a whole-machine rate.Azure's H100 SXM at “$12.29/GPU/hr” is an 8-GPU VM at $98.32 an hour — you cannot rent one GPU at that rate, and the same applies to the per-GPU figures divided out of CoreWeave, Oracle OCI and Google Cloud nodes throughout this guide. We print the node total beside every such figure; any page that prints the division without the total is making the card look like something it is not.
Do not let an attachable-GPU rate stand alone.Google Cloud's A100 80GB rate ($4.52/GPU/hr) bills the host VM the GPU attaches to on top. The rate is real; the bill is bigger.
Do not treat a spot price as a substitute for an on-demand price.Spot and preemptible capacity is a different product — cheaper because it can be taken back mid-job. Every price in this guide is on-demand, because that is what a renter replacing a sold-out card is actually buying. A spot figure quoted beside an on-demand rate, with the difference unlabelled, is not a comparison.
Do not rent from a price nobody will stand behind.On Nov 12, 2026, Spheron's own pages stated the H100 SXM5 at $2.75, $3.96 and $4.19 in three places on the same day — and its machine-readable price file said $3.96 while its own pricing FAQ said $5.15. Spheron sells GPU rental itself, which is exactly why its stated prices for everyone else's cards need checking against the provider's own page before they are worth acting on. A stock alert that ends in an unverifiable price has told you a card is gone and left you nowhere priced to go.
Do not skip the small print that is not small.Minimums (TensorDock's H100 rate needs 8 GPUs), VAT (Nebius's rates exclude it), and “from” prices that vary by instance size all change the real bill more than most headline differences do.

The worked comparison: 100 hours — one GPU

Assumptions, stated plainly: 100 hours of GPU time, on-demand, card for card, at the Nov 12, 2026 rates above. Hours are not jobs — a faster card may finish your job in fewer hours, and we hold no verified timings, so we price the hours and leave the speed judgement to you. Storage and downloads are excluded; they vary by provider and are not part of the card rate. What the table prices is the decision a sold-out message forces: pay more per hour for a closer card, or less for a further one.

Against that, price the wait honestly — an idle team, a missed deadline, a training run that starts next week instead of tonight. We put no figure on your deadline, because only you know it; but when the premium for the closest substitute is $0.90 an hour, “wait for the card I wanted” is usually the most expensive option on the page.

How we know

Every price in this guide is from GPUJournal's verified price board, checked Nov 12, 2026 on providers' own published pages and banked the same day (86 priced offers across 13 providers and 20 GPU variants): best verified on-demand offers — H100 SXM: TensorDock $2.25/GPU/hr at an 8-GPU minimum ($18.00/hr for 8 GPUs), RunPod Community $2.69; H200: RunPod Community $3.59; H100 PCIe: RunPod Community $1.99; H100 NVL: RunPod Community $2.59, sold as linked pairs; B200: RunPod Community $5.98; B300: Hyperstack $7.40; GB300: Verda $14.00; A100 80GB: Thunder Compute $1.09; RTX PRO 6000: RunPod Community $1.69; GH200: CoreWeave $6.50 (1-GPU instance). Node and VM figures are printed with their totals wherever a per-GPU figure is a division (CoreWeave 8-GPU nodes, Oracle OCI nodes, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud VMs). Nebius rates exclude VAT, as Nebius states. Verda's figures were read on verda.com on Nov 11 and Nov 12, 2026 (both sides of the Nov 12 rise); the fourteen-rise run and the GB300's $11.82 → $14.00 move since Oct 19 are our Price Watch record, kept daily since Oct 19, 2026. Lambda's B200 rise to $7.69 effective Nov 16, 2026 is Lambda's own announcement of Nov 6, 2026 — announced, not yet in effect; the board carries the current $6.69. Two honesty notes: RunPod Community's figures were corroborated in part on Nov 12 (5 of 11 via RunPod's own pricing page) with the remainder carried from the last full read, and the Spheron figures in “What not to do” are Spheron's own stated prices, read on its pages Nov 12, 2026 — reported as stated, never as verified prices, which is the point of the example. This guide reports no provider as sold out on Nov 12, 2026, because no record we checked says that; it is a plan for when you find one gone. Live board: Compare prices. Every verified change, dated both sides: Price Watch.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Everything in this box is GPUJournal's judgement on the verified record above it; the record itself is in the tables and the method note. We sell nothing and take no commission from any provider named here. Sold out is a routing problem, not a stopping problem. The renter who gets hurt is the one whose plan has a single card at a single provider in it: they pay the scramble price, or they wait. The fix costs nothing — know, before you need it, which card you would take instead and what it costs today. The honest shape of that plan, from the checked record: same card at a second provider first; one step up (H200, B300) when the job is deadline-shaped; one step down (PCIe, A100) when it is budget-shaped; and never a substitute chosen from a price that exists on only one aggregator's page. Prices will move — that is what our board and Price Watch are for — but the plan survives it, because it is a ranking, not a price list.

Deploy Praxis-1 on one H100

Runway's Praxis-1 is a 27B robot policy that genuinely runs on one rented GPU — but “deploy” is three different jobs: serve a ready-made policy, adapt one to your task with LoRA, or fine-tune the base checkpoint for your own rig. Each prices differently, and one of them is not a one-card job at all. This guide prices all three from our verified board, checked Nov 12, 2026 — starting from the fact most coverage skips: the base checkpoint cannot drive a robot until you fine-tune it.

The verdict

  • Run a ready policy on an H100 (DROID or YAM rig, BF16) — H100 PCIe at RunPod Community, no minimum listed — the cheapest one-card H100 route on the board. Runway's stated bar is one 80GB GPU; this is one. Catch: Runway's own measured runs are on SXM H100s — the fit is by the maker's stated requirement, not a benchmark we can cite.
  • The same, on the SXM card — H100 SXM at RunPod Community, no minimum listed. Catch: TensorDock's $2.25 wears the lower number but bills an 8-GPU minimum — $18.00/hr before you have run anything.
  • Cheapest card of any kind for the BF16 model — RTX PRO 6000 at RunPod Community (Blackwell) — a card Runway lists as running Praxis-1 out of the box. Catch: a workstation card, not a datacenter Hopper — you trade datacenter manners for 96GB at a lower rate.
  • The NVFP4 route (17.5GB in memory) — RTX 5090 at RunPod Community — the cheapest way to run a Praxis-1 policy at all. Catch: experimental and Blackwell-only (SM120: RTX 5090, RTX PRO 6000) — not on an H100, not on an L40S. Only the ready policies have NVFP4 checkpoints, and you still download the full 54.4GB.
  • Room to spare — H200 at RunPod Community. Catch: more than inference needs; it earns the premium for heavy evaluation batches and zero memory suspense.
  • Fine-tune for a new rig — Not a one-card job: Runway's recipe is one node of 8 × 80GB GPUs, ~15 hours measured — priced as a node in the tables below. Catch: the one-card fine-tune is LoRA, and it only adapts the DROID checkpoint, on the DROID rig. A different arm means the node.
Compare prices→Praxis-1 in the model catalogue→

What Praxis-1 is — and what it is not

Praxis-1 is a world action model for robots: a 27.2-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer that takes two camera feeds and a task string (“Put the red block in the bowl”) and predicts, together, the next chunk of video and the next chunk of robot motion — 24 commands at a time, at 15 Hz control. It is not a chatbot and not an image model; if your work doesn't end at a robot arm, this is the wrong download. What Runway released on Nov 11, 2026 — weights, inference code and fine-tuning code, all Apache 2.0, commercial use included — is a small family, and picking the right member is the first deployment decision. praxis-1-droid is the finished single-arm policy for the DROID rig (a Franka arm, exterior + wrist cameras); it is the checkpoint that tops RoboLab-120 on Runway's figures (46.2% success across 1,200 episodes — the maker's numbers, not measured by us), and it runs as a policy as downloaded. praxis-1-yam is the finished bimanual policy, for two YAM arms with three cameras. praxis-1-so101 is a fine-tune for the low-cost SO-101 LeRobot arm, added to the collection on Nov 12. praxis-1-base is the pretrained checkpoint the others were made from, trained on robot and human video across 18 embodiments: it has no action heads for any rig, so — in its own model card's words — “it does not run as a policy as is.” It exists to be fine-tuned; renting a GPU to “serve the base” buys a 54.4GB download and nothing that moves. Each policy also ships in a LeRobot layout (praxis-1-droid-lerobot and siblings) and, for the ready policies, in an NVFP4 build. Two frozen dependencies ride along, not included in the Praxis repos: the Wan2.2 VAE and the Qwen3.5-2B text encoder, each a separate download under its own licence — Apache 2.0 covers Praxis-1 itself, not them.

The H100 decision for this model is a terms decision, not a price decision: the two lowest SXM numbers split into a node commitment (TensorDock) and a true single card (RunPod Community). The fit maths: BF16 vs NVFP4

The arithmetic is the maker's own. 27.2B parameters at 2 bytes in BF16 is 54.4 GB of weights — the exact figure on the model card, in 17 safetensors shards. Runway's quick start states the requirement plainly: one CUDA GPU with at least 80 GB of memory, Python 3.12, the CUDA 13.0 driver; the LeRobot card repeats it (“Inference needs one 80 GB GPU”). On an 80GB card the weights leave 25.6GB for the VAE, the text encoder and the runtime — and the maker's measurements say the stack stays inside it: Runway's LoRA training run, which holds the whole frozen checkpoint plus adapters and optimizer state, peaks at 65 GiB on one 80GB card. Inference is the lighter job. The NVFP4 build is narrower than the headline suggests. Runway fine-tuned the ready policies with quantization-aware training on the routed MoE experts only; everything else stays BF16. You still download the full 54.4GB — the experts are packed to NVFP4 at load time, and in memory the policy shrinks from 54.4 GB to 17.5 GB (the maker's figure). Two hard limits: the path is labelled experimental, and it runs only on SM120 Blackwell cards — the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000. Not on Hopper (H100/H200), not on Ada (L40S). Which makes the board's cheapest 48GB card a dead end twice over: an L40S (RunPod Community $0.79/hr) can't hold 54.4GB in 48GB, and its architecture has no NVFP4 path in Runway's code. The same honesty applies to the A100 80GB (from $1.09/hr): the memory fits, but Runway doesn't list the A100 among the cards that run Praxis-1 out of the box, so this guide doesn't price it as a route.

Steps

1. The reference code (runwayml/praxis-1-oss)

Three documented ways in share one front door: Python 3.12, the CUDA 13.0 driver, one GPU with at least 80GB for anything BF16, and a Hugging Face login. Clone, install, download the checkpoint plus the two frozen dependencies, and serve with the shipped configs — configs/serve_droid.yaml for the single-arm policy, serve_yam.yaml for the bimanual. The same repo runs a built-in MuJoCo simulation: the sensible first hour is three episodes of block_in_bowl in the sim, before any real arm is involved. The install builds at least one component from source — Runway's own fresh-clone run on an H100 took 17 minutes end to end (13 of it installing, most of that compiling causal-conv1d; 3 downloading weights; 1.5 to load and run — the maker's figures, on their setup).

2. The LeRobot route

If your stack is already LeRobot, the -lerobot checkpoints drop in as a native policy: pip install “lerobot[praxis]”, then lerobot-eval --policy.path=runwayml/praxis-1-droid-lerobot --policy.device=cuda, or PraxisPolicy.from_pretrained(...) in code. Same weights, byte for byte; the repo adds the LeRobot config and the pre/post-processors.

3. Hosted and other engines

Runway's announcement also places Praxis-1 in vLLM-Omni and offers hosted inference on its Reactor platform — the zero-rental comparison point: if you only need to evaluate the policy briefly, weigh rented hours against simply calling the hosted version first. Reactor's pricing is not published in a form we could verify, so it is named here without a rate.

4. LoRA — the one-card fine-tune

If your robot is the DROID rig and the task is new, Runway documents a complete recipe (configs/finetune_droid_lora.yaml): the DROID checkpoint stays frozen while low-rank adapters train on the action expert — at the documented rank 16, 80 layers carrying 5.5M adapter weights in total. It runs on one 80GB GPU at a measured 65 GiB peak, and the maker's worked example — 1,200 steps of 16 windows, taught from 3,000 recorded demonstrations — takes about 5 hours on one H100. Recording those demonstrations in simulation takes another 1–2 hours of GPU time, and every save is a full 54GB checkpoint: save every 200–400 steps and rent the disk to match (six saves ≈ 324GB). The maker's results, stated plainly: about +10 success points on three of four test tasks; the fourth, the hardest, unmoved. And LoRA cannot help a different rig — it keeps the DROID heads and normalization, so other cameras or arms need the full recipe.

5. Full fine-tune — the node job

A new rig starts from praxis-1-base: compute your rig's normalization statistics (scripts/compute_norm_stats.py), grow the missing action heads (scripts/init_heads.py — allow about 55GB of ordinary CPU memory for this step), pass the documented overfit check, then train all weights (configs/finetune_base.yaml). Your data is a LeRobot v2.x tree in the DROID layout at 15 fps; the config defaults to the public DROID dataset, so the recipe runs as written. Runway's recipe table prices the hardware honestly — one node of 8 × 80GB GPUs — and its own worked run on 8 H100s (5,000 steps, 53.3 GiB per GPU) took 15.7 hours. Set expectations by the maker's scoreboard: that run produced a working policy (19.0% on their hard simulation suite) that does not match the shipped DROID checkpoint (56.5%) — one node-day buys a working policy for your rig, not a replica of theirs.

Alternatives

What a call costs in time — the maker's measurements only

On one H100 80GB at the default serving settings, Runway measured a median 501 ms per policy call for calls after the first (344 ms with video guidance at 1.0), each call returning 24 commands — 1.6 seconds of robot motion — so a call takes about a third of the time it commands. The first call of a process took 35 seconds (kernel compilation; warm-up is real). The inputs were synthetic camera frames, which Runway notes can differ from real ones. We have not benchmarked this model, and no one else's numbers were available to check.

Watch out — the base checkpoint is not a policy

No action heads, no normalization — it cannot run a robot until the full fine-tune. If a rig-ready checkpoint matches your hardware (DROID, YAM, SO-101), start there.

Watch out — the $2.25 headline is an 8-card bill

TensorDock's board-leading H100 SXM rate carries an 8-GPU minimum: $18.00/hr from the first minute. For one-card work the real floor is the PCIe card at $1.99.

Watch out — NVFP4 is Blackwell-only and experimental

SM120 cards only; the experts pack at load time, so the 54.4GB download happens either way; and there is no NVFP4 base — a new-rig fine-tune is a BF16 job.

Watch out — check the driver before you pay for hours

The documented stack wants the CUDA 13.0 driver and Python 3.12, and builds a kernel from source at install. An older provider image turns your first rented hour into systems administration.

Watch out — LoRA saves eat disk

Every save is a full ~54GB checkpoint; six saves ≈ 324GB before your dataset. Size the volume when you rent, not at step 1,000.

Watch out — judge fine-tunes closed-loop, not by loss

Runway's own warning, both recipes: training loss flattens while simulation scores still move by points between saves. Budget evaluation time — in the sim or on the arm — into every fine-tune.

Watch out — the dependencies have their own licences

The Wan2.2 VAE and Qwen3.5-2B text encoder are separate downloads under their own terms; Apache 2.0 covers Praxis-1, not them.

Watch out — Community tier means independent hosts

RunPod Community — where most of this guide's cheapest rates live — runs on independent hosts, not RunPod's vetted datacentres (that is RunPod Secure, at higher rates). A specific card's availability varies by the hour; if it's gone when you look, Secure is the same model on the other shelf.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Everything in this box is GPUJournal's judgement on the verified record above it; the record itself is in the tables and the method note. We sell nothing and take no commission from any route on this page. Praxis-1 is the rare frontier release whose rental maths is genuinely small: a working robot policy for a few dollars a day of experiments, and a documented adaptation recipe — LoRA — that costs about ten dollars of H100 time. The traps are all in the framing, not the model. “Runs on one H100” is true for serving and for LoRA, and quietly false for the job a new rig actually needs, which is an eight-card node-day; “NVFP4” sounds like a compression option for the H100 you were about to rent and is in fact a different, cheaper card entirely; and the cheapest H100 number on any board, ours included, is a node rate in a per-GPU costume. Rent the PCIe H100 — or the PRO 6000, if a workstation card fits your setup — serve the ready policy in simulation first, and let the fine-tune decision wait until the policy has failed at your task in a way LoRA can fix.

Deploy Inkling 2 Small — what it actually costs

Thinking Machines put the Inkling 2 Small weights on Hugging Face on Nov 12, 2026, under Apache 2.0 — and the first question every builder asks is the rental question. The honest answer starts with size: a 594-billion-parameter model whose own card asks for a GPU cluster with at least 500GB of memory. There is no single-card route. What there is: a cheapest verified way in at $14.36 an hour, a more comfortable one for 44 cents an hour more, and a clear set of people who should not rent at all and should use the APIs the maker lists instead. The model facts come from the maker's own card and repos, read on release day; the prices from our verified board, checked Nov 12, 2026.

The verdict

  • Cheapest verified — the maker's own example config — 4× H200 at RunPod Community — 564GB aggregated against the card's 500GB floor for the native NVFP4 checkpoint.
  • Comfortable — fewest GPUs, most room per card — 2× B300 at Hyperstack — 576GB; about 91GB per card left after the checkpoint loads, against about 43GB on the H200 route.
  • Same cheap cards, datacentre tier — 4× H200 at RunPod Secure — the same four cards, Secure tier instead of Community.
  • The MXFP8 checkpoint — priced, and not recommended — 8× H200 at RunPod Community — the card's cheapest MXFP8 example shape (800GB floor). Double the NVFP4 floor, for an evaluation gain the maker itself calls not meaningful.
  • Don't self-host — occasional or bursty use — The hosted APIs the card lists — NVIDIA, Fireworks, Together, Baseten, Nebius, Modal, Cloudflare, and the maker's own Tinker. No verified API price for this model exists in our records yet, so we print no break-even — price the APIs against the rental floor (about $345/day before your first token) and your real usage.
Compare prices→Inkling 2 Small in the model catalogue→

What Inkling 2 Small is

From the maker's own card, read Nov 12, 2026: a multimodal mixture-of-experts model — text and image in, text out — with 594 billion parameters in total and 17 billion active per token. A 48-layer decoder-only transformer; each token routed to 8 of 384 experts; local and global attention layers; a vision transformer for image input; a context window of 1 million tokens. It launched closed on Thinking Machines' Tinker platform on Nov 5, 2026; the weights landed on Hugging Face on Nov 12, 2026, under Apache 2.0, with day-one integration in SGLang, vLLM, TokenSpeed and Unsloth. Two checkpoints ship: the native NVFP4 build — the precision the model was trained in, and the one the card recommends — and an MXFP8 build. Full record: the model's catalogue entry on this site.

The memory maths

An MoE model carries a trap in its headline numbers. The 17B active figure is not the size of the download, the memory, or the rental. Every one of the 594 billion parameters sits in GPU memory whether a given token uses it or not — the active count shapes the compute per token; the total decides what you rent. Anyone who prices this as a “17B model” is about to be surprised by a cluster bill.

CheckpointOn disk (the repo's own file list)The maker's floorWhat the gap is for
NVFP4 — native, recommended393.5GB — 24 weight shards (about 390GB) plus the bundled speculator file (3.4GB)At least 500GB of aggregated VRAM (card's examples: 2× B300 or 4× H200)About 106GB above the file — working room for KV cache, activations and the framework. The card sets the floor; it does not itemise the gap, and neither do we.
MXFP8 — the alternative622.8GB — 49 weight shardsAt least 800GB of aggregated VRAM (card's examples: 4× B300 or 8× H200)About 177GB above the file, same job.

Why the NVFP4 file is bigger than the naive maths (594B × 0.5 bytes ≈ 297GB): it is a mixed build, not a uniform one. The repo's own metadata shows about 248GB of FP4-packed weights alongside about 128GB in FP8 and about 14GB in BF16 — and the vLLM recipe linked from the card explains the split: experts are NVFP4 in layers 0–39 and MXFP8 in layers 40–47. Four-bit is the bulk, not the whole. The context window deserves the same honesty. “1M tokens” is the model's ceiling, not a promise about what a 500GB cluster serves at full length to a crowd. The working, from the model's published config: 8 of its 48 layers attend globally (the other 40 use a 1,024-token sliding window, per the vLLM recipe), and a global layer's KV cache at BF16 costs 2 × 8 KV heads × 128 head-dim × 2 bytes = 4,096 bytes per token — about 32KB per token across the 8 global layers, so one sequence at the full 1M context carries roughly 33GB of KV cache alone (labelled assumptions: BF16 KV cache, per sequence; sliding-window layers excluded — their cache stops growing at the window). Against about 106GB of headroom, that is a handful of full-length sequences, not a crowd — the recipes set the context and batch you actually get. vLLM's verified configurations agree: on GB200 trays it verifies up to 262,144 tokens at TP4 and reserves the full 1,048,576 for TP8.

The configs, priced

The card names exactly two example configurations for NVFP4. Everything below that goes beyond them is labelled as what it is — memory arithmetic against the card's floor, not a maker's promise — and the serving recipes are the final arbiter of what runs well.

Two lessons in that table. First, the card's two examples land within 44 cents an hour of each other by different shapes — four mid cards against two big ones — so the choice is about headroom, not price: the B300 pair leaves about 91GB per card after the checkpoint loads, the H200 four about 43GB, and that difference is your room for KV cache and batch. Second, the cheap B200 rescues nobody: at $5.98 it is the board's best B200 rate, but clearing the floor takes three, and three cost more than either card example. A cheaper card you need more of is not a cheaper cluster. The minimums that bite. Some per-GPU rates on the board are divisions of whole machines. Oracle OCI's H200 ($10.00/GPU/hr) is an 8-GPU node at $80.00 an hour, take all eight or none; Azure's H200 ($10.60/GPU/hr) is an 8-GPU VM at $84.80 an hour; CoreWeave's ($6.31/GPU/hr) is an 8-GPU node at $50.44 an hour — a real route (1,128GB clears either checkpoint's floor), but priced as a node, because that is what you rent. Compare these node totals against the $14–18/hr shapes above, not the divided rates. The rest of the board, honestly. GB300 is listed per GPU-hour (Verda, $14.00), so two would cost $28.00/hr — double the B300 route, for a rack-scale part the card does not name; Oracle sells it only as a 4-GPU node at $72.00 an hour. The GH200 goes the other way: CoreWeave lists it at $6.50 as a 1-GPU instance with 96GB, so the floor takes six separate instances ($39.00/hr) before interconnect questions start. And no H100 configuration appears in this guide: the card's hardware story starts at the H200 and the B300, and we do not invent routes the maker has not documented. MXFP8's table is shorter still — 8× H200 at RunPod Community ($28.72/hr) or 4× B300 at Hyperstack ($29.60/hr) — because its honest use in a cost guide is as the priced warning in the watch-outs below.

The serving route, as documented

The software story is unusually well documented for a day-one release, because the maker shipped the integrations with the weights. The card names four local inference routes, each with its own recipe — SGLang, vLLM, TokenSpeed and Unsloth — plus Hugging Face's own stack, and three post-training routes: Miles, SkyRL and Snowflake Cortex Training. What the documentation also says, before your first invoice:

Who should not self-host

Anyone whose usage is occasional, bursty, or still being figured out. The rental floor is about $345 a day before your first token, and it runs while you sleep. The same weights are served by API at NVIDIA, Fireworks, Together, Baseten, Nebius, Modal and Cloudflare, and the maker runs them on its own Tinker platform and playground — all named on the card itself. We hold no verified per-token API price for this model as of Nov 12, 2026, so we print no break-even and invent none: price your expected token volume at those APIs against roughly $10,500 a month for an always-on cluster, and notice how much round-the-clock traffic it takes before renting wins.

The MoE trap17B active is the compute story; 594B total is the memory story, the download story and the rental story. Every sizing decision in this guide runs off the total. So should yours.

The card recommends NVFP4 for all use cases. So do the prices.

Live board: Compare prices. The model: Inkling 2 Small in our catalogue. The release: Inkling 2 Small weights are out.

Our reading

Inkling 2 Small is the first open-weights release of this size where the deployment question has a clean, priced answer on day one — the maker published real hardware floors, and the board already prices every card in them. The answer is narrower than the launch noise suggests: two configurations within 44 cents an hour of each other, a floor of about $345 a day, and an alternative checkpoint that costs double for nothing the maker will defend. Rent if you have training plans or traffic that never sleeps; everyone else is being sold a cluster when what they need is an API key and a weekend of honest evaluation. When verified API prices for this model reach our records, this guide's comparison gets its missing half — until then, the floor above is the number to beat, and it is dated today.
