Deploy MiniMax H3-Image on one GPU

MiniMax released the H3-Image weights on Nov 10, 2026: a 33.1-billion-parameter image model that generates and edits at up to 16 megapixels natively, in six sampling steps, and serves from a single GPU — the cheapest documented one-card route on our board is $1.69 an hour. The hard part is the licence, and it is not a footnote: the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License Agreement excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom, South Korea and the United States entirely, and requires MiniMax's prior written authorisation before anyone with over $1M in annualised revenue — or anyone offering the model as a hosted service — may use it at all. For most readers, the licence decides whether there is a deployment to price. This guide takes the decisions in the order they bind: licence first, memory second, rental third. The model facts come from MiniMax's own card, repo and LICENSE file, read Nov 13, 2026; the prices from our verified board, checked Nov 26, 2026.

The verdict

  • 1. May you run it at all? — the licence gate — The licence covers use only outside its Excluded Territories: the EU, the UK, South Korea and the USA. Use there — of the model or its outputs — is “not authorized” (Sections I.5, II, V.4). Excluded-territory readers: the licence itself points you to MiniMax to ask about a separate licence. No rental configuration fixes a territory problem.
  • 2. Do you need MiniMax's written authorisation first? — Yes, if your annualised revenue (yours and your affiliates') exceeds $1M, or you provide the model as a hosted service to third parties — Section IV.1, via MiniMax's platform console. Commercial products must also prominently display “MiniMax-H3-Image” on the user interface (Section IV.2). Authorisation is prior and written — apply before you rent, not after you launch.
  • 3. Cheapest documented one-GPU route — RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell at RunPod Community — a card MiniMax's own card names. SGLang publishes a measured one-card resident recipe for this 96GB card (with AdaLN precomputation); the full stack does not sit in 96GB untouched — the recipe manages placement.
  • The maker's headline card — H200 at RunPod Community — the frameworks' tested card: SGLang keeps all components resident when a GPU has at least 130 GiB free at startup, as tested on H200; vLLM's profiles were measured on H200.
  • Full residency, nothing offloaded — B200 at RunPod Community — vLLM's recipe calls full single-GPU residency (an estimated 135 GiB) “the natural choice on B200 and B300”. B300 at Hyperstack is the roomier step up.
  • Cheapest way in at all — the offload route — H100 PCIe at RunPod Community. An 80GB card cannot hold the ~135GB stack — residency is out by arithmetic. The frameworks document offload instead: vLLM's layer-offload profile peaks at 14.7 GiB of GPU memory (measured on H200); SGLang's H100 row is “component offload on one; resident on two”. Slower by design; native precision kept.
  • Don't self-host — You're in an Excluded Territory; your plan is to improve a different model on the outputs (Section V.3 forbids using them that way for any model outside H3-Image and its own derivatives); or your use is occasional — MiniMax sells the same model through its own API and apps. No verified per-image API price exists in our records yet, so we print no break-even — price the API against the rental floor (from $40.56/day before your first image) and your real volume.
Compare prices→MiniMax H3-Image in the model catalogue→

What H3-Image is

From MiniMax's own card, read Nov 13, 2026: one checkpoint that unifies text-to-image generation and image editing — an edit is simply a request that carries reference images (up to 16). The diffusion transformer is a dense, single-stream design of 33.1 billion parameters in 50 layers; the weights are BF16, with the embedding, timestep and output layers in FP32. It generates about 16-megapixel images natively — 4096×4096 at 1:1, up to 6272×2688 at 21:9, a working range of roughly 4–20 MP — with no upscaler, distilled to 6 sampling steps with no classifier-free guidance. The text encoder is the full Qwen3-VL text encoder from the base MiniMax-H3, used unchanged — and, critically for the memory maths below, it is not counted in the 68.65 GB checkpoint figure. MiniMax names five serving frameworks on the card: SGLang, vLLM-Omni, diffusers, LightX2V and ComfyUI, with a one-GPU start command for the first two. An optional prompt-expander companion, MiniMax-H3-Image-PE (NVFP4, 17.9 GB), ships under the same licence. Full record: the model's catalogue entry on this site.

The licence is the first deployment decision

This is a community licence written by MiniMax (licensor: Nanonoble Pte. Ltd.; licence date Nov 10, 2026), not a permissive open-source licence. We read the LICENSE file in full on Nov 13, 2026. Four of its terms decide deployments before any GPU is rented, quoted in substance with their section numbers — read the file itself before you rely on any of this; we are a journal, not your lawyer.

TermWhat it says
The territory clause (Sections I.3, I.5, II, V.4)Rights are granted “solely within the Applicable Territory” — worldwide excluding the “Excluded Territories”: the European Union, the United Kingdom, the Republic of Korea and the United States of America. Section V.4: you may not “use, reproduce, modify, distribute, or display” the model works or any of their Outputs outside that territory — “Any such use outside the Applicable Territory is not authorized by this Agreement.” Note the reach: not just where the GPU sits, but where the outputs are used. MiniMax says it keeps evaluating the excluded territories' laws and invites people there to contact it about a licence under “robust controls and guardrails” — a separate negotiation, not a download.
The authorisation clause (Section IV.1)“You shall obtain a separate, prior written authorization from MiniMax” — via the form on its platform console — if the Annualized Revenue of you and/or your affiliates exceeds 1 Million USD, or you provide Hosted Service(s) to any Third Parties. Hosted service is defined broadly: the model's functionality made available to third parties via API, web access or any other remote means. In plain terms: a public image API or customer-facing generator on these weights needs MiniMax's written yes first, wherever you are — and so does any company over the $1M line, even for internal use.
The display and distribution duties (Sections IV.2, III)A commercial product or service must “prominently display 'MiniMax-H3-Image'” on its user interface. Redistribute the weights and every recipient must get a copy of the agreement, modified files must carry prominent modification notices, and distributions outside a hosted service must include a NOTICE file with MiniMax's copyright line.
The output restriction (Sections V.3, I.11)You may not use the model, “or any of their Outputs or results”, to improve any other artificial intelligence model (other than H3-Image or its derivatives). The definitions make a model distilled from H3-Image, or trained on its synthetic outputs, a Model Derivative — so that route inherits this licence whole rather than escaping it. MiniMax claims no rights over your outputs (Section VI.4); it restricts feeding them into another model's training.

Three further terms belong in a deployment plan. Offer the model to the public and Section V.5 makes you operate safeguards, a violation-reporting mechanism and investigation/removal processes, with an Acceptable Use Policy (Exhibit A: 20 prohibitions, including undisclosed machine-generated content in public environments, impersonation without consent, and military use) incorporated by reference. Breach, and Section VIII.2 lets MiniMax terminate: you must stop, delete or destroy all copies, and notify downstream recipients. Disputes sit under Hong Kong law in Hong Kong courts (Section IX). All of it is decided before the rental — which is why this section comes before the prices.

The memory maths: 68.65 GB is not the model you run

The headline number on the card is the image checkpoint. The running stack is roughly twice it, because the text encoder is a separate component — loaded from the base MiniMax-H3 repository and not counted in that figure. From the card's own download table:

ComponentWhat it isSize (card's download table)
transformer/The DiT: BF16 weights, embedding/timestep/output layers in FP3266.28 GB
vae/The image VAE, FP322.34 GB
Heads, tokenizer, processorPer-step output heads (12 MB) + Qwen3-VL tokenizer/processor (23 MB)~0.04 GB
Image checkpoint totalThe card's Model Zoo figure for MiniMax-H3-Image68.65 GB
Text encoderThe full Qwen3-VL text encoder — not counted in the 68.65 GB figure; the pipelines load it from MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3, folder text_encoder/, per model_index.json and the card (“If you already have MiniMax-H3, it is not downloaded again”). The image repo also carries a bundled copy of the same folder66.7 GB
Full BF16 stackWhat a serving process actually loads, before activations~135.35 GB

The frameworks agree with the sum: SGLang's cookbook states that “downloading both checkpoints and the VAE requires about 135 GB”, and vLLM's recipe estimates full single-GPU residency at 135 GiB — weights plus the room a live process needs. (Units as each source prints them. The two sources also differ on disk: vLLM's own plan says “about 127 GB” — both figures stand as their sources print them.) The optional prompt expander adds 17.9 GB on top. Whoever budgets a 96GB card from the “68.65 GB” headline has under-budgeted by about 66.7 GB — the encoder is the trap in this release, and it is an arithmetic trap: the card's table is honest, the headline is just partial. There is no quantised checkpoint to rent down to. MiniMax's organisation publishes exactly three H3 repositories (checked Nov 13, 2026): the image model in BF16 only, the base H3, and the PE in NVFP4 — and the PE is a different, optional model, not a smaller H3-Image. What exists instead is framework-side quantisation: SGLang can quantise the DiT (optionally the encoder) to FP8/MXFP8 at load time from the BF16 checkpoint — its cookbook calls these “approximate modes” and warns that “quantization can change composition and reference identity”, which for an editing model is the product itself; vLLM-Omni's recipe states plainly that “quantization… [is] not qualified”. Treat load-time quantisation as an experiment you validate on your own reference images, never as the plan.

The serving route, as documented

The card's quick starts are one-GPU commands. vLLM-Omni: vllm serve MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image --omni; SGLang: sglang serve --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image (add --text-encoder-path if your encoder copy is local rather than in the Hugging Face cache). Both frameworks publish per-hardware recipes the card links to — SGLang's picker marks unmeasured combinations “unverified”, and its measured set covers H200/B300, AMD Instinct, one-card RTX PRO 6000 and DGX Spark; vLLM's profiles are H200-measured with configuration guidance for the rest. For lower latency both offer sequence parallelism across GPUs (Ulysses), and vLLM-Omni also splits the text encoder tensor-parallel — capacity first, speed second.

PointWhat the documentation says
The request contractSteps are fixed at 6 and guidance at 1 — other values are rejected; there is no negative prompt; one image per request; prompts are used as given, truncated at 4,096 tokens.
The small-request cost lineOutputs below the minimum generation area (default 2048×2048) are still generated on a canvas of at least 2048² and resized back, so a “small, cheap” 1024×1024 request costs a 2048² generation unless you deliberately lower min_generation_area per request — a cost line hiding in the API contract.
Prompt expansion is a separate stepMiniMax's API expands short prompts into the detailed descriptions this model expects (its H3-Image-Context-IR step); self-hosting that step means either their API anyway, or the local PE model — the extra 17.9 GB checkpoint above, under the same licence.

The offload routes sit below these: an H100 PCIe held around the clock at $1.99/hr is $1,452.70 a month — cheaper than the H200, dearer than the PRO 6000, and slower per image by construction. Read the table's shape: a day of honest evaluation costs less than a team lunch; the bill only becomes a strategy when the card never sleeps — exactly the point at which the licence's hosted-service authorisation, not the hourly rate, becomes the binding constraint on what you may do with it.

Who should not self-host

Four readers should stop before the rental, each for a different reason:

If this is youThe honest route
You are in the European Union, the United Kingdom, South Korea or the United StatesUnder this licence the conversation ends there, for the model and for its outputs; MiniMax's own route for you is to ask it for a separate licence.
Your plan is to improve a different model with these outputsSection V.3 forbids using the model or its outputs to improve any other AI model (other than H3-Image or its derivatives), and a model distilled from H3-Image counts as a derivative under Section I.11 — it inherits this licence whole: territory, authorisation and all.
You are planning a public hosted service and have not yet appliedThe authorisation in Section IV.1 is prior and written; renting first and applying later puts the launch on the wrong side of the agreement.
Your usage is a handful of images a weekThe same weights sit behind MiniMax's own API and apps (Hailuo), and the rental floor — from $40.56 a day before storage and your own serving work — buys a great deal of API usage first. We hold no verified per-image API price as of Nov 13, 2026, so we print no break-even: price your expected volume against roughly $1,234 a month for an always-on PRO 6000 and notice how much generation it takes before renting wins.

Watch-outs

The trapWhy it costs you
The territory follows the outputsSection V.4 covers the model's Outputs, not just the weights: serving from an in-territory GPU to users in an excluded one is not a workaround the agreement leaves open. Where your users are matters as much as where your GPU is.
The affiliates trap in Section IV.1The $1M line is the annualised revenue of you and/or your affiliates — a small subsidiary of a large group is over the line even if its own books are tiny.
The download is bigger than the headlineThe image repo alone is ~204 GB if you clone everything, because it carries native and diffusers copies of the transformer and VAE, plus a bundled copy of the text encoder — pull only what your framework needs, or provision ~135 GB for the full working set.
Offload is a host bill tooThe documented small-card routes stream weights from host RAM — SGLang's offload recipes assume a 256 GB-class host with local NVMe. A cheap GPU hour attached to an undersized host is not the documented recipe.
Quantisation changes the productLoad-time FP8/MXFP8 in SGLang is labelled approximate by its own cookbook, with composition and reference identity liable to change — for an editing model, validate on your own reference images before serving it to anyone. In vLLM-Omni it is not qualified at all.
Termination means deletionBreach the terms and the licence can be terminated with a duty to delete or destroy all copies and notify downstream recipients (Section VIII.2). Keep your compliance record as carefully as your checkpoints.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Everything in this box is GPUJournal's judgement on the verified record above it; the record itself is in the tables and the method note. We sell nothing and take no commission from any route on this page. Every deployment guide in this field starts with memory and ends with price. This one has to start with a map. H3-Image is a genuinely strong open image model at a genuinely small rental — a measured one-card route at $1.69 an hour is remarkable for a 33.1B model that paints 16 megapixels in six steps. But the licence draws a border through the middle of the market: the four territories where most GPU renters sit are outside it, the outputs inherit the border, and the two commercial triggers — $1M of revenue, or any hosted service — catch exactly the readers most likely to build a business on it. None of that makes the release less important; it makes the honest guide the one that says “check the map first” and means it as step one, not small print. For readers inside the territory and under the triggers, the rental maths above is as friendly as this class of model gets. For everyone else, the API — or a differently-licensed model — is the deployment, and knowing that before the first invoice is the whole value of reading the licence first.

/guide/gpu-rental-cost.html:
GPU PRICING →  ·  2026-11-14 · 13 min read

How much does it cost to rent a GPU in the cloud?

On the board we checked on Nov 14, 2026, the cheapest verified on-demand offers in the table below start at $0.34 an hour for an RTX 4090 and top out at $14.27 an hour for a GB300. That range is real, but it is not the whole answer. The lowest H100 SXM rate, TensorDock's $2.25 per GPU per hour, comes with an eight-GPU minimum — an $18.00 hourly commitment, not a $2.25 rental. This guide separates the sticker price from the amount you actually commit to, then adds the costs the hourly rate leaves out.

The verdict

  • Cards under a dollar an hour — RTX 4090 at $0.34, RTX A6000 at $0.35, RTX 5090 at $0.69, and L40S or L40 at $0.79 — the cheapest verified on-demand offers on the board checked Nov 26, 2026.
  • The A100 band — The A100 band starts just above a dollar an hour: A100 80GB at $1.09 and A100 40GB at $1.70.
  • The current data-centre flagships — The current data-centre flagships cost several dollars an hour: H200 at $3.59, B200 at $5.98, B300 at $7.40 and GB300 at $14.27.
  • The floor is not the bill — Those are floors, not averages and not quotes for every buying shape. The lowest H100 SXM rate, TensorDock's $2.25 per GPU per hour, comes with an eight-GPU minimum — an $18.00 hourly commitment, not a $2.25 rental.
Compare prices→Price Watch — every verified move→

The short answer

For a single hourly budget, use three bands from the Nov 14 board. Cards start below a dollar an hour: RTX 4090 at $0.34, RTX A6000 at $0.35, RTX 5090 at $0.69, and L40S or L40 at $0.79. The A100 band starts just above a dollar: A100 80GB at $1.09 and A100 40GB at $1.70. The current data-centre flagships cost several dollars an hour: H200 at $3.59, B200 at $5.98, B300 at $7.40 and GB300 at $14.27. Those are floors, not averages and not quotes for every buying shape. A floor can belong to a community tier, carry a minimum, or describe one variant while a similarly named variant costs more. The rest of this guide is about not mistaking the floor for the bill.

Why the same GPU can cost several times more

The spread is not a rounding error. In the Nov 14 snapshot, the range on a single card runs to several times its floor, before the buying shapes are even considered:

Some of that spread is the provider and service tier. Some is the machine wrapped around the GPU. Some is a per-GPU figure divided out of a whole node or VM. The name of the card alone does not make two offers equivalent.

What moves the price — the minimum setup: compare totals, not per-GPU stickers

The most expensive misunderstanding in GPU rental is also the simplest: a per-GPU rate is not the amount leaving your account when the offer is sold as a node, a VM or a multi-GPU minimum. GPUJournal prices viable multi-GPU offers by their minimum setup total wherever the snapshot gives that total. Date note: the TensorDock and CoreWeave rows below were re-read on Nov 14, 2026. The real bill beyond the sticker

The extraWhat it does to the bill
Idle timeA GPU bought by the hour charges for the shape of your working day, not only for the minutes a job is productive. Setup, data loading, debugging, failed runs and a machine left running while you decide what to do next all consume rented time if the instance remains live. The 730-hour column above is the warning: an always-on habit turns a modest hourly rate into a monthly commitment.
StorageDatasets, checkpoints, images and results need somewhere to live, and storage can remain after the GPU stops. Our Nov 14 snapshot verifies GPU rates, not a comparable set of storage prices, so this guide prints no storage fee. Add the provider's volume, disk and snapshot lines separately before calling a rate cheap.
Data transfer and egressMoving training data in and checkpoints or generated results out can add a transfer bill, especially when the GPU region and the data's home differ. The snapshot does not verify comparable egress rates across these providers, so no transfer figure is printed here. “No figure in our table” does not mean “no charge on the invoice.”
The host around the GPUSome prices are not complete machine prices. Google Cloud's A100 80GB rate in the snapshot is explicitly an attachable-GPU rate with the host VM billed on top. Node and VM rows have the opposite trap: the total is real, but the divided per-GPU figure can make an eight-GPU commitment look like a one-GPU rental.
Tax treatmentNebius's snapshot figures are marked “excl. VAT.” None of Nebius's rates leads the TL;DR table, but the warning generalises as a checking rule: do not compare a tax-exclusive quote with another provider's final payable amount without putting both on the same basis.
Restart costInterruptible work needs checkpoints and a restart plan. Even where the hourly rate is lower, a restart can buy setup and unfinished progress again. Our snapshot contains no spot rate, so it offers no honest way to total that trade-off here.

What moves the price — the buying basis, the region, the provider type and the date

The buying basis: on-demand, spot or term. Every price in the TL;DR table is on-demand. That matters because on-demand is the flexible reference rate: it is the price shape our snapshot can compare across providers without hiding a duration or interruption condition inside the number. Spot and interruptible capacity are a different bargain. The Nov 14 snapshot contains no offer labelled spot, so this guide prints no spot price and does not borrow one from another page. If you price spot elsewhere, compare it only after adding the cost of checkpointing, restarting and losing unfinished work. A lower interruptible rate is not cheaper if the job has to buy the same hours twice. Term and reserved prices are also not on-demand prices. The snapshot used here contains no verified term or reserved figure, so none is mixed into the table. A term quote belongs in a comparison only with its duration, minimum spend and cancellation or expiry terms printed beside it. Leaving those terms out makes a commitment look like a discount with no cost. Region is part of the price. A regional meter is not a worldwide quote. The snapshot identifies Microsoft Azure's H200 figure as an East US 2 meter: $10.60 per GPU per hour (a carried hyperscaler row verified Oct 27–28, 2026), divided from an $84.80 eight-GPU VM. It does not present that figure as Azure's price in every region, and neither does this guide. Before comparing two offers, put the region in the row. A cheaper card in the wrong place can also create a second cost when data has to move to it or results have to move back. The snapshot does not give us a verified cross-region price table, so this guide does not invent one. Provider type changes the shape of the offer. The snapshot's provider labels describe different buying shapes. Hyperscalers — Oracle OCI, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure in this snapshot — often price the GPU as part of a node or VM; Google Cloud's A100 80GB figure goes further and prices an attachable GPU while billing the host VM separately. Specialist GPU clouds — including CoreWeave, Nebius, Hyperstack, Verda, Thunder Compute and TensorDock — include both per-GPU offers and whole-node divisions, so the provider category alone still does not settle the comparison. RunPod Community supplies the cheapest verified offer for many cards in the TL;DR table, while RunPod Secure prices the same card family as a separate tier; on Nov 14, for example, H200 is $3.59 at RunPod Community and $5.29 at RunPod Secure. The lesson is not that one provider type is always cheaper. It is that the words around the number — Community, Secure, node, VM, attachable GPU, minimum — are part of the price. The date is part of the price. GPU prices are moving while you read. In the Nov 14 check, Verda rose for the 16th consecutive time, with all nine tracked cards up about 1% from Nov 13. Its GB300 has risen from $11.82 on Oct 19 to $14.27 on Nov 14 — 20.7% — in our dated record. That is why this guide prints the check date in every TL;DR row instead of presenting November's floor as a permanent market fact. It is also why stale comparison tables mislead. Vast.ai published a guide with this question as its title on Nov 13; our daily research note records that its competitor rows are stamped “checked July 20, 2026.” This guide does not reuse those rows. It answers from GPUJournal's Nov 14, 2026 snapshot.

Steps

1. Match the exact card and variant

H100 PCIe, H100 SXM and H100 NVL are separate rows for a reason. So are A100 80GB PCIe and A100 80GB SXM, and L40 and L40S.

2. Write the minimum total beside the per-GPU rate

If the shape is eight GPUs, a node or a VM, budget the whole-shape total — TensorDock's $18.00, CoreWeave's $50.44, or Microsoft Azure's $84.80 (a carried row verified Oct 27–28, 2026) — not the divided sticker.

3. Keep the basis, region and date in the row

On-demand is not spot; a term is not on-demand; East US 2 is not every region; Nov 14 is not July 20.

4. Price the finished stretch, then add what the sticker excludes

Start with 24, 168 or 730 hours, then add the host, storage and transfer lines from the actual provider quote. If one of those lines is missing, the comparison is not finished.

Compare prices→Price Watch — every verified move→

How we check

GPUJournal's Nov 14, 2026 snapshot contains 87 offers. Its source note records first-hand Nov 14 re-reads for Verda, RunPod Secure, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, TensorDock and Hyperstack, with RunPod Community corroborated in part and the remaining Community figures carried in the same board check. The hyperscaler rows used for buying-shape examples were carried from the board's earlier Oct 27–28, 2026 verification and were not re-read in the Nov 14 pass; the guide uses them to explain node and VM totals, not as the cheapest current offer for any card. Prices are read from providers' own published pages and banked by date. A change is reported in Price Watch only when the before and after figures are both in our records. Live board: Compare prices. Verified changes: Price Watch. What is deliberately not priced. Lambda is not in the tables: the Nov 14 research note says its current rates are login-gated and its public page prints announced Nov 16 rates, which are not yet in effect and are therefore not presented as current prices. nafnaf is not priced: the snapshot's carried figures sit behind a “No GPUs available right now” note, so they are not verified live offers for this guide. Spheron's stated marketplace figures are omitted, not treated as verified prices. SaladCloud figures mentioned in the daily research note are not used in the cheapest table because they are not offers in the banked snapshot's offer list and the note does not define the “High” tier as the same on-demand basis used above.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. The Nov 14 board does not describe one GPU market with one sensible average. It describes several markets sharing card names: community and specialist per-GPU floors, whole-node capacity divided back into per-GPU figures, regional hyperscaler VMs, and at least one attachable-GPU rate whose host is extra. The renter's advantage comes from matching the buying shape to the job, not from finding the smallest number on a page. A $2.25 rate with an $18.00 floor can be excellent for eight GPUs and irrelevant for one. A $14.27 GB300 can be a short evaluation or a $10,417.10 always-on month. The honest question is never only “what is the hourly rate?” It is “what exactly am I committing to, for how long, and what else will be billed?”

GB200 NVL72 pricing, minimums and lead times — the real total cost

A GB200 NVL72 is not a GPU you rent by the card. It is a 72-GPU rack — 36 GB200 Superchips in one NVLink domain — and almost every price quoted for it is a division of a whole-system price, not a rate you can buy one GPU at. On the board we checked on Nov 15, 2026, exactly two providers publish a verified on-demand price for it: Oracle OCI at $16.00 per GPU per hour and Google Cloud at $18.6875. But their smallest cheques differ by a factor of twenty-one: Oracle will sell you one 4-GPU node for $64.00 an hour, while Google’s own page sets an 18-VM minimum for this shape — 72 GPUs, the entire rack — so the smallest Google commitment is $1,345.50 an hour. This guide prices the rack, not the sticker.

The verdict

  • The smallest verified buy — Oracle OCI will sell you one 4-GPU node for $64.00 an hour — $16.00 per GPU per hour, verified Oct 27–28, 2026 and board-checked Nov 26, 2026. It is the smallest verified buy in this market.
  • The only verified rack minimum — Google Cloud’s own page sets an 18-VM minimum for this shape — 72 GPUs, the entire rack — so the smallest Google commitment is $1,345.50 an hour at $18.6875 per GPU, and $982,215 run around the clock for a 730-hour month.
  • Stated, not verified — CoreWeave states $42.00 an hour for a 4-GPU instance ($10.50 per GPU, a division) and Microsoft’s retail price list states $108.16 an hour for its 4-GPU VM ($27.04 per GPU, a division) — both read first-hand on Nov 15, 2026, and neither is a verified board offer.
  • No published lead time, and one no-price door — No provider publishes a delivery lead time for GB200 NVL72 capacity on its public pages — we read the public pricing and product pages of CoreWeave, Nebius, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Oracle OCI on Nov 15, 2026. Nebius, the third provider listed on our board for this system, publishes no price at all.
GB200 NVL72 on the board — every offer→Compare prices across all GPUs→

The short answer

If you need a full NVL72 rack and want a published price you can budget against today, there is exactly one verified route whose minimum is the rack itself: Google Cloud at $1,345.50 an hour — 18 VMs at $74.75, checked on our board Nov 15, 2026. Run that rack around the clock for a 730-hour month and the verified arithmetic is $982,215, before storage, data transfer and everything else a training programme consumes. If you do not need all 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain, the comparison changes completely. Oracle OCI’s verified node is $64.00 an hour — a buyable 4-GPU unit at $16.00 per GPU. CoreWeave states a cheaper per-GPU division, $10.50, on a $42.00 4-GPU instance (stated, read Nov 15, 2026). Microsoft’s retail list states the most expensive division, $27.04 per GPU on a $108.16 VM (stated, read Nov 15, 2026). Nebius, the third provider listed on our board for this system, publishes no price at all. So the spread that matters is not $16.00 versus $18.6875 — the two verified per-GPU figures sit within 17% of each other. It is the spread of minimum commitments: $42 to $64 an hour to start with a node, $1,345.50 an hour to start with a rack.

Every per-GPU figure in this table is a division. Nobody in it sells a single GB200 GPU by the hour: the smallest unit on sale anywhere is four GPUs. The two verified rows are the only GB200 NVL72 offers in GPUJournal’s Nov 15, 2026 snapshot (87 offers). The CoreWeave and Azure rows are provider-stated figures read first-hand on Nov 15, 2026; they are printed here because a buyer will meet them, and they are labelled stated because our board has not verified them as buyable offers. No spot, term or reserved figure appears in this table: the snapshot contains none for this system.

Cheapest verified routes, by what you actually need

What you needThe route
You need a few GB200 GPUs, not a rackOracle OCI’s verified 4-GPU node at $64.00/hr ($16.00/GPU/hr, verified Oct 27–28, 2026, board-checked Nov 15, 2026) is the smallest verified commitment in this market. CoreWeave states a lower entry — $42.00/hr for a 4-GPU instance (stated Nov 15, 2026) — worth quoting against Oracle, with the stated label kept in view.
You need the full 72-GPU NVLink domainGoogle Cloud’s verified rack total is $1,345.50/hr (18 × $74.75). At Oracle’s verified per-GPU rate, the same 72 GPUs total $1,152.00/hr — but that is arithmetic on Oracle’s rate, not a rack product Oracle lists; whether Oracle will assemble and price a full NVL72 for you is a sales question.
You are negotiating, not buying self-serveNebius lists GB200 NVL72 with no published price and routes large clusters to its sales team (its pricing page, read Nov 15, 2026). In a negotiation, the verified figures above are your anchors: $16.00 and $18.6875 per GPU per hour are published, dated, and checkable — a quote that lands far above them needs a reason attached.

What an hour becomes over time

Rack-scale prices are hourly the way mortgages are monthly: the unit is small, the commitment is not. The table below is simple arithmetic on the figures above — 24 hours, a 168-hour week, a 730-hour always-on month. Rows marked “rack-equivalent” multiply a 4-GPU unit price by 18 to reach 72 GPUs; they show what the rate implies at rack scale, not a listed rack product. Only Google’s row is a listed rack-scale minimum.

Read the gaps, not just the rows. At rack scale for a month, the difference between the cheapest stated division (CoreWeave, $551,880) and the most expensive stated division (Azure, $1,421,222.40) is about $869,000 — for the same 72 GPUs. The difference between the two verified routes (Google’s listed rack at $982,215 and Oracle’s rate extended to rack scale at $840,960) is about $141,000. These are the numbers a reservation negotiation is actually about.

Lead times and availability: what is actually public

Here is the honest answer first: no provider publishes a delivery lead time for GB200 NVL72 capacity on its public pages. We read the public pricing and product pages of CoreWeave, Nebius, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Oracle OCI for this guide (Nov 15, 2026), and not one states “order today, running in N weeks” for this system. A guide that prints a precise lead time for cloud NVL72 capacity is printing an estimate or a sales anecdote. What is public instead is the shape of each buying route — minimums, booking windows and term structures — and that is what a buyer can plan around:

What is publicThe detail
Minimum units are published; dates are notGoogle’s 18-VM minimum (a full rack) is stated on Google’s own page and recorded on our board. Every other seller’s smallest public unit is one 4-GPU node, VM or instance. Nobody attaches a delivery date to any of them.
Reservation structures are where the real differences sitSpheron’s Nov 13, 2026 comparison of reservation terms states that AWS sells GB200 only through EC2 Capacity Blocks that book at most eight weeks ahead, charge the full fee upfront and allow no cancellations; that Azure’s GB200 VM sits outside Azure’s capacity-guarantee product, leaving 1- or 3-year Reserved Instances that discount billing without guaranteeing capacity; and that CoreWeave’s new capacity is typically sold on multi-year contracts (a weighted average of about five years, per CoreWeave’s Q1 2026 earnings call as reported there). Those are Spheron’s stated findings, attributed because they describe contract terms we have not independently verified — but the questions they raise are the right ones to put to any seller.
Quote-only routes quote fast, on their own accountSpheron’s own GB200 listing states a quote back within one business day from an 8-GPU node minimum (Spheron’s pages, read Nov 15, 2026). Nebius publishes no equivalent promise; its page simply routes large clusters to sales.
The “6 to 12 months” figures are about buying hardware, not renting cloud capacityLead times in that range circulate in third-party analyses of purchasing NVL72 racks outright. They are not provider-published cloud delivery times, and this guide does not present them as such.

The practical consequence: if your programme has a hard start date, the lead time is a contract term to extract in writing from whichever seller you choose — it exists nowhere public to be looked up.

Watch-outs before you commit

Watch-outThe detail
Do not compare a division with a total“$10.50/GPU/hr” (CoreWeave, stated) and “$1,345.50/hr” (Google, verified) describe the same system at different slicing. Convert everything to the full shape you will actually run, for the full hours you will actually run it, before ranking anything.
GB300 NVL72 is a different systemThis guide prices GB200 NVL72 only. GB300 rows you will meet elsewhere — CoreWeave lists its GB300 NVL72 as “contact sales” (read Nov 15, 2026), and our board carries a GB300 label at $14.27/GPU/hr from Verda — are a newer rack generation with its own prices, not a discount on this one.
A retail meter is not a reservationAzure’s stated $108.16 VM meter (West US 2, Linux, Nov 15, 2026) does not include the reservation terms Azure actually sells this capacity under; region changes the meter, too — the same VM lists higher in several other regions of Microsoft’s price list.
Stated is not verifiedThe CoreWeave and Azure figures above are printed exactly as those providers publish them, read Nov 15, 2026. Our board has not verified them as buyable at those figures, and CoreWeave’s volume GB200 business is contract-led in practice. If a stated figure anchors your budget, get it confirmed in a quote before the budget hardens.
The rack is not the whole billStorage, data transfer, networking between racks, and the staff time of a multi-week negotiation all sit outside every figure in this guide. At $1,345.50 an hour, idle time is the most expensive line: a rack left running unused for one day burns $32,292.00 at Google’s verified rate.

What the headline rate hides

The per-GPU figure is a division, not a product. An NVL72 rack holds 72 GPUs in 18 compute trays, and every seller slices it the same way: a 4-GPU unit — two Superchips — is the atom. Oracle calls it a node, Google and Microsoft call it a VM, CoreWeave calls it an instance. When a page says “$16.00 per GPU,” it means “$64.00 for the 4-GPU unit, divided by four.” No checkout anywhere sells one GB200 GPU for one hour. A comparison that treats the divided figure as buyable understates the smallest commitment four times over before it starts. Google’s minimum is the whole rack. The second thing the sticker hides is the minimum. Google’s own page notes an 18-VM minimum for this shape (recorded on our board, checked Nov 15, 2026). Eighteen 4-GPU VMs are 72 GPUs: Google is not selling you a slice of an NVL72, it is selling you an NVL72. That makes Google’s $18.6875 the only verified per-GPU figure in this guide that is also a true rack rate — and it makes its $1,345.50 hourly floor twenty-one times Oracle’s $64.00 entry point. Neither is “cheaper” in the abstract. They are different products wearing the same per-GPU costume. A published meter is not the same as capacity you can start. Microsoft’s retail price list publishes a real hourly meter for its ND GB200 v6 VM — $108.16 in West US 2 for Linux, read Nov 15, 2026. A meter existing is not the same as on-demand capacity sitting open: our board carries no Azure GB200 offer — a published meter is not an offer we have verified as buyable self-serve, and Spheron’s Nov 13 summary describes Azure GB200 access as running through Reserved Instances. Treat the $27.04 division as a stated reference price for negotiations, not as a rate you can spin up against this afternoon.

GB200 NVL72 on the board — every offer→Compare prices across all GPUs→

How we check

GPUJournal’s Nov 15, 2026 snapshot contains 87 offers read from providers’ own published pages and banked by date. For GB200 NVL72 the board carries exactly three listings: Oracle OCI and Google Cloud with verified on-demand prices (first verified Oct 27–28, 2026, and still listed in the Nov 15, 2026 board check), and Nebius as quote-only with no published price. Rack totals are arithmetic on those verified figures, labelled wherever the multiplication goes beyond the shape the provider lists. The CoreWeave and Azure figures are stated: CoreWeave’s pricing page was read first-hand on Nov 15, 2026 (GB200 NVL72 4-GPU instance, $42.00/hr on-demand, spot not offered; its GB300 NVL72 is “contact sales”), and Microsoft’s retail price list was read the same day (ND128isr GB200 v6, $108.16/VM/hr for Linux in West US 2; Microsoft’s documentation specifies four Blackwell GPUs and two Grace CPUs per VM). Nebius’s pricing page, read the same day, lists GB200 NVL72 with no price in either its preemptible or on-demand column. RunPod’s pricing page (read Nov 15, 2026) lists no GB200 NVL72, and Hyperstack’s (read Nov 15, 2026 by our raw-page method, 13 rows) lists none either. Live board: https://gpujournal.ai/compare-prices. The system: https://gpujournal.ai/gpu/gb200-nvl72. What is deliberately not priced. AWS carries no GB200 NVL72 offer on our board, so no AWS price appears in this guide’s tables; the Capacity Block terms quoted in the lead-times section are Spheron’s stated summary of AWS’s structure (their guide, Nov 13, 2026), not our verified finding. Lambda’s current rates sit behind a login (checked Nov 15, 2026), so Lambda is not priced here either. Spheron’s own marketplace figures are never treated as verified prices on this site; where Spheron’s claims are mentioned, they are attributed to Spheron. No lead time is printed anywhere in this guide, because no provider publishes one — that absence is reported, not filled.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. The GB200 NVL72 market, as published, is thinner than it looks. Strip away the divisions and there are two verified on-demand prices, one stated instance price, one stated retail meter, and a row of quote-only doors. Spheron’s Nov 13 piece argues the real blocker is reservation fine print rather than price, and on AWS and Azure it makes that case well — but it never totals a rack, and it omits the two providers (Oracle and Google) whose published rates let a buyer total one today: $64.00 an hour to start at node scale, $1,345.50 an hour at rack scale, $982,215 for an always-on month. Price is not the whole decision at this end of the market. It is, however, a knowable number — and a buyer who walks into a quote-only negotiation knowing the verified rack total negotiates from a different position than one who knows only a per-GPU sticker.

PROVIDER COMPARISONS →  ·  2026-11-19 · 16 min read

Serverless GPU inference compared — AWS Lambda GPU functions vs RunPod Serverless vs keeping an instance

“Serverless GPU” now means two very different bills. RunPod Serverless charges for the seconds a worker actually runs. AWS’s new Lambda GPU functions, launched Nov 18, 2026, charge for EC2 instance time your capacity sits provisioned — plus a 9.75% management fee and $0.20 per million requests — with no per-request duration charge at all. And the third option is the oldest one: rent the GPU by the hour and pay for its idle time yourself. This guide prices all three shapes from the providers’ own published rates, checked Nov 19, 2026, works the cost of a million requests at two request lengths, and finds the utilisation line where the always-on instance starts winning.

The verdict

  • AWS Lambda GPU functions — EC2 instance time while capacity is provisioned, plus a 9.75% management fee on the On-Demand price and $0.20 per million requests — no per-request duration charge. Best for event-driven inference already inside AWS, and models that pack many concurrent requests onto one GPU.
  • RunPod Serverless (Flex workers) — Per second a worker runs, from worker start until it fully stops, rounded up to the nearest second — L40S class $1.89/hr of busy time, L4 class $0.75/hr. Best for bursty or unpredictable inference with no AWS tie-in; the widest GPU menu of the two serverless routes, up to B300.
  • Always-on instance — Flat per-hour rate, 24/7, idle included — the cheapest verified L40S on our board is $0.79/hr at RunPod Community, $576.70 for a 730-hour month. Best for steady traffic: it beats RunPod Serverless once the GPU is busy more than about 41.8% of the month, and beats AWS’s provisioned g6e once capacity would sit provisioned more than about 38.7% of the time.
Compare always-on GPU prices across every provider→The AWS Lambda GPU launch, as reported Nov 18→

The short answer

If your traffic is spiky, low or unpredictable, rent seconds, not hours. RunPod Serverless Flex is the purer serverless of the two: a worker that has scaled down bills nothing, and you pay only for start, execution and a short idle tail. On the two card classes both providers offer, its busy-hour rate is also the lower one — $0.75/hr for the L4 class against an effective $0.88/hr for AWS’s L4 instance (g6.xlarge), and $1.89/hr for the L40S class against an effective $2.04/hr for AWS’s L40S instance (g6e.xlarge), each AWS figure being the EC2 On-Demand rate plus the 9.75% fee, checked Nov 26, 2026. If your workload lives inside AWS — triggered by S3, SQS, EventBridge or any of Lambda’s 200-plus event sources, billed on the same account, with Savings Plans already in place — Lambda GPU functions are the integration play, and their economics hinge on one feature RunPod does not have: an execution environment can serve up to 48 concurrent requests on one GPU. Serve requests one at a time and AWS is the most expensive route per request in this guide; pack them concurrently and the same instance-hour divides across all of them. If your traffic is steady, skip both. The cheapest verified L40S instance on our board, RunPod Community at $0.79/hr (checked Nov 19, 2026), beats RunPod Serverless once the GPU is busy more than about 41.8% of the month, and beats AWS’s provisioned g6e once capacity would sit provisioned more than about 38.7% of the time. Past those lines you are paying serverless prices for an always-on workload.

TL;DR — the three routes side by side (rates checked Nov 19, 2026)

RouteHow you payBest forThe catch
AWS Lambda GPU functions (Lambda Managed Instances on EC2 G-series)EC2 instance time while capacity is provisioned, + 9.75% management fee on the On-Demand price, + $0.20 per million requests. No duration charge per request.Event-driven inference already inside AWS; spiky traffic if you switch scale-to-zero on; models that pack many concurrent requests onto one GPU.It is not pay-per-request compute. The default keeps a warm baseline (minimum 3 execution environments), scale-to-zero is opt-in, and new accounts may start with a G-series quota of 0.
RunPod Serverless (Flex workers)Per second a worker runs, from worker start until it fully stops, rounded up to the nearest second. L40S class $1.89/hr of busy time; L4 class $0.75/hr.Bursty or unpredictable inference with no AWS tie-in; the widest GPU menu of the two serverless routes, up to B300.Cold start and a 5-second idle tail after each burst are billed time. Per busy hour it costs more than the same card rented as an instance.
Always-on instance (a rented GPU, e.g. a RunPod Pod)Flat per-hour rate, 24/7, idle included. Cheapest verified L40S on our board: $0.79/hr (RunPod Community), $576.70 for a 730-hour month.Steady traffic, latency-sensitive serving, anything busy more than about two-fifths of the day on an L40S.You pay for every idle hour, and scaling, patching and availability are your job.

The headline comparison, on the L40S class at 2 seconds per request, sequential serving: a million requests cost $1,050.00 on RunPod Serverless and $1,134.89 on AWS Lambda GPU (g6e.xlarge) — while a RunPod Community L40S instance costs $576.70 for the whole month whether it serves one request or millions, up to its throughput. Serverless wins on volume you do not have; the instance wins on volume you do. The break-even maths is below, with every assumption stated.

Shape one: AWS Lambda GPU — instance time plus 9.75%

AWS announced GPU support for Lambda Event Functions on Nov 18, 2026: functions run as container images on Lambda Managed Instances built from EC2 G-series hardware, and AWS handles drivers, CUDA versions, provisioning and routing. The launch families are G4dn (T4), G5 (A10G), G6 and Gr6 (L4), G6f and Gr6f (fractional L4) and G6e (L40S), with 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory per function — AWS positions it for inference and custom models, not training or large foundation models. The pricing, from AWS’s own Lambda pricing page, read Nov 19, 2026, has exactly three components: EC2 instance charges for the instances Lambda provisions in your capacity provider, at standard EC2 pricing — Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply to this part. A compute management fee of 9.75% for GPU G-series instance types (15% for CPU types) — read the pricing page’s own worked example carefully: the fee is calculated on the EC2 On-Demand price, even when a Savings Plan has discounted the instance charge itself; the discount shrinks your instance line, it does not shrink the fee. And request charges of $0.20 per million requests — and that is all: the pricing page states plainly that Managed Instances functions do not pay separately for the execution duration of each request. So an AWS GPU function is not billed like a Lambda function, and it is not billed like RunPod Serverless. You pay for provisioned instance time — the hours your capacity exists — at the EC2 rate plus 9.75%, plus twenty cents per million requests. What a request costs you is therefore decided entirely by how much provisioned time it consumes and how many requests share that time. The EC2 rates below are AWS’s own published On-Demand prices for US East (N. Virginia), Linux, from the AWS Price List file published Nov 18, 2026 and read Nov 19, 2026:

Instance (GPU)EC2 On-DemandWith the 9.75% feeKept warm 24/7 (730 hrs)

Effective hourly figures are the EC2 rate × 1.0975, computed exactly ($0.8833, $1.1041 and $2.0424) and rounded for display; the monthly column is the exact figure × 730 hours. The request fee is on top and is negligible at these volumes: $0.20 per million requests. AWS bills EC2 instance time per second with a 60-second minimum, per its On-Demand pricing page. Regions other than US East (N. Virginia) price differently; this guide uses the one region throughout so the three routes stay comparable.

Shape two: RunPod Serverless — per second a worker runs

RunPod Serverless turns a container into an autoscaling endpoint. Its pricing documentation, read Nov 19, 2026, is unusually explicit about the meter: you are billed from when a worker starts until it fully stops, rounded up to the nearest second, across three phases — cold start (worker start until your handler is ready, mostly model loading; pulling the container image and downloading cached models normally happen while scaled down and are not billed), execution time, and an idle timeout after the last job (default 5 seconds) during which the worker waits for more work. A worker that has scaled down is not billed. Two worker types sit on that meter: Flex workers start on demand and scale to zero when there are no requests, at the standard per-second rate — this is the serverless default and the only publicly priced tier. Active workers run 24/7, which removes cold starts — but RunPod publishes no rate for them; its documentation says only that discounts are “available through sales inquiry.” Any comparison you read that prints an Active-worker price is quoting a negotiated or stale figure, not a list price; this guide prices Flex only. On cold starts, RunPod claims sub-200ms starts on FlashBoot-optimised workers and “low single digit seconds” on standard container workers — the publisher’s figures, from its own comparison page, not independently measured; a large model loading into GPU memory is the real-world cold start, and RunPod bills you for it.

Worked examples: what a million requests cost — L40S class, the class all three routes offer

Shape three is the baseline both serverless shapes have to beat: a GPU you simply rent. From our board snapshot, checked Nov 19, 2026, the L40S — the card class all three routes can serve — costs $0.79/hr at RunPod Community and $1.09/hr at RunPod Secure, per-GPU on-demand, billed per second while the pod runs. A Community L40S kept for a 730-hour month costs $576.70; a Secure one, $795.70. No request fees, no management percentage, no per-second worker meter — and no autoscaling, no managed drivers, and a bill that runs at full rate at 4 a.m. when nobody is calling. Every other provider on the board prices the same shape; the L40S also lists at Nebius $1.55/hr (a from-price, excl. VAT), CoreWeave $2.25/hr and Verda $2.08/hr in the same snapshot, which is why this guide uses the cheapest verified row as the baseline: it is the bar serverless has to clear, not the average. Assumptions, stated once and used throughout: requests are served sequentially, one at a time per GPU (concurrency 1), each taking exactly 2 seconds or exactly 10 seconds of GPU time. A million sequential requests at 2 seconds each consume 555.6 GPU-hours; at 10 seconds, 2,777.8 GPU-hours. RunPod Serverless is charged for execution time only in the main tables — no cold starts, and requests are assumed to arrive back-to-back so the 5-second idle tail is paid once per burst, not per request; the worst case, where every request sits alone and pays the tail, is costed separately below. AWS is charged for exactly the instance-hours the sequential work consumes, as if capacity provisioned and released perfectly with scale-to-zero on, plus the $0.20 request fee; real deployments also pay a termination tail of a few minutes per scale-in, which this model excludes and the watch-outs cover. The always-on instance is charged its flat monthly rate — at a volume of exactly one million requests in the month, the whole month’s rent is the cost of those million requests. All figures are arithmetic on the verified rates above, computed by script.

Two honest qualifiers. First, the idle tail: if your traffic is so sparse that every request arrives alone, each RunPod request also pays the worker’s 5-second idle timeout. In that worst case the L40S figures become $3,675.00 (2s requests) and $7,875.00 (10s), and the L4 figures $1,458.33 and $3,125.00 — sparse traffic is where the idle-timeout setting earns its keep, and lengthening it to dodge cold starts quietly converts a serverless endpoint into a part-time instance. Second, concurrency: the sequential model is the worst case for AWS and the natural case for a single-stream worker. An AWS execution environment can serve up to 48 concurrent requests; under the stated assumption of perfect packing — every instance-hour fully shared — a million 2-second requests on a g6e would cost $23.84 at concurrency 48 and $142.04 at concurrency 8. Treat those as the floor the arithmetic allows, not a forecast: real packing is set by GPU memory and how parallel your model actually runs, and AWS scales on CPU utilisation and concurrency saturation signals, not on your hopes.

The break-even lines

Serverless and instance pricing cross at a utilisation, and on the L40S class the lines are close together:

ComparisonThe instance wins once the GPU is busy…

In request volume, at the Community pod’s $576.70 month: RunPod Serverless on the L40S class matches it at about 549,000 requests a month if each request takes 2 seconds, and at about 110,000 requests a month at 10 seconds each. Below those volumes, per-second billing is cheaper than the rent. Above them, you are paying a premium for flexibility you no longer use. The same shape of line exists on every card class — divide the flat hourly rate by the serverless hourly rate and you have the utilisation where the instance takes over.

Cold starts and warm floors — the part the pricing pages put elsewhere

RouteThe detail
AWSLambda Managed Instances does not scale like classic Lambda. AWS’s scaling documentation, read Nov 19, 2026, says scaling is asynchronous, driven by CPU utilisation and multi-concurrency saturation, and that traffic more than doubling within five minutes can throttle while capacity catches up. The default minimum is 3 execution environments across Availability Zones — a warm floor you pay for in provisioned instance time (environments pack onto instances, so the floor is not automatically three whole instances, but it is not zero either). Scale-to-zero exists but is a setting, not the default: set the minimum to 0 with a maximum above 0, and an idle function’s environments stop and its instances terminate, with charges running until termination completes, usually within minutes. The first invocation after that is throttled with an HTTP 429 while an environment starts — “typically a few minutes,” in AWS’s words, and longer for functions with long initialisation, which a GPU model load is. AWS’s own recommendation is to keep a minimum of at least 1 environment for latency-sensitive work, and 3 for AZ redundancy.
RunPodThe cold start is inside the bill by design: the meter starts when the worker starts, and the start phase — mostly your model loading into GPU memory — is charged at the same per-second rate. FlashBoot and model caching are RunPod’s mitigations, and its sub-200ms FlashBoot figure is the publisher’s claim for optimised workers. The 5-second default idle timeout is the other dial: long enough to absorb a burst, short enough that sparse traffic pays it constantly. There is no warm floor on Flex unless you buy one — Active workers are exactly that, at a price RunPod does not publish.
The instanceNo cold start, no throttle window, no scaling signal — the GPU is simply there. That is what the flat rate buys, and for latency-sensitive steady work it is often the real reason to pay it, ahead of the break-even arithmetic.

Watch-outs before you commit

Watch-outThe detail
New AWS accounts may not be able to run a GPU function at all on day oneAWS’s launch post warns that new accounts may start with a G-series quota of 0 — the “Running On-Demand G and VT instances” quota — and must request an increase before anything runs. Budget the request into your launch plan; it is a limit increase, not an instant toggle.
The 9.75% fee is charged on the On-Demand price, not on what you actually pay for the instanceAWS’s own pricing example computes the management fee from the undiscounted On-Demand rate while the instance line enjoys a Savings Plan discount. Commitments shrink one line of the bill and leave the other untouched.
“Serverless” at AWS does not mean the meter stops at zero by defaultWith the default minimum of 3 execution environments, an idle GPU function still holds provisioned capacity. Scale-to-zero must be switched on, and switching it on buys the 429-and-wait restart described above.
RunPod bills the cold start and the tailWorker start until handler-ready is charged, and so is the idle timeout after every burst. A 30-second job behind a 90-second model load is a 120-second bill, plus the tail. The execution timeout setting is the guard against a runaway job billing unattended — set it deliberately.
There is no published Active-worker priceRunPod’s docs route Active discounts through sales. If your design needs an always-warm RunPod worker, its true comparison is the pod price — $0.79/hr Community for an L40S — not a serverless rate.
Storage rides along on bothRunPod charges container disk at about $0.10/GB/month and network volumes at $0.07/GB/month under 1TB (its docs, read Nov 19, 2026). AWS functions get up to 32GB of ephemeral storage in the launch configuration; anything persistent lives in S3 or EBS at their own rates, which this guide does not price.
Data transfer is the quiet lineAWS gives 100GB of data transfer out to the internet free per month across services (its EC2 pricing page, read Nov 19, 2026); beyond that, per-GB rates apply. Neither provider’s per-GB transfer rates are in any figure in this guide — check them before a media-heavy launch rather than assuming either way.
Regional prices move the AWS columnEvery AWS figure here is US East (N. Virginia) On-Demand. G-series capacity and price vary by region, and Lambda picks among the instance types you allow — allow several, as AWS’s own walkthrough does, or a capacity crunch in one family becomes your outage.

Who should pick which

RouteWhen it wins
RunPod ServerlessPick RunPod Serverless if your inference is bursty, experimental or low-volume, you want the widest GPU menu of the two serverless routes (the only one that reaches H100, H200 and B300), and you can tolerate a billed cold start. Below roughly 549,000 two-second requests a month on an L40S class workload, it beats the cheapest instance rent; below 41.8% utilisation it beats it at any request length.
AWS Lambda GPU functionsPick AWS Lambda GPU functions if the workload is born inside AWS — event sources, VPC, IAM and billing already there — and especially if your serving stack packs concurrent requests onto one GPU, because concurrency is the lever that turns AWS’s provisioned-time pricing from the most expensive column into the cheapest. Switch scale-to-zero on for anything latency-tolerant, and file the G-series quota increase before launch day.
The always-on instancePick the always-on instance if traffic is steady past the break-even lines, if cold starts and throttle windows are unacceptable, or if you simply want the serving stack you already know. On the L40S, $576.70 a month at RunPod Community is the number both serverless routes have to beat, and at real volume neither does.

How we check

AWS pricing structure — the three components, the 9.75% GPU management fee, the $0.20 per million requests, the absence of a per-request duration charge, and the fee being computed on the On-Demand price in AWS’s worked example — is from the AWS Lambda pricing page, read first-hand Nov 19, 2026. EC2 On-Demand rates (g6.xlarge $0.8048/hr, g5.xlarge $1.006/hr, g6e.xlarge $1.861/hr, US East (N. Virginia), Linux) are from AWS’s Price List offer file for Amazon EC2, version published Nov 18, 2026, extracted and cross-checked against the file’s own price descriptions on Nov 19, 2026; EC2 per-second billing with a 60-second minimum and the 100GB free data-transfer allowance are from AWS’s EC2 On-Demand pricing page, read the same day. Scaling behaviour — asynchronous scaling, the default minimum of 3 execution environments, scale-to-zero as an opt-in setting, 429 throttling on restart from zero, “typically a few minutes” to first environment, and charges continuing until instance termination completes — is from AWS’s Lambda Managed Instances scaling documentation, read Nov 19, 2026. Launch scope (families, 3–48GB accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per environment, quota warning) is from AWS’s Nov 18, 2026 announcement as reported in our story of the same day. RunPod Serverless mechanics — billing from worker start to full stop rounded up to the nearest second, the three billed phases, the 5-second default idle timeout, Flex versus Active, and storage rates — are from RunPod’s Serverless pricing documentation, read Nov 19, 2026; the Flex rate ladder is from RunPod’s pricing page, read the same day. Instance prices are GPUJournal’s Nov 19, 2026 board snapshot: RunPod Community L40S $0.79/hr, RunPod Secure L40S $1.09/hr, Nebius L40S $1.55/hr (from-price, excl. VAT), CoreWeave L40S $2.25/hr, Verda L40S $2.08/hr. Every total, per-million figure and break-even in this guide is arithmetic on those inputs, computed by script; the worked-example assumptions (sequential serving, stated request durations, perfect-packing concurrency labelled as a floor) are stated where the figures appear. What is deliberately not claimed: no latency, throughput or tokens-per-dollar figure appears here as our finding. RunPod’s sub-200ms FlashBoot figure is printed as the publisher’s claim. No Active-worker rate is printed, because RunPod publishes none. No AWS figure uses a region other than US East (N. Virginia), a Savings Plan discount, or a fractional-GPU (G6f) configuration. The concurrency figures are arithmetic under a stated perfect-packing assumption, not measurements. Egress beyond AWS’s free 100GB is flagged, not priced.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. The interesting thing about AWS’s entry is what it declines to be. RunPod Serverless is a meter on GPU time; Lambda GPU is a managed fleet with a Lambda-shaped front door, priced like one — instance hours plus a percentage. That makes the honest comparison less “which serverless is cheaper” and more “what is your traffic’s shape.” Spiky and small: rent seconds. Steady and packed: the AWS percentage buys real operational relief, and concurrency does the rest. Steady and simple: the flat hourly instance remains the price both newcomers have to beat, and on today’s verified rates, past two-fifths utilisation, neither beats it.

Deploy Inkling 2 Mini — how to run it and what it actually costs

Inkling 2 Mini is the rare new model that is a one-card job. Thinking Machines Lab released the weights on Nov 20, 2026 as a single checkpoint of about 20GB — a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts whose middle layers loop three times per token — and the cheapest verified card that a serving framework has actually verified for it rents for $0.69 an hour. This guide works the two honest routes: run the checkpoint exactly as shipped on one 32GB card, or run it dequantized at full precision on an 80GB card — what each route needs, which serving commands are documented today, and what each costs at prices checked Nov 26, 2026. It also names the cheap cards that look like they fit and, as of today, are not verified to run it.

The verdict

  • Native checkpoint — cheapest verified — The checkpoint exactly as shipped (NVFP4 / MXFP8, 19.5GB file) on one RTX 5090 at RunPod Community — the cheapest card that clears the lab's 32GB floor and appears in a framework's verified matrix for this model: SGLang's cookbook verifies this exact card, single GPU, with context capped at 65,536 tokens (32,768 with speculative decoding on) to fit the KV cache.
  • Native checkpoint — room to breathe — The same shipped precision on a 96GB RTX PRO 6000 at RunPod Community, SGLang-verified on one GPU — three times the card memory, about six times the KV headroom once the weights are loaded. For long context and bigger batches.
  • Full precision — cheapest memory that fits — The checkpoint dequantized to a ~52.8GB BF16 working set on an A100 80GB at Thunder Compute, the cheapest 80GB rental on the board. Two cautions ride with this row: there is no official BF16 download, and no framework lists the A100 for this model — the framework check is still on you.
  • Full precision — framework-verified — The same ~52.8GB BF16 working set on an H100 PCIe at RunPod Community — vLLM verifies the H100 for this model, and its recipe caps context at 262,144 tokens there.
  • The tempting rows — NOT verified for this model today — RTX A6000 at Thunder Compute ($0.35/hr, $255.50/mo) and L40S at RunPod Community ($0.79/hr, $576.70/mo) are real prices for real cards — but neither vLLM's recipe nor SGLang's verified matrix lists an Ampere or Ada card for this model, and at 48GB both are also too small for the dequantized full-precision load. Cheap is only cheap if it runs; the verification detail is in the serving section.
Compare GPU prices across every provider→Inkling 2 Mini in the catalogue — every card ranked→

The short answer

Rent one RTX 5090 and run the checkpoint as shipped. The weights file is 19.53GB (plus a 0.64GB bundled draft head for speculative decoding), the lab's own hardware floor is a GPU with 32GB or more of VRAM, and SGLang's cookbook has a verified single-GPU recipe for exactly this card — with one honest limit: on 32GB it caps the context at 65,536 tokens (32,768 with speculative decoding on) to fit the KV cache. At RunPod Community's $0.69/hr, checked Nov 21, 2026, that is $503.70 for a 730-hour month. If you need long context or several long sessions at once, step up to the 96GB RTX PRO 6000 at $1.69/hr rather than to a data-centre card: same shipped precision, SGLang-verified on one GPU, and three times the card memory — about six times the KV headroom once the weights are loaded. If you need the model at full BF16 precision — for fine-tuning, evaluation against the lab's numbers, or because your stack dequantizes on load anyway — you are renting an 80GB card and paying $1.09–$1.99/hr, and you should read the full-precision section first: Thinking Machines does not publish a BF16 checkpoint, so that route starts with a conversion, not a download.

What you are actually downloading — model card and repo file listing, read Nov 21, 2026

The factThe detail
26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active per tokenA 24-layer decoder-only transformer with sparse MoE feed-forward layers: each token routes to 8 of 128 experts. The middle 12 layers (6–17) run three times with shared weights, so each token makes 48 layer visits, and the lab counts 5.4B effective active parameters once the extra passes are included.
One checkpoint file of 19.53GBmodel-00001-of-00001.safetensors, plus mtp.safetensors at 0.64GB — the bundled DSpark draft head used for speculative decoding. The whole repo, tokenizers included, is 20.19GB. The card's “about 20GB” is exact.
Mixed precision, as trainedThe routed experts of layers 0–19 are NVFP4 and layers 20–23 are MXFP8 (the repo config confirms a ModelOpt NVFP4 quantization setup). This is the model's native format, not a post-release squeeze — there is no higher-precision original to download.
Multimodal, 1M-token contextText and image in, text out, via a 23-layer vision encoder. Context window up to 1M tokens (the config's maximum position count is 1,048,576).
Licence: Apache 2.0Declared on the card — the details, and one honest footnote, are in the licence table below.

Route one: the 20GB checkpoint on a single card (prices checked Nov 21, 2026)

This is the route the model was built for. The lab lists three supported hardware classes on the card: one NVIDIA DGX Spark, Apple silicon with 32GB or more of memory, and other GPUs with 32GB or more of VRAM recommended. Note the floor is the maker's: the 20.19GB of files would physically squeeze onto a 24GB card, but the lab does not recommend it, and the frameworks' own context caps below show why — what is left after the weights is what your conversations live in.

Why the 5090 is the headline: it is the cheapest card on our board that clears the lab's 32GB floor and appears in a framework's verified matrix for this specific model. The A6000 at $0.35/hr is cheaper and bigger on paper — but “the lab says 32GB+ GPUs generally” is not the same as “a serving stack has run this looped, NVFP4-native model on Ampere.” Until a framework verifies it, treat the A6000 and L40S rows as an experiment you would be running, not a deployment you are buying.

The memory maths: why context, not weights, sets your card

Worked from the repo's own config, Nov 21, 2026. Inkling 2 Mini keeps 48 KV caches — one per layer visit, because every pass through the looped core keeps its own keys and values (the vLLM recipe and the Transformers documentation both state this).

The figureHow it is derived
4,096 bytes per token, per cacheEach cache costs, per token, 8 KV heads × 128 head dimension × 2 (keys and values) = 2,048 values, which at BF16 is 4,096 bytes per token per cache.
About 206GB — the impossible boundIf all 48 caches grew to the full sequence, a 1M-token context would need about 206GB of KV cache — impossible, and not what happens: 20 of the 24 stored layers are sliding-window layers whose caches stop growing at the config's 1,024-token window. Only the 4 full-attention layers' caches grow with your context.
Roughly 17GB to 35GB for one 1M-token sequenceDepending on how many of those 4 full-attention layers sit inside the looped core (the split is not published), the KV cache for one full 1M-token sequence works out at roughly 17GB to 35GB — arithmetic under a stated assumption, not a measurement.
About 11.8GB left on a 32GB cardOn the RTX 5090 the weights and draft head take 20.19GB of the 32GB, leaving about 11.8GB for KV cache, activations and the runtime — plan your context around the caps, not around the 1M on the box.

The operative numbers are the frameworks' own: vLLM fits about 1.8 concurrent 1M-token requests on one GB200 (192GB), caps H100 and DGX Spark at 262,144 tokens, and SGLang caps the 32GB RTX 5090 at 65,536 (32,768 with the draft head on).

Route two: full precision — the BF16 working set

There is no official BF16 checkpoint. The lab ships NVFP4/MXFP8 only, so a “full-precision deployment” means one of two things, and both start from the same arithmetic: 26.4B parameters × 2 bytes = 52.8GB of weights (script-computed from the card's parameter count; a community BF16 conversion measures 52.2GB on disk, which corroborates the derivation).

The routeWhat it means
Transformers dequantizes on loadThe Transformers documentation states plainly that both checkpoints' NVFP4 and MXFP8 layers are dequantized when loading — so a Transformers deployment carries a ~52.8GB working set even though the download is 20GB. That is the honest way to run it for research, fine-tuning prep and evaluation; it is not the fast serving path (attention runs in eager mode only in this first implementation, contributed to Transformers on Nov 21, 2026).
Community GGUF conversionsllama.cpp-format conversions include a BF16 build at 52.2GB — a third-party dequantization, not a lab artifact, and as of today the looped model needs an unmerged llama.cpp pull request (ggml-org/llama.cpp#32695) to load at all. Labelled here as community and unproven for production, because that is what it is.

Memory consequence: 52.8GB of weights plus KV cache does not fit a 48GB card at all, and fits an 80GB card with roughly 27GB to spare. The cheapest 80GB rentals on our board, checked Nov 21, 2026: A100 80GB at Thunder Compute, $1.09/hr ($795.70/month), and A100 80GB PCIe at RunPod Community, $1.19/hr ($868.70/month). One caution that belongs with those prices: neither vLLM's recipe (Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark) nor SGLang's matrix (B300/GB300, B200/GB200, H200, RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090, DGX Spark, AMD MI350X/MI355X, TPU7x) lists the A100 for this model — the A100 rows are the cheapest memory that fits the BF16 working set, with the framework check still on you. The cheapest full-precision home that a framework has verified is the H100: vLLM-verified, $1.99/hr at RunPod Community ($1,452.70/month), context capped at 262,144 tokens in its recipe. Who this route is for: fine-tuners and evaluators who need the weights at full precision, and teams whose existing stack is Transformers-shaped. Who it is not for: anyone serving traffic. The native checkpoint is the model as trained — serving it dequantized buys you memory bills, not accuracy the lab ever claimed.

Serving: what is documented today (framework pages read Nov 21, 2026)

FrameworkWhat is documented
vLLM — dedicated reciperecipes.vllm.ai/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini. Until support lands in a vLLM release, the recipe specifies the pinned image vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini. Its documented serve command, with the bundled DSpark speculative decoding enabled: vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini --tensor-parallel-size 1 --reasoning-parser inkling --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'. The recipe verifies the model on GB200, B300, GB300, H100, H200 and DGX Spark; TP1 is its recommended shape (“the most efficient way to serve the model”), with the full 1,048,576-token context on one GB200 and a 262,144-token cap on H100 and DGX Spark. Drop the speculative-config line and you have the plain decode setup.
SGLang — full cookbookA full cookbook page with verified launch recipes per platform, using the pinned image lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini. Its verified matrix is the widest of the three: B300/GB300, B200/GB200, H200, RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090 and DGX Spark on one GPU each (TP1/EP1), plus AMD MI350X/MI355X and TPU7x images. The recipes pass --reasoning-parser inkling and --tool-call-parser inkling2 explicitly, and --enable-multimodal for image input. On the RTX 5090 its context caps are 65,536 tokens (Balanced) and 32,768 (DSpark).
Hugging Face Transformers — the research routeThe architecture (Inkling2LoopForConditionalGeneration) was contributed to Transformers on Nov 21, 2026, with official model documentation and a pipeline example: pipeline("image-text-to-text", model="thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini", dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto"). Proven as a documented route, with the documentation's own caveats attached: the quantized layers are dequantized on load (so budget the ~52.8GB working set, not 20GB), and attention runs in eager mode only. This is the research and integration route, not the throughput route.

Named honestly — listed, community, or not yet verified

RouteStatus today
llama.cpp / GGUFListed by the lab for quantized GGUF versions, but the looped architecture loads only via an unmerged pull request (ggml-org/llama.cpp#32695) as of Nov 21, 2026, and the GGUF files themselves are community conversions. Fine for local experiments; not a production serving route today.
TokenSpeed and NVIDIA DynamoNamed on the lab's card as supported frameworks. We did not verify a model-specific recipe for either first-hand today, so this guide asserts nothing about their setup or hardware.
Ollama and MLX buildsThe lab lists Ollama on Apple silicon, and community MLX conversions exist — desktop routes, outside this guide's rental scope.
Ampere and Ada cards (A100 serving, A6000, L40S, RTX 4090)No framework verification for this model found today. The 24GB RTX 4090 fails earlier anyway: the lab's floor is 32GB+ and the files alone are 20.19GB.

The lab's benchmarks, in the lab's own frame

Every number in this table is Thinking Machines' own published table from the model card — the lab's harnesses and settings, not independent results, and not ours. The comparison is against the dense Qwen3.8-27B, the comparison the launch leans on.

SWE-bench Verified (bash only)79.2%77.8%
