The honest summary of the lab's own framing: a 3.4B-active MoE that ties a dense 27B on the lab's headline index and beats it on the lab's coding benches, while trailing it on several agentic, knowledge-work and vision rows of the same table. The card is also unusually plain about the weak spots — multi-turn conversation, factual recall bounded by size, and agents that “may take destructive actions… without confirmation” in the lab's own words. Budget your own evaluation before believing any row, in either direction.

Licence — Apache 2.0, and the contrast is real

The pointThe detail
Apache 2.0, declared on the cardThe card declares Apache 2.0, and the repository metadata agrees. Apache 2.0 is the whole licence: use it commercially, serve it, fine-tune it, with no revenue trigger, no user-count trigger and no separate licence to negotiate. Set that beside the Tencent Hy licences examined elsewhere on this site — where reselling inference above a $50M revenue line or 100M monthly users needs a separate licence — and the contrast is exactly as clean as it looks: nothing in the Apache 2.0 text reaches into your business that way.
Footnote one: no standalone LICENSE fileAs of Nov 21, 2026 the repo's file listing contains no standalone LICENSE file — the licence is declared on the card and in the repo metadata; keep a copy of the card with your deployment records.
Footnote two: an Acceptable Use Policy linkThe card also links the lab's Model Acceptable Use Policy alongside the licence, as it did for Inkling 2 Small — a policy link to read, not a licence condition we can quote you chapter and verse on here. Neither footnote changes the headline.

Watch-outs before you rent

Watch-outThe detail
Looped-model support is days oldThe card itself warns that “support for looped models in local runtimes is new, and speed varies by runtime and hardware.” vLLM support lives in a pinned image, not a release; Transformers support was contributed the day this guide was drafted. Pin your images and expect movement.
Context on the box is not context on your card1M tokens is the model's maximum. The verified caps today: 65,536 on a 32GB 5090 (SGLang), 262,144 on H100 (vLLM), the full 1,048,576 only on a GB200 in vLLM's verified set. Size your card to the context you will actually run.
The agent warnings are the lab's, and they are bluntThe card reports repetitive reasoning loops in debugging, tool use that is less reliable than larger models, and possible destructive file actions without confirmation. Its own advice: sandbox agentic workloads, require confirmation before irreversible actions, and cap output tokens and agent turns.
Reasoning effort never fully turns offSetting it to minimum does not disable reasoning (card, limitations) — and with 48 layer visits per token, compute per token is higher than the 3.4B active figure suggests. Do not budget throughput off the active-parameter count alone.
Speculative decoding gains are prompt-dependentvLLM's recipe notes DSpark acceptance depends on prompts and temperature — random-token benchmarks accept almost nothing. Benchmark on text that looks like your traffic.
The cheap-card trapThe two cheapest ≥32GB rows on the board (A6000 $0.35/hr, L40S $0.79/hr) are not in any framework's verified matrix for this model today, and both are too small for the dequantized load. Verify before you commit a month to them.

Who should run this, and how

Your workloadThe route
Coding-agent and tool-use workloads on a budgetThe native route on an RTX 5090 at $0.69/hr. That is the deployment the release was designed for — one card, the shipped precision, SGLang's verified recipe, sandboxed per the lab's own advice.
Long-document and long-session servingThe RTX PRO 6000 at $1.69/hr. The 96GB is not about the weights; it is about KV cache headroom the 32GB card does not have.
Fine-tuning, evaluation, researchThe BF16 route on an 80GB card — Transformers dequantizes on load, and the varloop research checkpoint (released alongside, loop passes adjustable from the research repo) exists for exactly this audience. Pay the $1.09–$1.99/hr knowing the A100 rows carry a framework check and the H100 row is the verified one.
Production serving at volumevLLM or SGLang on Hopper or Blackwell, where both frameworks have verified the model — and run your own benchmark first, because every performance claim available today is the maker's.

How we check

Model facts — 26.4B total / 3.4B active / 5.4B effective parameters, 24 layers with the middle 12 looped three times, 8 of 128 experts, NVFP4 experts in layers 0–19 and MXFP8 in layers 20–23, 1M-token context, the 32GB+ hardware recommendation and the Apache 2.0 declaration — are from Thinking Machines Lab's Hugging Face model card, read first-hand Nov 21, 2026. Checkpoint sizes (19.53GB main file, 0.64GB DSpark draft, 20.19GB total) are the repository's own file sizes via the Hugging Face API, read the same day. Architecture figures used in the KV maths — 8 KV heads, 128 head dimension, 1,024-token sliding window, 48 caches at one per layer visit — are from the repo's config.json and the Transformers model documentation, read Nov 21, 2026; the 20 sliding-window / 4 full-attention layer split is from the vLLM recipe. Serving verification is from the frameworks' own pages read the same day: the vLLM recipe (pinned image, serve command, verified hardware, context caps, ~1.8 concurrent 1M-token requests on GB200, DSpark prompt-dependence), the SGLang cookbook (pinned image, verified matrix including RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 at TP1, parser flags, 5090 context caps), and the Transformers documentation (dequantize-on-load, eager attention, pipeline example, contributed Nov 21, 2026). Prices are GPUJournal's Nov 21, 2026 board snapshot: RTX 5090 RunPod Community $0.69/hr and Secure $1.39/hr; RTX PRO 6000 RunPod Community $1.69/hr and Nebius $1.80/hr; RTX A6000 Thunder Compute $0.35/hr; L40S RunPod Community $0.79/hr; A100 80GB Thunder Compute $1.09/hr and RunPod Community PCIe $1.19/hr; H100 PCIe RunPod Community $1.99/hr; H200 RunPod Community $3.59/hr. Monthly figures are hourly × 730. The BF16 weight figure (52.8GB) is arithmetic — 26.4B × 2 bytes — corroborated by a community BF16 GGUF conversion's measured 52.2GB on disk. The KV range (17–35GB at 1M tokens) is arithmetic under a stated assumption about the unpublished full-attention layer split, presented as a range for that reason. What is deliberately not claimed. No throughput, latency or tokens-per-dollar figure appears here as our finding — we ran no benchmarks, and every benchmark number printed is the lab's own table, labelled as such. No serving route is asserted beyond what the framework's own page documents: TokenSpeed and NVIDIA Dynamo are named as lab-listed only, llama.cpp GGUF is labelled community-plus-unmerged-PR, and Ampere/Ada cards are labelled unverified for this model because neither vLLM's recipe nor SGLang's matrix lists them as of Nov 21, 2026. The proposal-stage estimate of “~80GB” for the BF16 route did not survive the arithmetic and is not used: the derived figure is 52.8GB.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. The interesting thing about Inkling 2 Mini is not the loop; it is the shape of the bill. A frontier-adjacent coding model whose honest deployment is a $0.69-an-hour consumer card changes who gets to experiment: the rental question stops being “can we afford the cluster” and becomes “is a days-old runtime stable enough to build on.” On today's evidence the weights, the licence and the price are the solid parts. The runtimes are the moving part — and this guide's verified/unverified split is the map of exactly where the ground is still soft.

MODEL DEPLOYMENT →  ·  2026-11-22 · 16 min read

Deploy Hy4 on an 8-GPU node — the FP8 route, costed

Hy4 is Tencent's 770-billion-parameter flagship, and its FP8 checkpoint measures 786.31GB on disk — which is why every serving recipe is built around a single node, eight GPUs or four of the largest cards. This guide works the deployment the way a renter has to: the measured weights, the memory arithmetic that rules the H100 out outright, the two documented serving routes with their exact launch commands, what a node costs at prices checked Nov 22, 2026, and the licence clause that has to be read before the node is rented, not after.

The verdict

  • 8 × H200 — cheapest documented shape — Per-GPU rate × 8. Both frameworks document exactly this shape (TP8); whether a given provider sells you all eight in one node is a checkout question, not a pricing-page one.
  • 4 × B300 — half the GPUs, similar money — SGLang documents this shape (TP4 on B300/GB300); vLLM's recipe is TP8-only. Per-GPU rate × 4.
  • 8 × H200 — sold as a node — The per-GPU figure is normalised from CoreWeave's own 8-GPU node price — this row is a node you can actually buy as a node.
  • 8 × B200 — headroom and Blackwell — 749.7GB spare after the FP8 weights, against 341.7GB on H200 — the room shows up as KV cache and batch size. Per-GPU rate × 8.
  • 4 × GB300 — sold as a node — Oracle's offer is a 4-GPU node at $72.00/node/hr, matching SGLang's TP4 GB300 shape. Premium iron, premium bill.
  • The BF16 route — 8 × B300 — Full precision weighs 1,548.93GB and fits no smaller single node in either framework's documentation. The FP8 route is the deployment; this is 2.06× its cheapest monthly bill.
  • NOT an option — 8 × H100 — 8 × 80GB = 640GB of memory against 786.31GB of FP8 weights. The weights alone do not fit, before any KV cache. Cheapest H100 row shown (TensorDock, 8-GPU minimum) only to close the question.
Compare GPU prices across every provider→Hy4 in the catalogue — every card ranked→

The short answer

Rent eight H200s (or four B300s), download tencent/Hy4-FP8, and serve it with one of the two pinned images Tencent points to — vLLM's vllm/vllm-openai:hy4 or SGLang's lmsysorg/sglang:hy4 — at tensor parallelism 8 (or 4 on B300-class cards under SGLang). The cheapest verified version of that node on our board, checked Nov 22, 2026, is RunPod Community's H200 at $3.59 per GPU per hour: $28.72 an hour for the node, $20,965.60 for a 730-hour month. Everything else in this guide is the working behind those three sentences — the measured weights, the memory arithmetic that rules the H100 out and the BF16 checkpoint off a single H200/B200 node, the exact commands, and the licence gate. One disambiguation that matters, because the names are close: this guide is about Hy4, the 770B flagship whose weights landed Nov 20, 2026. It is not about Hy4 Flash, the 220B/12B sibling released Nov 17 — a different model with a different bill, covered by its own guide.

What you are actually downloading — model cards, configs and file listings, read Nov 22, 2026

The factThe detail
770B total parameters, 49B active per token770B total parameters in the language backbone, 49B active per token (plus 1.23B of vision encoder and the 3.3B DFly2 drafter — about 774B stored in total). 78 layers: the first is a dense FFN, the other 77 are MoE with 256 routed experts plus 1 shared, top-8 routed experts firing per token. Attention is gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention over multi-head latent attention, with a sparse indexer selecting the top 2,048 positions per token.
The FP8 checkpoint measures 786.31GBThe FP8 checkpoint (tencent/Hy4-FP8) measures 786.31GB — 245 safetensors shards, summed from the repo's file listing. The card's “about 0.79TB” is honest rounding. It is block FP8 (e4m3, 128×128 blocks) for the routed experts and most projections; the vision tower, the first layer's attention and dense MLP, the shared experts, the DSA indexer and lm_head stay in BF16 — which is why the file is bigger than a naive one-byte-per-parameter figure (~774GB).
The BF16 checkpoint measures 1,548.93GBThe BF16 checkpoint (tencent/Hy4) measures 1,548.93GB, also 245 shards; the pre-trained base (tencent/Hy4-base) measures 1,542.35GB. The serving recipes are written for the FP8 build; the BF16 build's role in the frameworks' own documentation is mostly as a warning (see the memory section).
Context: 1,048,576 tokensContext: 1,048,576 tokens, confirmed in the repo config (max_position_embeddings) and the card. What the recipes have actually been evaluated at is a shorter story — vLLM's recipe starts from an evaluated window of 131,072 tokens and states plainly that a full 1M-token request has not been validated for it.
MultimodalText, image and video in, text out, with computer use across CLI and GUI. The vLLM recipe's default allows one image per prompt and video off, as on the card.
The DFly2 drafter is inside both checkpointsFive draft layers that share the target model's KV cache and sparse indices, so speculative decoding costs no extra KV memory. Tencent's card credits it with constant draft cost regardless of context length; that is Tencent's claim, stated as theirs.
Licence: Tencent Hy LicenseThe Tencent Hy License, version 1.0 — Apache-derived, with the §10 gate covered in its own section below. The repo metadata tag is license:other; there is no Apache 2.0 grant here, whatever you may have read about the earlier Hy4-preview checkpoint, which is a separate release under a different licence.

The memory maths: why the node looks like this — worked from the measured checkpoint and the repo config, Nov 22, 2026

The figureHow it is derived
98.3GB of weights per GPU at TP8The FP8 weights are 786.31GB. Split eight ways at tensor parallelism 8, that is 98.3GB of weights per GPU before KV cache, activations or the runtime — the single number that decides every card verdict below.
8 × H100 (80GB each, 640GB total): does not fitThe weights alone exceed the node's whole memory by 146.3GB, and the per-GPU share (98.3GB) exceeds one card (80GB) on its own. No context length, batch size or framework flag fixes a weights-don't-fit problem. This is the honest negative: the H100 is simply not a Hy4 card at FP8, and at BF16 it is not close.
8 × H200 (141GB each, 1,128GB total): fits, with 341.7GB to spareAbout 42.7GB per GPU after weights for KV cache and working room. vLLM's recipe states the FP8 build needs about 944GB of aggregate GPU memory; an H200 node clears that with 184GB spare. This is the documented, cheapest shape.
8 × B200 (192GB each, 1,536GB total): fits with 749.7GB spareNote the near-miss in the other direction: 4 × B200 is 768GB, which is less than the 786.31GB of weights — there is no four-B200 shortcut, which is exactly why SGLang's four-GPU recipes are B300/GB300-only.
4 × B300 (288GB each, 1,152GB total): fits with 365.7GB spareThe TP4 shape SGLang documents.
BF16 is a different purchase1,548.93GB of weights exceeds even 8 × B200 (1,536GB) by 12.9GB — SGLang's cookbook says in so many words that the BF16 weights exceed TP8 on H200/B200 and TP4 on B300/GB300, with no BF16 recipe offered. vLLM puts the BF16 aggregate requirement at about 1,859GB and its example shape is 8 × B300 (2,304GB). On one node, full precision means B300-class cards or nothing.
KV cache, worked from the configThe attention is MLA, so each token's cache is the latent vector — kv_lora_rank 512 plus the 64-dimension RoPE key — 576 values per layer per token. At BF16 that is 1,152 bytes × 78 layers = 89,856 bytes per token. One full 1,048,576-token sequence therefore carries about 94.2GB of KV cache across the node: about 11.8GB per GPU if the cache is sharded evenly at TP8, up to the full 94.2GB per GPU in layouts where each rank holds the whole latent cache — the frameworks' parallelism options (DP-attention and decode context parallelism in SGLang) move you between those ends, so the honest figure is the range, with the layout named. The DSA indexer's own keys are excluded — the config does not give a derivable per-token size for them once IndexCache cross-layer reuse is accounted for, and we do not guess. The DFly2 drafter adds no KV of its own (it shares the target's cache, per the card and both framework pages). At the vLLM recipe's evaluated 131,072-token window, the same arithmetic gives about 11.8GB per sequence across the node — which is why the recipes' real constraint is the KV pool, not the 1M on the box.

Serving: what is documented today — proven routes (framework pages read Nov 22, 2026)

FrameworkWhat is documented
vLLMTencent's card points to a dedicated recipe (recipes.vllm.ai/tencent/Hy4) and a pinned official image, vllm/vllm-openai:hy4. The card's own launch line, reproduced exactly: "docker run --gpus all --privileged --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface -e VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 vllm/vllm-openai:hy4 tencent/Hy4-FP8 --dtype bfloat16 --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image":1,"video":0}' --tensor-parallel-size 8 --enable-auto-tool-choice --reasoning-parser hy_v4 --tool-call-parser hy_v4 --speculative-config '{"num_speculative_tokens":5,"method":"dfly"}' --attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE --port 8000 --served-model-name hy4" The recipe's own conditions, stated on its page: one 8-GPU NVIDIA node; the FP8 build needs about 944GB of aggregate GPU memory and the BF16 build about 1,859GB (its BF16 example is 8 × B300); host memory and disk must hold the checkpoint (786GB FP8 / 1,549GB BF16, 245 shards each). Release vLLM does not have this model yet — v0.34.0 does not register the architecture, and 0.35.0 will be the first release with it — so today the route is the pinned image or a nightly wheel. DFly2 requires the data, pipeline and context parallel sizes to stay at 1, which is why the recipe is single-node TP only. AMD Instinct is explicitly not supported in vLLM: its ROCm port has neither the vision encoder nor the DFly2 drafter. The recipe starts from an evaluated window of 131,072 tokens with 32 concurrent sequences; the card's launch line sets no cap and so serves the full 1M window, and the recipe states a full 1M-token request has not been validated.
SGLangA full cookbook page with a command generator and two strategies, using the pinned official image lmsysorg/sglang:hy4 (multi-arch, x86 and Arm). The card's launch line, reproduced exactly: "docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:hy4 ; docker run --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 lmsysorg/sglang:hy4 sglang serve --model-path tencent/Hy4-FP8 --tp 8 --speculative-algorithm DFLY --port 8000 --served-model-name hy4" The cookbook documents the FP8 checkpoint at TP8 on 8 × H200/B200 and at TP4 on 4 × B300/GB300, with automatic memory sizing — no recipe pins a context length, so the server takes the declared 1,048,576 and the KV pool bounds what actually fits at once. Its two strategies split on the drafter: Low-Latency runs DFly2 speculative decoding for interactive traffic, High-Throughput drops it for multi-user and batch traffic. Two conditions worth knowing before you build on the Low-Latency recipe: DFly2 verifies drafts greedily, so requests that set sampling parameters (temperature, top_k, top_p) are rejected unless they also force greedy decoding; and grammar-constrained tool calls are refused there too — the cookbook routes both to the High-Throughput recipe. Its worked examples were run on H200. For the BF16 checkpoint the cookbook offers no recipe at all: “the weights exceed TP8 on H200/B200 and TP4 on B300/GB300.”

Named honestly — listed, testing-only, or not documented

RouteStatus today
GGUFTencent's AngelSlim project publishes a Hy4 GGUF build, and the card describes it as provided “for end-to-end testing purposes.” That is the maker's own framing — a testing artifact, not a documented production serving route, and no node recipe accompanies it.
TransformersThe repos declare the transformers library in their metadata, but neither Tencent's card nor the frameworks' pages document a Transformers serving route for Hy4, and we found none today. The documented deployment routes are the two pinned images above; treat anything else as an experiment you are running.
AMD / ROCmExplicitly unsupported in vLLM (above), and SGLang's Hy4 cookbook documents NVIDIA shapes only. There is no documented AMD route for this model today.
Anything below eight Hopper-class cards, or four B300-classNo recipe exists, and the memory maths in this guide shows why — the FP8 weights alone need 98.3GB per GPU at TP8. Pipeline-parallel or multi-node shapes beyond the recipes are undocumented for Hy4 as of today; DFly2 in vLLM actively requires the parallel sizes that would enable them to stay at 1.

Licence — the §10 gate sits in the decision path (Tencent Hy License, version 1.0)

The pointThe detail
§10.2, quoted exactly“if You operate a MaaS business, You must obtain a separate written license to use the Work or any Derivative Works from Licensor (including by email), in either of the following cases: (a) if Your aggregate worldwide gross revenue exceeds US$50 million (or the equivalent in other currencies) in any consecutive 12-month period, whether or not such revenue is derived from the Work or any Derivative Works, before using (or continuing to use) the Work or any Derivative Works; or (b) before using the Work or any Derivative Works in or for any product or service provided by You that has more than 100 million monthly active users in any calendar month.”
“MaaS” is defined broadly (§10.1)Giving third parties remote access to model inference or fine-tuning, e.g. via API — though end-user products that confine the model to specific features or workflows, without general-purpose model access, are excluded from the definition.
The revenue trigger is your whole business§10.2(a) counts aggregate worldwide gross revenue “whether or not such revenue is derived from the Work.”
Internal use is carved out (§10.3)§10.2 “does not apply to Your use of the Work or any Derivative Works solely for internal purposes, provided that neither the Work, any Derivative Works, nor their outputs are made available to third parties.” Licensing requests go to hy_partners@tencent.com (§10.4).
What this means in the decision pathIf you are renting the node to run Hy4 for your own organisation, §10.3 covers you and the licence otherwise behaves like its Apache base. If you are renting it to sell inference, you are a MaaS business by the licence's definition, and the two triggers — US$50M worldwide revenue in any 12 months, or a product over 100M monthly active users — decide whether Tencent's written licence has to come before your first rented hour. Below both lines, no separate licence is required by §10. That ordering is the point of printing it here: the check costs an email; discovering it after a month at $28.72 an hour costs more.

Watch-outs before you rent

Watch-outThe detail
The 1M context is declared, not validatedvLLM's recipe evaluates 131,072 tokens and states a full 1M-token request has not been validated for it; SGLang pins no context cap and lets the KV pool decide. Budget your context from the KV arithmetic (about 94.2GB per full-length sequence across the node), not from the number on the box.
You are deploying on pinned imagesRelease vLLM (v0.34.0) does not register this architecture at all; the routes are Tencent-tagged images (:hy4) or nightlies, with 0.35.0 slated as the first release carrying it. Pin the tags, and expect the ground to move when the release lands.
The download is part of the deployment786.31GB of shards — 1,548.93GB for the BF16 build — has to land on the node before anything serves, and vLLM's recipe calls for host memory enough to load the checkpoint. On a rented node, that transfer and staging time is billed time; stage the checkpoint before you start the serving clock where the provider allows it.
DFly2's fast path is greedy-only in SGLangThe Low-Latency recipe rejects sampled and grammar-constrained requests by design; if your traffic samples, you are on the High-Throughput recipe and should benchmark that one.
Tencent's own limitation statement is plainThe card says a notable gap remains to top proprietary models on research-level mathematics, long-horizon coding, model self-improvement and advanced visual question answering. Every benchmark on the card is Tencent's own evaluation; no independent evaluation exists yet. Evaluate on your own workload before the monthly commitment, not after.
Per-GPU prices are not node pricesMost rows in the cost tables are a verified per-GPU rate multiplied by the GPU count. An 8-GPU NVLink node in one chassis is a specific product; where the distinction matters, the node-priced rows (CoreWeave, Oracle) are the ones that remove the doubt.

Who should run this, and how

Your workloadThe route
Internal teams evaluating a flagship open modelThe FP8 route on 8 × H200 at the cheapest verified row. §10.3 keeps internal use clear of the gate, the recipes are documented end to end, and $28.72/hr buys a real answer about whether 49B-active flagship quality changes your product.
Inference resellers below the §10 triggersThe same node, with the licence arithmetic done first and kept on file. Your constraint is not the hardware table; it is the revenue and user-count lines, and they are measured on your whole business and your whole product.
Anyone above either triggerThe first step is an email to hy_partners@tencent.com, not a rental. The guide's prices will still be here when the written licence is.
Throughput-first serving on newer siliconSGLang's TP4 shape on 4 × B300 — near-identical monthly money to the H200 node at Hyperstack's rate, with the High-Throughput recipe for sampled, multi-user traffic.
Full-precision researchThe BF16 checkpoint on 8 × B300, knowing it is 2.06× the FP8 node's monthly cost and that SGLang offers it no recipe — vLLM's aggregate figure and example shape are the documentation that exists.
Everyone elseIf your workload fits a smaller open model, it almost certainly costs a tenth of this node. Hy4's bill is a flagship bill; rent it for the work only a flagship does.

How we check

Model facts — 770B backbone parameters (49B active per token, plus the 1.23B vision encoder and 3.3B DFly2 drafter, ~774B stored), 78 layers (1 dense, 77 MoE), 256 routed experts plus 1 shared with top-8 firing, gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention over MLA with a top-2,048 sparse indexer, 1,048,576-token context — are from Tencent's Hugging Face model cards for tencent/Hy4-FP8 and tencent/Hy4 and the repos' config.json, read first-hand Nov 22, 2026. Checkpoint sizes are measured, not quoted: the safetensors shard sizes in each repo's file listing (Hugging Face API) sum to 786.31GB for Hy4-FP8 (245 shards), 1,548.93GB for Hy4 (245 shards) and 1,542.35GB for Hy4-base (280 shards). Card capacities (H100 80GB, H200 141GB, B200 192GB, B300 288GB) are the makers' headline HBM figures; no verdict in this guide flips at the lower HGX-board variants (180GB B200 / 270GB B300) — FP8 still fits, BF16 still does not. The KV figure is arithmetic from the config: (kv_lora_rank 512 + qk_rope_head_dim 64) × 2 bytes × 78 layers = 89,856 bytes per token; the DSA indexer's keys are excluded as not derivable from the config under IndexCache reuse, and DFly2 adds no KV by design. Serving verification is from the frameworks' own pages read Nov 22, 2026: the model card's Deployment section (both launch lines reproduced verbatim), the vLLM recipe (pinned image, TP8-only shape, ~944GB FP8 / ~1,859GB BF16 aggregate requirements, v0.34.0 not registering the architecture, 131,072-token evaluated window, 1M unvalidated, AMD unsupported) and the SGLang cookbook (TP8 H200/B200 and TP4 B300/GB300 shapes, BF16 offered no recipe, DFly2 greedy-only and grammar restrictions, examples run on H200). The licence quotations are from the LICENSE file (Tencent Hy License, version 1.0) shipped in both repos, read the same day. Prices are GPUJournal's Nov 22, 2026 board snapshot: H200 — RunPod Community $3.59, Hyperstack $3.99, RunPod Secure $5.29, Nebius $5.40 (excl. VAT), CoreWeave $6.31 (normalised from its $50.44/node/hr), Verda $7.043; B200 — RunPod Community $5.98, Hyperstack $6.00, Lambda $7.69, RunPod Secure $7.99, CoreWeave $8.60 (from $68.80/node/hr), Verda $9.747; B300 — Hyperstack $7.40, RunPod Secure $8.99, Nebius $9.50 (excl. VAT); GB300 — Oracle OCI $18.00 (4-GPU node at $72.00/node/hr); H100 SXM — TensorDock $2.25 (8-GPU minimum) shown only for the does-not-fit row. Node totals are per-GPU × GPU count and monthly figures are node-hourly × 730, computed exactly, except CoreWeave and Oracle, whose node prices are the providers' own. What is deliberately not claimed. No throughput, latency or tokens-per-dollar figure appears here as our finding — we ran no benchmarks, and the only performance-adjacent claims printed (DFly2's constant draft cost, the recipes' evaluated windows) are attributed to Tencent or the frameworks. Tencent's benchmark tables are not reproduced: they are the maker's own evaluations, our story covers the release, and no independent evaluation exists yet. No serving route is asserted beyond what the card, the vLLM recipe and the SGLang cookbook document: the GGUF build is labelled testing-only in the maker's own words, Transformers is labelled undocumented for this model, and multi-node shapes are labelled undocumented. Tencent's API prices for Hy4 are not used — we did not verify them from a Tencent source today. The proposal-stage “~0.79TB” for the FP8 checkpoint survives only as the card's rounding; the guide's working figure is the measured 786.31GB.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Hy4 is the first open flagship where the deployment question is not really technical. The recipes are short, pinned and documented; the memory maths is unforgiving but simple; the board gives you the node for a known price. The two genuine decisions are commercial: whether FP8's halved bill beats BF16's precision for your workload, and whether §10's triggers put a Tencent email ahead of your first invoice. A guide that priced the node without printing the licence would have answered the easy half.

MODEL DEPLOYMENT →  ·  2026-11-24 · 19 min read

Deploy ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview — what its FP8+FP4 weights need, priced

Baidu has open-sourced the first post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash: a 280B mixture-of-experts model with 14B active per token, a 1M-token context window and an Apache 2.0 licence, shipped in three builds — a default build whose routed experts are 4-bit (165.91GB measured), an FP8 build for hardware without FP4 kernels (301.87GB) and a BF16 build (599.59GB). Unusually for preview weights, the serving support is real on day one: SGLang publishes a cookbook with a verified hardware matrix, and vLLM serves it through Baidu’s own plugin. Just as unusually, Baidu says in plain words on the model card that this is “an intermediate checkpoint from post-training” and that training is not finished. This guide prices the documented routes against our board, works the memory maths build by build — including the shapes that fail by single-digit gigabytes — and keeps the preview caveat where it belongs: in the decision, not in a footnote.

The verdict

  • FP8+FP4 build — SGLang, verified — Blackwell only: the FP4 experts are SM100-only, and B300 is the one shape SGLang marks fully verified for this build. B300 supply on the board is thin — five offers, against eight for H100 SXM. 2 × B300 at Hyperstack — $14.80/hr, $10,804.00/mo.
  • FP8 build — SGLang, verified on H100 — The Hopper route, with a Hopper ceiling: on 80GB cards the documented context tops out at 262,144 tokens — the 1M window does not fit this shape. TensorDock’s rate carries an 8-GPU minimum, which happens to be exactly this recipe. 8 × H100 SXM at TensorDock — $18.00/hr, $13,140.00/mo.
  • FP8+FP4 build — 4-GPU node recipes — Both frameworks publish 4-GPU commands, but read the fine print: SGLang’s FP4 recipe borrows the FP8 GPU count for expert parallelism and is not in its verified set on B200, and vLLM’s FP4 recipe was tested on GB200 trays. 4 × B200 at RunPod Community — $23.92/hr, $17,461.60/mo.
  • FP8 build — capacity only, unproven — The cheapest FP8 route on paper — and nobody documents it. SGLang’s hardware matrix omits the H200 entirely; the weights fit with room to spare, but you would be the first to publish the recipe. Arithmetic, not a route. 4 × H200 at RunPod Community — $14.36/hr, $10,482.80/mo.
  • BF16 build — SGLang, verified — The full-precision weights Baidu recommends as the fine-tuning start, at exactly double the FP4 node’s money. 4 × B300 at Hyperstack — $29.60/hr, $21,608.00/mo.
  • BF16 build — two-node Hopper — Both frameworks put BF16 on H100 at two nodes of eight. Two separate rentals, and the interconnect between them is yours to arrange. 16 × H100 SXM at TensorDock, two nodes of eight — $36.00/hr, $26,280.00/mo.
Compare GPU prices across every provider→The Base model this checkpoint was post-trained from→

The short answer

If you have Blackwell, download baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Preview (the FP8+FP4 build, 165.91GB measured) and serve it with SGLang on 2 × B300 — the shape SGLang itself marks fully verified — at $14.80 an hour, $10,804.00 a month at Hyperstack’s board rate, checked Nov 26, 2026. If you have Hopper, the build changes, not just the node: the FP4 experts cannot run, so take the FP8 repository (301.87GB) on the documented 8 × H100 shape at $18.00 an hour at TensorDock, and accept the 262,144-token context ceiling that comes with 80GB cards. And whichever route you take, take it by the hour first: Baidu calls this checkpoint intermediate, post-training is still running, and the official release will supersede it. The rest of this guide is the working behind those sentences. Monthly figures in the verdict table are the hourly rate × 730 hours, computed exactly. “Verified” means the framework’s own documentation uses that word for that shape (SGLang’s cookbook, checked Nov 24, 2026); every other shape is labelled with what it actually is. The memory maths behind each row — and the shapes that fail — are worked in full below.

What you are actually downloading — model cards, configs and file listings, read Nov 24, 2026

From the three repositories’ model cards, configs and file listings, read Nov 24, 2026 — sizes measured from the repositories’ own file lists through the Hugging Face API, not quoted from announcements.

The factThe detail
280B total parameters, 14B active per tokenBaidu’s figures, stated on the card and cookbook alike. The architecture, from the repo config: 43 layers — 1 dense plus 42 mixture-of-experts layers with 512 routed experts, 10 firing per token, plus 1 shared expert, in a 2048-dimension latent space; hidden size 4,096; vocabulary 201,216. SGLang’s cookbook adds the accounting note: the 280B includes the input embedding and output head and excludes the 0.36B ECHO draft layer.
Attention is hybrid, and it is why the context claim is plausible37 layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA), which caches one entry per 128 tokens of history plus a 128-token sliding window; the other 6 keep token-level history through MLA with sparse attention (DSA), attending to the top 2,048 selected positions. The config’s per-layer compression list (128 for the HCA layers) matches the card’s description.
Context: 1,048,576 tokensIn the config (max_position_embeddings). The card says mid-training extended the training context from 128K to 1M; both serving recipes below default to a 131,072-token window, and the gap between the box and the recipes is a real planning fact (see the memory section).
Three builds, three measured sizesThe default repo — blockwise FP8 for most weights, routed experts in MXFP4 — measures 165.91GB (154.51 GiB, the “~155 GB” the frameworks quote; 128 shards). The FP8 repo measures 301.87GB (281.14 GiB). The BF16 repo measures 599.59GB (558.41 GiB). A naive 280B × 2 bytes derivation gives 560GB for BF16 — the measured repo runs 39.59GB (7.1%) above it, which is why this guide plans from measurements.
The precision split, from the default repo’s quantization configNon-expert weights in blockwise FP8 (128×128 blocks, e4m3), routed experts in MXFP4 run as W4A8 — 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations — with quantization-aware training, so, in Baidu’s words, “the released weights deploy directly in W4A8, with no extra conversion or calibration.” The KV cache is FP8 and the DSA indexer runs in FP4.
DSpark ships inside every buildA 3-layer draft head for speculative decoding, conditioned on the target’s last three layers, proposing blocks of up to 7 tokens (the config’s draft block size is 7). It is part of the download and of both documented serving recipes — not an add-on fetched elsewhere. Baidu claims an average acceptance length above 5.5 on real multi-turn conversations; that is Baidu’s figure, not a measurement of ours.
Thinking is on by defaultThe model reasons before it answers (the reasoning lands in a separate response field), with reasoning_effort low / medium / high and high the default. Sampling defaults from the checkpoint’s generation config, per the SGLang cookbook: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95.
What Baidu says this checkpoint is — its own words“ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is an intermediate checkpoint from post-training. It already performs competitively among models of its size, but some capabilities may still fall short because training is not finished. Post-training is ongoing.”
Licence: Apache 2.0Verified from the licence file inside the repositories, not just the metadata. The scope limit Baidu prints is in the licence section below: it covers the Preview weights only.

The weights, and where they fit: the memory maths — worked from the measured checkpoints, Nov 24, 2026

Every figure below is the measured safetensors total for the build, against raw card capacity. Weights are the floor, never the whole budget: KV cache, activations and framework workspace all eat from what is left, and the last part of this section is about exactly that.

The buildThe maths
The FP8+FP4 build (165.91GB) — Blackwell’s buildOn 2 × B300 (576GB) it leaves 410.10GB of headroom — the verified SGLang shape is roomy, not tight. On 4 × B200 the weights split to 41.48GB per GPU. On a single B300 (288GB) the capacity arithmetic also works — 122.10GB spare — and Baidu’s plugin documentation lists one 288GB GPU as the smallest home for this build; the published launch commands, though, are 4-GPU node commands, so treat one-card serving as documented capacity, not a published recipe. The honest negatives: two 80GB cards miss it outright — 160GB of capacity against 165.91GB of weights, short by 5.91GB before a single token of KV cache. And two popular paper fits are kernel-blocked, not memory-blocked: 2 × H200 (282GB, 116.10GB spare) and 3 × A100 (240GB, 74.10GB spare) both hold the file, but Hopper has no FP4 kernels and Ampere has neither FP4 nor FP8 — Baidu’s own instruction for such hardware is to change builds, below.
The FP8 build (301.87GB) — the Hopper fallbackOn the documented 8 × H100 shape the weights split to 37.73GB per GPU, leaving real room for KV and workspace. The trap shape is 4 × H100: 320GB of capacity against 301.87GB of weights “fits” with 18.13GB to spare — 4.53GB per GPU for everything else, which is not a serving budget; neither framework publishes it, and the documented H100 shape is eight cards. Two more negatives worth printing: 2 × H200 cannot hold this build at all (282GB against 301.87GB — short by 19.87GB), and 4 × H200 (564GB, 75.47GB of weights per GPU) fits on capacity but appears in no framework’s matrix — the TL;DR’s unproven row.
The BF16 build (599.59GB) — the fine-tuning startVerified on 4 × B300; documented at 8 × B200 (74.95GB of weights per GPU) and at two nodes of 8 × H100. The negative that catches people: 4 × H200 misses it — 564GB against 599.59GB, short by 35.59GB. One 4-GPU node of 192GB cards (768GB) holds the weights on capacity, and Baidu’s plugin notes it leaves little room for KV cache; the plugin’s own BF16 commands run data-parallel 8 across two 4-GPU nodes.
KV cache — stated structurally, because a point figure would be inventedThis architecture does not keep a conventional per-token cache: 37 of 43 layers cache one compressed entry per 128 tokens, and the 6 sparse-attention layers keep FP8 KV but attend to at most 2,048 selected positions. Baidu publishes no per-token KV byte figure and the public config does not determine one honestly, so this guide does not print one. What the frameworks do publish are the operative limits, and they are the numbers to plan with: the recipes default to 131,072 tokens of context; on 8 × 80GB cards the FP8 build tops out at 262,144 tokens per the plugin documentation — “1M does not” fit; and SGLang’s cookbook warns that at a full 1,048,576-token context on 2 × B300, concurrent requests fall to single digits, because each GPU’s KV pool must hold whole 1M-token requests, with tens of GB of activation memory needed for a 1M-token prefill on top. The 1M window is real; serving it at volume is a different purchase from serving the model.

Serving: what is documented today — proven routes (framework pages read Nov 24, 2026)

FrameworkWhat is documented
SGLangA dedicated cookbook for this model (its documentation page was updated Nov 24, 2026, the day of this guide) with a hardware × precision matrix and per-recipe launch commands. Its verification statement, in its own terms: on B300 every recipe (FP4, FP8 and BF16) is verified; the FP8 high-throughput recipe is also verified on GB300, B200, GB200 and H100; the remaining recipes follow from the same memory budget and are not yet verified. Its matrix’s smallest GPU counts: FP4 — 2 × B300/GB300, 4 × B200/GB200, none on H100 (SM100 only); FP8 — 2 × B300/GB300, 4 × B200/GB200, 8 × H100; BF16 — 4 × B300/GB300, 8 × B200, 2 trays of GB200, 2 nodes × 8 × H100. The card’s own SGLang command — DSpark on, 131,072-token context — reproduced exactly: "docker run -d -it --name ernie55 --gpus all --network host --ipc host -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface lmsysorg/sglang:latest ; docker exec -it ernie55 bash ; sglang serve --model-path baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Preview --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --tp 4 --attn-dp-size 4 --context-length 131072 --max-running-requests 128 --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --reasoning-parser ernie55 --tool-call-parser ernie55 --enable-dp-lm-head --trust-remote-code" Read the recipe’s settings as intent: 4-way parallelism, a 131,072-token window rather than the config’s 1,048,576, DSpark speculative decoding on, and --trust-remote-code — the repos ship their own modelling code and the documented routes use it. The cookbook’s fastest decode path additionally uses HALOps, PaddlePaddle’s operator library, installed from PaddlePaddle’s own package page rather than PyPI, into the SGLang environment — see the speed section.
vLLM, through Baidu’s plugin (not mainline)vLLM serves this checkpoint through vLLM-ERNIE, Baidu’s plugin package, installed into the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, unmodified. The vLLM project marked the support itself: its blog carried a day-0 post on the plugin on Nov 24, 2026, and its recipes site has a full ERNIE-5.5-Flash page — which states that the FP4 recipe was tested on full 4-GPU GB200 trays and is offered on Blackwell only. Mainline vLLM without the plugin does not document this model: vLLM’s supported-models documentation, checked Nov 24, 2026, lists the ERNIE 4.5 family and no ERNIE 5.5 entry. Install and the card’s FP4 command, reproduced exactly: "uv venv --python 3.12 ernie5-venv ; source ernie5-venv/bin/activate ; uv pip install vllm==0.32.0 ; uv pip install git+https://github.com/baidu/vLLM-ERNIE.git ; export VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 ; vllm serve baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Preview --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --data-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-model-len 131072 --reasoning-parser ernie5 --tool-call-parser ernie5 --enable-auto-tool-choice --attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"mxfp4"}' --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'" The plugin’s own smallest-count table is a capacity table, by memory class: at 288GB per GPU — FP4 1 GPU, FP8 2, BF16 4; at 192GB — FP4 2, FP8 4, BF16 8 (or two nodes of 4); at 80GB — FP4 4, FP8 8, BF16 two nodes of 8. Two of its notes deserve quoting rather than paraphrase: on 80GB GPUs, FP8 serves on 8 GPUs at --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 with up to --max-model-len 262144 — “1M does not” fit; and the FP4 command’s MXFP4 indexer setting “needs Blackwell-architecture data-center GPUs” — elsewhere, drop it and keep the FP8 indexer. The FP8 command in the same source adds --moe-backend humming, recommended on Blackwell; on Hopper, keep the default.

Named honestly — not documented for this checkpoint

RouteStatus today
Mainline vLLM, no pluginNot documented — the supported-models list checked today carries ERNIE 4.5 only. If a tutorial shows ERNIE 5.5 serving on a bare vLLM install, it is omitting the plugin step.
FastDeploy / PaddlePaddle servingNot documented for this checkpoint. FastDeploy’s supported-models list, checked Nov 24, 2026, covers the ERNIE 4.5 family and no 5.5 Flash Preview entry; Baidu’s model card names SGLang and vLLM and nothing else. PaddlePaddle’s presence in this release is real but narrower: HALOps, its operator library, accelerates the SGLang route — it is a kernel package inside someone else’s server, not a serving route of its own here.
TransformersThe repos declare the transformers library and ship custom modelling and tokenisation code — which is why both servers demand --trust-remote-code — but neither the card nor the repos document a Transformers serving recipe. Loading the weights in Transformers is an experiment, not a documented route.
Anything on A100 / AmpereNo framework lists it. The FP8 and FP4 builds need post-Ampere kernels outright, and the BF16 build’s documented homes start at H100 nodes. The 3 × A100 capacity fit for the default build, printed in the memory section, is arithmetic with no serving route behind it.

The speed claim, read carefully

The claimThe detail
1,074 tokens per second — LMSYS, Nov 23, 2026The number attached to this launch comes from the LMSYS team’s own blog post about its SGLang work — a primary source for the claim, with its conditions printed. What it is: single-stream decoding (batch size 1) on four SM100 (Blackwell) GPUs, with 55K input tokens and 1K output tokens, DSpark speculative decoding enabled, HALOps kernels installed, on an SGLang build taken from a pull request. What it is not: a throughput figure for a loaded server. Two conditions deserve plain print. First, the DSpark acceptance length in the headline runs was simulated — set to 5.5 by environment variable rather than measured from the model’s own drafts (a second figure, about 1,310 tok/s, uses a simulated 7.2). Second, batch-1 decode speed is the metric a single interactive user feels; it says nothing about how many tokens per second the node produces under concurrent load, and neither Baidu nor SGLang publishes an aggregate throughput table for this checkpoint. That is why this guide contains no cost-per-token section: with no sustained aggregate rate from any primary source, a tokens-per-dollar figure would be arithmetic built on an assumption, and we do not print those as results. When an aggregate benchmark from the maker or a framework exists, the break-even can be worked; today it cannot, honestly.

The preview caveat, and the licence — Apache 2.0, Preview weights only

The pointThe detail
Preview first, because it prices the commitmentBaidu states on the card that this is an intermediate checkpoint, that “some capabilities may still fall short because training is not finished”, and that post-training is ongoing with an official release to follow. Three practical consequences for a renter. The weights you download can be superseded — behaviour, scores and possibly the serving recipes will move at GA, so pin the exact repository revision in anything you build (the default repo’s revision at the time of checking is recorded in this guide’s audit note). Evaluate by the hour or the week, not by the quarter: every route in the TL;DR is an on-demand board rate, and that is the right shape of commitment for an unfinished checkpoint. And hold production migrations until GA — the preview’s own maker does not describe it as finished. (Context, for readers who met this model earlier: a Preview API has been live on Baidu’s Qianfan platform since Nov 11, 2026; what is new this week is the weights.)
The licence is Apache License 2.0Verified three ways on Nov 24, 2026: the license: apache-2.0 declaration in each repository’s Hugging Face metadata, the licence line on the model card, and the LICENSE file inside the repositories, whose text is the Apache License 2.0 itself. Read plainly, that is the permissive grant: use, modify and serve commercially, with no revenue threshold and no user-count trigger of the kind §10 of the Tencent Hy licence imposes on Hy4.
Baidu’s scope sentence, quoted exactly“This license covers the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview weights only. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base remains under its own license, the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0.”
Where the clean grant stopsThe clean Apache grant travels with the Preview weights and stops there: if your work also touches the Base checkpoint — the fine-tuning starting point this family’s tooling was built around — the Base’s own licence agreement governs that part, and it is not Apache.

Watch-outs before you rent

Watch-outThe detail
The 2 × 80GB trapThe default build misses two H100s by 5.91GB of weights alone. Any “runs on two cards” claim for this checkpoint means two large cards — 141GB Hoppers hold the file but cannot run its FP4 experts; the two-card documented routes are Blackwell (2 × B300) or the FP8 build on bigger Hopper counts.
The 4 × H100 trapThe FP8 build’s weights-only arithmetic fits four 80GB cards with 4.53GB per GPU to spare — for KV cache, activations and workspace combined. Both frameworks document eight. Rent the documented shape; the four-card version is a forum experiment you would be running on your own invoice.
“Verified” has a scope, and SGLang prints itFully verified means B300 (all precisions) plus the FP8 high-throughput recipe on GB300, B200, GB200 and H100. FP4 on B200, BF16 on B200, and every other cell of the matrix are the framework’s own words for it: recipes that “follow from the same memory budget and are not yet verified.” They will very likely work; they are not yet the framework’s promise.
The H200 is absent from the matrixThe board’s most-rented Hopper-class card appears in neither SGLang’s cookbook matrix nor any published recipe for this checkpoint, despite the capacity fitting comfortably for the FP8 build. If your fleet is H200s, you are early — budget setup time accordingly, or take the documented 8 × H100 shape.
The 1M context is a configuration, not a default, and it costs concurrencyBoth documented commands set 131,072 tokens. Raising the window to 1,048,576 is supported, but SGLang’s own guidance drops concurrent requests to single digits on 2 × B300 at that length, a 1M-token prefill needs tens of GB of activation memory on top of the weights, and on 80GB cards the documented ceiling is 262,144. Price the context you will actually serve.
1,074 tok/s is a decode figure with a simulated acceptance lengthSingle stream, four Blackwell GPUs, DSpark acceptance set by simulation (5.5; 7.2 for the ~1,310 figure). It is evidence the serving stack is fast for one user; it is not a capacity plan, and it is not a cost per token.
You are serving on pinned, moving groundThe vLLM route is a plugin on one exact release (vllm==0.32.0); the SGLang low-latency path was built from a pull request plus an operator library installed from PaddlePaddle’s package page; both servers require --trust-remote-code. Pin every version, and expect the recipes to be revised as the support mainlines.
Thinking is on by default, and it is billed in timeEvery response reasons first, at the high effort setting unless you lower it. Latency budgets and per-request costs that assume direct answers will be wrong until you set enable_thinking or reasoning_effort deliberately.
Every benchmark on the card is Baidu’s ownThe card says so itself: all ERNIE scores are from Baidu’s evaluations, on Baidu’s chosen harnesses, with some rival scores also marked as Baidu’s runs. The 20-benchmark table (Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 46.5, AutomationBench at 61.9 among them) is the maker’s evidence for an unfinished checkpoint. No independent evaluation exists yet.
The download is part of the deployment165.91GB for the default build — 301.87GB for FP8, 599.59GB for BF16 — lands on the rented machine before anything serves. On hourly rentals, staging is billed time; on the two-node BF16 route it is billed twice.

Who should run this, and how

Your workloadThe route
Agent and coding shops evaluating open weightsThis checkpoint’s pitch — long-horizon agent work at 14B active — is aimed at you, and the evaluation is cheap to run properly: the verified 2 × B300 FP4 route at $14.80/hr, by the hour, against your own tasks. Baidu’s benchmark table is a reason to test, not a result.
Blackwell renters who want the documented pathSGLang on B300 is the one configuration in this launch that a framework calls fully verified for the default build. If the work matters, start there rather than chasing the cheaper-on-paper cells of the matrix that no framework has verified yet.
Hopper fleetsThe FP8 build on 8 × H100 at $18.00/hr is a real, framework-verified route — with the 262,144-token context ceiling on 80GB cards understood before you promise anyone a long-context service. H200 owners: see the watch-out; your card is not in the matrix yet.
Fine-tuners and researchersBaidu recommends the BF16 repo as the fine-tuning start and documents Megatron-Bridge support; rent 4 × B300 ($29.60/hr) by the hour for the work, and keep the Base checkpoint’s separate licence in view if your pipeline touches it.
Production rentersWait. The maker calls the checkpoint intermediate and its training unfinished; the official release is the production event. Until then, the hosted Preview API on Qianfan exists for evaluation traffic you do not want to stand up hardware for — and anything you build on these weights should pin the revision, because the GA drop will not ask your permission to differ.

How we check

Model facts — 280B total parameters and 14B active per token (Baidu’s figures), 43 layers (1 dense, 42 MoE), 512 routed experts plus 1 shared with top-10 firing in a 2048-dimension latent space, hidden size 4,096, vocabulary 201,216, 1,048,576-token context, hybrid attention (37 HCA layers caching one entry per 128 tokens plus a 128-token sliding window; 6 MLA-DSA layers with top-2048 selection), DSpark draft head (3 layers, block size 7, target layers 40–42), thinking on by default — are from the model cards and config.json files of baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Preview, baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Preview-FP8 and baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Preview-BF16 on Hugging Face, read first-hand Nov 24, 2026; the parameter accounting (280B includes embedding and output head, excludes the 0.36B ECHO layer) and the sampling defaults (temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95) are from SGLang’s cookbook for the model. Checkpoint sizes are measured, not quoted: the safetensors file sizes in each repo’s listing (Hugging Face API, blob listing) sum to 165.91GB for the default FP8+FP4 build (128 shards plus the FlashIndexer file; 154.51 GiB, the frameworks’ “~155 GB”), 301.87GB for the FP8 build (281.14 GiB; frameworks quote ~280 GB) and 599.59GB for the BF16 build (558.41 GiB; frameworks quote ~560 GB, which is also the naive 280B × 2 bytes derivation — the measured repo exceeds it by 39.59GB). The precision split (blockwise FP8 at 128×128 blocks in e4m3; routed experts MXFP4 as W4A8; FP8 KV cache; FP4 DSA indexer) is from the default repo’s quantization_config and the card’s model overview. Repository dates are the Hugging Face API’s own records: all three Preview repos were created on Nov 23, 2026 (09:00–09:01 UTC) and the default repo was last modified Nov 24, 2026 (07:17 UTC); Baidu’s public release in Beijing time is Nov 24, 2026. Serving verification: SGLang’s ERNIE-5.5-Flash cookbook (docs.sglang.io; page updated Nov 24, 2026) for the hardware × precision matrix, the verification scope quoted in the serving section, the long-context guidance and the HALOps notes; the model card’s Deployment section for the SGLang and vLLM commands (reproduced verbatim); Baidu’s vLLM-ERNIE repository (README, read Nov 24, 2026) for the plugin’s install, its capacity table by memory class, the 80GB context ceiling and the Blackwell indexer note; vLLM’s recipes page for baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash for the FP4 testing scope (GB200 trays, Blackwell only); vLLM’s supported-models documentation (checked Nov 24, 2026 — ERNIE 4.5 family only) for the mainline statement; FastDeploy’s supported-models list (checked Nov 24, 2026 — ERNIE 4.5 family only) for the FastDeploy statement. The 1,074 tok/s figure and its conditions (four SM100 GPUs, batch size 1, 55K input / 1K output, HALOps 0.2.0, SGLang built from PR #52603, DSpark acceptance length simulated at 5.5, ~1,310 tok/s at a simulated 7.2 with block size 7) are from the LMSYS blog post “Toward the Decode Limit: ERNIE 5.5 Flash at 1074 tokens/s on SGLang” (Nov 23, 2026) and SGLang’s cookbook summary of it; both are the framework team’s reported measurements, not ours. Baidu’s DSpark acceptance claim (average acceptance length above 5.5 on real multi-turn conversations) is from the model card and is attributed wherever used. The licence is Apache License 2.0 as declared in each repo’s Hugging Face metadata and card and as the text of the LICENSE file inside the repos (read Nov 24, 2026); the Preview-only scope sentence is quoted from the card’s License section. Rental prices are GPUJournal’s Nov 24, 2026 board snapshot with the same-day corrections (price-history/corrections.md) applied — Verda’s corrected Nov 24 rates replace the snapshot’s banked Verda figures wherever Verda appears: B300 — Hyperstack $7.40, RunPod Secure $8.99; B200 — RunPod Community $5.98, Hyperstack $6.00; H200 — RunPod Community $3.59; H100 SXM — TensorDock $2.25 (8-GPU minimum at that rate, $18.00/hr true total), RunPod Community $2.69; GB300 — Verda $15.31 (corrected). Monthly figures are hourly × 730; node figures are the per-GPU rate × the GPU count. All computed by script. What is deliberately not claimed. No throughput figure appears here as our measurement, and no cost-per-token or break-even figure is computed for this checkpoint: the only speed evidence in primary sources is a single-stream decode measurement with a simulated acceptance length, and no sustained aggregate throughput is published by Baidu, SGLang or vLLM — arithmetic on an assumed rate would be an assumption wearing a result’s clothes. No KV-cache bytes-per-token figure is printed: the hybrid HCA + MLA-DSA design does not determine one from the public config, so the guide prints the frameworks’ operative context limits instead. No serving route is asserted beyond the documentation named: the 4 × H200 FP8 row is labelled capacity-only because no framework publishes it; FP4 on B200 is labelled with SGLang’s own “not yet verified” scope; FastDeploy, mainline vLLM and Transformers are labelled undocumented for this checkpoint on the evidence of their own lists and the card. Baidu’s benchmark table is not reproduced as findings — it is the maker’s own evaluation of an unfinished checkpoint, and the guide says so. Qianfan API pricing is not quoted: it was not verified first-hand from Baidu’s pricing pages for this guide, so the hosted route is named without a price.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. This launch inverts the usual preview pattern. Normally the weights arrive half-served and the frameworks catch up over weeks; here the serving story is the finished part — a framework cookbook with a verified matrix, a vendor plugin with a day-0 blog post, a speculative-decoding head trained alongside the model — and it is the checkpoint itself that its maker describes as unfinished. That combination argues for a specific renter posture: spend freely on evaluation, because the deployment risk has been unusually well retired, and commit to nothing the GA release would make you redo. The teams who get this release right will be the ones who can say, on the day the finished weights land, exactly what the model does on their own workloads — measured on rented hours, not on a contract signed against a preview.

Deploy Ternary Bonsai 2.5 on one small card — what 6 GB of weights actually costs to run

PrismML’s Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B is a 27B agent model whose weights are ternary — every weight is −1, 0 or +1 — so the fastest checkpoint measures 5.99 GB on disk (the maker headlines 5.93 GB) against 53.8 GB for the same model at FP16. That makes the rental question almost absurdly simple: every single card on our board can hold it, so the decision is not which card fits but which card is worth paying for, which of the three file packings your runtime will actually load, and whether the maker’s own speed tables — the only speed figures that exist for this model — justify skipping the ordinary 4-bit build of the base model instead. This guide works the arithmetic, prices the honest single-card routes, and prints the traps: the fastest file needs PrismML’s own llama.cpp fork, and the file that runs on stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage on an old build.

The verdict

  • RTX 4090 · 24 GB — cheapest honest route — Fits, with at least 14 GB to spare against the 8–10 GB working set worked out below. The maker’s tables put it at 112 tok/s plain and 204 tok/s with the MTP head. RunPod Community · RTX 4090 — $0.34/hr, $248.20/mo.
  • RTX A6000 · 48 GB — Fits. Not in the maker’s speed tables — capacity is certain, speed is unmeasured by anyone. Thunder Compute · RTX A6000 — $0.35/hr, $255.50/mo.
  • RTX 5090 · 32 GB — Fits. 163 tok/s plain and 305 tok/s with the MTP head — the fastest small card in the maker’s tables; on those tables it decodes about 1.45× faster than the RTX 4090 plain and about 1.5× with MTP, for about twice the money. RunPod Community · RTX 5090 — $0.69/hr, $503.70/mo.
  • L40S · 48 GB — Fits. 95 tok/s plain in the maker’s table; no MTP figure is published for this card. RunPod Community · L40S — $0.79/hr, $576.70/mo.
  • A100 80GB — Fits. 107 tok/s plain and 171 tok/s with the MTP head, on the maker’s tables. Thunder Compute · A100 80GB — $1.09/hr, $795.70/mo. · $1.09/hr at Thunder Compute
  • RTX PRO 6000 · 96 GB — Fits. 158 tok/s plain and 277 tok/s with the MTP head, on the maker’s tables. RunPod Community · RTX PRO 6000 — $1.69/hr, $1,233.70/mo.
