The short answer

Rent the RTX 4090 on RunPod Community at $0.34 an hour, $248.20 a month (checked Nov 25, 2026), download the PTQ1_0 file (5.99 GB measured), and run it in PrismML’s llama.cpp fork — the only runtime that loads the fast packings today. PrismML’s own table puts that card at 112 tokens/s plain and 204 tokens/s with the built-in MTP draft head. If you refuse third-party forks on principle, the fallback is the Q2_0 file (7.67 GB) on stock llama.cpp — but only on build b11556 or newer; older stock builds load it without a warning and produce garbage. And if your workload is ordinary chat rather than tool-calling agents, read the Q4 section before renting anything: the maker’s own benchmarks say the ternary model’s edge is specifically agentic, and a normal Q4_K_M build of the base model (16.46 GB) fits the same 24 GB card. “Fits” in the table above is judged against the working set worked out in this guide — about 8–10 GB total at the maker’s own 32K-context quickstart shape on one request slot — not against the 5.99 GB file alone. Every card on the board fits; the six rows are the cheapest single-card offers, ranked by price, not by value.

What you are actually downloading — the model card and file listing, read Nov 25, 2026

From the repository’s model card and file listing — sizes measured from the repository’s own file list through the Hugging Face API, not quoted from the announcement.

The factThe detail
27.36B total parametersA ternary release of Qwen3.8-27B: 24.35B language parameters (64 blocks) + 2.54B embedding/lm-head + a 0.47B vision tower. The GGUF language file itself carries 26,895,998,464 parameters (the repository’s GGUF metadata); the vision tower ships as a separate optional file and is never loaded for text work. Architecture: hybrid attention (about 75% linear / 25% full attention), SwiGLU MLP, RoPE, RMSNorm; context 262,144 tokens.
PTQ1_0 — the fast, small packing: 5.99 GB (5.58 GiB)PrismML llama.cpp fork only; upstream merge under review. With the MTP head built in: 6.23 GB (5.81 GiB), fork only.
PQ2_0: 7.25 GB (6.76 GiB)PrismML llama.cpp fork; the packing benchmarked on Apple Metal. With the MTP head: 7.49 GB (6.98 GiB).
Q2_0 — the stock-compatible packing: 7.67 GB (7.15 GiB)Stock llama.cpp, build b11556 or newer. With the MTP head: 7.91 GB (7.37 GiB).
Vision projector (mmproj), optional: 0.63 GB (Q8_0) / 0.93 GB (BF16)Loaded only when an image arrives.
One honest discrepancy, printed rather than smoothed overThe card headlines the PTQ1_0 file as “5.93 GB”. The file in the repository measures 5,993,834,848 bytes — 5.99 GB, about 1% larger. Nothing in this guide plans from the headline; every fit judgement uses the measured file.
The MTP head costs 0.24 GBThe PTQ1_0 file grows from 5.99 GB to 6.23 GB with it built in — one extra draft layer, made by PrismML. What it buys is in the speed section.
Reasoning is on by defaultThe model thinks before answering, at xhigh effort by default (medium for shorter traces; low is not supported and behaves like xhigh). The maker’s sampling for thinking mode: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20 — and pass --min-p 0, because llama.cpp defaults to 0.05.
Licence: Apache 2.0Declared in the repository metadata, stated in the card’s licence section, and the repository carries the full Apache 2.0 licence text as its LICENSE file. The scope note is in the licence section below.

The 6 GB arithmetic: how 27B fits in 6 GB

Worked from the format description on the model card and the measured file, Nov 25, 2026.

The stepThe maths
A ternary weight carries log₂3 ≈ 1.585 bits of informationIt is one of three values, {−1, 0, +1}. That is the floor, not the file.
The scales add 0.125 bits per weightWeights are stored in groups of 128 with one shared FP16 scale per group (“Ternary g128”): 16 ÷ 128 = 0.125 bits per weight. Floor plus scales: 1.71 bits per weight before any packing overhead.
The maker states 1.76; the measured file works out at 1.78 bits per parameterThe maker states 1.76 bits per weight for the PTQ1_0 packing (“dense trits”); the measured file is 5,993,834,848 bytes × 8 ÷ 26,895,998,464 parameters = 1.78 — the small remainder is GGUF metadata and the tensors that are not ternary. Claim, format maths and file all land within 0.07 bits of each other.
The rotation costs nothingEach matrix is stored in a blockwise Hadamard-rotated basis, folded into the weights offline; the runtime applies the matching transform to activations. It costs no extra bits and no extra weight traffic — but it is why the runtime needs Hadamard (FWHT) kernels, which is the root of the fork situation in the serving section.
Against FP16: 8.97× smallerThe same language model at 16 bits is 26,895,998,464 × 2 bytes = 53.79 GB (the maker’s 53.8 GB). 53.79 ÷ 5.99 = 8.97× — the maker’s “~9× smaller” checks out against the measured file.
Why the other packings are biggerPQ2_0 spends a full 2-bit slot on every trit (7.25 GB), and Q2_0 is llama.cpp’s standard 2-bit type (7.67 GB). Same weights, three storage layouts — the differences are layout and kernel speed, not model quality.

The file is not the footprint: the working set

Weights are the floor, never the whole budget. KV cache, activations and the runtime’s buffers eat from what is left, and PrismML’s own card carries the one measured datapoint that exists: in its known-issues section, a community report on an RTX 3080 10 GB measured about 9.5 GB of total GPU memory with the server’s default four request slots, and about 7.8 GB after limiting it to one slot (-np 1), desktop usage included. The maker’s quickstart runs at a 32,768-token context.

The judgementThe basis
Plan on roughly 8–10 GB totalFor the PTQ1_0 file at a 32K context on one request slot — the measured 7.8 GB, plus margin for your own desktop/driver overhead. Against that band, every card in the TL;DR table (24 GB and up) fits with at least 14 GB to spare.
The full 262K context costs more KV room, and nobody publishes the numberThe hybrid backbone helps — only about a quarter of the 64 blocks keep a full token-by-token KV cache, the rest are linear-attention layers — but neither PrismML nor the runtime publishes a per-token KV figure for this model, so this guide does not invent one. llama.cpp prints the cache size it allocates at load; raise -c in steps and read it. Even a several-fold KV growth over the 32K band stays inside a 24 GB card, but treat 262K on a small card as “verify at load”, not as promised.
Serving more than one user at once is a different shapeThe maker’s server guidance for limited VRAM is one slot (-np 1); the default four slots share a unified KV cache and pushed a 10 GB card to about 9.5 GB. No primary source publishes a sustained multi-user throughput figure for this model, so this guide prints none: what is priced here is a single-agent, single-slot deployment, which is what the model is built for.

Serving reality: one runtime family, and it is not vLLM

This checkpoint exists only as GGUF and MLX packs — PrismML’s own download documentation lists no safetensors release, and that single fact decides the serving table. Proven below means the maker’s card or the framework’s own documentation names this model, its files or its architecture; everything else is printed as what it is.

The routeThe record
PrismML llama.cpp fork (CUDA, Metal, CPU, SYCL) — Proven, the reference routeThe only runtime that loads PTQ1_0 and PQ2_0. The card’s tested commands, pinned binaries and presets live in the maker’s Bonsai-demo repository, which the card calls “the source of truth for running these models”.
Stock llama.cpp, build b11556 or newer — Proven, Q2_0 file onlyUpstream merged Bonsai 27B-family support (ggml-org/llama.cpp#29600) and the FWHT kernels it needs. On an H200 the maker measures stock llama.cpp decoding the Q2_0 file at 109 tok/s against 150 on the PrismML runtime — stock works, the fork is faster. Trap: older stock builds load Q2_0 with no warning and produce garbage. Check llama-cli --version first; the same applies to apps that bundle their own llama.cpp.
MLX (the -mlx-2bit pack) — Proven, Apple Silicon onlyA text-only MLX build exported from the PQ2_0 file, with a bundled loader for the Hadamard transforms; the maker measures it on an M5 Pro at 21.7 tok/s decode against 30.2 for llama.cpp on the same machine. Not a rental route — no provider on our board rents Apple Silicon — but it is the documented route if the “small card” is a Mac.
vLLM — Not available for this checkpointThere is no safetensors release for vLLM to load, and vLLM’s own GGUF support is documented as highly experimental and now lives in an out-of-tree plugin; neither vLLM nor the plugin names this model or its qwen35 hybrid-attention architecture. Do not plan a vLLM deployment around this model today.
SGLang — Not available for this checkpointNo SGLang documentation names this model, and there is no safetensors or documented GGUF route for it. Same conclusion as vLLM, for the same reason.
Transformers — Not availableThe release ships GGUF and MLX packs only; there is no Transformers-format checkpoint to load.
The reference route, in the maker’s own commandshf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-GGUF Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf --local-dir . — then: ./bin/llama-cli -m Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0 -p “Explain quantum computing in simple terms.” -n 16384. From the model card’s quickstart, read Nov 25, 2026. -ngl 99 offloads every layer; -c sets the context, up to 262144; -n 16384 leaves room for the thinking trace — the card warns that a small cap ends generation mid-thought. For the server, tool calling and the MTP variants, the card defers to the Bonsai-demo repository’s run scripts; on a small card add -np 1 to the server command. Swap the file for Q2_0 and the binary for stock llama.cpp b11556+ if you take the stock route.

Speed: the maker’s tables, and the MTP head

Every figure in this section is PrismML’s own published measurement, on PrismML’s runtime, and GPUJournal has not re-run any of them. There are two tables on the card and the maker is explicit that they must not be read against each other: the plain table is llama-bench (synthetic tokens, tg128 decode, batch 1, flash attention on), while the MTP table times llama-server on 36 real prompts (chat, agents and tool calls, documents, code, reasoning), each ratio comparing two runs on one machine. That is why the same card shows different “plain” numbers in the two tables — an RTX 5090 is 163 tok/s in one and 174 in the other. MTP is multi-token prediction — PrismML’s term, defined on the card: the -mtp.gguf variants carry one extra layer, a draft head built by PrismML, that guesses the next few tokens; with speculative decoding the full model checks all the guesses in one pass and keeps only the tokens it would have produced itself. The maker’s check on an H200 puts the mean KL divergence between drafting on and off at 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ — output-equivalent up to the rounding noise of checking several tokens at once, on the maker’s measurement (not yet checked on Metal, SYCL or the NPU, the card notes). The cost is prefill: the head makes its own pass over the prompt, slowing prefill by 9–23% on NVIDIA GPUs at the released settings.

The cardThe maker’s figures
RTX 4090Plain (llama-bench tg128, PTQ1_0): 112 tok/s decode, 3,452 tok/s prefill. MTP table (llama-server): 111 tok/s off, 204 tok/s on — 1.83×.
RTX 5090Plain: 163 tok/s decode, 4,198 tok/s prefill. MTP: 174 off, 305 on — 1.75×.
L40SPlain: 95 tok/s decode, 3,018 tok/s prefill. No MTP row — the maker did not publish one — so the TL;DR prints its plain figure only.
A100Plain: 107 tok/s decode, 1,405 tok/s prefill. MTP: 105 off, 171 on — 1.63×.
RTX PRO 6000Plain: 158 tok/s decode, 4,283 tok/s prefill. MTP: 158 off, 277 on — 1.76×.
H100 / H200 (for scale)Plain: 186 / 189 tok/s decode, 2,987 / 2,962 tok/s prefill. MTP: 184 → 282 (1.53×) / 194 → 296 (1.53×).
Reading the MTP tablellama-server, 36 real prompts, PTQ1_0, released build, drafting setting “3, 0.1” (tokens drafted per pass, minimum draft probability; the RTX 4090 row ran at “3, 0”). The card also prints a “+kernels” column that is a few percent higher — those kernels are still in testing, not in the released build, so this guide does not use those numbers anywhere. The maker’s summary range: MTP speeds decode by 1.5–1.8× on NVIDIA GPUs. Drafting pays only when the head guesses right, which depends on the text; agent and tool-call prompts are the workload the head was built and measured on.

When the ordinary Q4 build of the base model is the better buy

The honest alternative is not another ternary file — it is the base model, Qwen3.8-27B, in a normal 4-bit GGUF. The canonical Unsloth UD-Q4_K_M build measures 16.46 GB (16,464,440,224 bytes, recorded byte-exact in a community repository that byte-matches the canonical build; treat the last decimal as community-recorded, not Qwen-published). That is 2.75× the PTQ1_0 file — and it still fits a 24 GB card, which is why this section exists. Choose by workload, using the maker’s own published evaluation of its model against the conventional low-bit builds of the same base (all figures PrismML’s, thinking mode, from the model card).

The build (maker’s table)The figures
Bonsai 2.5 PTQ1_0 (1.76 bpw) — 5.99 GB measuredTool calling (5-benchmark average) 77.2 · agentic coding (3-benchmark average) 54.2 · general capability (16-benchmark average) 82.1.
Qwen3.8 FP16 — 53.8 GBTool calling 77.7 · agentic coding 60.5 · general capability 84.3.
GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS (3.00 bpw) — 10.1 GBTool calling 75.3 · agentic coding 55.5 · general capability 81.7.
Unsloth UD-IQ2_XS (2.27 bpw) — 7.6 GBTool calling 75.3 · agentic coding 47.8 · general capability 77.5.
Take the ternary build when the work is agenticOn the maker’s own numbers it matches FP16 on tool calling (77.2 against 77.7) at one ninth of the file, and keeps 90% of FP16 on agentic coding (54.2 against 60.5; DeepSWE 27.0 against 30.1, SWE-bench Verified 75.6 against 80.6). No conventional build under 10 GB is close on tool calling. It is also the only build here that leaves a 24 GB card mostly empty — room for a long context, a second slot, or a second model.
Take Q4_K_M when the work is ordinary chat, summarising or draftingThree reasons. First, runtime freedom: a Q4_K_M file loads in every stock llama.cpp build, Ollama and LM Studio, with no fork and no version trap — the ternary fast files load in exactly one fork today. Second, the maker’s table has no Q4 row: the conventional builds Bonsai 2.5 beats are 2–3 bit builds, and nothing in the maker’s published evidence says the ternary file beats a competent 4-bit build outside the agentic benchmarks it leads on. Third, general capability is where the ternary model’s gap to FP16 actually sits (82.1 against 84.3, with math the widest single gap at 3.1 points, on the maker’s averages) — if your workload lives there, the extra 10.5 GB of Q4 weights is the conservative buy, at the same RTX 4090 money.
Either way, the card money is the sameBoth files fit the RTX 4090 at $0.34/hr; the Q4 build leaves roughly 5–7 GB of a 24 GB card for KV at a working context, the ternary build leaves about 16 GB. The choice is quality profile and runtime, not price — which is exactly why the ternary headline (“27B in 6 GB!”) should not make the decision for you.

Honest negatives

The draft’s warning box, carried in full.

The negativeThe detail
The fast file needs the maker’s forkPTQ1_0 and PQ2_0 are rejected by stock llama.cpp as unknown types. PTQ1_0 is under upstream review (the card cites the open upstream PRs); until it lands, the fastest route depends on PrismML-Eng’s llama.cpp fork and its release cadence. The maker’s own demo repository is the pinned, tested path — follow it, not a random fork build.
The stock route has a silent-failure trapStock llama.cpp older than b11556 loads the Q2_0 file without any warning and produces garbage (the card’s words). Any app that bundles its own llama.cpp — desktop chat apps included — needs an engine built from b11556 or newer. Version-check before you debug the model.
Every speed figure here is the maker’sPrismML measured its own model on its own runtime; GPUJournal has not independently re-run a single number, and no third party had published a replication by Nov 25, 2026. The two tables also use different methods and disagree with each other by up to ~7% on the same card’s plain decode — read each table on its own terms, as the maker instructs.
The headline size is the maker’s rounding, not the file“5.93 GB” is the card’s number; the file measures 5.99 GB. Immaterial to every fit in this guide, printed because this guide plans from measurements.
No multi-user serving story is documentedThe priced shape is one agent, one slot. The card’s server material is about presets and flags, not sustained concurrent throughput, and no primary source publishes tokens/s under batch load for this model. If you need to serve a team, that measurement does not exist yet — you would be making it.
The L40S is half-documented, and the RTX A6000 is unmeasuredThe L40S appears in the maker’s plain-decoding table (95 tok/s) but has no MTP row, so its with-head speed is unpublished by anyone. The RTX A6000 does not appear in the maker’s tables at all: it fits, it is cheap, and its speed on this model is unmeasured.
Thinking is not optional decorationThe model reasons at xhigh by default and a small generation cap ends output mid-thought; agent loops should budget the trace tokens, and low effort silently behaves like xhigh.

The licence — Apache 2.0

From the repository itself, read Nov 25, 2026.

The factThe detail
Apache 2.0, verified three waysThe repository metadata declares license: apache-2.0; the model card’s licence section states “Released under Apache 2.0”; and the repository carries the full Apache 2.0 text as its LICENSE file (10,174 bytes).
NOTICE and provenanceThe repository also carries a NOTICE.txt with upstream attribution — the base model is Qwen’s Qwen3.8-27B — and the provenance of the MTP draft head included in the -mtp variants. There is no custom licence, no non-commercial clause and no separate terms file in the repository: what the metadata says is what the repo contains. As always, the licence covers the weights as released by PrismML; your obligations for the base model’s own terms are yours to check if your use goes beyond running these files.
Compare GPU prices across every provider→The model page for Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B→

How we check

Model facts are from PrismML’s Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-GGUF model card and the repository file listing via the Hugging Face API (revision 28a7093cc25bc151cc2b284c5570f12ce343fdcf), read first-hand Nov 25, 2026: parameters, architecture, packings, commands, known issues, benchmark and speed tables, licence. Every checkpoint file was measured byte-exact from that listing, which is why this guide plans from 5.99 GB where the card headlines 5.93 GB. PrismML’s download documentation (docs.prismml.com) gives the repository inventory for the 27B — GGUF, GGUF-MTP and MLX packs, no safetensors release — and that single fact decides the serving table; vLLM’s documented characterisation of its own GGUF support (highly experimental, now in an out-of-tree plugin) was checked the same day. The Q4 comparison size — the canonical Unsloth UD-Q4_K_M build of Qwen3.8-27B, 16,464,440,224 bytes — is recorded byte-exact in the fraQtl Hi-Fi repository’s byte-matched comparison table: a community record, labelled as such wherever it is used. Prices are GPUJournal’s board snapshot of Nov 25, 2026 (87 offers, check_type corroboration; its source line names TensorDock and nafnaf.ai as carried): RTX 4090 RunPod Community $0.34, RTX A6000 Thunder Compute $0.35, RTX 5090 RunPod Community $0.69, L40S RunPod Community $0.79, A100 80GB Thunder Compute $1.09, RTX PRO 6000 RunPod Community $1.69 — monthly = hourly × 730, computed exactly. TensorDock’s RTX 4090 figure in the snapshot is a carried Managed Containers page figure and is not used in the table; the table’s RTX 4090 row is RunPod Community, corroborated Nov 25. What is deliberately not claimed: no speed figure appears here as our finding — every decode and prefill number is PrismML’s own published measurement, labelled the maker’s, with its method; no per-token KV figure is derived, because no primary source publishes one; no sustained multi-user throughput is stated, because none exists in a primary source.

MODEL DEPLOYMENT →  ·  2026-11-25 · 17 min read

Deploy Hy4 Flash — the FP8 setup on two H200s, costed

Tencent's Hy4 Flash is a 220B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only about 12B parameters per token — but memory is always the full 220.3B, because every parameter has to sit in GPU memory whether a given token uses it or not. At FP8 the weights occupy about 220GB, which fits two H200s with room to spare; at BF16 they occupy about 440GB and need four. On the cheapest verified H200 rate on our board, checked Nov 25, 2026, the FP8 pair costs $7.18 an hour. This guide shows the memory maths, the serving routes Tencent actually documents — both written for tensor-parallel 8, so the two-GPU run is a memory fit, not a published recipe — what each setup costs across every H200 offer on the board, and the licence clause, §10.2 of the Tencent Hy License, that a commercial hoster needs to read before the download finishes.

The verdict

  • FP8 — 2 × H200 (282GB; weights ≈220GB) — The cheapest verified FP8 setup, at RunPod Community's $3.59/GPU/hr. A memory fit, not a published recipe: both of Tencent's serving recipes are tensor-parallel 8. RunPod Community · 2 × H200 — $7.18/hr, $5,241.40/mo.
  • FP8 — 2 × H200 — The same memory-feasible shape at Hyperstack's $3.99/GPU/hr. Hyperstack · 2 × H200 — $7.98/hr, $5,825.40/mo.
  • BF16 — 4 × H200 (564GB; weights ≈440GB) — Full precision at RunPod Community's $3.59/GPU/hr. Three H200s give 423GB, less than the ≈440GB of weights — four cards is the floor. RunPod Community · 4 × H200 — $14.36/hr, $10,482.80/mo.
  • BF16 — 4 × H200 — Full precision at Hyperstack's $3.99/GPU/hr. Hyperstack · 4 × H200 — $15.96/hr, $11,650.80/mo.
  • FP8, the shape Tencent's own recipe uses — 8 × H200 (tensor-parallel 8) — The maker-documented shape: the only serving recipes Tencent publishes, for vLLM and for SGLang, are both written for tensor-parallel 8. At RunPod Community's $3.59/GPU/hr. RunPod Community · 8 × H200 — $28.72/hr, $20,965.60/mo.
Compare GPU prices across every provider→The model page for Hy4 Flash→

The short answer

If you want the cheapest defensible Hy4 Flash deployment today, rent two H200s and run the FP8 checkpoint: $7.18 an hour at RunPod Community's verified $3.59 per GPU (checked Nov 25, 2026), $5,241.40 for an always-on month. The FP8 checkpoint is a separate repo (tencent/Hy4-flash-FP8) and it is the checkpoint both of Tencent's serving recipes point at — FP8 is not a compromise you make to save money here, it is the maker's own production build. If you need full BF16 precision — for evaluation work, fine-tuning headroom, or because your pipeline distrusts 8-bit weights — the same model needs four H200s and the cheapest verified total doubles to $14.36 an hour. There is no single-GPU route in Tencent's documentation at either precision, and on the H200 this guide prices, even FP8 needs two cards; nor is there a smaller official quantisation beyond a GGUF build Tencent provides, in its own words, “for end-to-end testing purposes.” And before any of that matters commercially: Hy4 Flash is not Apache 2.0. It ships under the Tencent Hy License, whose §10.2 requires a separate written licence from Tencent if you run it as a model-as-a-service business past either of two size triggers. Most self-hosters never trip it. An API reseller at scale trips it on day one. Read the TL;DR table's last row before you budget on the first one: the two-H200 FP8 setup is a memory fit — the weights provably fit in 282GB, with about 62GB left for KV cache and runtime overhead — but nobody's published recipe yet documents a two-GPU run. Treat $7.18/hr as the floor the memory maths allows and $28.72/hr as the price of the shape the maker actually documents, until a two-GPU recipe is proven. Monthly figures are the hourly total × 730 hours, always-on.

The memory maths — the card's component table (Tencent's model card, read Nov 18, 2026)

Everything in this section is arithmetic on figures from Tencent's own model card. Two things in the table surprise people. First, nearly a third of the model — 63.5B parameters — is Engram embedding tables, not transformer layers; they still occupy memory in full. Second, the “12B active” headline (the card's table: 11.3B text + 0.43B vision activated per token) describes compute per token, not memory. Memory is always the full 220.3B. Sizes are decimal gigabytes at exactly 1 or 2 bytes per parameter, before framework overhead, activation memory and KV cache — which is why the setups keep headroom rather than filling cards to the byte.

Component (card's table)Parameters · at FP8 (1 byte/param) · at BF16 (2 bytes/param)

What fits where — and the 1M context and its KV cache

The shapeThe working
FP8 on 2 × H200An H200 carries 141GB, so two cards give 282GB against ≈220GB of weights — about 62GB of headroom for KV cache and runtime. This is the cheapest memory-feasible shape.
BF16 on 4 × H200Three H200s give 423GB, which is less than ≈440GB of weights — so four cards (564GB) is the floor at full precision, with about 124GB of headroom.
FP8 on H100 SXM (80GB)Weights alone need three cards (240GB) and leave almost nothing for cache; four cards (320GB) is the practical floor — 4 × $2.69 at RunPod Community = $10.76/hr (checked Nov 25, 2026), which is more than the two-H200 setup. The H200 is simply the right card for this model.
The 1M context and its KV cache — smaller than you fearA 1M-token context usually means a KV cache that eats the GPU. Hy4 Flash is built to avoid exactly that, and the card's configuration lets you check the claim yourself. Its attention is Multi-head Latent Attention with a compressed KV of 512 dimensions plus a 64-dimension RoPE key — 576 values per token per layer. Only 12 of its 42 layers are sparse full-context layers; the other 30 are sliding-window layers that cache just 512 tokens each. The arithmetic, assuming a BF16 cache and that the sparse layers cache the compressed latent for every position: 12 layers × 576 values × 2 bytes ≈ 13.8KB per token, so a full 1,048,576-token sequence costs about 14.5GB of KV cache per sequence; the 30 sliding-window layers add under 20MB. Halve it if the cache is held at FP8. The DFly2 drafter adds no KV of its own — the card states it shares the target model's cache. Tencent's own version of this claim is that the design cuts KV cache to 1/24 of Hy3's and 1/6 of Hy4's; that comparison is the publisher's, but the per-token arithmetic above is derivable from the published configuration, with the assumptions stated. Per-sequence is the operative phrase: a serving node running many long-context sessions in parallel multiplies that 14.5GB by the number of concurrent full-length sequences, and that — not the weights — is what will cap your batch size on the two-H200 setup.

The serving route, as it actually stands (verified from primary sources, checked Nov 18, 2026)

RouteWhat is documented
vLLM serves it today — through Tencent's pinned image, not the stock releaseThe model card's Deployment section gives an official prebuilt image, vllm/vllm-openai:hy4-flash, serving the FP8 checkpoint with tensor-parallel 8, the FLASHMLA_SPARSE attention backend, DFly2 speculative decoding (5 speculative tokens), and Tencent's hy_v4 tool-call and reasoning parsers. The card also links an official Hy4 Flash recipe on vLLM's recipe site. But vLLM's own supported-models list, checked the same day, names the HYV4 architecture against Hy4-preview only — Hy4 Flash does not appear in the stock release's model list yet. So the honest statement is: a maker-maintained vLLM build serves it now; mainline vLLM support is not yet listed.
SGLang is the second documented routeAlso via a pinned image (lmsysorg/sglang:hy4-flash, x86 and Arm), also tensor-parallel 8, with DFly speculative decoding. The card links an SGLang cookbook for the model.
Transformers support is written but not mergedThe card tells you to install Transformers from a specific pull request (PR 50903) “until then” — its words are that support “will be merged into the transformers main branch soon.” A plain pip install transformers does not run this model today.
Both recipes are tensor-parallel 8Neither Tencent recipe documents 2, 4 or any other GPU count. Changing the tensor-parallel size to fit two H200s is the obvious experiment, and it may work — but no source we read documents it, so this guide does not present the two-GPU run as a proven recipe. It presents it as what it is: memory-feasible, recipe-unproven.
Practical settings from the cardReasoning runs in two modes, reasoning_effort “high” (default, thinking on) and “no_think”; Tencent recommends temperature 0.9 and top_p 1.0. The base repo (tencent/Hy4-flash-Base) is a pre-trained checkpoint, not a chat model — deploy the instruct or FP8 repo, not the base, unless pre-training is your job.
On speed, this guide prints no throughput figure of its ownNobody independent has measured one yet. The only number in circulation is Tencent's: the card says that combining megakernels, 4-bit quantisation and DFly2 “pushes decoding speed past 150 tokens/s.” Note the conditions — that claim belongs to a 4-bit configuration, not to the FP8 build this guide costs, and it is the publisher's own figure, unverified by any third party as of Nov 18, 2026. Budget on the rental totals, not on that number.

The licence: read §10 before you build on it (Tencent Hy License, Version 1.0)

The pointThe detail
Not Apache 2.0Hy4 Flash is released under the Tencent Hy License, Version 1.0. The licence file, read in the model repo on Nov 18, 2026, says in its own header that it is derived from the Apache License 2.0 “with modifications, mainly the additional commercial terms for large Model-as-a-Service businesses in Section 10” — and that it “is not the Apache License, Version 2.0.” This is a change from Hy4 preview, which shipped under plain Apache 2.0.
§10.1 — what “MaaS” means“MaaS means giving third parties remote access to model inference or fine-tuning (e.g., via API), allowing them to submit inputs or specify parameters or training data.” — §10.1, with two carve-outs: end-user products where the model's capabilities are confined to specific features or workflows without general-purpose model access, and merely relaying requests to an independently operated third-party model service.
§10.2 — the triggers“If You operate a MaaS business, You must obtain a separate written license… (a) if Your aggregate worldwide gross revenue exceeds US$50 million… in any consecutive 12-month period, whether or not such revenue is derived from the Work…; or (b) before using the Work… in or for any product or service provided by You that has more than 100 million monthly active users in any calendar month.” — §10.2, summarised only in the connective wording; the triggers are quoted exactly.
The revenue trigger is your whole company's revenue, not your model revenue§10.2(a) counts aggregate worldwide gross revenue “whether or not such revenue is derived from the Work.” A company with $60M of unrelated revenue that exposes Hy4 Flash through a public API needs Tencent's written licence before it starts — or must stop using the weights. The licence says the separate licence can be granted “including by email,” and names its contact: hy_partners@tencent.com (§10.4).
Internal use is fully exempt§10.3: §10.2 “does not apply to Your use of the Work… solely for internal purposes, provided that neither the Work, any Derivative Works, nor their outputs are made available to third parties.” Run it for your own team, your own research, your own back office — §10 never engages.
A product feature is not MaaS; an API isUnder §10.1's carve-out, a product that uses the model inside confined features — a document assistant inside your own app, say — is not MaaS even at scale, though the 100M-MAU trigger in §10.2(b) is written separately and applies to “any product or service,” so a feature-confined product past 100M monthly users should still take advice before assuming it is clear. Selling general-purpose inference or fine-tuning access is MaaS by definition.
The clause travels with the weightsSection 4 of the licence provides that any licence terms you pass on for the Work or a derivative must not “remove, limit, or conflict with Section 10,” and that §10 “shall continue to apply to every recipient.” Fine-tunes, quantisations and merges are all defined as Derivative Works. You cannot launder the trigger away by re-releasing a fine-tune.
Below both triggers, the licence is permissive in practiceAn independent hoster under $50M revenue and under 100M MAU may run a paid API on these weights without a separate licence, on the licence's own text. That is a genuinely open door for small and mid-size inference businesses — with a ceiling built into it. This section is a plain-English reading of the licence text, not legal advice. The triggers are quoted from the Tencent Hy License v1.0 file in the tencent/Hy4-flash repo, read Nov 18, 2026; if your business sits anywhere near either line, read the file itself and take advice before you build on the weights.

Watch-outs before you commit

Watch-outThe detail
Every benchmark is Tencent's ownThe numbers circulating for this model — a 42.1 score on Tencent's internal WorkIndex benchmark, a blind test of 85 of Tencent's own WorkBuddy users scoring satisfaction 2.79/4 against Claude Haiku 5.5's 2.81/4, cost-per-task comparisons against Tencent's own API prices — were all produced by the publisher. No independent evaluation existed when we checked on Nov 18, 2026. Treat the quality claims as unverified until an outside evaluator publishes; the cost and memory figures in this guide do not depend on them.
You are pinned to Tencent's framework buildsThe working vLLM and SGLang routes are model-specific prebuilt images maintained for this launch. Fixes and features arrive on the image maintainer's schedule, not the frameworks'. Mainline vLLM lists Hy4-preview, not Hy4 Flash (checked Nov 18, 2026), and Transformers support sits in an unmerged pull request. Expect launch-month friction and pin your image versions.
The two-GPU recipe gap is the budget riskThe gap between the memory-feasible setup ($7.18/hr) and the maker-documented shape ($28.72/hr) is a factor of four. Do not sign a month of two-GPU capacity on the assumption that tensor-parallel 2 works until you have run the pinned image at that size yourself.
Community capacity is community capacityThe cheapest rate in this guide, RunPod Community at $3.59/GPU/hr, is marketplace capacity: availability varies by region and hour, and a two-GPU pair in the same place is not guaranteed to be there when you scale. The board's H200 page shows the current spread; re-check before a long run.
Do not download the wrong repoThree repos landed within minutes of each other on Nov 17, 2026: the instruct model, the FP8 build, and a pre-trained base that does not follow chat instructions. Production serving wants the FP8 repo; chat evaluation wants the instruct repo; the base is for fine-tuners.
The Engram tables are not optional63.5B of the 220.3B parameters are N-gram embedding tables. Any plan that budgets memory from the “155.5B backbone” figure alone under-budgets by nearly 30% — the tables load in full alongside the backbone.

How we check

Model facts — parameter counts, architecture, context length, sampling recommendations, framework recipes — are from Tencent's Hy4 Flash model card on Hugging Face, read first-hand on Nov 18, 2026; the licence summary and quotations are from the Tencent Hy License v1.0 file in the same repository, read the same day. vLLM's supported-models list was read on Nov 18, 2026 and names HYV4 against tencent/Hy4-preview and tencent/Hy4-preview-FP8 only. Prices are GPUJournal's Nov 25, 2026 board snapshot: 87 offers read from providers' own published pages and banked by date; H200 offers in it are RunPod Community $3.59, Hyperstack $3.99, RunPod Secure $5.29, Nebius $5.40 (excl. VAT), CoreWeave $6.31 (normalised from an 8-GPU node at $50.44/node/hr), Verda $7.184, Oracle OCI $10.00 (8-GPU node at $80.00/node/hr) and Microsoft Azure $10.60 (8-GPU VM at $84.80/VM/hr, East US 2). Setup totals and monthly figures are arithmetic on those verified rates (× 730 hours for a month), labelled wherever a per-GPU division is extended to a shape the provider does not list at that size. Weights sizes are arithmetic on the card's parameter table at 1 byte (FP8) and 2 bytes (BF16) per parameter. The KV-cache figure is arithmetic on the card's published attention configuration (MLA kv_lora_rank 512, RoPE head dimension 64, 12 sparse layers, 30 sliding-window layers at 512 tokens), with its assumptions stated in the text; it excludes indexer state, framework padding and activation memory. What is deliberately not claimed. No throughput, latency or tokens-per-dollar figure appears in this guide as our finding: the only speed claim in circulation is Tencent's own (past 150 tokens/s, under a 4-bit configuration with megakernels and DFly2), printed above as the publisher's claim with its conditions, and no independent benchmark of Hy4 Flash existed when we checked on Nov 18, 2026. Tencent Cloud's own API prices for this model circulate in secondary reporting in RMB and via third-party routers; they are not printed here because we did not verify a USD list price on Tencent's own pages for this guide. No two-GPU serving run is claimed as proven: the recipes Tencent publishes specify tensor-parallel 8.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. Hy4 Flash is priced by its maker to be served, and the serving maths is genuinely friendly: a 220B-class model whose FP8 weights fit a two-GPU rental at $7.18 an hour, with a KV design that makes its 1M context cheap to hold, is a different economic object from the 220B models that needed a full node. But the two honest asterisks are both Tencent-shaped. The framework support is a pair of pinned images and an unmerged pull request, and the licence quietly converts “open weights” into “open below $50M of company revenue” for anyone selling inference. Neither is a reason to walk away. Both are reasons to read §10 before the download finishes, and to test the two-GPU run before the month-long rental starts.

Deploy Sarvam-105B-1711 on one RTX PRO 6000 — and the $0.15/Mtok break-even

Sarvam's 105B checkpoint is the rare open-weight release whose pitch is a single workstation card: the NVFP4 build measures 70.15GB on disk and is documented by its maker to run on one 96GB RTX PRO 6000, at $1.69 an hour on the cheapest verified row of our board (checked Nov 25, 2026). In the same announcement, Sarvam cut its hosted price to a blended $0.15 per million tokens — and this guide works the honest break-even from Sarvam's own published throughput table. The answer is stark: at the throughput Sarvam itself measures on this card, the break-even volume is about 57 times what the card can produce in a month. You rent this card for control, not for savings — and the guide shows the arithmetic that proves it, both ways.

The verdict

  • Self-host NVFP4 — 1 × RTX PRO 6000 — Break-even at 8.22 billion tokens/month — a sustained 3,130 tok/s, around the clock, all month. Sarvam's own model card measures this card's peak aggregate throughput at 54.9 tok/s, so the break-even volume is ~57× the most the card can produce in a month (~144M tokens). On cost alone, this route never wins — it is a control and on-premises purchase. RunPod Community · RTX PRO 6000 — $1.69/hr, $1,233.70/mo.
  • Sarvam hosted API — 100M tokens/month costs $15; 1 billion costs $150; the self-host card's whole month costs the same as 8.22 billion API tokens. “Blended” is Sarvam's own 3 input : 1 output mix of its Token Factory rates (₹10 in / ₹25 out per million). Those rates are marked introductory, through the end of 2026, on Sarvam's pricing page — the $0.15 has an expiry date on its inputs.
  • Self-host BF16 — 2 × H200 — Break-even at 34.94 billion tokens/month — a sustained 13,296 tok/s. Full precision, and the maker's documented shape (tensor parallel 2). But Sarvam publishes no throughput table for the BF16 build, so this break-even is a volume you must hit, not a rate anyone has demonstrated. The NVFP4 build is the deployment this checkpoint is documented around. RunPod Community · 2 × H200 — $7.18/hr, $5,241.40/mo.
Compare GPU prices across every provider→The release story — Sarvam-105B-1711 open weights→

The short answer

Download sarvamai/sarvam-105b-1711 (the NVFP4 build, 70.15GB measured), serve it on one RTX PRO 6000 with the vLLM commands Sarvam prints on the model card — tested by the maker on vLLM 0.33.0, tensor parallel 1 — and the cheapest verified way to rent that card on our board, checked Nov 25, 2026, is RunPod Community at $1.69 an hour, $1,233.70 for a 730-hour month. Then make the hosting decision with open eyes: Sarvam sells the same model, hosted, at a blended $0.15 per million tokens, and at that price the rented card only pays for itself above 8.22 billion tokens a month — a volume Sarvam's own throughput table says this card cannot reach. Self-host because the weights must sit on your premises, under your control, in your jurisdiction. Do not self-host this checkpoint on this card to save money. The rest of this guide is the working behind those sentences. Monthly figures are the hourly rate × 730 hours, computed exactly. All throughput figures in this guide are Sarvam's own published measurements, labelled vendor-reported; we ran no benchmarks.

What you are actually downloading — model cards, repository configs and file listings, read Nov 23, 2026

Sizes measured from the repositories' own file lists, not the announcement's rounded figures.

The factThe detail
105B total parameters, 10.3B active per tokenThe maker's figures, stated on both cards. The architecture, from the repo config: 32 layers — the first dense, the other 31 mixture-of-experts with 128 routed experts, 8 firing per token, plus 1 shared expert per layer. Attention is multi-head latent attention (MLA) with a 512-rank latent KV, the DeepSeek pattern. Our own check of the config's expert maths accounts for ~103B of the 105B before attention and routers, so the maker's headline is consistent with the shipped config.
The NVFP4 build (sarvamai/sarvam-105b-1711) measures 70.15GB on disk64.64GB of main weights in 4 shards, plus the 5.51GB DSpark draft model the repo ships alongside. The announcement's “65 GB” is the same total read in GiB (65.33 GiB); the guide works in the measured GB figures. It is a mixed-precision build, per the repo's quantization config: the routed experts — the bulk of the model — are NVFP4 (4-bit), while attention, the shared experts and the first layer's dense MLP are MXFP8 (8-bit), and the routers and language-model head stay in BF16.
The BF16 build (sarvamai/sarvam-105b-1711-bf16) measures 218.23GB212.07GB of main weights in 43 shards, plus a 6.16GB DSpark draft. A naive 105B × 2 bytes gives 210GB, so the measured file is the honest planning figure.
Context: 163,840 tokensDeclared in the config (max_position_embeddings), extended from a 4,096 base by YaRN rope scaling. Note the gap between the box and the recipes: Sarvam's own serving commands and its own benchmark setup both run the model at 131,072 tokens.
DSpark is in both reposA draft model for speculative decoding (5 draft tokens in the maker's published throughput runs). It is part of the download and part of the documented serving recipe, not an optional extra you fetch elsewhere.
What the checkpoint is for, in the maker's framingA “Flash-Lite” model for high-volume conversational, voice-agent and agentic work, post-trained from the February Sarvam 105B for tool calling, instruction following, agentic tasks and Indian languages. Thinking is on by default (temperature 1.0 recommended with it, 0.6 without).
Licence: Apache 2.0Declared in both repos' metadata — with one nuance printed in the licence section below. There is no revenue or user-count gate of the kind the Tencent Hy licence imposes; the contrast is real and worth having in writing.

The one-card route: the memory maths — worked from the measured checkpoint and the repo config, Nov 23, 2026

The card is an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell with 96GB — the capacity Sarvam's own card names for its throughput test.

The figureThe working
Weights: 70.15GB64.64GB main + 5.51GB DSpark draft. On a 96GB card that leaves 25.85GB of raw headroom for KV cache, activations and the runtime.
Inside the maker's own recipe budgetSarvam's serving commands set --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92, a budget of 88.32GB on this card. After the 70.15GB of weights, 18.17GB remains inside that budget for KV cache and working room. That is the number to plan with — not the 96 on the box.
KV cache, worked from the configMLA stores a compressed latent per token — kv_lora_rank 512 plus the 64-dimension RoPE key, 576 values per layer per token, across 32 layers. In the FP8 KV format the recipe specifies (--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3), that is 18,432 bytes per token: about 0.92GB per 50,000-token sequence, 2.42GB per sequence at the recipe's 131,072-token setting, and 3.02GB at the full 163,840 the config declares. Eight concurrent 50k-context sequences — the top of Sarvam's published test on this card — carry about 7.37GB of KV, comfortably inside the 18.17GB. At BF16 KV precision every one of those figures doubles.

Serving: what is documented today, and what is not

RouteStatus today
vLLM — proven, documented by the maker, with exact commandsBoth model cards carry a “vLLM hosting” section, “Tested with vLLM 0.33.0”, with the environment the maker specifies and two serve commands (with and without DSpark speculative decoding). vLLM's own documentation also carries a Sarvam MLA implementation (the SarvamMLAForCausalLM architecture in its supported-models documentation), and the cards' commands still pass --trust-remote-code — the repos ship their own modelling code, and the documented route uses it. Read the recipe's own settings as the maker's intent: one GPU (--tensor-parallel-size 1), a 131,072-token window rather than the config's 163,840, FP8 KV cache, and 256 maximum sequences — a ceiling the memory maths, not the flag, will govern in practice.

The hosted price, verified from Sarvam's own pages

The $0.15 figure is Sarvam's own, from its Nov 22, 2026 announcement: “Our inference optimisations have also cut its blended price by two-thirds, from $0.44 to $0.15 per million tokens.” Three things about it that the headline hides, all from Sarvam's own material read Nov 23, 2026.

The pointThe detail
“Blended” has a definition, and it is a mixThe announcement's own pricing footnote: blended prices are computed at 3 input tokens : 1 output token, from Token Factory list prices. A workload that generates more output than that mix — long reasoning traces, for instance, with thinking on by default — blends dearer than $0.15; an input-heavy workload blends cheaper. Reasoning tokens are billed as output, per the pricing page.
The underlying rate card is in rupees, and it is a split, not a blendSarvam's API pricing page lists Sarvam 105B at ₹10 per million input tokens, ₹0.25 per million cached input, ₹25 per million output, the same on every plan, excluding GST. Our arithmetic on the maker's own footnote (₹10/₹25 at the 3:1 blend, converted at the ₹90-per-dollar rate the announcement itself uses) gives ₹13.75 blended, or $0.1528 — the announced $0.15, confirmed as arithmetic.
The rates are introductory, with a stated horizonThe pricing page marks the Sarvam 105B rates “Introductory pricing … through the end of 2026.” The $0.44 is the previous blended figure as Sarvam states it in the announcement; Sarvam's current pricing page does not print it. When the introductory rates lapse, the break-even in the next section moves — in self-hosting's favour — by whatever the new blend is.
Rate limits are part of the hosted offerThe pricing page lists the Sarvam-105B models at 60 requests/minute on pay-as-you-go, 200 on Pro, 300 on Growth. High-volume self-hosters are sometimes really buying their way out of a rate limit, not out of a per-token price — a legitimate reason, but a different one from cost.

The break-even, worked honestly

Method and assumptions, stated before the numbers. Self-host cost is the card's rent for a 730-hour month, run around the clock — the only way renting competes with a per-token price. The API side is Sarvam's blended $0.15 per million tokens at the maker's 3:1 input:output mix. Break-even volume = monthly rent ÷ $0.15, in tokens. Required sustained throughput = that volume ÷ the 2,628,000 seconds in the month — the rate the card would have to average, day and night, with no idle second. Where a throughput is Sarvam's published measurement, it is labelled vendor-reported with its test conditions; where a throughput is an assumption, the table says so in its heading. Electricity, storage, and your own operations time are excluded on the self-host side; API-side extras (GST for Indian entities, per the pricing page) are excluded on the other. Both exclusions favour neither side enough to change the conclusion, which is not close.

The lineThe working
The headline lineAt the cheapest verified card rate ($1.69/hr, $1,233.70/month), break-even against $0.15 per million tokens is 8.22 billion tokens a month. Producing them in a 730-hour month means sustaining 3,130 tokens per second — every second, all month.
What the card actually does — Sarvam's own throughput tableSarvam's model card publishes its own throughput table for this checkpoint on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96GB), measured with DSpark speculative decoding, FP8 KV cache, thinking on, at 50,000-token context — the maker's numbers, vendor-reported. At 1 concurrent user: 30.9 tok/s total throughput, 61.8 tok/s per user, time to first token p50 8.1 s. At 4 users: 43.9 tok/s total, 14.4 per user, 8.5 s. At 8 users: 54.9 tok/s total, 12.2 per user, 19.5 s.
The peak, run flat out for a monthTake the table's peak — 54.9 tok/s aggregate at 8 concurrent users — and run it flat out for a month: 144.3 million tokens. That volume on the API costs $21.64. The rented card costs $1,233.70 for the same month, an effective $8.55 per million tokens — 57 times the API price. The break-even volume (8.22 billion) is ~57× the maximum the card can produce at its maker's measured rate. There is no utilisation trick that closes a gap of that shape: the card would need to be 57 cards.
One discrepancy, printedSarvam's announcement says the model on this card reaches “99 tokens per second per user.” The model card's own published table for this checkpoint peaks at 61.8 tok/s per user, at a single user. The guide works from the card's table — it is the checkpoint's own documentation, with its test conditions printed — and treats the 99 as an announcement headline the card's table does not reproduce.

The BF16 route: full precision, two cards

The BF16 build is the same checkpoint at full precision, and Sarvam documents its serving shape on its card: the same vLLM recipe at tensor parallel 2. The memory arithmetic decides the node: 218.23GB of weights splits to 109.11GB per GPU at TP2, and inside the recipe's 0.92 utilisation budget a card must offer at least ~118.6GB — which is why the sensible node is 2 × H200 (141GB each): budget 129.72GB per GPU, weights 109.11GB, room left for the BF16 KV cache (36,864 bytes per token from the config — 4.83GB per 131,072-token sequence before it is split across the pair). The honest negatives: two RTX PRO 6000s total 192GB, less than the 218.23GB of weights — the one-card story does not stretch to two of the same card; a single B200 (192GB) does not hold it either; and three 80GB cards pass the raw arithmetic (72.74GB per GPU against a 73.6GB budget) with no headroom worth the name and no documented recipe — arithmetic, not a route. Who is this route for? Workloads where the NVFP4 quantisation itself is the question — evaluation against the BF16 reference, research on the checkpoint, or a quality bar the 4-bit build demonstrably misses on your own tests. Sarvam's own benchmark table puts the two builds within a point or two of each other almost everywhere (its runs, its harness — see the watch-outs). What the BF16 route is not is a throughput play: Sarvam publishes no BF16 throughput table, so nobody can honestly quote you its tokens per second, and its break-even is a volume target, not a demonstrated rate.

The pointThe detail

Watch-outThe detail

Thinking is on by default in this checkpoint and reasoning tokens bill as output on the API — a reasoning-heavy workload blends above $0.15, which quietly improves the self-host comparison. How we check

Model facts — 105B total parameters and 10.3B active per token (the maker's figures), 32 layers (1 dense, 31 MoE), 128 routed experts plus 1 shared with top-8 firing, MLA attention with kv_lora_rank 512 and a 64-dimension RoPE key, 163,840-token declared context — are from the config.json files and model cards of sarvamai/sarvam-105b-1711 and sarvamai/sarvam-105b-1711-bf16 on Hugging Face, read first-hand Nov 23, 2026; the config-derived expert maths (~103B before attention and routers) is our consistency check on the maker's 105B, not a recount. Checkpoint sizes are measured, not quoted: the safetensors file sizes in each repo's listing (Hugging Face API) sum to 70.15GB for the NVFP4 build (64.64GB main weights in 4 shards + 5.51GB DSpark draft; 65.33 GiB in binary units, which is the announcement's “65 GB”) and 218.23GB for the BF16 build (212.07GB in 43 shards + 6.16GB DSpark; 203.24 GiB). The quantization split (routed experts NVFP4; attention, shared experts and layer-0 dense MLP MXFP8; routers and lm_head unquantised) is from the NVFP4 repo's quantization_config. KV figures are arithmetic from the config: (512 + 64) values × 32 layers = 18,432 bytes per token at FP8, 36,864 at BF16. Serving verification: the model cards' “vLLM hosting” sections (tested with vLLM 0.33.0; environment block and DSpark command reproduced verbatim; the BF16 card's shape is tensor parallel 2), vLLM's supported-models documentation (a Sarvam MLA implementation, SarvamMLAForCausalLM, is listed), and SGLang's documentation, in which no Sarvam entry could be found today — SGLang is therefore labelled undocumented for this checkpoint, as is any Transformers serving recipe (the repos ship custom modelling code but document no Transformers route). Throughput figures are Sarvam's published tables from the NVFP4 model card (DSpark, FP8 KV cache, thinking on, prefix cache cleared per level, reasoning prompts): RTX PRO 6000 at 50k context — 30.9 / 43.9 / 54.9 tok/s aggregate at 1 / 4 / 8 users; B200 at 128k context — 5,354 tok/s at 64 users, 7,490 at 128. All are vendor-reported; we ran no benchmarks. The announcement's “99 tokens per second per user” for the PRO 6000 appears in Sarvam's blog (Nov 22, 2026) and is not reproduced in the card's table; the guide says so where it matters. Hosted pricing: the announcement's blended $0.44 → $0.15 per million tokens and its blend definition (3 input : 1 output, Token Factory list prices, ₹90 per dollar) are Sarvam's; the underlying rates — ₹10 input / ₹0.25 cached input / ₹25 output per million tokens, introductory through the end of 2026, GST excluded, reasoning billed as output, 60/200/300 requests-per-minute limits by plan — are from Sarvam's own API pricing page (docs.sarvam.ai), read Nov 23, 2026; the blend arithmetic (₹13.75 → $0.1528) is ours, computed from those figures. The licence is Apache 2.0 as declared in both repos' Hugging Face metadata; neither repo contains a standalone LICENSE file as of Nov 23, 2026, and the guide says so. Rental prices are GPUJournal's Nov 25, 2026 board snapshot: RTX PRO 6000 — RunPod Community $1.69, Nebius $1.80 (excl. VAT), CoreWeave $2.50 (High-Memory variant, normalised from $20.00/node/hr), RunPod Secure $2.69, Verda $3.041, Oracle OCI $4.50 (from an 8-GPU node at $36.00/node/hr), Google Cloud $5.1749195 (1-GPU VM); H200 — RunPod Community $3.59, Hyperstack $3.99, RunPod Secure $5.29. The RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q row (nafnaf.ai, $0.752) is a different variant whose board figure is carried, not re-verified, and is excluded from every table. Monthly figures are hourly × 730; break-even volumes are monthly rent ÷ $0.15; required sustained rates are those volumes ÷ 2,628,000 seconds; effective self-host $/Mtok at a given throughput is monthly rent ÷ (throughput × 2,628,000 ÷ 1,000,000). All computed by script. What is deliberately not claimed. No throughput figure appears here as our measurement — every rate is Sarvam's published table (vendor-reported, conditions printed) or a labelled assumption in the sensitivity table. No serving route is asserted beyond the cards' own vLLM documentation: SGLang and Transformers are labelled undocumented for this checkpoint, and community quantisations are named as community work. No BF16 throughput is quoted, because Sarvam publishes none. The $0.44 previous blended price is Sarvam's statement in its announcement; it is not printed on Sarvam's current pricing page and we do not present it as independently verified. Where our own Nov 22 story's rounded figures differ from the measurements in this guide — the NVFP4 size (story: 65GB; measured: 70.15GB, the same total in GiB), the BF16 size (story: about 198GB; measured main weights: 212.07GB, 197.50 GiB), the B200 rate at 64 users (story: about 6,000 tok/s, the announcement's rounding; the card's table: 5,354) — the measured and tabled figures in this guide are the ones to use, and the differences are unit and rounding differences in the maker's own material, recorded in the audit note.

Our reading

Our reading — interpretation, not fact. This release is two announcements wearing one coat: a genuinely useful one-card deployment, and a hosted price cut so deep it undercuts the deployment it arrived with. Both can be true, and for Sarvam both are useful — the weights prove the model is open, the API price is where the volume goes. For a renter, the discipline is to keep the two decisions separate: custody is a reason to rent the card; cost, at $0.15 a million, is not. A guide that printed the one-card route without the maker's own throughput table would have sold you the coat without mentioning the weather.

MODEL DEPLOYMENT →  ·  2026-11-25 · 17 min read

Deploy Soma-1X Lite — paper records to structured data on one small card, priced

Amini’s Soma-1X Lite does one job: it takes a page — a typed form, a handwritten letter, a table, a faded scan — and returns the page as structured data, one labelled block per element with its position on the page, tables as HTML and maths as LaTeX. It is a 2.21-billion-parameter vision-language model whose whole weights file measures 4.43 GB, so the rental question is not whether it fits — every card on our board holds it several times over — but which serving route actually runs it today, what a page costs on the one throughput figure the maker publishes, and where the traps are: the model only answers properly with its own trained prompts and thinking switched off, the card prints no context length, and the 4-bit quantisations people usually reach for do not exist because the maker’s own tests found they degraded the layout detection. This guide works the arithmetic and prices the honest single-card routes.

The verdict

  • RTX 4090 · 24 GB — cheapest honest route — Fits — the default buy for a digitisation workstation or a single-stream parsing job. No pages-per-hour figure exists for this card — see the cost section before quoting one. RunPod Community · RTX 4090 — $0.34/hr, $248.20/mo.
  • RTX A6000 · 48 GB — Fits. One cent more than the 4090 for twice the memory — the room is batch headroom for many pages in flight at once, not fit. Thunder Compute · RTX A6000 — $0.35/hr, $255.50/mo.
  • RTX 5090 · 32 GB — Fits. The newer card if your pipeline is decode-bound; nobody has published a Soma throughput figure for it. RunPod Community · RTX 5090 — $0.69/hr, $503.70/mo.
  • L40S · 48 GB — Fits. The datacentre-shaped option at the same memory as the A6000. RunPod Community · L40S — $0.79/hr, $576.70/mo.
  • RTX PRO 6000 · 96 GB — the maker’s benchmark card — Fits. The only card with a published throughput claim: Amini’s up to 15,000 pages/hour, which at this price is about $0.11 per 1,000 pages — our arithmetic on the maker’s unverified figure. RunPod Community · RTX PRO 6000 — $1.69/hr, $1,233.70/mo.
Compare GPU prices across every provider→The model page for Soma-1X Lite→

The short answer

Rent the RTX 4090 on RunPod Community at $0.34 an hour, $248.20 a month (checked Nov 25, 2026) and serve the BF16 weights with vLLM — the maker’s own card ships a vllm serve command and the architecture is on vLLM’s supported list — or run it in Transformers with the maker’s quickstart code if a notebook-shaped job is all you need. Feed it the repository’s own system_prompt.txt and user_prompt.txt, and switch thinking off: with thinking on, the answer lands in the wrong field or comes back empty. If the job is a national-scale archive and you are buying on cost per page, the only defensible number anyone publishes is Amini’s own — up to 15,000 pages an hour on an RTX PRO 6000 — and at our board’s best verified price for that card (RunPod Community, $1.69 an hour) that works out at about $0.11 per 1,000 pages, about $113 per million pages, against the roughly $0.22 per 1,000 Amini quotes from an AWS rate. Both figures rest on the maker’s throughput claim, which nobody has independently re-run; treat them as the claim’s arithmetic, not as a measurement. Monthly = hourly × 730, computed exactly. “Fits” in the table above is judged against the working set worked out in this guide — roughly 6–8 GB all-in at the maker’s own 32K serving shape — not against the 4.43 GB file alone. Every card on the board fits this model; the five rows are the cheapest single-card offers, ranked by price. The one figure that should drive a bigger purchase is throughput, and the only throughput claim that exists is the maker’s, on the most expensive card in the table.

What you are actually downloading — the model card, config and file listing, read Nov 25, 2026

From the repository’s model card, config and file listing — sizes measured from the repository’s own file list through the Hugging Face API, not quoted from the announcement.

The factThe detail
A vision-language fine-tune of Qwen3.5-2B, 2,213,241,664 parameters at BF16Trained by Amini with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning (RLVR/GRPO) on document parsing. Architecture Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration: a 24-layer text tower (hidden size 2,048) with hybrid attention — 18 linear-attention layers and a full-attention layer every fourth (6 in total, 8 query heads, 2 KV heads, head dimension 256) — in front of a 24-layer vision tower (hidden size 1,024, 16-pixel patches). Embeddings tied.
One weights file: model.safetensors measures 4,426,558,864 bytes — 4.43 GB (4.12 GiB)The parameter count cross-checks exactly: 2,213,241,664 × 2 bytes = 4,426,483,328, with the remaining 75,536 bytes the file’s header. The tokenizer is a separate 19,989,339-byte file; the processor and chat template ship alongside.
One honest discrepancy, printed rather than smoothed overOur own Nov 25 story and catalogue entry record this file as 4,455,280,241 bytes (4.46 GB), read earlier the same day. The repository was modified again at 21:35 UTC on Nov 25 — after those reads — and the file in the repository tonight measures 4.43 GB, about 0.65% smaller. (The story and catalogue figures were corrected the same day, Nov 25, 2026.) Nothing in this guide plans from the earlier figure; every fit judgement uses the measured 4.43 GB.
The job it doesInput is one document image (PDF pages are rendered to images first — the card’s own snippet uses PyMuPDF at a 1,792-pixel long edge). Output is one <block> per page element in reading order, each with a semantic label (text, heading, caption, footnote, page header/footer, annotation, image, chart, diagram, map, stamp, signature, table, equation) and a position box on a 0–1000 grid; tables come out as HTML and mathematics as LaTeX. It is a document parser, not a chatbot: the shipped chat template itself redirects non-document requests back to documents.
Thirteen languages listedEnglish, French, Spanish, Swahili, Yoruba, Hausa, Wolof, Lingala, Xhosa, Afrikaans, Kinyarwanda, Chichewa and Sango. The African-language coverage is the point of the model, not a footnote: the maker’s transcription evaluation is over ten African languages (see the quality section).
Context — the card does not state one, so read the config carefullyThe model card prints no context length. The config’s ceiling is max_position_embeddings 262,144, but the maker’s own serving examples — the vLLM command on the card and the GGUF repository’s llama.cpp and Ollama setups — all cap the working context at 32,768. This guide prices and plans at 32K, the maker’s own shape, and treats 262K as an unproven config ceiling, not a working context.
The prompts are part of the modelThe repository ships the exact system_prompt.txt (4,897 bytes) and user_prompt.txt (50 bytes) the model was trained with, and every one of the maker’s code paths loads them. Generation is greedy in the maker’s examples (temperature 0, do_sample=False) with up to 16,384 new tokens per page, and thinking is disabled everywhere (enable_thinking=False).
Licence: Apache 2.0Declared in the repository metadata and stated in both repositories’ licence sections. One gap worth printing: neither repository carries a standalone LICENSE file; the licence section links out to the Apache text instead. The scope note is in the licence section below.

The working set: why 4.43 GB of weights is a 6–8 GB job

Weights are the floor, never the whole budget — but this is a small model with a hybrid backbone, and the arithmetic is unusually kind. Worked from the config, Nov 25, 2026.

The stepThe maths
Weights: 4.43 GB at BF16The measured file. The GGUF route is smaller still — see the serving section.
KV cache is small by construction: 12,288 bytes, about 12 KB per tokenOnly the 6 full-attention layers keep a token-by-token cache; the 18 linear-attention layers carry a fixed-size state per sequence instead of one that grows with context. Per token, the full-attention cache is 6 layers × 2 KV heads × 256 head dimension × 2 (keys and values) × 2 bytes = 12,288 bytes. At the maker’s 32,768-token serving cap that is 0.40 GB per sequence; even at the config’s 262,144 ceiling it is 3.22 GB per sequence. The config publishes no size for the linear-attention state, so this guide does not invent one — it is fixed per sequence rather than per token, and the planning band carries a general allowance for it.
A page is a bounded input: at most about 3,100 image tokensAt the maker’s own render size (1,792-pixel long edge), a page costs at most about 3,100 image tokens (a 56 × 56 grid at one token per 32 × 32 pixels, from the vision tower’s 16-pixel patches and 2 × 2 merge) — derived from the config and the card’s PDF snippet, not measured. The output side is the bigger budget: the maker’s examples allow up to 16,384 generated tokens for one dense page.
Plan on roughly 6–8 GB totalFor the BF16 model at the maker’s 32K shape, one stream: 4.43 GB of weights, up to ~0.4 GB of KV per sequence at that cap, plus the vision encoder’s activations and runtime buffers inside the band. Against that, the cheapest card in the TL;DR table (24 GB) fits with at least 16 GB to spare — which is batch headroom: at the 32K cap, each additional page in flight costs at most ~0.4 GB of KV, so a 24 GB card has room for dozens of concurrent pages before memory, not compute, becomes the limit. Nobody publishes a measured concurrency figure for this model; that sentence is arithmetic, not a benchmark.

Serving reality: four documented routes, one of them an hour old

Unusually for a release-day model, every major route is documented somewhere primary. Proven below means the maker’s card or the framework’s own documentation names this model, its files or its architecture; the one route that is proven only at family level is printed as exactly that.

The routeThe record
Transformers — Proven, the reference routeThe repository’s library is Transformers, the card’s quickstart loads Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration directly, and the config records the stack it was saved with: transformers_version 5.21.0. That version is a real watch-out — this is a Transformers 5.x architecture (qwen3_5); older 4.x installs do not know the model type. Install current, as the card’s own pip install -U line does.
vLLM — Proven, the serving routeThe card ships a complete vllm serve command (BF16, tensor parallel 1, --max-model-len 32768, thinking disabled via chat-template kwargs), and vLLM’s own supported-models documentation lists Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration as natively supported. Same version warning as Transformers, sharper: containers pinned to an old Transformers are documented failing on this architecture family, so use a current vLLM rather than a stale vendor image. The maker’s command, verbatim: vllm serve AminiTech/Soma-1X-lite --served-model-name soma-1x-lite --dtype bfloat16 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --max-model-len 32768 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'
SGLang — Supported by architecture, Soma not namedSGLang’s Qwen3.5 documentation covers the family and lists the dense 2B (Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B) among its available models, hybrid attention and all — but it names the base model, not Soma, and it requires SGLang installed from the main branch. Expect it to work because the architecture is registered; do not treat it as maker-tested.
llama.cpp / Ollama (GGUF) — Proven, the local route, published hours after the weightsAmini’s own GGUF repository (created Nov 25, 2026, 21:31 UTC) ships two builds plus the vision encoder the document files need: Q8_0 at 2.01 GB — the maker’s recommended build — and BF16 at 3.78 GB, with the mmproj vision file at 0.67 GB required alongside either. The card’s llama.cpp command needs a recent build with Qwen3.5 support; the same files run on CPU. The maker states both builds produced near-identical output to the Transformers original in its checks — and that 4-bit quantisations degraded layout detection in its tests and are deliberately not provided. There is no official Q4 for this model; if a community Q4 appears, it is exactly the build class the maker measured failing.
However you serve itLoad the repository’s system_prompt.txt and user_prompt.txt — every maker code path does — and keep thinking off. The GGUF card’s warning is the sharpest statement of why: in Ollama, leave thinking on and the parse lands in the thinking field while the message content comes back empty.

What a page costs: the maker’s one number, and its limits

Amini publishes exactly one throughput figure for this model, and the whole cost story hangs off it, printed here with its provenance intact: up to 15,000 pages per hour on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000, from Amini’s launch post and press release (Nov 25, 2026), where the maker prices it at about $0.22 per 1,000 pages using an AWS on-demand rate of about $3.36 an hour for that card. The maker’s arithmetic checks out (3.36 ÷ 15 = $0.224). GPUJournal has not re-run the throughput figure, and no third party had published a replication by Nov 25, 2026. The per-page figures are our arithmetic on Amini’s unverified “up to 15,000 pages/hour” claim — hourly price ÷ 15. “Up to” is the maker’s own wording: a dense handwritten page and a clean typed page are not the same job, and the claim’s page mix is Amini’s, not stated per page type.

RTX PRO 6000 routeThe cost (prices checked Nov 25, 2026)
RunPod Community — our board’s best verified price for the card: $1.69/hrAbout $0.11 per 1,000 pages; about $113 per 1M pages.
Nebius: $1.80/hrAbout $0.12 per 1,000 pages; about $120 per 1M pages.
RunPod Secure: $2.69/hrAbout $0.18 per 1,000 pages; about $179 per 1M pages.
Amini’s own AWS-based estimate: about $3.36/hrAbout $0.22 per 1,000 pages; about $224 per 1M pages.
Run continuously at the claimed rateOne PRO 6000 clears about 10.95 million pages a month; at RunPod Community money that is the $1,233.70 monthly row in the TL;DR buying roughly eleven million parsed pages — again, the claim’s arithmetic, not a measurement.
Why the cheap cards carry no per-page figureThe 15,000 pages/hour claim is for the RTX PRO 6000 specifically. A 2B model will parse pages on an RTX 4090 — it fits trivially — but nobody, maker included, has published a pages-per-hour figure for it, and this guide does not move the PRO 6000 number across cards. If your job is a fixed archive on a deadline, the PRO 6000 row is the only one that can be planned against a published rate; if your job is a steady trickle of pages, the 4090 at $0.34 an hour is the rational buy and its per-page cost is simply unmeasured.
There is no hosted API price to compare againstAs of Nov 25, 2026, Amini publishes no per-page API price for Soma-1X Lite, and no Hugging Face inference provider serves it. The honest comparison is the one above: the maker’s self-host estimate against our board’s prices for the same card. Anyone quoting you a hosted Soma price today is quoting the wider Amini platform, not this open model — check which one the quote is for.

Quality: the maker’s benchmarks, printed as the maker’s

Every figure in this section is Amini’s own published evaluation, read from the model card on Nov 25, 2026; GPUJournal has not re-run any of them, and no independent replication existed by publication. They are printed because they are the only quality record that exists for a release-day model — and because the African-language table is the part of the record no rival publishes at all.

The claimThe detail
olmOCR-Bench: 84.7 overallThe maker’s reported evaluation; open-weight comparison scores are sourced by the maker from the public leaderboard, and the API-model scores on its chart are drawn from third-party published evaluations — the chart is a comparison the maker assembled, not a single head-to-head run.
OmniParse-Bench: 84.37 overall, 86.53 with the maker’s multi-pass harnessThe largest gain is on tables (+5.0). The harness is the maker’s inference wrapper, not a different model — budget the extra passes if you plan to use it.
African-language transcription: 2.90% mean character error rateAcross ten African languages on 435 held-out document pages (the maker’s internal test set), the lowest of the five open-weight document models the maker evaluated, and best in seven of the ten languages. The character-retention detail is the figure that matters for archive work: Hausa hooked letters retained 93% (rivals 0–60%), Yoruba dots-below 99% (rivals 31–69%), Lingala open vowels 87% (rivals 0.2–25%) — the maker’s table, printed as such.
What the card does not claimNo general reasoning, writing or coding scores, because that is not the model’s job; and no throughput figure for any card but the RTX PRO 6000. The absences are part of the record.

Watch-outs before you commit

The honest negatives, from the draft as audited.

The watch-outThe detail
Every performance number here is the maker’sBenchmarks, character error rates and the 15,000 pages/hour throughput are Amini’s own evaluations, published on release day and not independently replicated by Nov 25, 2026. The per-page costs in this guide are arithmetic on the throughput claim, labelled as such wherever they appear.
The weights file changed size on release dayThe repository was modified at 21:35 UTC on Nov 25, after our story’s read; the file measures 4.43 GB tonight against the 4.46 GB recorded this afternoon. Immaterial to every fit in this guide, printed because this guide plans from measurements — and because a release-day repository can move again; re-check the file size when you download.
The card states no context lengthThe 262,144 in the config is a positional ceiling, not a promise: every serving example the maker ships caps at 32,768. A document page does not need more — a page is a few thousand image tokens — but anyone planning to feed the model long multi-page context is outside the documented shape.
Thinking must be off, and the failure is silentLeave it on in Ollama and the parse arrives in the thinking field with empty content; the model was trained to parse with its shipped prompts and thinking disabled. Use the repository’s prompt files verbatim — paraphrasing the system prompt is debugging a model you did not train.
There is no 4-bit build, on purposeThe maker tested lower-bit quantisations, found layout detection degraded, and withheld them. The Q8_0 GGUF (2.01 GB plus the 0.67 GB vision file) is the small-file route; a future community Q4 is unendorsed by the only party that has measured the difference.
The stack is youngThe architecture needs Transformers 5.x-era tooling; pinned vendor containers are documented failing on this model family. And the config carries one MTP (multi-token prediction) layer, but no card documents a speculative-decoding route for it — this guide prices none.
A parser is not a digitisation programmeThe model reads a page; scanning, storage, search, access control and human review of low-confidence reads are still yours to build. Its output preserves positions precisely so a reviewer can check a block against the page — plan the review step, especially for records with legal weight.
