How we check

Model facts are from Amini’s Hugging Face repositories AminiTech/Soma-1X-lite (model card, config.json and repository file listing via the Hugging Face API, revision 8f320903089dcc088eb8c87f08f5ea164339992b, last modified Nov 25, 2026 21:35 UTC) and AminiTech/Soma-1X-lite-GGUF (created Nov 25, 2026 21:31 UTC) — parameters, architecture, files, prompts, commands, benchmarks, licence — read first-hand Nov 25, 2026. Checkpoint size is measured, not quoted: model.safetensors is 4,426,558,864 bytes (4.43 GB), cross-checked exactly against 2,213,241,664 BF16 parameters (params × 2 + the 75,536-byte safetensors header = the file). Our Nov 25 story and catalogue entry first recorded 4,455,280,241 bytes (4.46 GB) from afternoon reads; the repository was modified again at 21:35 UTC and both were corrected to the measured figure the same day. GGUF sizes are measured from that repository’s listing: Q8_0 2,012,011,264 bytes (2.01 GB), BF16 3,775,707,904 bytes (3.78 GB), mmproj F16 668,227,104 bytes (0.67 GB). KV arithmetic is from the config: only 6 of the 24 layers are full-attention (2 KV heads × 256 head dimension), so the cache is 12,288 bytes per token — 0.40 GB at the maker’s 32,768-token serving cap, 3.22 GB at the config’s 262,144 ceiling; the config publishes no linear-attention state size, so the 6–8 GB working-set band carries a stated general allowance and is labelled planning, not measurement. Serving verification: the model card’s own Transformers quickstart and vllm serve command; vLLM’s supported-models documentation (Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration listed as natively supported, checked Nov 25, 2026); SGLang’s Qwen3.5 documentation (the family including the dense 2B listed, Soma not named, main-branch install required — labelled at exactly that strength); the GGUF repository’s llama.cpp and Ollama instructions. Throughput and benchmarks are Amini’s published claims (model card and the maker’s Nov 25, 2026 launch post): up to 15,000 pages/hour on one RTX PRO 6000 and the maker’s AWS-based estimate of about $0.22 per 1,000 pages at about $3.36/hr (the maker’s arithmetic verified: 3.36 ÷ 15 = $0.224); the per-page costs in this guide are our arithmetic on that claim (hourly ÷ 15) and are never extrapolated to any other card. No hosted API price exists to compare: the Hugging Face API shows no inference-provider mapping for the repo and Amini publishes no per-page API price for this open model, and the guide says so instead of inventing one. The licence is Apache License 2.0 as declared in both repositories’ Hugging Face metadata and licence sections (verified Nov 25, 2026); neither repository carries a standalone LICENSE file — the declaration is metadata and a linked reference to the Apache text, and the guide prints that gap. The base model, Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B, is a fine-tune parent rather than a separate download here; the weights as released by Amini are the Apache 2.0 artefact. As always, the licence covers the weights as released; what your institution may do with the records you parse through it is a question about the records, not the model. Rental prices are GPUJournal’s Nov 25, 2026 board snapshot (87 offers, corroboration check), read with price-history/corrections.md (the corrections touch Verda figures in the Nov 24 snapshot only; no figure used in this guide is affected): RTX 4090 RunPod Community $0.34, RTX A6000 Thunder Compute $0.35, RTX 5090 RunPod Community $0.69, L40S RunPod Community $0.79, RTX PRO 6000 RunPod Community $1.69, Nebius $1.80, RunPod Secure $2.69. Monthly figures are hourly × 730; all computed by script. None of the guide’s rows come from the snapshot’s carried exceptions (TensorDock, nafnaf).

That makes the rental question almost absurdly simple: every single card on our board can hold it, so the decision is not which card fits but which card is worth paying for, which of the three file packings your runtime will actually load, and whether the maker’s own speed tables — the only speed figures that exist for this model — justify skipping the ordinary 4-bit build of the base model instead. AMD launches Instinct MI450X: 288 GB of HBM4 for Helios — and an MLPerf claim 30% above Vera Rubin

Nov 12, 2026

AMD added a second Helios GPU on Nov 12, 2026: the Instinct MI450X, with 288 GB of HBM4 against the MI455X's 432 GB but the same compute, bandwidth and connectivity — a cheaper-memory option for workloads that fit. Alongside it, AMD published its own MLPerf testing putting the MI455X at 21,333 tokens per second per GPU on DeepSeek-R1, up to 30% above NVIDIA Vera Rubin's latest published MLPerf offline result.

Image: AMD via amd.com

What shipped, from AMD's own Newsroom release (Nov 12, 2026), read first-hand: the Instinct MI450X is a new GPU option for the AMD Helios rackscale platform. It carries 288 GB of HBM4 per GPU while delivering the same core compute, memory bandwidth and scale-up and scale-out connectivity as the MI455X, which keeps 432 GB for larger models, longer contexts and higher concurrency. Both run on the same Helios architecture and ROCm software stack, so Helios customers now pick their memory tier per workload instead of paying for 432 GB everywhere. AMD's product page lists the MI450X as CDNA 5 on a TSMC 2nm/3nm process with 320 billion transistors, 23.3 TB/s of peak HBM bandwidth, 40.3 PFLOPs of peak MXFP4 matrix throughput, 3.6 TB/s of UALoE scale-up bandwidth and direct liquid cooling, with a launch date of 11/12/2026.

The benchmark claim, labelled as AMD's own testing: AMD Performance Labs measured the MI455X on Helios at 21,333 tokens per second per GPU running DeepSeek-R1 in an MLPerf Inference Offline configuration in October 2026, and compares it with NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72's published MLPerf Inference v6.1 Closed Division result (entry 6.1-0106, retrieved from mlcommons.org on Nov 11, 2026) — up to 30% higher throughput on that comparison. AMD also calculates up to 20% higher HBM bandwidth and higher scale-up bandwidth than Vera Rubin from published specifications. These are AMD's figures and calculations, not measured by us, and system configurations vary.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Nobody rents a single MI450X — Helios is a rackscale system, and this launch matters to renters one step removed: the MI400 series is the hardware the next wave of AMD capacity at GPU providers will be built from, and a 288 GB tier gives those providers a lower-memory, lower-cost configuration to buy for inference fleets whose models fit inside it, alongside the 432 GB flagship. The MLPerf number is the other half of the story: AMD is publicly claiming inference leadership over Vera Rubin on a standard benchmark, on its own testing — the claim NVIDIA's published result will be re-run against as Helios systems reach customers. Watch for the first providers to list MI400-series capacity; that is when this becomes a price on the board.

NEWS →  ·  Open weights · Thinking Machines

Inkling 2 Small weights are out: the 594B model lands on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0

Nov 12, 2026

Thinking Machines kept its promise on schedule: Inkling 2 Small, launched closed on its Tinker platform on Nov 5, 2026, put its full weights on Hugging Face on Nov 12, 2026 under Apache 2.0. It is a 594-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 17 billion active per token and image input — and serving it yourself starts with a multi-GPU cluster: the model's own card puts the native NVFP4 checkpoint at a GPU cluster with at least 500 GB of aggregated memory, met by 2× B300 or 4× H200.

Image: Thinking Machines via thinkingmachines.ai

What shipped, from Thinking Machines' own Nov 12, 2026 update to its launch post and the model's Hugging Face card, both read first-hand: the weights are downloadable under Apache 2.0 (the card's licence field reads apache-2.0), integrated on day one with SGLang, vLLM, TokenSpeed and Unsloth, post-trainable with Miles, SkyRL and Snowflake Cortex Training, and available by API at NVIDIA, Fireworks, Together, Baseten, Nebius, Modal and Cloudflare. The model itself: a 48-layer decoder-only MoE routing each token to 8 of 384 experts, a 292-million-parameter vision encoder for image input, variable reasoning effort, and a context window of up to 1 million tokens. At its Nov 5 launch the lab reported a score of 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — the lab's figure, not measured by us.

The hardware, in the card's own words: the main NVFP4 checkpoint — the precision the model was trained in, and the one the card recommends — requires a GPU cluster with at least 500 GB of aggregated VRAM, with 2× NVIDIA B300 or 4× NVIDIA H200 as the card's example configurations. The alternative MXFP8 checkpoint requires at least 800 GB, met by 4× B300 or 8× H200, and the card says its 1–2-point evaluation gain over NVFP4 is not meaningful in practice. There is no single-card route to this model at any precision the maker ships.

What it means if you rent GPUs

This is a cluster rental, priced like one. At the board's checked prices of Nov 12, 2026, the card's two NVFP4 example setups price out close together: 4× H200 at RunPod Community's $3.59/hr per GPU is $14.36/hr in total, and 2× B300 at Hyperstack's $7.40/hr is $14.80/hr — roughly $10,500–$10,800 a month run around the clock, before storage and your own serving work. That is the honest comparison to set against the hosted APIs the same announcement lists. The model is now in our catalogue (linked below), where its page works through every fit from the same memory arithmetic. A deployment guide — what it actually costs to run Inkling 2 Small well, and where the API beats renting — is proposed to the editor, not published by this sweep.

RunPod for Agents: one prompt sets up your coding agent to rent and run GPUs

Nov 12, 2026

RunPod's November update to RunPod for Agents (published Nov 10, 2026 and updated Nov 12, 2026) lets a coding agent set itself up from a single prompt — “Read agents.runpod.io and set up Runpod for me” — then deploy and manage Pods, endpoints and volumes through RunPod's plugins for Claude Code and ChatGPT and a hosted MCP server that now carries its own knowledge base.

Image: RunPod via runpod.io

What is in the update, from RunPod's own blog post, read first-hand: one-prompt setup works from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more; the hosted MCP server gains a knowledge base (lookup-concept, search-concepts, list-guides, read-guide and search-docs, which returns its sources), read-only and destructive labels on every tool so clients can auto-approve reads and ask before deletes, and new tools for global volumes, secrets and organisations, plus report_feedback for agents to flag a wrong tool or guide. RunPod counts 10 new skills since August, a Terraform provider 2.0 and a TypeScript SDK — both generated from the same REST v2 API as the MCP server — and mounting or unmounting up to four network volumes on existing Pods. One customer result is named: Open Source Films reports roughly 10× project and build throughput running agents on RunPod — the customer's figure, quoted by RunPod.

The image above is RunPod's own screenshot of its ChatGPT plugin listing: the plugin browses GPUs and live stock, launches and controls Pods, deploys Serverless endpoints and tracks spend, with sign-in by OAuth and no API key stored.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Every major GPU provider is now racing to be the cloud a coding agent operates, not just the one a human clicks through — and this update is RunPod's fullest version of that pitch: current docs and tested skills beside the API, so the agent stops guessing at outdated commands. For renters the detail that matters is the permission design: read-only and destructive tool labels decide what your agent may do without asking, on an account where a wrong call spends real money by the hour. Set those labels before you hand an agent a GPU account — ours included.

NEWS →  ·  Inference software · LMSYS Org

NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google and Meta launch the SGLang Consortium to steer open-source inference

Nov 12, 2026

LMSYS Org launched the SGLang Consortium on Nov 12, 2026 at the first SGLang Summit in San Francisco, with NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Cloudflare, Modal and RadixArk as founding members. The group gives the companies that run the open-source inference engine at the largest scale a standing seat in its roadmap — while SGLang's maintainers keep technical decisions and code acceptance.

Image: LMSYS Org via lmsys.org

What was announced, from LMSYS Org's own post (Nov 12, 2026), read first-hand: each founding member designates a technical representative and joins two roadmap meetings a year, contributing engineering expertise, deployment feedback, testing resources or joint development, with working groups between meetings and public updates on direction. The shared work focuses on frontier-model support, reasoning and multimodal workloads, distributed inference and hardware optimisation. LMSYS says SGLang — part of the PyTorch ecosystem — runs on hundreds of thousands of GPUs and powers production inference for companies including Meta, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Thinking Machines Lab, Cloudflare, Reflection and Modal, and cites Deloitte's estimate that inference will account for roughly two-thirds of all AI compute in 2026.

The quotes set the terms. Ying Sheng of RadixArk, for the SGLang team: “The teams running SGLang at the largest scale see what inference needs next before anyone else does.” NVIDIA's Ian Buck: “Better software helps developers get more performance from NVIDIA compute.” AMD's Ramine Roane pointed to SGLang running across hardware, including AMD Instinct GPUs. The consortium was announced in the opening keynote of the inaugural SGLang Summit, held Nov 12–13 at Fort Mason Center with more than 100 speakers.

What it means if you rent GPUs

The inference engine is where a rented GPU's money is won or lost: the same card serves more tokens, or fewer, depending on the software on top of it. SGLang is one of the two engines most open-weight deployments on rented hardware actually run, and it now has a formal industry body — chip makers included — steering its roadmap toward the frontier models and distributed setups renters serve. For builders the practical watch is what lands from it: day-one support for new weights drops (Inkling 2 Small, above, shipped with SGLang integration on day one) and hardware optimisation that shows up as throughput on the GPUs already on the board.

NEWS →  ·  Open weights · Salesforce

Salesforce's SOV-Transcribe-1 is the new #1 open-weight speech model — and it needs a big-memory card

Nov 13, 2026

Salesforce released SOV-Transcribe-1 on Hugging Face on Nov 12, 2026 under Apache 2.0: a 26.6-billion-parameter speech model (4.6 billion active) that ranks #1 among open-weight models for non-streaming speech-to-text on Artificial Analysis, at a 2.28% word error rate. Its BF16 checkpoint is about 53 GB, so running it yourself starts on an 80 GB-class GPU.

Image: Salesforce via huggingface.co

From Salesforce's own announcement on Hugging Face (Nov 12, 2026), read first-hand: SOV-Transcribe-1 pairs a Whisper large-v3 encoder with a Gemma 4 MoE decoder, is non-streaming only, covers seven languages, and was tested on audio up to 30 minutes. Its 2.28% AA-WER beats NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (2.81%) and Mistral's Voxtral Small (2.77%) on Artificial Analysis's index, where it ranks #1 open-weight and #7 overall (rankings as of Nov 12, 2026). It also leads open-weight models on BeSimple's VoiceCodeBench entity test — recovering 93.4% of key entities such as emails and account numbers — and supports instruction-based style steering and keyword context biasing. Serving is via a vLLM plugin or Transformers; the technical report is still to come.

The hardware maths, from the model's own card: the BF16 checkpoint is about 53 GB, which does not fit a 48 GB card. On this board the cheapest verified way in is a single A100 80GB — Thunder Compute at $1.09 an hour, checked today — with the RTX PRO 6000's 96 GB the roomier single-card option, from $1.80 an hour at Nebius.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Transcription is one of the clearest sovereign-AI use cases — call recordings and dictation that cannot leave your own infrastructure — and the best open option now needs datacenter-class memory rather than a workstation card. That is a rental-shaped problem: an A100 80GB at about a dollar an hour, switched on only when there is audio to process, against closed per-minute APIs. The model is in our catalogue from today, with the GPU maths on its page.

/story/agnes-2-5-pro-theta-weights-nov-1.html:
NEWS →  ·  Open weights · Agnes AI

Agnes 2.5 Pro Theta weights are out: a 187.8B multimodal MoE under Apache 2.0 that starts at four H200s

Nov 15, 2026

Agnes AI has published the BF16 weights of Agnes 2.5 Pro Theta on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0 — 187.8 billion parameters, a 375.5 GB download, and a model card that names four H200-class GPUs as the practical starting point. The model was API-only before this release; the weights, the custom code and the publisher's own benchmark chart are now public.

Image: Agnes AI via huggingface.co

What shipped, from the Hugging Face model card (Agnes-AI/Agnes-2.5-Pro-Theta), read first-hand on Nov 15, 2026, with the repository's last update stamped Nov 15, 2026 in Hugging Face's own API: a multimodal mixture-of-experts checkpoint with 187,763,545,616 total parameters, 52 text decoder layers, 512 routed experts per MoE block with top-10 routing plus a shared expert branch, and a configured context limit of 262,144 tokens — the card states plainly that the context figure is a configuration limit, not a benchmarked claim. The BF16 weights ship in 105 safetensors shards totalling 375.5 GB (about 349.7 GiB), with the model implementation, tokenizer, chat template and image/video processors, under the Apache 2.0 licence. The code is custom: loading it requires trust_remote_code=True, and the card's own quickstart uses eager attention with device_map set to auto, which it notes is not tensor parallelism.

The scores, labelled as the publisher's own snapshot: the card's benchmark chart puts Theta at 92.9 on GPQA Diamond, 90.5 on LiveCodeBench v6, 84.7 on AA-LCR, 82.6 on IFBench and 64.1 on SWE-bench Pro, ahead of NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B, Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on five of its eight benchmarks — DeepSeek's entry beats it on SciCode, HLE-Diamond and GDP.pdf. Agnes itself warns these scores summarise a publisher-provided chart, not a reproducible evaluation bundle: no prompts, sampling settings or raw run logs are included. Treat them as the maker's claims until an independent run exists.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters and builders the useful part of this card is that it does its own hardware maths honestly: the unquantised payload alone is about 349.7 GiB, so Agnes names a system with four H200-class GPUs as the practical capacity starting point and at least 400 GB of storage for one local copy. By our catalogue method that is the honest floor — four 141 GB H200s give 564 GB of aggregate memory, enough for the BF16 weights plus the runtime overhead the card warns about. The watch-outs are equally plain: serving-engine support is unproven (the card says optimised vLLM/SGLang compatibility must be checked for this custom implementation before deployment), the benchmark lead is the maker's own snapshot, and a 375 GB download is a real cost in time and storage before the first token. We have added Agnes 2.5 Pro Theta to the model catalogue with the memory maths shown; if a verified serving route lands, its page will say so.

/story/qwen4-max-launch-nov-16.html:
NEWS →  ·  Model launch · Alibaba Qwen

Qwen4-Max is live: a 2.4-trillion-parameter flagship at $1.50 per million input tokens — API only, with open weights promised for the smaller models

Nov 16, 2026

Alibaba's Qwen team has made Qwen4-Max generally available: a 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts flagship with native vision and a one-million-token context, priced on QwenCloud at $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output — 25% below its own predecessor. There are no weights to rent a GPU for: Max is API-only, and the open-source release Qwen promises is for the smaller models in the family, with no names or dates yet.

Image: Alibaba Qwen via qwen.ai

What shipped, from Qwen's own launch post ('Qwen4-Max: Your New Teammate Has Arrived', qwen.ai, read first-hand on Nov 16, 2026) and Reuters' same-day report: Qwen4-Max is built on the new Qwen4 architecture — a sparse mixture-of-experts model with a 2.4-trillion-parameter backbone, 71 billion parameters activated per token, plus 328 billion N-gram embedding parameters. It takes text, image and video input natively, works over a one-million-token context window, and can return up to 393,216 output tokens per QwenCloud's model page. Access is through the QwenCloud API (model ID qwen4-max, live Nov 16 after a Token-Plan-only preview that opened Nov 11), Qwen Studio and Qwen's own apps. The preview ID, qwen4-max-preview, is a separate thing: it stays on the Token Plan until it is retired on Nov 25 — the generally available model is not affected.

The price, from QwenCloud's published rates checked Nov 16, 2026: $1.50 per million input tokens, $4.50 per million output tokens and $0.075 per million cached input tokens — against $2.00 / $6.00 / $0.25 for Qwen3.8-Max, a 25% cut on input and output and 70% on cached input. Qwen's own efficiency figures (the maker's numbers, not independently rerun at launch) say the model also uses fewer tokens per task: on its Work360 suite the average cost per task falls from $4.43 to $1.67 while the score rises from 47.74 to 52.69. On Alibaba's own 16-benchmark chart the model leads on four (including Agents' Last Exam and DeepSWE) and trails rivals clearly on others, including ProgramBench and Terminal-Bench — read the chart as the maker's case, not a verdict.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters the honest headline is the one in Qwen's closing paragraph: 'Max is only the first look at Qwen4. Smaller models in the family are coming to open source.' No smaller Qwen4 weight had been released as of Nov 16 — there is no Qwen4 repository in Qwen's Hugging Face organisation — so today this launch changes API maths, not rental maths: a hosted flagship got 25% cheaper per token, and every self-hosting comparison now has a lower API bar to beat. The rental story starts when a smaller Qwen4 weight actually lands with a licence and a parameter count we can do memory maths on; our model catalogue will carry it then, with the GPU arithmetic shown, and not before. Until then, treat any 'deploy Qwen4-Max on your own GPUs' offer with suspicion — there are no official weights to deploy.

/story/nvidia-rubin-hpc-nov-16.html:
NEWS →  ·  GPU hardware · NVIDIA

NVIDIA announces Rubin HPC: a new GPU with more than 50,000 CUDA cores for science and engineering, due in 2028

Nov 16, 2026

Announced today at SC26 in Chicago, Rubin HPC is a new GPU in NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform, built for the simulation and data-processing work behind science, engineering and analytics — with a record count of more than 50,000 CUDA cores on a single GPU, a sparse-data acceleration capability, and seventh-generation NVLink. NVIDIA expects it in 2028, and gives no memory, power, performance or price figures.

Image: NVIDIA via blogs.nvidia.com

What NVIDIA announced, from its own blog post published Nov 16, 2026 at 16:00 UTC and read first-hand: Rubin HPC is designed for the pattern scientific computing shares across climate models, engineering simulation, genomic analysis and financial risk — an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers scattered values, calculates, and repeats at enormous scale. The GPU pairs its record CUDA core count with a sparse data acceleration capability intended to keep those cores fed, and a balanced design that scales data movement and compute together rather than compute alone. NVIDIA names the workload patterns it targets: sparse matrix operations, stencil computations, sorting and reductions. Seventh-generation NVLink accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity. Ian Buck, NVIDIA's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing: “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery.” The post closes with the only availability line given: Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.

What was not announced matters as much for anyone planning hardware: NVIDIA published no memory capacity or bandwidth, no power figure, no FP64 or other performance numbers, no rack or node configuration, and no price. The announcement also landed inside a wider SC26 package from NVIDIA the same afternoon — a Vera CPU rack-scale platform for HPC (192 Vera CPUs per rack, systems from Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro expected from early 2027) and the Nemotron for Science open package — but Rubin HPC is the only new GPU in it.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters and builders this is a roadmap signal, not a bookable card: nothing here changes what can be rented today or in 2027, and with no memory or performance figures there is no honest way to price it against the current board. The signal itself is still worth having on the record. NVIDIA is splitting the Vera Rubin family, adding a purpose-built sibling for simulation-class work — the sparse, data-movement-bound workloads the AI training cards are not shaped for — and tying it to agents that run simulations to test candidate materials, molecules and designs. Anyone whose rental spend is scientific computing now has a dated marker: the HPC-specific Rubin part is a 2028 story, so buying and renting decisions for the next two years still run on today's H100, H200, B200 and GB300-class hardware. We will track Rubin HPC as NVIDIA publishes real specifications, and we will not list it on the board until there is a dated price to verify.

/story/hugging-face-openrouter-nov-16.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · Hugging Face · OpenRouter

Hugging Face hands its inference routing to OpenRouter — and your own provider keys stop working

Nov 16, 2026

Hugging Face has switched Inference Providers — the service builders use to call open-weight models hosted by outside providers — from its own custom router to OpenRouter's. Language-model requests now go to whichever of more than 80 providers offers the best live mix of price, speed and reliability, and a failed call is retried on another provider inside the same request. The trade-off is a breaking change: you can no longer use your own provider API keys for language models.

Image: Hugging Face via huggingface.co

What changed, from Hugging Face's own blog post published Nov 16, 2026 and read first-hand: every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can now be called with a Hugging Face token through the same API, with the provider picked per request. OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers; OpenRouter's own announcement puts 160 models from 38 labs live on Hugging Face this way today. Its recently rebuilt routing — which scores providers on live price, speed and reliability instead of lowest list price alone, and moves traffic away from a provider that slows down or starts failing — cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3% in OpenRouter's measurements; OpenRouter's post adds that the rebuilt routing cost 6.0% more per request in its October experiment. Builders can still steer with a suffix on the model id (:cheapest, :fastest, or a named provider), routing is cache-aware so a conversation stays on the provider holding its prompt cache, and model pages gain Providers and Metrics tabs showing each provider's live price, speed and uptime. Pricing itself does not change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, with no Hugging Face markup on top.

The breaking change is stated plainly by Hugging Face: because language-model requests now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, custom provider keys no longer work for those models — you can still pin a provider by suffix or switch providers off in settings, and your code stays the same. Image, video and audio generation are untouched: they keep running directly through Inference Providers, and custom keys for image and video providers keep working. Hugging Face also published the usage picture behind the move: open-weight models rose from 26.8% of the tokens OpenRouter served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, peaking at 77.5% in July, with weekly open-weight volume up more than 60-fold in a year. This week's most-used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one — DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, at 59.2 trillion tokens — and Hugging Face puts open-weight models at about a quarter of the closed-model price on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output, against $1.27 and $6.36.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For model builders this is the serving layer consolidating in public: the Hub where open weights are published now rents its request routing to the largest multi-provider gateway, which means the provider behind a Hugging Face call is chosen by live measurements, not by the caller's own key or contract. That is good news for reliability — a failing provider no longer fails your request — and it makes the per-provider price, speed and uptime tables on each model page a genuinely useful comparison surface. It is also a real loss of control for teams who negotiated their own provider deals: those keys, and any pricing attached to them, no longer apply to language models on Hugging Face. The numbers in the announcement underline why this desk tracks open weights so closely: at 71.7% of tokens on the biggest gateway, open-weight serving is no longer the alternative route — it is most of the traffic, and the cheapest verified way to run those same models yourself is the board we check every day.

/story/openai-gpt-6-2-astra-sol-nov-17.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · OpenAI

OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol: frontier API price cut 20%, live in Work, Codex and the API today

Nov 17, 2026

OpenAI released two models today, Nov 17, 2026: GPT-6.2 Astra, its new frontier model for the hardest projects, and GPT-6.2 Sol, an efficient everyday model that nearly matches Astra on real-world coding at about a fifth of the cost. Both are live in ChatGPT Work and Codex and in the API. Astra's API price falls 20% on its predecessor, to $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output; Sol holds its predecessor's $2 and $10. Both models are closed — there are no weights to rent a GPU for — so this launch matters as the price bar every self-hosting decision is measured against.

Image: OpenAI via community.openai.com

What OpenAI announced, from its own announcement post published Nov 17, 2026 and read first-hand (with the launch thread on X at 17:54 UTC): GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, and to developers in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol, with the high-speed Ultrafast mode available — Pro 500 subscribers get Ultrafast with either model, and Pro 200 subscribers get it for the first time, starting with Sol. The rollout does not add either model to regular Chat. Astra, OpenAI says, sets new highs on evaluations across professional work and scientific research at less than a third of the cost per task of GPT-6 Astra; on Agents' Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra at extra-high effort scores 5.2 points above GPT-6 Astra at maximum effort at less than half the cost per task. Astra is also OpenAI's most capable model yet for cybersecurity, jumping 22 points over GPT-6 Astra on its ExploitBench Internal Port evaluation — and because of that capability, both models launch with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance, with work under way to give approved defenders reduced-refusal access through Daybreak. All benchmark figures are OpenAI's own.

The pricing is the part builders will price against. Astra costs $8.00 per million input tokens and $40.00 per million output tokens in the API — a 20% cut from GPT-6 Astra's $10 and $50, with cached input down 60% to $0.40 per million on OpenAI's API documentation. Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's rates exactly: $2.00 in, $0.10 cached in, $10.00 out per million. OpenAI's claim for Sol is that it nearly matches Astra where it counts for agent work: on FrontierCode 2.0, which tests merge-ready changes to real codebases, Sol finishes within about half a point of Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost. Independent scoring is already landing: Artificial Analysis puts Astra at 62.1 and Sol at 57.3 on its Intelligence Index. Neither model is open-weight — no weights, no licence, no self-hosting route was announced.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and model builders, a closed launch like this changes no board price and adds nothing to the catalogue — but it moves the number every deployment plan is compared against. The frontier API just got 20% cheaper per token, and on OpenAI's own figures the cost per finished task fell by half or more, which pushes the break-even usage level for renting GPUs and self-hosting an open-weight model higher: you now need more volume, or a stronger privacy and control case, before the rented route wins on cost alone. Sol holding $2 and $10 while closing most of the gap to the frontier model is the volume story — that is the rate high-throughput agent workloads will be benchmarked against. We will keep tracking the open-weight answers to this pair in the catalogue, priced from the board we check every day.

/story/lambda-cpo-photonics-nov-17.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · Lambda · NVIDIA

Lambda connects more than 10,000 Blackwell Ultra GPUs with NVIDIA Photonics — the first large-scale co-packaged optics deployment

Nov 17, 2026

Announced on Nov 16, 2026 at SC26, Lambda has deployed NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged-optics switches to connect more than 10,000 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs at its Quebec campus — what Lambda calls the world's first large-scale deployment of the technology. In Lambda's own measurements against conventional pluggable optics, throughput was identical, latency was lower at every scale tested, and the optics ran 15 degrees cooler. This story was held yesterday for an official image; NVIDIA's SC26 hub has since published Lambda's photograph of the installation, and it runs with the story.

Image: Lambda via blogs.nvidia.com

What was announced, from Lambda's Nov 16, 2026 announcement (Business Wire, 08:45 ET) and NVIDIA's own blog post the same afternoon: the deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches — 144 ports at 800Gb/s, liquid-cooled, with 18 removable external light sources — to connect more than 10,000 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs, in GB300 NVL72 racks on NVIDIA's account, at Lambda's Quebec campus. The campus figures are Lambda's: 142MW of power secured, nearly 100% renewable energy, a guaranteed PUE of 1.2, and free cooling for up to 80% of the year. Co-packaged optics puts the optical conversion on the switch itself instead of in pluggable modules at the rack edge, which is why the networking layer — usually a fixed tax on large training runs — is the claim here.

Lambda's measured comparison against pluggable optics: identical throughput, with latency lower at every scale — 3.8% lower at rack scale and 10.1% lower at pod scale — and a median optics temperature of 36°C against 51°C. The bigger numbers in NVIDIA's post — up to 5x power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability for Photonics — are NVIDIA's general claims for the technology, not figures measured at Quebec, and no switch count, absolute latency baseline or independent test was published. Treat the Quebec numbers as the deployer's own measurements, labelled as such.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters this is not a price or a product you can book — it is a signal about where large-cluster economics move next. On a multi-thousand-GPU training rental, the network decides how many of the GPU-hours you pay for turn into finished work; a networking layer that measurably cuts latency and runs cooler at 10,000-GPU scale is Lambda's argument that its clusters deliver more productive hours per dollar than the same GPUs wired conventionally. The honest renter's response is to ask for the evidence per deployment — Lambda has now published its own, which gives buyers a concrete set of figures to ask rival cluster providers to match. Single-card and small-cluster renters are unaffected today; the board's Lambda prices are unchanged.

/story/nvidia-earnings-q3-fy27-nov-17.html:
NEWS →  ·  Earnings · NVIDIA

NVIDIA revenue hits $115.8 billion, beating its own guide — Data Center $107.6 billion as Vera Rubin ships

Nov 17, 2026

NVIDIA reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 results after the close today, Nov 17, 2026, and beat the guide it set in August on every headline line: revenue of $115.8 billion against guidance of $108.0 billion plus or minus 2%, gross margin of 74.8% against 74.0% guided, and Data Center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% on a year ago. The release also confirms Vera Rubin NVL72 has shipped — the fastest product ramp in the company's history, with racks already running at CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud and Nebius — and guides next quarter to $130.0 billion. This was the first earnings report under interim CEO Colette Kress.

Image: NVIDIA

The quarter, from NVIDIA's own results release published Nov 17, 2026 (GlobeNewswire, 21:20 UTC) and read first-hand: revenue was $115.8 billion ($115,844 million) for the quarter ended Oct 25, 2026 — up 20% on the previous quarter and 103% on a year ago, against the $108.0 billion plus-or-minus-2% guidance NVIDIA gave on Aug 26. GAAP gross margin was 74.8% and non-GAAP 74.9%, against 74.0% guided; GAAP earnings were $2.70 a share and non-GAAP $2.68, against consensus of about $2.47; net income was a record $65.3 billion. Data Center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 21% on the quarter and 110% on a year ago — against $89.0 billion in the second quarter — and Edge Computing added $8.2 billion. Kress, in the release: “Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”

The renter-relevant half of the release is Vera Rubin and the outlook. NVIDIA says it ramped production and began shipping Vera Rubin NVL72 in the quarter — “the fastest product ramp in the company's history” — with racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius, and SpaceXSI coming online soon; the same release records general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud and of Google Cloud's Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances. For the fourth quarter, which includes an additional week, NVIDIA guides revenue to $130.0 billion plus or minus 3%, with GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins of 71.0% to 72.0% — a step down from this quarter's 74.8%, which the release frames as the Rubin ramp — and it assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China in that outlook.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and builders this is the demand verdict behind the whole board. Data Center revenue doubling in a year, a $130 billion guide for next quarter, and Rubin already shipping at five of the clouds this desk tracks means Vera Rubin capacity will be scarce and contracted first — no provider has published an on-demand Rubin rate yet, and tonight's numbers give none of them a reason to discount early capacity. The softer margin guide is the one caution in the release: ramping Rubin costs money before it earns it, which is a supplier's problem, not a renter's discount. Read alongside our own dated record — Verda's eighteenth rise this morning, Lambda's rises in effect since Nov 16 — the pattern is consistent with demand still running ahead of supply (our reading of the evidence, labelled as interpretation; supplier revenue is not rental pricing, and no rental price changed tonight).

/story/sage-s2-1-flash-nov-17.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Shanghai AI Laboratory · InternLM

Sage S2.1 Flash: a 320B open science-agent model under MIT, with weights live and an eight-H200 reference setup

Nov 17, 2026

Shanghai AI Laboratory's InternLM team uploaded the weights of Sage S2.1 Flash to Hugging Face on Nov 15, 2026: a scientific multimodal agent model of 320 billion parameters (321.3 billion by the repository's own file metadata) with 18 billion active per token, released under the MIT licence in both full-precision and FP8 builds. Through its Sage SciPerception layer it reads more than ten kinds of scientific input — molecular graphs, crystal structures, protein sequences and 3D structures, spectra, X-ray diffraction, ECG, EEG and more — alongside text and images. This desk held the story for an official image; the model's card has since been published in full, the maker's own architecture diagram is in the repository, and it runs with the story. Every benchmark below is the maker's own — no independent harness has tested this model yet.

Image: Shanghai AI Laboratory / InternLM via huggingface.co

What dropped, from the model's own Hugging Face repositories, read first-hand: Sage S2.1 Flash is built on the GLM-5.3-Flash architecture, with 45 layers and 288 routed experts in its own config file, a maximum context of 1,048,576 tokens, and code and weights under the MIT licence — no revenue cap and no use restrictions beyond the licence notice. The full-precision weights total 642.8 GB across 129 files; an FP8 build is published alongside, at about 321 GB by the same file metadata. The scientific side is the point of the model: Sage SciPerception encoders project each scientific input type into the same representation space as text, so the model can run multi-round analysis — reading evidence, calling tools and specialist software, checking intermediate results and adjusting — rather than answering from a single pass. Deployment guides are published for vLLM, SGLang and LMDeploy; the maker's own example runs the model on eight H200 GPUs in tensor parallel, and the guides require custom code to be trusted at load time.

The maker's own evaluation, published on the model card: across its 15-benchmark headline comparison against five rivals, Sage S2.1 Flash placed first on four benchmarks and second on seven. Its clearest first is MLE-bench Lite, the machine-learning engineering test, at 90.3 against DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017's 89.2; it also leads its table on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), Harvey LAB (25.0) and SpreadsheetBench 2 (37.1), and scores 87.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. These are InternLM's own measurements under its own harnesses, published with unusually full evaluation settings on its release site — detailed, but still the maker's numbers, with no independent replication and no hosted provider price anywhere yet. The model is now in our catalogue with its sizes worked from the repository's own files.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For model builders this is the largest open-weight science-agent release yet, and the licence is the cleanest kind: MIT, so a lab or a company can run it commercially without negotiating anything. The honest cost side is the footprint. At full precision this is a node, not a card — the maker's own reference setup is eight H200s, which at the cheapest verified H200 rate on our board (RunPod Community, $3.59 per GPU per hour, checked Nov 17, 2026) is about $28.72 an hour before storage and your own serving work; the FP8 build, at roughly half the memory, is the realistic starting point for smaller clusters, by memory arithmetic alone. Whether it earns that rent depends on benchmarks nobody independent has run yet — the maker's table is strong on exactly the agentic, tool-using work research labs pay for, and this desk will treat the first independent results, when they land, as the follow-up story.

/story/rtx-spark-desktops-nov-18.html:
NEWS →  ·  Hardware · NVIDIA

RTX Spark desktops go on sale: 128GB of unified memory in a mini PC from ASUS, Dell and MSI

Nov 18, 2026

NVIDIA's RTX Spark compact desktops are on sale from today, Nov 18, 2026 — machines from ASUS (the ProArt GR1X pictured), Dell and MSI that put a 20-core Grace CPU and a Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores in a mini-PC box, with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to a petaflop of AI performance. NVIDIA says the systems run supported large language models of up to 120 billion parameters locally. Acer, GIGABYTE and HP mini PCs and a Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box follow later. NVIDIA's announcement lists no per-system prices.

Image: NVIDIA via blogs.nvidia.com

The announcement, from NVIDIA's own blog post of Nov 18, 2026: RTX Spark pairs the Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU on one package with 10GbE networking, aimed at local AI work — agents, fine-tuning and inference — rather than at a datacenter. The 128GB of unified memory is the specification that matters: it is addressable by both the CPU and the GPU, which is what lets a desktop hold a 120B-parameter model that would need a datacenter card or a multi-GPU rental in a conventional PC. NVIDIA also used the post to note native Windows-on-Arm Adobe applications accelerated with TensorRT-RTX and Blender 5.3 support for DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction. Secondary coverage (Gizmodo, Nov 18) puts the desktop ecosystem's starting price at about $4,400 per NVIDIA — that figure is not in NVIDIA's own post and is labelled here as reported, not announced; the earlier RTX Spark laptops, on shelves since October, started at $2,599.

Context from this desk's own coverage: the RTX Spark laptops reached shelves in October alongside a 64GB DGX Spark variant, and NVIDIA showed a four-node DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit at SC26 this week (512GB of combined memory across four GB10 nodes). The desktops extend the same Grace Blackwell package from laptops and developer kits into machines a studio or a small team can simply buy.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters this is the buy side of the buy-versus-rent line, priced in one box. A team running an always-on agent or a fine-tuning loop on a single rented card pays by the hour, every hour; a 128GB desktop that holds a 120B model locally pays once. The honest limits are the same ones this desk applies to any single device: one GPU's compute, no NVLink path to a second box for training at scale, and memory that is large but fixed — a model or a context that outgrows 128GB still belongs on rented datacenter cards. What changed today is that the option is actually on sale, from three makers, rather than announced.

/story/tencent-hy4-flash-open-weights-no.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Tencent

Tencent releases Hy4 flash weights: a 220B MoE with 12B active and a 1M context — under a licence with a $50M trigger

Nov 18, 2026

Tencent published the weights of Hy4 flash on Nov 17, 2026 — three repositories (the instruct model, an FP8 build, and the pre-trained base) on Hugging Face, ModelScope and GitCode, a day after the model reached Tencent's API. The card, read first-hand by this desk, totals 220 billion parameters with about 12 billion active per token, native image input and a context window of 1,048,576 tokens. The release ships not under the plain Apache 2.0 of Tencent's earlier Hy models but under the Tencent Hy License, whose section 10.2 requires a separate written licence from model-as-a-service operators above US$50 million in revenue or 100 million monthly users. The picture is Tencent's own diagram of DFly2, the built-in speculative-decoding drafter that ships inside the model.

Image: Tencent via huggingface.co

What is in the repositories, from the model's own card: the 220B total is a 155.5B-parameter language backbone plus 63.5B of Engram N-gram embedding tables, a 0.43B SigLIP2 vision encoder and the 0.85B DFly2 drafter; per token it activates 11.3B text parameters plus the vision encoder. The backbone has 42 layers — one dense, 41 MoE layers with 512 routed experts of which 16 fire per token — hybrid sparse and sliding-window attention, and a KV cache Tencent says is one twenty-fourth the size of Hy3's. Serving recipes are published for vLLM and SGLang, including an official prebuilt vLLM image; Tencent says that combining 4-bit quantisation with DFly2 pushes decoding past 150 tokens per second (the maker's own figure). The licence is the change from family practice: Hy3 and the Hy4 preview shipped under Apache 2.0; Hy4 flash's Tencent Hy License v1.0 is an Apache derivative adding section 10.2 — above US$50M worldwide gross revenue in any 12 months, or over 100M monthly active users, a model-as-a-service operator needs Tencent's separate written licence; section 10.3 exempts internal use.

The evidence is, so far, entirely Tencent's. On its internal WorkIndex suite the maker scores Hy4 flash at 42.1 against the Hy4 preview's 39.7, at one thirteenth of the preview's cost per task; in its own blind test with 85 internal users across 259 tasks, satisfaction was 2.79 out of 4 against Claude Haiku 5.5's 2.81, with the lowest cost per task and the shortest median completion time (6.7 minutes) in its set. No independent harness has scored the model — Artificial Analysis has no page for it as of Nov 18 — and support in the Transformers library is still a pull request, not a release. The model is now in our catalogue with its sizes worked from the card's own parameter table.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For self-hosters the serving maths are friendly for a model this size: only 12B parameters are active per token, and the FP8 build — about 220GB by memory arithmetic from the card's parameter count — fits on two H200s (282GB combined), which at the cheapest verified H200 rate on our board (RunPod Community, $3.59 per GPU per hour, checked Nov 18, 2026) is about $7.18 an hour before storage and your own serving work; the full-precision build, about 440GB, wants four H200s on the same arithmetic. The watch-out is not the hardware, it is the licence: a small team can self-host freely, including commercially, but a hosted service that grows past the $50M revenue or 100M-user lines owes Tencent a separate agreement first — exactly the kind of clause to read before building a product on these weights, and the reason this desk does not file Hy4 flash under plain open-source licences in the catalogue.

/story/anthropic-ipo-priced-nov-18.html:
NEWS →  ·  AI labs · Anthropic

Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 a share — above the range, upsized to 980 million shares

Nov 18, 2026

Anthropic priced its initial public offering on Nov 18, 2026 at $83.00 a share — above the $70 to $78 range it filed on Nov 10 — and enlarged the offering from 825 million to 980 million shares, the company announced this evening. The shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Nov 19, 2026 under the symbol ANT, with the offering expected to close on Nov 20. At the announced terms the base offering is worth $81.34 billion before underwriting discounts (our arithmetic from Anthropic's figures); Reuters, reporting the same terms, puts the raise at $81.31 billion and calls it the largest stock-market debut on record, eclipsing SpaceX's June offering.

Image: Anthropic via anthropic.com

The pricing, from Anthropic's own announcement published Nov 18, 2026 and read first-hand: of the 980,000,000 Class A shares, 956,351,354 are sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 by certain selling stockholders, and Anthropic receives no proceeds from the stockholders' shares. At $83, the shares Anthropic itself is selling are worth about $79.4 billion before discounts and expenses (our arithmetic). Anthropic has also granted the underwriters a 30-day option on up to a further 147,000,000 shares — up from the 123,750,000-share option in the filed terms. A registration statement for the shares was declared effective by the SEC on Nov 18, 2026, and the final prospectus is available through the lead underwriters, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. Anthropic states no valuation in the announcement; the roughly $1.5 trillion fully diluted figure in press coverage is a press calculation, not a company figure.

The side deal this desk has tracked since the terms were set on Nov 10 is unchanged in the prospectus and is not part of the pricing announcement: seven technology companies — AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC — have agreed to buy an aggregate $26.0 billion of non-voting Class N stock in a private placement at the IPO price. Reuters, reporting from the IPO filing, adds the demand context behind the pricing: Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate reached $81 billion at Oct 31, it spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, and it has committed to nearly $900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Google — all filing figures as reported by Reuters, not figures in tonight's pricing release.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and builders, tonight's pricing is the demand story of the year landing in cash. The largest frontier-lab listing on record has just raised roughly $79 billion of new money for the company itself at a price above its own range, with the GPU supply chain — the chip designers, the memory maker and the foundry — buying a further $26 billion alongside. A buyer with Anthropic's filed compute commitments, now funded at this scale, competes for the same accelerators, the same HBM and the same data-center capacity that rental prices are made of. That does not set any single rental price — no provider rate changed tonight, and our evening check found the board flat — but it is consistent with the pattern our dated record keeps showing, from Verda's three straight rise days this week to Lambda's rises now in effect: demand funded at a scale that supply has not caught. Trading opens Nov 19 as ANT; the first trade, not the pricing, is the market's own verdict, and we will report it as such.

/story/aws-lambda-gpu-support-nov-18.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · Amazon AWS

AWS Lambda now runs GPU functions — serverless inference on EC2 G-series at the EC2 rate plus 9.75%

Nov 18, 2026

Amazon announced on Nov 18, 2026 that AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances — generally available the same day. You ship a container image, Lambda provisions and scales the GPU capacity behind it, and the bill is the underlying EC2 instance fee plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. The launch families are the EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e), and AWS positions the feature plainly: optimised for inference rather than training, and for custom models rather than large foundation models.

Image: Amazon Web Services via aws.amazon.com

How it works, from AWS's own announcement post, read first-hand: GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (OCI) images of up to 32 GB, with up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory and 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory; each execution environment can serve up to 48 concurrent requests, a capacity provider can scale to 15,000 vCPUs, and the extended timeout reaches 90 minutes for asynchronous and event-source invocations. Lambda supplies curated base images — including vLLM and SGLang serving images — and handles drivers, CUDA versions, provisioning and routing. In AWS's own worked example, a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct model went from a Hugging Face model ID to a live OpenAI-compatible endpoint in about 10 minutes, with no inference code written (AWS's figure, from its own demo). One practical catch is in the same post: new accounts may start with a G-series quota of 0 and must request an increase before anything runs.

The pricing structure is the part renters should note, because AWS prints it in the announcement itself: the EC2 instances run On-Demand, existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply to the instance fee, and an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation can be matched to a capacity provider for predictable availability. On top of the instance fee sit the 9.75 percent GPU management fee and $0.20 per million requests — there is no per-token or per-second GPU price of AWS's own here, so the effective cost of an inference still depends on how well concurrent requests pack onto the GPU you are paying for, which is exactly what the per-environment concurrency setting (up to 48) is for. AWS says GPU utilisation and memory metrics appear in CloudWatch and the console alongside standard function metrics.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For model builders this is a new shape of GPU rental from the largest cloud: not an instance you keep, but a function that happens to run on a GPU, triggered by the same 200-plus AWS event sources as any Lambda function and billed off published EC2 rates plus a stated percentage. The honest limits are AWS's own: the G-series is the small-to-mid inference tier (3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory per function), the feature is for inference and custom models rather than training or large foundation models, and the headline price is a structure, not a number — your real cost per request is set by utilisation, the same arithmetic that decides whether any rented GPU is cheap. Against the serverless-GPU specialists, AWS's offer is integration and the EC2 rate card; against raw EC2, it is the 9.75 percent that buys you not operating the fleet. We are adding Lambda GPU functions to our provider watch on those stated terms; no Lambda rate sits on our price board, because AWS publishes no single GPU hourly rate for this feature — the board only carries rates we can verify as numbers.

/story/ovhcloud-olala-mini-open-weights-.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · OVHcloud

OVHcloud's Olala mini weights are live: a 6.8B MoE with 1B active, Apache 2.0 — that only OVHcloud's forks can run today

Nov 19, 2026

OVHcloud published the weights of Olala v1.0 mini 7A1B today, Nov 19, 2026, launching the model formally at its AI Summit in Paris. The model card — read first-hand by this desk — corrects the launch material in one place: the model totals 6.8 billion parameters, not 7 billion, with about 1 billion active per token, across 36 layers of which only seven are attention layers and the other 29 are Mamba-3 state-space layers, each followed by a mixture-of-experts block with 256 routed experts of which six fire. The context window is 32,000 tokens, the licence is plain Apache 2.0 with no revenue or user-count trigger, and the picture is OVHcloud's own diagram of the architecture from the model card.

Image: OVHcloud / OVHai LLM via huggingface.co

What is in the repositories, from the card itself: the final post-trained model, a pre-trained base, an SFT build, and summarise and translate variants, plus GGUF and MLX routes. OVHcloud says the model was trained on 12.8 trillion tokens on the JUPITER, Jean Zay and MeluXina supercomputers, pre-trained in English and 36 other languages, and is already in production at the search engine Qwant for flash answers. The honest watch-out is the serving stack: upstream vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio cannot load the new olala architecture yet — self-hosting today means OVHcloud's own forks (a vLLM fork or its pre-built Docker image, and its llama.cpp fork for the GGUF route). The card's vLLM route wants a 24GB or larger NVIDIA GPU and was tested on L4 and L40S cards; the GGUF route runs in 6 to 14GB. OVHcloud's own launch material says the model runs on a GPU with as little as 8GB — that is the maker's figure for the quantised route, attributed as such.

The same summit brought a second announcement, folded in here because OVHcloud's release for it carries no image of its own: a 55-product launch that adds NVIDIA B300 and Rubin R200 GPUs and the RTX PRO 6000 to OVHcloud's Bare Metal and Public Cloud lines. OVHcloud states its data-centre capacity could supply up to 60,000 B300 GPUs or 35,000 R200 GPUs — a company-stated capacity figure, not installed, priced inventory; no GPU prices were published in the release, and several of the 55 products are December previews rather than available today. This desk will treat OVHcloud as a board candidate when priced, bookable GPU rows appear.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For self-hosters this is the small end of the board done properly: an Apache 2.0 model with no licence trigger, sized so that one modest card holds it — about 13.6GB at full precision by memory arithmetic from the card's parameter count, and far less quantised — from a European provider whose pitch is sovereignty. The trade is maturity: the architecture is days old, the serving tools are the maker's forks rather than the upstream projects most teams already run, and every performance figure so far is OVHcloud's own. The model is now in our catalogue with its sizes worked from the card.

/story/cloudflare-clairic-open-weights-n.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Cloudflare

Cloudflare open-weights Clairic: 27B and 9B extraction models under Apache 2.0

Nov 19, 2026

Cloudflare released the full weights of Clairic and the new Clairic-flash on Nov 18, 2026, under Apache 2.0 — two purpose-built extraction models that turn text, images and PDFs into typed values, estimates and forecasts, rather than chat replies. Clairic is a 27B model built on Qwen3.8-27B; Clairic-flash is a 9B model built on Qwen3.5-9B. Both also run hosted on Workers AI at $0.24 and $0.10 per million input tokens respectively, with no charge for output tokens — and both are $0.10 until Dec 1, 2026. The picture is Cloudflare's own extraction comparison from its announcement.

Image: Cloudflare via blog.cloudflare.com

What the release contains, from Cloudflare's announcement and the models' own cards: a typed-output head alongside the weights, per-field confidence and null-probability scores, and special heads for estimates, forecasts and arithmetic. Clairic reads up to four images or PDF pages per request. Cloudflare is plain that the evidence is its own: it states there are no public extraction benchmarks yet, and its headline figures are internal — on its fresh-text test set Clairic extracted 335 of 336 fields correctly and Clairic-flash 328, against 295 for the hosted preview these models replace; on synthetic receipts both scored 576 of 576. Treat those as the maker's measurements, not independent results.

The hosted price is the comparator a self-hoster has to beat: input tokens only, at $0.10 per million for Clairic-flash and $0.24 for Clairic after the Dec 1 promotion ends. The models are now in our catalogue, labelled as specialised extraction models — their fit maths describes an extraction workload, not a general chat deployment.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters this is a different shape of job from the chat models that fill most of the catalogue: document pipelines — invoices, receipts, forms — where the rental unit is one modest GPU, not a cluster. By memory arithmetic the 27B model at full precision is about 54GB, one H100, L40S or A100 80GB class card; the 9B flash model is about 18GB, one consumer 24GB card. Whether self-hosting beats the hosted per-token price depends on volume, which is exactly the break-even question the catalogue entry now frames.

/story/anthropic-ant-first-trade-nov-19.html:
NEWS →  ·  Markets · Anthropic

Anthropic closes its first day at $97.17: up 17% on the IPO price after a $111.50 open

Nov 19, 2026

Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market today, Nov 19, 2026, under the ticker ANT — and the first day is now complete. The first trade came just before noon Eastern, at $111.50 a share, up 34.3% on the $83.00 initial public offering price set the evening before. The stock touched $115.10 at its high and $92.72 at its low, and closed at $97.17, up $14.17 or 17.07% on the IPO price (Nasdaq data; the Associated Press and CNBC carry the same close). About 840 million shares changed hands — roughly 86% of the 980 million shares sold in the offering. In after-hours trading the shares slipped further, to $92.60 at 8 p.m. Eastern, down 4.70% on the close; that last figure is a quote-feed print (Finnhub), not a wire-reported price. This story was first published intraday and has been updated with the closing figures. The picture is Anthropic's own artwork from its IPO site.

Image: Anthropic via ipo.anthropic.com

The offering itself, from Anthropic's own pricing announcement of Nov 18, 2026: 980,000,000 Class A shares at $83.00 — 956,351,354 sold by the company and 23,648,646 by selling holders, above the $70 to $78 range the roadshow had carried — for gross proceeds of about $81.3 billion, the largest initial public offering on record, with an underwriters' option for up to 147,000,000 more shares and the offering expected to close Nov 20. Co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell this morning. Separately from the public raise, the filings carry a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price to strategic partners reported to include NVIDIA, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Micron and TSMC — the chip and cloud suppliers buying into their own customer at the offering price.

The full first-day record, on Nasdaq's figures: open $111.50, high $115.10, low $92.72, close $97.17 — the close is 12.9% below the opening print, so the day's honest shape is a strong debut that faded, not a straight climb. Volume was about 840 million shares (CNBC's data puts it at 839.6 million). At the close the market valued Anthropic at about $1.27 trillion on shares outstanding (Nasdaq's listing basis) and about $1.75 trillion fully diluted (CNBC's figure) — two different bases, printed separately here because morning coverage's roughly $2 trillion was the fully diluted value at the open. The debut also closed up on a sharply down day for the wider market: the S&P 500 fell 2.0% and the Nasdaq Composite 2.3% on Nov 19 (Associated Press). For one line of local colour: NVIDIA, an investor in that $26 billion placement, closed the same session at $145.98, down 3.30%.

Why a stock-market debut sits on a GPU journal's front page: Anthropic is one of the largest buyers of GPU compute in the world. Its prospectus reports about $900 billion of compute commitments and an annualised revenue run-rate of about $81 billion at Oct 31, 2026, and the money raised is raised against that build-out. The first-day verdict matters to everyone renting capacity out: a trillion-dollar-plus public valuation for a frontier lab is capital that keeps flowing into data centres, chips and contracted GPU supply — the demand side of every price this board tracks.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and builders, today's trade is a demand signal, not a rental fact: nothing about ANT's debut changes a single price on the board, and this desk does not treat a first-day pop as proof of anything except appetite. The fade is part of the record and is printed here rather than smoothed over: $111.50 at the open, $97.17 at the close, $92.60 after hours. What the debut does confirm is the scale of the financing now standing behind AI compute demand — $81.3 billion of public money plus a $26 billion strategic placement, much of it from the companies that sell the hardware. That is the same demand pressure this desk has been logging in smaller type all autumn, in Verda's twenty rise days since Oct 23 and the board's other dated increases.

/story/nvidia-microsoft-vera-rubin-azure.html:
NEWS →  ·  Clouds · NVIDIA + Microsoft

Vera Rubin NVL72 is running in Azure data centres — and VM access is expanding, as a preview

Nov 19, 2026

At Microsoft Ignite today, Nov 19, 2026, NVIDIA said Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centres, and that the two companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by them. NVIDIA's own post calls it Azure's Vera Rubin preview — and preview is the operative word: the announcement publishes no price, no region list, no VM series name and no general-availability date. The picture is NVIDIA's own announcement art for the post.

Image: NVIDIA via blogs.nvidia.com

What NVIDIA's post (Nov 19, 2026, 20:00 UTC, read first-hand by this desk) actually says: the Rubin systems are in place in Azure data centres, providing infrastructure for reasoning, agentic applications and large-scale training and inference; confidential computing is being extended to bare-metal and rack-scale Rubin infrastructure, with NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation; and the two companies are working on power efficiency with NVIDIA MaxLPS. The performance colour is Blackwell, not Rubin numbers: in MLPerf Training v6.1, Azure scaled to 10,240 GPUs on GB200 NVL72 systems training DeepSeek-V3, the largest scale in the round, and in MLPerf Inference v6.1 Azure's GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65, as cited by NVIDIA.

The same post widens Microsoft Foundry's open-model shelf: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super (long-running agents) and Lightning (fast responses and tool use) are available on Foundry Managed Compute, with Bolt and Transcribe listed as coming soon, alongside Nemotron Embed, Rerank, Parse and Content Safety models; Foundry Managed Compute now supports deploying custom model weights, and the serverless Programmed Training route handled EY's adaptation of Nemotron models for purchasing-record classification — a 55% accuracy improvement on EY's evaluation dataset at 15 times lower cost than proprietary frontier models, both figures NVIDIA's, from its customer example. Beyond Azure, Azure Local will also support RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, and GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs gain Direct Stream in a limited preview, with public preview planned for early 2027.

The honest framing for the scoreboard: Azure is not first with Rubin. Oracle announced general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 on OCI on Oct 27, 2026, and CoreWeave and Google Cloud have earlier Rubin deployments. Microsoft's step is a preview expansion by the largest cloud of the three — a supply signal, not a bookable product. No Azure Rubin rate exists to check, so nothing about this announcement changes a single price on this board today.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters and builders, this is the next generation announcing its queue position. Rubin-class racks running inside Azure data centres means the capacity the whole market is waiting on is physically arriving at hyperscale; what would make it a booking fact — a VM series, regions and a price — is exactly what the announcement does not contain. This desk will treat the preview as real and the timeline as unstated, and will check Azure's own pages for the first priced Rubin VM the way it checks every other provider: from the provider's own figures, dated.

/story/tencent-hy4-open-weights-nov-20.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Tencent

Tencent releases the Hy4 weights: a 770B flagship you can download — under a licence with a $50M trigger

Nov 20, 2026

Tencent published the full Hy4 weights today, Nov 20, 2026 — the instruct model, an FP8 build and the pre-trained base, on Hugging Face, ModelScope and GitCode, a fortnight after the model reached Tencent's API. The model card, read first-hand by this desk, totals 770 billion parameters with 49 billion active per token, across 78 layers with 256 routed experts of which eight fire, a native vision encoder, a built-in speculative-decoding drafter, and a context window of 1,048,576 tokens. The picture is Tencent's own benchmark chart from the model card. The release does not ship under the plain Apache 2.0 of Tencent's earlier Hy models: it uses the Tencent Hy License, whose section 10 requires a separate written licence from model-as-a-service operators above US$50 million in revenue or 100 million monthly users.

Image: Tencent via huggingface.co

What is in the repositories, from the card itself: Hy4 at about 1.55 terabytes, Hy4-FP8 at about 0.79 terabytes, and the Hy4 base at about 1.54 terabytes, plus a system card. The 770B backbone figure excludes a 1.23B vision encoder and the 3.3B DFly2 drafter, which reuses the model's own KV cache so speculative decoding adds no separate cache. Serving recipes are published for vLLM and SGLang with tensor parallelism across eight GPUs; Tencent ships a prebuilt vLLM image for the FP8 build. Every benchmark on the card is Tencent's own evaluation — the base model scores 91.6 on MMLU and 73.9 on MMLU-Pro in its tables, ahead of the DeepSeek and house baselines it lists — and the card is candid about the gap that remains to the top proprietary models on research-level maths and long-horizon coding. Treat the numbers as the maker's measurements, not independent results.

The licence is the part a renter has to read before the parameter count. Section 10 of the Tencent Hy License — the same clause that shipped with Hy4 flash on Nov 17 — means an operator selling Hy4 inference as a service needs Tencent's separate written licence once its worldwide gross revenue passes US$50 million in any twelve months or its product passes 100 million monthly active users. Purely internal use is exempt. Below those lines the licence is Apache-derived and the weights are free to download and run.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters this is a node-scale decision, not a single-card one. By memory arithmetic from the card's own figures, the FP8 checkpoint alone is about 770GB of weights before any KV cache — an eight-GPU node of H200 or B200 class cards is the realistic serving unit, which is exactly the shape of Tencent's own eight-way tensor-parallel recipe; at full precision the weights are about 1.54TB and the job becomes multi-node. The model is now in our catalogue with its sizes worked from the card, and the open-versus-closed maths for a model this size turns on the licence line as much as the hourly rate: self-hosting is unrestricted for internal use, while reselling Hy4 inference at scale is a negotiation with Tencent first.

/story/verda-b200-first-cut-nov-20.html:
NEWS →  ·  Price Watch · Verda

Verda cuts its B200 price — the first cut after a month of rises

Nov 20, 2026

Verda cut the on-demand price of its NVIDIA B200 today, Nov 20, 2026, from $9.796 to $9.747 per GPU hour — down 0.50%, and the first cut this desk has recorded from the provider since its rise run began on Oct 23. The cut is narrow and it is not a turn: on the same read, six of Verda's other tracked GPUs rose about 1% for a fifth straight day. The chart is this desk's own daily record of Verda's B200 price, read on Verda's own pages.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on verda.com/gpu-instances and verda.com/pricing

The B200's own path, from our daily record: $9.14 on Nov 8, rising on Nov 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17 and 18 to $9.80, flat on Nov 19, and cut to $9.75 today (board rounding; the unrounded read is $9.796 to $9.747). The rest of today's Verda read, both of the provider's pages agreeing exactly: GB300 $14.86 → $15.01, B300 $12.92 → $13.05, H200 $6.97 → $7.04, H100 SXM $5.45 → $5.51, A100 80GB $2.45 → $2.47 and RTX PRO 6000 $2.95 → $2.98, each up about 1%; A100 40GB held at $1.73 and L40S at $2.08. The GB300 has now risen 27.0% since Oct 19, from $11.82 to $15.01.

Nothing else on the board moved today. Lambda, RunPod Secure and Community, Nebius, CoreWeave, Thunder Compute, SaladCloud and TensorDock's headline rates were all re-read unchanged on Nov 20, and Hyperstack's thirteen on-demand rows are unchanged by the raw-page read. Verda's B200 at $9.75 remains well above the board's best B200 offers — RunPod Community lists $5.98 and Lambda $7.69 — so the cut changes Verda's own trajectory, not the cheapest way to rent the card.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters the honest reading is a mixed signal, printed as one. A month of near-daily rises across one provider's whole range is consistent with growing demand — that has been this desk's labelled interpretation of the pattern since October. One half-percent cut on one card, on a day when six siblings rose again, does not reverse that reading; it does end the claim that every Verda card only moves one way. If the cuts broaden, or the B200 falls again tomorrow, the story changes — the daily record will show it either way.
