/story/inkling-2-mini-open-weights-nov-2.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Thinking Machines

Inkling 2 Mini weights are out: a looped 26.4B that ships in a single 20GB checkpoint — and leads its class at agentic coding

Nov 20, 2026

Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini with open weights today, Nov 20, 2026, under Apache 2.0 — a looped mixture-of-experts model whose middle layers run three times per token, giving 48 layer visits from 24 stored layers. The model card, read first-hand by this desk, totals 26.4 billion parameters with 3.4 billion active per token (5.4 billion effective once looping is counted), takes text and image input, carries a context window of up to 1 million tokens, and ships as a single checkpoint of about 20GB in its native NVFP4 and MXFP8 precisions — no conversion loss, because it was trained in the precision it ships in. The card's own hardware floor is one DGX Spark, an Apple silicon machine with 32GB or more, or another GPU with 32GB or more of memory recommended. The picture is Thinking Machines' own architecture diagram from the release.

Image: Thinking Machines Lab via huggingface.co

What was released, from the announcement and the model card: a 24-layer decoder whose middle 12 layers repeat three times with shared weights; each token routes to 8 of 128 experts; attention is a hybrid of local and global layers; a vision transformer feeds images into the same hidden space. Alongside it sits a research variant, TML-d24-varloop-research, which lets researchers vary the loop count from one to five passes — the lab is explicit that one reason for this release is to let the community study whether looped models stay monitorable, and its own tests found the chain of thought stayed legible as loops rose while no-CoT reasoning improved (the variable-loop model's no-CoT time horizon rose from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 at three). Serving support is there on day one: vLLM, SGLang, Hugging Face Transformers, TokenSpeed, NVIDIA Dynamo, Unsloth and llama.cpp GGUF builds, and Ollama on Apple silicon. The weights are also on the lab's Tinker platform for inference and customisation. As with its sibling, the card links the lab's Model Acceptable Use Policy alongside the Apache 2.0 licence.

The benchmark claims are the lab's own tables, printed here as its measurements, not independent results: Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model under 100B total parameters on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and the Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%) in Thinking Machines' comparison, scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified, and ties the dense Qwen3.8-27B at 20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — a 27B dense model matched by a 3.4B-active MoE, on the lab's numbers. One third-party data point exists: Stanford researchers with early access measured intelligence per watt on a DGX Spark (128GB) and scored Inkling 2 Mini 0.703, ahead of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 0.430 and Gemma-4-26B-A4B at 0.159 in their study. The card is equally plain about the weak spots, and they are printed here too: multi-turn chat and many-constraint instructions trail Qwen3.8-27B (50.0% on MultiChallenge, 33.4% on ComplexConstraints in the lab's table), factual knowledge is bounded by the model's size, and support for looped models in local runtimes is new, so speeds vary by runtime and hardware — the card's own warning.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters this is the opposite end of the Inkling family from its sibling. Inkling 2 Small, whose weights landed on Nov 12, is a cluster rental — its cheapest verified way in was $14.36 an hour. Inkling 2 Mini is a single-card job: the checkpoint is about 20GB as shipped, and while that file would physically fit a 24GB card, the maker's own recommendation is 32GB or more — the headroom is what the KV cache eats, especially anywhere near the 1M-token context. On the board's checked prices of Nov 20, 2026, the cheapest verified 32GB-class door is an RTX 5090 on RunPod Community at $0.69 an hour (RunPod Secure lists $1.39), and an RTX PRO 6000 — 96GB, room for long contexts and bigger batches — starts at $1.69 on RunPod Community and $1.80 on Nebius. Run it at full precision instead and the arithmetic changes: 26.4 billion parameters at two bytes is about 53GB of weights, one 80GB-class card. The model is now in our catalogue with its sizes worked from the card. A deployment guide — how to run Inkling 2 Mini and what it actually costs, against the dense 27B it ties — is proposed to the editor, not published by this sweep.

/story/anthropic-ipo-close-day-two-nov-2.html:
NEWS →  ·  Markets · Anthropic

Anthropic closes its IPO with $119.5 billion raised — and ANT ends day two at $88.91, down 8.5%

Nov 20, 2026

Anthropic announced today, Nov 20, 2026, that its initial public offering has closed — with the underwriters' option exercised in full, taking the public raise to about $93.5 billion, and the concurrent $26 billion private placement closed alongside it, for about $119.5 billion raised in total. The market's second verdict was cooler than its first: ANT closed its second day at $88.91, down 8.5% from the $97.17 first-day close, after touching $83.05 intraday — five cents above the $83.00 IPO price. The picture is Anthropic's own artwork from its IPO site, as on our first-day story; the company's closing announcement itself is text-only.

Image: Anthropic via ipo.anthropic.com

The closing, from Anthropic's own announcement of Nov 20, 2026, read first-hand by this desk: 1,127,000,000 Class A shares at $83.00, including the full exercise of the underwriters' option on a further 147,000,000 shares — 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 by selling stockholders, for gross proceeds of about $93.5 billion, of which about $91.6 billion went to Anthropic. The private placement closed at the same time: 313,253,007 non-voting Class N shares at the same $83.00 to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners, for about $26.0 billion. Combined gross proceeds: about $119.5 billion. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the book; Morgan Stanley was also the stabilisation agent, and Reuters' reading of the full greenshoe exercise is worth printing with its attribution: because the underwriters covered their short from the company rather than in the market, the stabilisation buying that could have supported the shares below $83 is now gone.

Day two, on the session record: ANT opened at $89.86, traded between $92.56 and $83.05 — the low came at 12:49 p.m. Eastern, five cents above the IPO price — and closed at $88.91, down $8.26 or 8.50% on the day (the closing figure is the one carried by the exchange-data feeds and CNN; a minority of market write-ups printed $88.30, and we do not use it). The close still sits 7.1% above the $83.00 offer price, so the honest two-day shape is: priced above its range, up 17.07% on day one, half that gain given back on day two. The slide was not Anthropic's alone: Nov 20 was a broad AI sell-off in which the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.3% and lost its gains for the year, with the chip names down hard alongside (market coverage of the session). In after-hours trading ANT slipped further to $87.80 at 8 p.m. Eastern — that last figure is a quote-feed print (Finnhub), not a wire-reported price.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and builders, the offering is now a completed fact rather than a roadshow promise: about $91.6 billion of new money sits inside the company whose prospectus reports roughly $900 billion of compute commitments, and the $26 billion placement puts the GPU supply chain itself — the two big GPU designers, the memory maker, the foundry and the two largest clouds — on its shareholder register at the offering price. That is the demand side of this board's prices, funded. Day two's fade is the counterweight, and it is printed here rather than smoothed: the market's appetite at $111.50 was not its appetite at the close, and the stabilisation bid that underwrote the first two days is spent. Nothing in today's close changes a single rental price — our evening check found every board provider flat — but the capital that will compete for accelerators, HBM and data-centre capacity over the next build cycle is now raised, dated and on the record.

/story/sk-hynix-mars-sc26-nov-21.html:
NEWS →  ·  Hardware · SK hynix

SK hynix demos MARS at SC26: a rack-scale memory pool built for KV cache

Nov 21, 2026

SK hynix used SC26 in Chicago (Nov 15–20) to demonstrate MARS, its Memory-centric AI Rack System: a rack-level pool of CXL memory — DRAM and SSD tiers — that servers and GPUs share for KV cache, instead of every GPU carrying its own copy. The photograph is SK hynix's own, from its Newsroom report of Nov 20, 2026, and shows the MARS exhibit on the show floor. MARS is a demonstration, not a product on sale: SK hynix published no price, no availability date and no measured uplift figure in its report.

Image: SK hynix via news.skhynix.com

What was shown, from SK hynix's own report: three MARS demonstrations — pooled CXL memory and CXL hybrid memory (DRAM plus SSD) sharing KV cache at rack level; AI-agent serving running over a computational memory pool that connects multiple servers and GPUs; and a multimodal demo sharing CPU-generated tokens through the same pool. Alongside MARS, SK hynix showed KV Cache Offloading over CXL, which it says it verified with SK Telecom in a real LLM inference environment, plus Compute-using-DRAM and its Custom HBM Array work. The report is a booth report from a conference of about 10,000 visitors and 500 exhibitors — evidence of direction, not of a shipping system.

The problem MARS aims at is real and priced daily on our board. In long-context and agentic inference serving, the binding constraint is increasingly KV-cache memory, not raw compute: context windows of a million tokens multiply the cache every concurrent session needs, and today that cache lives in GPU HBM — the most expensive memory in the rack. A shared CXL pool would let a rack hold far more cache in cheaper DRAM and SSD tiers and share it across servers, which is why the HBM market leader showing this design matters even at demo stage.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters the honest position is: nothing here can be rented yet, and SK hynix has attached no numbers to it. What MARS signals is where the memory industry expects inference economics to move — cache capacity pooled at rack scale rather than bought GPU by GPU. If pooled-memory serving reaches products, the maths of long-context serving changes: fewer, cheaper GPUs could hold the same concurrent sessions. Until a provider lists it with a price, it stays a direction to watch, and this desk will treat any future quantified claim as the maker's own until independently measured.

MemT-1.0-Pro: a 554B memory-native model built on NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Ultra, open-sourced today

Nov 24, 2026

MemTensor today, Nov 24, 2026, released and open-sourced MemT-1.0-Pro, a memory-native model built on NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Ultra backbone and trained with NVIDIA's Megatron tooling: 554 billion total parameters, 59 billion active, with a fixed-size persistent memory state instead of an ever-growing context cache. The picture is the maker's own architecture image from its release. One caution is printed up front, because it decides who can use this commercially: the weights carry the OpenMDW-1.1 licence, not a clean permissive one.

Image: MemTensor via PRNewswire

What shipped, from MemTensor's own release of Nov 24, 2026 and the model's Hugging Face card, both read first-hand: a 554B-total / 59B-active model on the NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B backbone, with 4.23B trainable memory parameters and a fixed-size persistent memory state — the maker puts the storage saving at roughly 66× against a full KV cache at 128K of history. The maker's own reported scores average 53.08 across 11 memory benchmarks (the best among the parametric-memory methods it evaluated), with BEAM-1M at 41.80 and MemoryAgentBench at 23.87 — and the release itself notes that strong textual-memory systems remain ahead on some evaluations. These are the maker's figures, not independently re-run by this desk.

The licence is the story's fine print, printed exactly as the card states it: OpenMDW-1.1, following the Nemotron backbone. That is not Apache 2.0 or MIT, and this desk does not list the model as clean commercial open weights — anyone planning a paid deployment should read the licence terms first. The research paper behind the family dates to October, and the smaller Nano and Flash tiers to Oct 20; today's release is the Pro tier's own announcement.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For builders, the interest is the serving shape, not the parameter count alone. A memory-native model holds its state in a fixed-size memory rather than a KV cache that grows with every token of history, which is aimed squarely at long-running agents — the workloads where context storage, not raw compute, becomes the bill. At 554B total parameters this is still a multi-GPU node model by any memory arithmetic, and the OpenMDW-1.1 licence, not the hardware, is the first gate a commercial renter has to clear. It is a research-grade release with a real idea inside it, published with its maker's own caveats attached — which is how this desk prefers to receive them.

NEWS →  ·  Models · Ant Group · inclusionAI

Ling-3.2-air: Ant Group drops a 124B MIT-licensed multimodal MoE — a four-GPU node job

Nov 23, 2026

Ant Group’s inclusionAI published the weights for Ling-3.2-air on Hugging Face on Nov 23, 2026, with no launch post — the model card is the announcement. It is a native multimodal mixture-of-experts model (text, image and video in) with 124 billion total parameters and only 5.5 billion active per token, a 262,144-token native context, block-FP8 weights and the MIT licence, so it can be self-hosted commercially today. The picture is the model’s own architecture diagram from its card.

Image: inclusionAI (Ant Group) via huggingface.co

What shipped, from the model’s own Hugging Face card and repository record, read Nov 23, 2026: a hybrid-linear MoE — 35 Kimi Delta Attention layers and 7 gated MLA layers in a 5:1 mix, 512 routed experts with 8 active per token plus one shared expert, a vision encoder for image and video input, and a 157,184-token vocabulary. The weights ship in block FP8 (roughly 129 GB across the repo’s shards) under the MIT licence, public and ungated. SGLang support is day-0: the card’s recommended recipe runs the full 256K context at tensor parallel 4, and a vLLM fork recipe is published alongside.

The gains are as reported on the card, against its predecessor Ling-3.0-flash-VL: AutomationBench-AA rises from 15.7% to 61%, the GDP.pdf all-pass rate from 8.4% to 16%, AA-Briefcase v1.1 Elo from 987 to 1,340, and Terminal-Bench 4.0 from 0% to 27%. The card also reports a score of 23 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1. These are the maker’s own published figures, not independently re-run by this desk — the pattern they describe is a document-and-workflow-automation specialist, not a general reasoning leap.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For builders, the honest headline is the serving shape. Only 5.5B parameters fire per token, but all 124B have to sit in memory: the card’s own recipes put it on four 141 GB-class GPUs (H200-class) or a four-GPU Blackwell node (B300 / GB300) at tensor parallel 4, or eight 80 GB cards (H100-class) at tensor parallel 8. That is a node rental, never a single card — the same class of commitment as its 560B sibling Ling-3.1-flash-1019, at roughly a quarter of the weight. What you get for the node is an MIT-licensed multimodal model aimed squarely at document processing and workflow automation, with day-0 SGLang support and no licence negotiation. It is in the model catalogue now, with the fit maths on its page.

AWS makes EC2 G7 bare metal generally available — eight RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell GPUs in US East (N. Virginia)

Nov 23, 2026

Amazon announced on Nov 23, 2026 that the metal size of its EC2 G7 instances is now generally available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region — the bare-metal version of the G7 family AWS launched in June, built on NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. A G7 metal instance carries eight of those GPUs with 32 GB of memory each (256 GB in total), custom Intel Xeon 6 processors, 192 vCPUs, 768 GiB of system memory and 700 Gbps of Elastic Fabric Adapter networking. The picture is AWS's own EC2 G7 artwork. AWS printed no price for the metal size in the announcement itself.

Image: Amazon Web Services via aws.amazon.com

What was announced, from AWS's own What's New post of Nov 23, 2026, read first-hand by this desk: the metal size is aimed at workloads that need direct access to bare metal — physical AI simulations, AI agent sandboxes and graphics work, plus the specialist cases AWS names in the same post: a custom virtualization stack, hypervisor-level GPU drivers, or licensing-restricted applications. It can be bought as On-Demand Instances, Spot Instances, or as part of Savings Plans, and started from the AWS console, CLI or SDKs. The wider G7 family's headline figures are AWS's own, from its June launch: up to 4.6 times the AI inference performance and up to 2.1 times the graphics performance of the previous G6 generation.

The GPU itself, from NVIDIA's own product page: the RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition is a single-slot, passively cooled card at 165 watts, with 32 GB of GDDR7 memory at 800 GB/s, fifth-generation Tensor Cores with FP4 support, and up to two MIG instances of 16 GB each. Eight of them in one bare-metal host is therefore a 256 GB pool of modest, power-efficient Blackwell cards rather than one large accelerator — a shape built for many concurrent inference, simulation or graphics jobs, not for training a large model on a single device.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, this is a narrow but real addition: bare metal is the option you take when a hypervisor in the way is the problem — your own virtualization stack, a driver level the cloud does not offer, or a licence that demands physical hardware. Most GPU renters do not need it, and the ordinary virtualised G7 sizes (which AWS expanded to more regions on Nov 10) remain the default door into this GPU on AWS. Two honest limits: the metal size is in one region only at launch, US East (N. Virginia), and AWS's announcement carries no price — the rate has to be read in the EC2 console or pricing pages before any cost comparison is possible, so this desk prints none. AWS sits in our Reference tier rather than on the verified single-card board, and nothing in this announcement changes a board price.

/story/nvidia-ceo-reinstated-nov-23.html:
NEWS →  ·  Companies · NVIDIA

NVIDIA's board reinstates Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director — 11 days after his resignation

Nov 23, 2026

NVIDIA announced today, Nov 23, 2026, that its board has voted unanimously to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as President, Chief Executive Officer and board director, effective immediately — eleven days after the resignation this desk reported on Nov 12. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, continues as Chief Financial Officer, and Harvey C. Jones remains board chair. The photograph is NVIDIA's own Newsroom file photo of Huang with Vera Rubin racks at GTC Taipei — a file photo of the chief executive, not a picture of today's decision.

Image: NVIDIA via nvidianews.nvidia.com

What was announced, from NVIDIA's own release of Nov 23, 2026 (13:55 UTC, read first-hand by this desk): the board said it had received input from senior levels of the United States government and is confident the reinstatement poses no national security risk. The independent-director committee investigation into reporting that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort will proceed to its conclusion, with Huang's support and cooperation. The same release creates two new structures: a National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors, and a Chief Compliance Officer role reporting to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, for which a search was announced. Huang, in the release: ‘I am honored to return to NVIDIA.’

The sequence matters and is short. Huang resigned on Nov 12, 2026; Kress held the chief executive role on an interim basis for eleven days while remaining CFO; today's vote restores the pre-Nov 12 leadership in full, with the investigation still open as the one unresolved thread. Nothing in today's release changes any product, price or availability fact this desk tracks — no roadmap, allocation or export position was announced alongside the personnel decision.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and buyers, this is the removal of a leadership cloud, not a change to supply. Every provider on our board ultimately rents capacity built on one supplier's roadmap, allocation and export-control posture, and for eleven days that supplier's top job was formally unsettled. It is settled now. The durable detail for this market is the new furniture: export control and compliance now sit in a named board committee and a dedicated officer role at NVIDIA, in the same week that US remote-access rules for advanced chips are being contested — the channel through which future chip-availability decisions for China and South-East Asia will run. This desk prints no share-price figure for the move: the numbers circulating today are secondary market coverage, not a primary source, and the rental board itself did not move on the news — today's check found Verda's scheduled-looking rise and nothing else.

NEWS →  ·  Models · Sarvam AI

Sarvam-105B-1711 open weights: a 105B model whose 65GB build runs on one RTX PRO 6000 — and a hosted price cut from $0.44 to $0.15

Nov 22, 2026

Sarvam AI of Bengaluru released Sarvam-105B-1711 on Nov 22, 2026 — a new open-weight checkpoint of its Sarvam 105B mixture-of-experts model (105 billion parameters in total, about 10.3 billion active per token), trained on the company's upgraded B200 infrastructure for high-volume conversational, voice and agentic work. The weights are published on Hugging Face in BF16 (about 198GB) and in a 65GB NVFP4 build that Sarvam says runs on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. The picture is Sarvam's own artwork for the release. In the same announcement, Sarvam cut its hosted blended price from $0.44 to $0.15 per million tokens — a two-thirds cut that moves the self-host break-even this desk watches.

Image: Sarvam AI via sarvam.ai

What was released, from Sarvam's own announcement of Nov 22, 2026, read first-hand by this desk: the -1711 checkpoint keeps the 105B MoE shape and is aimed at conversational and agentic serving at volume. Sarvam's serving claims are its own and are printed as vendor-reported: the 65GB NVFP4 build runs on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96GB) at 99 tokens per second per user, and its 4-bit B200 serving reaches about 6,000 tokens per second per GPU across 64 concurrent users. Its quality claim is likewise its own table: an eight-benchmark conversational-agent average rising from 42.6 for the previous checkpoint to 73.9 for -1711. None of these figures is independently measured yet, and this desk treats them as the maker's numbers until someone else reproduces them.

The price move is part of the same release and is Sarvam's own: the hosted blended rate falls from $0.44 to $0.15 per million tokens, which Sarvam attributes to inference optimisations. A two-thirds cut in the hosted price is the number a renter has to beat by self-hosting — at $0.15 per million tokens, the volume at which renting a GPU around the clock wins over the API rises sharply, and the honest comparison is now: one workstation card, running all month, against fifteen cents per million tokens with no operations at all.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters this is the single-card end of the open-weight market doing something the cluster end cannot: a 105B-class model that fits one 96GB card in the precision it ships in. On the board's checked prices of Nov 23, 2026, the cheapest verified RTX PRO 6000 door is RunPod Community at $1.69 an hour (Nebius lists $1.80, RunPod Secure $2.69) — about $1,234 for a full month of one card, before storage and your own serving work, against Sarvam's hosted $0.15 per million tokens. Which side wins is pure arithmetic on your token volume, and the break-even just moved against self-hosting for all but the heaviest users. The BF16 build (about 198GB) is a different job — three 80GB-class cards or two 141GB H200s at tensor parallel — and the NVFP4 route is the one that makes this checkpoint a one-card story. A deployment guide costing both routes against the hosted price is proposed to the editor, not published by this desk.

/story/sensenova-u1-6-nov-24.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · SenseTime

SenseNova U1.6: SenseTime's open 8B image model checks its own text and redraws it — on one 24 GB card

Nov 24, 2026

SenseTime released SenseNova U1.6 on Nov 24, 2026: an 8-billion-parameter open-weight image model, Apache 2.0, whose headline feature is native self-correction — after a first render it re-reads its own image, checks the text in it against the prompt, and redraws the errors, for up to five rounds. The picture is SenseTime's own before-and-after pair from its official showcase: on the left the first pass garbles two lines of the poster's small print; on the right the corrected pass renders them clean. The weights are BF16 and total about 35 GB, and a hands-on ComfyUI report puts peak memory at 18–21 GB — one 24 GB card.

Image: SenseTime via github.com/OpenSenseNova

What shipped, from the model's own Hugging Face card, read first-hand by this desk: a native unified multimodal checkpoint (mixture-of-transformers) for image generation and image editing, BF16 sharded safetensors totalling 35.07 GB as measured from the repository's own file list, released under Apache 2.0 — commercial use allowed. The card is explicit that the U1.6 self-correction and interleaved protocol needs the matching SenseNova-U1 runtime from SenseTime's GitHub; alongside the main checkpoint sit Native and GGUF variants and 4-step and 8-step LoRA adapters, in Python and ComfyUI formats. SenseTime's stated gains — an aesthetic score about 10% above U1.5 in its own user evaluations, and its UltraTextBench score rising from 86.04 to 92.28 with self-correction on — are the maker's figures, reported here as stated, not independently re-run by this desk.

The serving shape, from a hands-on ComfyUI write-up (a third-party test, labelled as such): native ComfyUI support with official Comfy-Org templates, ComfyUI 0.46 or later, a Turbo mode at 8 steps and a Quality mode at 50, default output of 2368×1760, and peak VRAM of 18–21 GB tested on an RTX 3090. The model's own showcase is unusually honest about the weak side: SenseTime itself notes that its rendering of limbs still has flaws, and the card warns that complex layouts, dense text and long multi-reference edits may need further validation.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For image builders this is the rare frontier-feature release that lands on the card they already rent. Garbled text is the standing failure of open image models — the thing that makes a generated poster unusable commercially — and U1.6 attacks it inside the model rather than with an external checker, at a size that fits a single 3090 or 4090 instead of a datacentre node. Apache 2.0 means the corrected output can be sold. The honest limits travel with it: the speed and quality numbers are the maker's or a single hands-on report, the self-correction rounds cost extra passes of compute, and the checkpoint is inseparable from SenseTime's own runtime. A model page is added to the catalogue with this story, and the deploy maths for one 24 GB card is proposed as a guide for approval.

/story/ernie-5-5-flash-preview-nov-24.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Baidu

ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview weights are out: Baidu's 280B Apache 2.0 MoE lands — an intermediate checkpoint, labelled as one

Nov 24, 2026

Baidu has published the weights of ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on Hugging Face: a 280-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 14 billion active per token, a 1,048,576-token context and the Apache 2.0 licence on the Preview weights. Three builds ship — the default FP8+FP4 build at 165.91 GB as measured, an FP8 build at 301.87 GB and a BF16 build at 599.59 GB — each carrying the DSpark speculative-decoding draft head. The picture is Baidu's own benchmark chart from the model card. Baidu is explicit that this is an intermediate checkpoint: post-training is still underway, and the finished release will supersede it.

Image: Baidu via huggingface.co

What shipped, from the model's Hugging Face card and this desk's own measurements of the repositories: 43 layers (1 dense, 42 MoE), 512 routed experts with top-10 routing plus one shared expert, served by SGLang (the card's recipe runs tensor parallel 4) or by vLLM 0.32.0 through Baidu's own vLLM-ERNIE plugin — mainline vLLM does not document this model. On Baidu's own 20-benchmark table the Preview leads Claude Opus 5.5 on AutomationBench (61.9 against a self-evaluated 58.0, per the chart's own asterisk) and trails it on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (46.5 against 63.6). Every score on that chart is Baidu's, with rival figures marked self-evaluated where Baidu evaluated them itself; this desk has not re-run them.

The licence needs one precise sentence, because it changed from the Base model: Apache 2.0 covers the Preview weights only. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, published on Nov 5, stays under Baidu's separate Base Model License Agreement v1.0, with its geographic and revenue conditions — do not carry the Preview's clean licence backwards onto the Base checkpoint. The Preview has been served on Baidu's Qianfan API since Nov 11; only the weights are new.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters, the shape is the news: a 280B MoE whose default build is already quantised to FP8+FP4 at about 166 GB is a four-GPU node job, not a rack — and the FP4-expert path makes it a Blackwell story, with the FP8 build as the Hopper fallback. This desk's deploy guide, published today, works every documented route against checked board prices (cheapest documented: SGLang on 2 × B300 at $14.80 an hour). The caveat is Baidu's own and it is printed in the standfirst for a reason: rent by the hour, pin the revision, and expect the finished checkpoint to replace this one. A catalogue entry for the Preview is added with this story — until today the catalogue carried only the Base model.

/story/kolibri-1-1-nov-23.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Aleph Alpha

Kolibri 1.1: Aleph Alpha's sovereign 75B MoE claims 3.4× less GPU time per task

Nov 23, 2026

Aleph Alpha released Kolibri 1.1 on Nov 23, 2026, its German–English sovereign open-weight model: 75 billion total parameters, 3.44 billion active, Apache 2.0. The pitch is serving cost — a new sparse-attention design and leaner reasoning that the maker says cut GPU time per task by 3.4× against Kolibri 1.0. The picture is Aleph Alpha's own chart from the model card: benchmark score against GPU-hours per 1,000 tasks, with 1.1 on the efficiency frontier at 73.2 points and 0.21 GPU-hours where 1.0 needed 0.72.

Image: Aleph Alpha via huggingface.co

What shipped, from the model's Hugging Face card and Aleph Alpha's own release, both read first-hand: each token attends to the 2,048 most relevant plus the 128 most recent tokens, layers share KV cache, and the model emits about 41% fewer output tokens per task; native context is 262,144 tokens (1,048,576 maximum, with up to 262K recommended). The efficiency figures are the maker's own modelling from vLLM 0.33 throughput on one 8 × B200 node with 8-bit weights — 0.208 against 0.718 GPU-hours per 1,000 tasks — not an independent measurement. The honest counterweight is on the same card: its τ-bench average fell against 1.0 (67.1 against 69.7), and below 8K of context 1.1 decodes slower than 1.0. The weights take about 77.6 GB; the card's minimum serving shapes are 2 × H100 SXM, 2 × H200, 1 × B200 or 1 × B300, and official GGUF builds ship alongside for llama.cpp.

Context: Kolibri 1.0 arrived on Oct 3, 2026, so this is a seven-week iteration, and it lands after the September agreement to combine Cohere and Aleph Alpha — background reported by secondary sources, printed here as context, not as part of the release.

What it means if you rent GPUs

A brief, deliberately: Kolibri is a niche sovereign-European model, not a general renter headline — but its claim is exactly this desk's home ground, cost per task. A 75B model whose weights fit one H200, B200 or B300, claiming a third of the GPU time per task, is a serving-cost story a renter can check against board prices, and the maker's own card prints the regression (τ-bench) next to the gain, which is how releases should read. The 3.4× figure is modelled, not measured by this desk, and is labelled that way everywhere it appears here. A catalogue entry is added with this story.

/story/ternary-bonsai-2-5-27b-nov-24.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · PrismML

Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: a 27B agentic model in 5.93 GB — FP16-level tool calling on one small card

Nov 24, 2026

PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B on Nov 24, 2026: a 27-billion-parameter model built on Qwen3.8-27B, written in ternary 1.76-bit weights, so the whole model is a 5.93 GB GGUF file against 53.8 GB at FP16 — Apache 2.0. The upgrade over Bonsai 2 is agentic staying power: on PrismML's own benchmarks it averages 77.2 across five tool-calling suites against 77.7 for the full-precision model, and its agentic-coding score rises from about 63% of FP16 to about 90%. The picture is the cover of PrismML's own whitepaper for the release, with its headline figures.

Image: PrismML via github.com/PrismML-Eng

What shipped, from the model's Hugging Face card, PrismML's release post and its whitepaper, all read first-hand by this desk: a hybrid-attention 27B (24.35B language weights, a 0.47B vision tower shipped as a separate optional file, 262,144-token context), released as GGUF builds — PQ2_0, PTQ1_0 and Q2_0, each also in a multi-token-prediction variant that the maker says decodes 1.5–1.8× faster. It runs via llama.cpp on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs and via MLX on Apple devices. On the maker's own table, SWE-bench Verified rises from 60.8 (Bonsai 2) to 75.6 against the FP16 base model's 80.6, DeepSWE from 0 to 27.0, and Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 52.8 to 60.1; AppWorld recovers from 51.2 to 90.5 against 93.2 at FP16. Every one of those scores is PrismML's, measured its way, and is reported here as the maker's — this desk has not re-run them. Its stated speeds are likewise the maker's: 291 tokens a second on one H100 and about 204 on an RTX 4090, both with MTP on.

The honest edges travel with the release: general capability still trails FP16 (82.1 against 84.3 averaged over the maker's five categories), LiveCodeBench dipped slightly against Bonsai 2 on the same table (83.0 against 83.8), and a ternary model this compressed lives or dies on long tool chains — exactly the workload its maker says it fixed, and exactly what an independent re-run should test first.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters and builders this moves the floor, not the ceiling: a 27B-class agent that fits in under 6 GB runs on the cheapest card on the board — or on a laptop, with no rental at all — and Apache 2.0 lets it ship inside a product. The comparison that matters is against ordinary low-bit GGUF builds of the same base model, which the maker's table puts behind it on tool calling at larger sizes. Treat the benchmark claims as the maker's until a third party reproduces them; the file sizes, licence and formats are facts from the repository itself. A catalogue entry is added with this story, and a one-small-card deploy guide is proposed for approval.

/story/together-preemptible-ga-nov-24.html:
NEWS →  ·  Providers · Together AI

Together AI makes preemptible GPU clusters general: the same GPUs at a flat half of on-demand

Nov 24, 2026

Together AI announced on Nov 24, 2026 that preemptible compute is now generally available on Together GPU Clusters — Kubernetes and Slurm, in all regions, including clusters that run entirely on preemptible nodes. The deal is simple: the same NVIDIA GPUs at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate, billed sub-hourly, in exchange for accepting that Together can reclaim a node with a five-minute drain warning. The picture is Together's own artwork for the announcement.

Image: Together AI via together.ai

The rates, from Together's own cluster pricing documentation, read first-hand: preemptible HGX H100 at $1.99 a GPU-hour against $3.99 on-demand, H200 at $2.99 against $5.99, B200 at $4.09 against $8.19 and B300 at $4.99 against $9.99. The rate is fixed, not a bid — it does not move with a spot market. When Together reclaims a node, pods get SIGTERM and up to five minutes (a terminationGracePeriodSeconds of up to 300) to checkpoint and exit; the cluster then refills toward its preemptible target on its own as spare capacity returns. Usage is metered every one to two minutes, so a node that lives twelve minutes bills about twelve minutes.

What general availability adds over the earlier preview: Slurm clusters alongside Kubernetes, and preemptible-only clusters — with the maker's own warning attached: keep at least one standard node if your shared storage must stay reachable at all times, and keep coordinators, login pods and user-facing replicas on standard capacity. There is no minimum node lifetime.

What it means if you rent GPUs

A brief, because the fact is small and clean: a flat, published half-price tier for interruptible cluster work is now a standing option renters can price against — against spot and preemptible offers elsewhere, and against holding standard capacity sized for a peak. It suits exactly the work that checkpoints well: sweeps, evals, distillation, batch inference. It is not a board price — Together is not a tracked board provider here — and the five-minute drain is the whole catch, printed up front: a multi-day run without checkpointing gets nothing from this tier.

Sakana AI announces Namazu Small: a 30B reasoner that outscores a 120B rival on its maker's chart — no weights yet

Nov 25, 2026

Sakana AI announced Sakana Namazu Small on Nov 25, 2026: a 30-billion-parameter reasoning model built on the pretrained base of NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Nano, then continued-pretrained and post-trained in-house. On Sakana's own chart it averages 60.1 across 25 benchmarks against 56.2 for NVIDIA's 120B Nemotron 3 Super and 50.2 for the Nano base it starts from. The picture is Sakana's own benchmark chart for the announcement. One limit is printed up front: there are no weights, no licence and no context length yet — this is an announcement, not a release you can run.

Image: Sakana AI via sakana.ai

What Sakana states, from its own announcement page read first-hand: Namazu Small is a reasoning model aimed at everyday conversation, web-search research and long-document reading with evidence-based answers. Its maker's grouped scores put its strength exactly there — web search 59.9 against the 120B Super's 54.6, context grounding 67.1 against 56.4 — while knowledge is the weak group: 53.2 against the Super's 57.8, and Sakana itself notes knowledge tasks barely improved over the base. Every score is Sakana's, measured its way; this desk has not re-run any of them.

What is not stated matters as much: the announcement names no weights release, no Hugging Face repository, no licence and no context length, so nothing about running it can be priced or planned today. Sakana says an on-premises offering is planned, with details promised in early-to-mid December 2026.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters and builders this is a diary item with a strong claim attached, not a deployable model: a 30B-class reasoner that genuinely outscores a 120B rival on research-style work would be a one-or-two-GPU serving story the day its terms land — and only then. Until Sakana publishes weights or on-prem terms, there is nothing to rent for it and no price to check. The desk will re-check when the December details arrive.

NVIDIA posts Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B weights: a 30B autoregressive image model — research-only licence

Nov 24, 2026

NVIDIA published the weights of Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B on Hugging Face on the evening of Nov 24, 2026: a 30-billion-parameter image generation model with 3 billion active per token, built as the raster rendering engine of NVIDIA's Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation ‘Pixel as Code’ framework. It is autoregressive, not diffusion — a hybrid Mamba-2/attention mixture-of-experts initialised from Nemotron 3 Nano. The picture is NVIDIA's own example-output sheet from the repository. The licence is the decision point, and it is restrictive: NVIDIA's own licence text limits the work to non-commercial use — research or evaluation only.

Image: NVIDIA via huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B

What shipped, verified first-hand against the repository itself: 61 files including 33 safetensors shards, the repository last modified Nov 25, 2026 at 03:19 UTC after the weights landed the previous evening; a bundled image tokenizer ships in a subfolder of the same repository. NVIDIA's benchmark claims are for the full VisualCreation system (harness plus repair loop), not the bare weights: GenEval 92.86 against GPT Image 2's 89.00 and LongTextBench 97.98 against 96.00 on NVIDIA's own table, while GenEval2 on the same material favours GPT Image 2 (81.00 against 65.43). Those are NVIDIA's figures, reported as NVIDIA's — this desk has not re-run them.

The licence, read first-hand in the repository's LICENSE file today: the NVIDIA License's use limitation (section 3.3) states the work and any derivative works may only be used non-commercially — ‘for research or evaluation purposes only’ — with commercial use reserved to NVIDIA and its affiliates. The Hugging Face card files the licence as ‘other’, which is why the exact text matters more than the label.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters the sizing is friendly and the terms are not: by the desk's arithmetic the 30B weights are about 60 GB at BF16 before the tokenizer and activations — one 80 GB-class card territory in principle, though no serving recipe has been verified by this desk — but no paid image product can be built on these weights under a research-or-evaluation-only licence. Treat it as an evaluation download: useful for testing autoregressive image generation on rented time, unusable as the engine of a commercial service until NVIDIA changes the terms. A catalogue entry is added with this story, with the licence printed in full.

/story/tencent-hy-mt3-nov-24.html:
NEWS →  ·  Open weights · Tencent Hunyuan

Tencent open-sources Hy-MT3: translation models for 102 languages, 1.8B to 30B-A3B, Apache 2.0

Nov 24, 2026

Tencent Hunyuan released the Hy-MT3 translation family on Nov 24, 2026 — three checkpoints on Hugging Face, ModelScope and GitHub: Hy-MT3-1.8B and Hy-MT3-7B (dense) and Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (a mixture-of-experts flagship with about 3 billion active per token), expanding coverage from Hy-MT2's 38 languages to 102, all under Apache 2.0, in BF16, FP8 and GGUF builds. The picture is Tencent's own results chart from the flagship's model card. A brief, because the facts are clean: permissive terms, small footprints, one honest context limit.

Image: Tencent Hunyuan via huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-MT3-30B-A3B

The verified shape, from the three repositories themselves: an 8,192-token context — modest, and translation-shaped rather than a defect — with Tencent also open-sourcing its TransRubric scoring suite alongside the models. One discrepancy is worth printing: the flagship card's metadata tag says 99 languages while its body text and paper say 102; this desk reports 102 as the maker's stated coverage and flags the tag as inconsistent. Tencent's own quality claims against Hy-MT2 (43% fewer mistranslations, 74% fewer omissions and additions, 40% fewer instruction-following errors) are the maker's, unverified independently.

The builds matter for small hardware: the 1.8B ships as a GGUF small enough for consumer cards and CPU-class jobs, the 7B is a one-small-card model, and the 30B-A3B flagship is about 60 GB at BF16 or about 30 GB at FP8 by the desk's arithmetic — one 80 GB or 48 GB card territory in principle.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Translation is one of the easiest workloads to price honestly, and this family covers the whole ladder in one release: a free-to-ship Apache 2.0 licence, a GGUF build that needs no datacentre card at all, and a flagship that fits the single-card end of the board. The 8K context is the watch-out — document-scale translation means chunking, which is normal for the task but should be planned, not discovered. A catalogue entry for the flagship is added with this story.

/story/soma-1x-lite-nov-25.html:
NEWS →  ·  Models · Amini

Amini's Soma-1X Lite: a 2B open-weight model that turns paper records into structured data on one GPU

Nov 25, 2026

Amini released Soma-1X Lite on Nov 25, 2026: a 2.2-billion-parameter vision-language model, Apache 2.0, built to convert paper records — typed forms, handwriting, tables, faded scans — into structured, machine-readable data that preserves layout and reading order. The weights are a single 4.43 GB file, verified from the repository by this desk, and the licence is Apache 2.0 in both the model card and the README — commercial use allowed. The picture is Amini's own hero image from the model repository: its wordmark over a mosaic of the historical documents the model is built to read. Amini's pitch is sovereign digitisation: the model is small enough to run inside an institution's own infrastructure, so the records never leave it.

Image: Amini via huggingface.co/AminiTech/Soma-1X-lite

What shipped, verified first-hand from the Hugging Face repository (AminiTech/Soma-1X-lite, created Nov 25, 2026): 2,213,241,664 parameters at BF16 in one model.safetensors file of 4,426,558,864 bytes; architecture Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration, a fine-tune of Alibaba's Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B base; an image-text-to-text pipeline whose structured output is one block per page element with position boxes on a 0–1000 grid, tables as HTML and mathematics as LaTeX. The card lists thirteen languages, among them French, Spanish, Swahili, Yoruba, Hausa and Wolof — a list that matches its target: archives and government records across Africa and beyond. The card states no context length, and none is claimed here.

Amini's own figures, reported as the maker's and not independently re-run by this desk: 84.7 on olmOCR-Bench and 84.37 on OmniParse-Bench (86.53 with multi-pass), a 2.90% mean character error rate across ten African languages, and throughput of up to 15,000 pages per hour on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000, which Amini prices at about $0.22 per 1,000 pages using an AWS on-demand rate of about $3.36 an hour for that card.

What it means if you rent GPUs

The sizing is the story for renters: at 4.43 GB of weights this model fits comfortably on any card on our board, down to the cheapest 24 GB cards — the RTX PRO 6000 in Amini's benchmark is a throughput choice, not a fit requirement. Run the maker's own throughput claim against the board's best verified price for that card (RunPod Community at $1.69 an hour, checked Nov 25, 2026) and the arithmetic gives about $0.11 per 1,000 pages — our arithmetic on Amini's unverified throughput figure, printed as such, not a measurement. The honest watch-outs: every performance number above is the maker's, the model is a fine-tune of a 2B base rather than a new architecture, and a 2B document model will not match frontier hosted OCR APIs on hard pages — its case is cost, privacy and running where the records already are. A catalogue entry is added with this story.

/story/verda-first-cut-nov-26.html:
NEWS →  ·  Prices · Verda

Verda cuts prices for the first time: seven cards fall in one day, five by about 6%

Nov 26, 2026

Verda cut seven of its nine tracked on-demand GPU rates on Nov 26, 2026 — its first cut after rises on Nov 23 and Nov 24 and a flat Nov 25. GB300 fell $15.31 to $14.41 and B300 $13.31 to $12.53 (both −5.9%); H200, H100 SXM and RTX PRO 6000 each fell about 5.8%; B200 and A100 80GB fell by smaller steps. A100 40GB and L40S held. The chart is this desk's own record of Verda's published rates, read on Verda's own pages on both days — the subject of this story is our own price data, so our chart is the evidence.

Image: GPUJournal Price Watch — the desk's own chart of Verda's published rates

The verified moves, from Verda's own pricing and GPU-instances pages read first-hand on Nov 25 and Nov 26, 2026 and agreeing exactly on both days: GB300 $15.31 → $14.41, B300 $13.31 → $12.53, H200 $7.184 → $6.768, H100 SXM $5.619 → $5.293, RTX PRO 6000 $3.041 → $2.864, A100 80GB $2.482 → $2.410, B200 $9.844 → $9.603. Spot rates on the same page sit at exactly half the new on-demand rates, so the cut runs across the page rather than touching one table.

Context a renter should keep: this is a reversal, not a return to cheap. The Nov 23–24 rises were larger than today's falls on most cards, so even after the cut GB300 at $14.41 remains well above its levels from earlier in November. Verda remains one of the board's pricier providers on most of these cards — the board's best offers did not change today.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For renters the practical point is timing: a provider that rose twice in three days has now cut once, which makes Verda's rates a moving target worth re-checking at booking rather than budgeting from a screenshot. For the market read (our interpretation, labelled as such): the autumn pattern of rises — Nebius on Oct 1, RunPod Secure on Oct 14, Verda repeatedly since Oct 23 — was consistent with growing demand; today's broad cut breaks the ‘everyone only rises’ run without reversing it. The next dated test is Dec 1, when Crusoe's pre-announced rises take effect.

NEWS →  ·  Open weights · Ant Group

Ant Group open-sources Ming-Image-0.2-Design: a design image model under MIT, validated on one 80 GB GPU

Nov 26, 2026

Ant Group's inclusionAI team listed the weights of Ming-Image-0.2-Design on Nov 25, 2026 and announced it on Nov 26: a design-focused text-to-image and image-editing model aimed at e-commerce hero images, UI drafts and spatial renderings, under the MIT licence. Ant's own validated setup is a single CUDA GPU with 80 GiB of memory — H100, H200 or A100 80GB territory. The picture is Ant Group's own example art from the model repository. Ant claims the model ranks first among open-weight models on Artificial Analysis's AA-Image-T2I v2.1 chart at 1,095 Elo as of Nov 25 — Ant's claim, reported as Ant's; this desk has not re-run it.

Image: Ant Group inclusionAI via huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ming-Image-0.2-Design

What shipped, verified first-hand against the repository: the Hugging Face repo inclusionAI/Ming-Image-0.2-Design (created Nov 25, 2026, still being updated Nov 26) carries the MIT licence in its own metadata, defaults to 2048×2048 output at 12 sampling steps, and Ant recommends serving it with vLLM-Omni. A companion model, Ming-Image-0.2-Design-Layer — which splits a design into transparent layers down to character parts — is promised for next week; that is a diary item, not a release. The model's parameter count (reported as 6B in coverage reading the card) is not stated in the card sections this desk could verify, so it is flagged here rather than printed as fact in the catalogue maths beyond the maker's own 80 GiB validation.

The licence is the clean part: MIT is as permissive as open weights get — commercial use, modification and redistribution are all allowed — which puts this release at the opposite end of the terms spectrum from yesterday's research-only NVIDIA image model.

What it means if you rent GPUs

For GPU renters and builders this is a tidy single-card sizing story: a commercially usable design-generation model whose maker validated it on one 80 GB card can be trialled for the price of a few H100 or A100 hours instead of a closed image API subscription, and the layer-splitting sibling due next week is the part design teams will actually watch. A catalogue entry is added with this story, carrying the maker's validated-hardware note in place of unverified parameter arithmetic.

/story/patram-1-5-nov-26.html:
NEWS →  ·  Open weights · BharatGen

BharatGen launches Patram 1.5: a 7.8B document model built for messy Indian paperwork, on one 24 GB GPU

Nov 26, 2026

BharatGen launched Patram 1.5 on Nov 26, 2026: a vision-language model that reads, parses, answers questions on and extracts from scanned, handwritten, stamped and mixed-language Indian documents — and is designed to say when it cannot answer rather than guess. The weights are Apache 2.0, verified from the repository by this desk, and BharatGen's own sizing guidance puts the model on a 24 GB GPU. The picture is BharatGen's own announcement art: Patram 1.5 pulling a clean billing-history table out of a Maharashtra electricity bill. BharatGen is India's sovereign AI programme, backed by the Department of Science and Technology and the IndiaAI Mission and anchored at IIT Bombay. This story was held this morning until the maker's own imagery could be verified and self-hosted; it is published now that it has been.

Image: BharatGen via bharatgen.com

What shipped, verified first-hand from the Hugging Face repository (bharatgenai/Patram1.5-7B, weights updated Nov 26, 2026): 7,760,786,896 parameters — 7.8B against the 7B headline figure — in three BF16 safetensors shards totalling about 15.5 GB; an image-text-to-text pipeline covering OCR (this release adds what BharatGen calls OCR 3.0), key-value extraction, table and chart understanding and multi-turn chat over documents. The licence is Apache 2.0 in the repository's own metadata: commercial use allowed. BharatGen's models page lists Patram 1.5 in November 2026 and states its models are open weights under Apache 2.0; the launch is corroborated the same day by The Hindu BusinessLine and Inc42.

BharatGen's own evaluation, reported as the maker's and not independently re-run by this desk: 49 tests — 34 public benchmarks plus 15 PatramBench tasks BharatGen built from 8,773 pages and 11,828 items of Indian documents — against 20 image-reading models of up to 763B parameters and seven specialist OCR systems. PatramBench itself is promised on Hugging Face ‘in the coming days’, so the home benchmark cannot yet be checked by anyone outside BharatGen.

What it means if you rent GPUs

This is the second sovereign document model in two days — Amini's Soma-1X Lite landed Nov 25 — and the pattern is the story: document AI that runs on one modest card, inside the institution's own walls, under a licence that allows commercial use, aimed at exactly the paperwork (bills, forms, lab reports, land and identity documents) that hosted APIs handle worst and charge most for. The sizing maths is friendly: about 15.5 GB of BF16 weights against BharatGen's 24 GB guidance means one RTX 4090-class card or one small cloud GPU, not a datacenter booking. The honest watch-outs: every benchmark number is BharatGen's own, the repository card still presents an access form before download (access is stated to be granted straight away, and the licence is Apache 2.0 regardless), and a model tuned for Indian documents and languages should be tested on your own pages before it is trusted with them. A catalogue entry is added with this story.

/story/nemotron-3-5-parse-open-data-nov-.html:
NEWS →  ·  Open data · NVIDIA

NVIDIA opens Nemotron 3.5 Parse's training data and recipe — and clocks 20.44 pages a second on one H200

Nov 26, 2026

NVIDIA published the training data, fine-tuning recipe and speed work behind its compact document-parsing model Nemotron 3.5 Parse on Nov 26, 2026: three synthetic datasets totalling about 18.9 million image-and-annotation pairs, a public supervised-fine-tuning to GRPO recipe, and a speculative decoder, DFlash2, that NVIDIA measures at 20.44 pages per second on a single H200 at high concurrency. The model itself is not new — it is a 0.63B parser published earlier in 2026 under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence — what opened today is everything around it. The picture is NVIDIA's own first figure from the post: a page on the left, the model's structured extraction of it on the right.

Image: NVIDIA via huggingface.co

What shipped, from NVIDIA's own post (Hugging Face, published Nov 26, 2026, 05:05 UTC) and verified against the repositories by this desk: Synthetic Charts V1 (9.98 million chart pairs), Synthetic Tables V1 (1 million table pairs) and OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 (7.9 million multilingual pages); all three dataset cards list the CC-BY-4.0 licence in their own metadata, checked first-hand today. The recipe runs NeMo Automodel SFT then NeMo RL GRPO with vLLM generating candidates. On NVIDIA's matched development checkpoints — its own caveat: not the final model — the overall score rose 66.24 to 71.38 after GRPO, loop-flagged pages fell 126 to 29 and pages hitting the 9,000-token cap fell 185 to 35. Optional double- and triple-pass reprocessing adds 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass, at lower throughput.

The speed figures are NVIDIA's own measurements on one H200 in BF16 over the same 2,078 ParseBench pages: DFlash2 — a draft model proposing up to 32 tokens, about 14 accepted on average — lifts throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512 against Parse 3.5 with speculation off; at 512 that is 20.44 pages per second with DFlash2, 13.48 without, and 2.98 for the older Parse 2.0.

What it means if you rent GPUs

Run NVIDIA's own high-concurrency figure against the board and the workload gets a price: 20.44 pages a second is about 73,600 pages an hour, and at the board's best verified H200 rate (RunPod Community, $3.59 an hour, checked Nov 26, 2026) that is roughly $49 per million pages parsed — our arithmetic on NVIDIA's unverified throughput figure, printed as such, not a measurement. The bigger deal for builders is the data: document parsing is the unglamorous workload underneath most RAG and agent pipelines, and NVIDIA has now given away the synthetic data and the training recipe to adapt a small parser to your own document types instead of paying a hosted OCR API per page forever. The honest watch-outs: the throughput and quality numbers are NVIDIA's, on NVIDIA's own benchmark pages; the development-checkpoint gains are not the shipped model's scores; and the model's OpenMDW-1.1 licence is a model licence, not Apache or MIT — read it before building a product on the weights. BharatGen's open-weight document vision-language model, launched Nov 26, 2026 under Apache 2.0 (licence verified in the repository metadata): 7,760,786,896 parameters in about 15.5 GB of BF16 weights, built to read, parse, question and extract from scanned, handwritten, stamped and mixed-language Indian documents, and designed to decline rather than guess when it cannot answer. Worth knowing

NVIDIA's compact document-parsing model (0.63B parameters, image-text-to-text, OpenMDW-1.1 licence): turns page images into reading-order structured data — content classes, bounding boxes, tables and charts as records — for RAG and agent pipelines. The model itself was published on Hugging Face earlier in 2026 (repository created Sep 3, 2026); it is catalogued here with NVIDIA's Nov 26, 2026 release of its training data and recipe: three synthetic datasets (Synthetic Charts V1 9.98M pairs, Synthetic Tables V1 1M, OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 7.9M; dataset cards list CC-BY-4.0), a public SFT-to-GRPO fine-tuning recipe, and the DFlash2 speculative decoder. NVIDIA's own measurements on one H200 in BF16: 20.44 pages/second at concurrency 512 with DFlash2 (13.48 without; Parse 2.0: 2.98), 7.62x at concurrency 1 — the maker's figures, not independently measured. Small enough for any single card on the board; the H200 figure is a throughput reference, not a fit requirement.
